name: Alaska Beacon
title: Independents, Democrats out-fundraise Republican incumbents in most Alaska House races
description: A Fairbanks fire captain’s campaign raised over $72,000. A retired Kodiak school teacher and union leader’s campaign raised nearly $71,000. A Clam Gulch fisherman’s campaign raised over $45,000. All three candidates are independents running for Republican-held seats in the Alaska State House.  Democratic and independent candidates for the Alaska State House[...]
text:
A campaign sign for Cliff Groh, candidate for Alaska House District 18 is seen in the Muldoon neighborhood of northeast Anchorage on Sep. 23, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)A Fairbanks fire captain’s campaign raised over $72,000. A retired Kodiak school teacher and union leader’s campaign raised nearly $71,000. A Clam Gulch fisherman’s campaign raised over $45,000. All three candidates are independents running for Republican-held seats in the Alaska State House. 
Democratic and independent candidates for the Alaska State House are largely out-fundraising Republican opponents in races for Republican-held seats. Of 17 seats held by Republicans that have a Democratic or independent challenger, that challenger is outraising the Republican in 11 races.
According to campaign disclosure reports filed with the Alaska Public Offices Commission ahead of the August primary election, Democratic and independent candidates outpaced Republicans in fundraising for races in Fairbanks, Anchorage, the Kenai Peninsula and Kodiak and Prince William Sound. Some are political newcomers and some have run for the Legislature before.
Jenny-Marie Stryker, executive director of the Alaska Democratic Party, said she’s not surprised. 
”When donors are giving overarchingly to one side of the movement, it’s because they’re looking for something different. And they’re clearly taking a look at the other side and seeing that they have a better return on their investment when they’re investing in coalition-minded leaders, who really want to put Alaska first,” she said.
There are some notable exceptions. Six Republican incumbents — mostly in the Matanuska-Susitna Borough — have out-fundraised Democrat and independent opponents.     
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE 

All forty members of the Alaska State House are up for re-election. In the 34th Alaska State Legislature, there was a tight margin between the 21-member multipartisan House Majority caucus and the 19 members of the all-Republican House Minority caucus leading to close votes on major legislation. If one or more Republican held seats flip, it could boost the majority caucus — made up of a mix of Republicans, Democrats and independents — and its priorities.  
Alaska House Representatives serve two-year terms, representing roughly 18,335 Alaskans in each district.
Campaign donations are just one way to gauge support for candidates. Financial disclosures include donations from individuals, industry and political interest groups, and political action committees.
In several races, Democratic and independent candidates gathered donations from a variety of individual Alaskans. Some are backed by unions, political interest groups or the Alaska Democratic Party. In some competitive races, some candidates — Republicans, Democrats and independents — gave large donations or personal loans to their own campaigns. 
The majority of Alaska’s approximately 603,000 voters are unaffiliated with a political party. A September report by the Alaska Division of Elections shows that 63% were registered as nonpartisan or undeclared in the August primary. 
An estimated 23.5% of voters are registered Republican and 11.6% registered Democrat. The remaining roughly 3% of voters are registered with a variety of other small political parties. 
Candidates of all political affiliations are making their bids for those independent voters. The ranked choice general election is just six weeks away. 
An independent is leading in donations and primary votes in Fairbanks 
In Fairbanks, independent Joy Beth Cottle has a significant financial advantage over  Republican Harmony Tomaszewski. The two are running for a seat vacated by Tomaszewski’s husband, former Republican Rep. Frank Tomaszewski, who is running for the Alaska Senate. House District 34 extends across Steele Creek, Two Rivers, Eielson Air Force Base and Salcha. 
Joy Beth Cottle is running to represent House District 34 in 2026. (Photo courtesy of Joy Beth Cottle)
Harmony Tomaszewski is running to represent House District 34 in 2026. (Photo courtesy of Harmony Tomaszewski)
Cottle, a fire captain and paramedic based in Delta Junction, has raised more than $72,000 as of the week before the election. Dozens of small, individual donors have contributed to Cottle, as well as larger donations from unions representing laborers, plumbers and pipefitters, and public employees. Political action committees for Fairbanks Firefighters, the local Teamsters union and NEA-Alaska, the public teachers union, donated to Cottle’s campaign. 
Republican Harmony Tomaszewski, a small business owner in Fairbanks, raised nearly $34,000 as of a week before the election. She raised a variety of large and small donations from individual donors and the Republican Women of Fairbanks. She also gave a $5,000 personal loan to the campaign. 
Former Republican Sen. Rob Myers of Fairbanks — who is vacating the seat that Rep. Frank Tomaszewski is running for — donated $2,000 to Harmony Tomaszewski’s campaign. 
In the primary election, Cottle won by just 280 votes, or 53% of the vote, compared to Tomaszewski who won 47% of votes cast in the district.  
Cottle said her district has been particularly impacted by the increases in cost of fuel driven by the Trump administration’s U.S. war on Iran. “A lot of people are hurting specifically because of this war,” she said. 
“Some of the platforms and initiatives from the GOP aren’t as popular these days because people are trying to fill their fuel tanks. I know up here in Fairbanks, just about every door that I knock, people are waiting for their PFD, but they also know that’s not going to be enough to get their fuel tanks filled. And we’re looking at really high energy costs going into the winter as well,” she said.
Nearby in Fairbanks’ House District 33 race, independent Pepper McFarland and Republican Barbara Haney are challenging Republican incumbent Mike Prax, who has held the seat representing the North Pole and Badger areas since 2019. 
McFarland, a teacher based in North Pole, has out-fundraised both Republican opponents, though she trailed them in votes in the primary election. 
A week before the primary, she reported collecting nearly $23,000 from dozens of donors as well as unions like the Alaska State Employees Association and NEA-Alaska teachers union.     

Rep. Mike Prax, R-North Pole speaks on the House floor on the operating budget on Apr. 13, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 


Comparatively, incumbent Republican Mike Prax reported bringing in $13,500 as of a week before the primary election, but $10,000 of that Prax donated to his own campaign.
Republican challenger Barbara Haney, a retired economist and former assembly member with the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly, reported roughly $7,400 in contributions as of a week before the primary.
In the primary election, Prax led by just 105 votes, or 37%. Haney had 34%, followed by McFarland with 28.8% of votes cast in the district.
Prax said this is his first election with political challengers — in prior elections he was the only candidate running. He said he thinks that was driven by differences in education funding policy, particularly with McFarland, which he said is one of the top issues he’s hearing about from voters in his district.
An independent leads in campaign donations and primary support in Kodiak 
In House District 5, which includes coastal communities of Kodiak Island and Prince William Sound, independent Kathy Simpler has an edge on Republican Sheldon Prout. The Kodiak residents are running for the seat vacated by former Republican Rep. Louise Stutes who is running for the Alaska Senate.
Sheldon Prout is running to represent House District 5 in the 2026 election. (Photo courtesy of Sheldon Prout)
Kathy Simpler is running to represent House District 5 in 2026. (Photo courtesy of Kathy Simpler)
Simpler, a former Kodiak elementary school teacher and union leader, raised over $70,700 as of a week prior to the election. The donations came from a variety of small and large donors, as well as unions: the Alaska Public Employees Association, NEA-Alaska teachers union — where she’s served as director since 2022 — the local Teamsters and the Anchorage Firefighters Union’s political action committee.
Prout, a Republican and commercial fisherman, raised over $21,400 in large and small donations one week before the primary, including $2,500 in donated snow crab for a reception at the fisheries tradeshow Comfish.
Simpler won the primary by 781 votes with 61% of the vote, while Prout had 38.5% of the vote and 1,319 votes. 
Independent seeks to unseat Republican incumbent in Homer 
In the southern Kenai Peninsula, independent Brent Johnson is running once again to unseat Republican incumbent Sarah Vance, who has represented the district since 2019. He has a very slight financial edge, as of the most recent financial reporting, and took a greater share of the vote in the primary election.
Johnson is a commercial fisherman and former Kenai Peninsula Borough Assemblymember from Clam Gulch, and unsuccessfully ran against Vance, of Homer, in 2024. 
Brent Johnson is running to represent House District 6 in the 2026 election. (Photo courtesy of Brent Johnson)
Rep. Sarah Vance, R-Homer, speaks Friday, April 26, 2024, on the floor of the Alaska House of Representatives. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Johnson raised more than $45,000 as of a week before the primary, from large and small donors and the Alaska Public Employees Association union. He also made a personal donation of $20,000 to his own campaign. 
Vance raised nearly $45,000 as of a week before the primary, from large and small donors, including $1,000 from current Republican Sen. Rob Yundt of Wasilla.  
In the primary election, Johnson won by 890 votes with 56.8%, while Vance landed 43% of votes.
Democrats lead in fundraising in races for Republican-held seats in Anchorage
Democrat Cliff Groh and Republican Dan Sager are running for a seat vacated by Republican Rep. David Nelson who is not seeking re-election.  Anchorage’s House District 18 includes Government Hill, Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson and a small section of Muldoon. 
Groh, a former prosecutor, has far outraised Sager — and any other state House candidate — and won the primary election. Groh raised nearly $152,000, with donations from dozens of Alaskans, as well as from the Alaska House Democratic Campaign Committee, public employee, construction and firefighters unions. He also wrote a $3,000 check to his own campaign.
Dan Sager, candidate for House District 18.
Cliff Groh, candidate for House District 18 in the 2026 election. (Photo courtesy of Cliff Groh)
Groh held the seat in 2023 and 2024 but lost a bid for re-election to Nelson in 2024 by just 22 votes. 
Sager, a sales manager for a manufacturing company and a political newcomer, has raised over $12,600 as of a week before the election, from a variety of donors including from Anchorage Republican groups. He also donated $3,000 to his own campaign. 
In the primary election, Groh won by 327 votes with 67% of the vote, while Sager won nearly 33%. 
Groh said he’s raised so much money in part because he has worked hard at his campaign, which he began last year, making calls and walking door-to-door speaking with residents. He noted that campaigns are expensive in his district: with more than half of residents living on Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, it’s more difficult to reach voters. “So I have to send the mailers, you know, mail pieces to them to reach them. So my campaign has a program for that, and that, of course, costs money,” he said. 
He said he’s had support from the Alaska Democratic Party and political consultants, but hopes his experience and vision garners support from voters.
In South Anchorage’s House District 15, long-time Republican incumbent Mia Costello is running for re-election against Democratic challenger Denny Wells, who raised more money than her and led in primary votes. 
Mia Costello, incumbent candidate for House District 15. Photo provided by candidate.
Denny Wells is a candidate for House District 15 in 2026. (Photo courtesy of Denny Wells)
The district includes Campbell Lake, Sand Lake, Bayshore and Dimond High School. Wells, a business owner, ran against Costello  for the seat in 2022 and 2024. Costello has held the seat since 2011.
In the primary, Wells won by 244 votes — winning nearly 53% of the vote; Costello won 47.2% of votes cast in the district.
Wells had raised nearly $23,000 as of a week before the primary, plus another $3,500 in donations a day before the election, totalling more than $26,000 by the primary election. He saw small and large donations from individual donors, as well as funds from the Alaska Democratic Party, the Alaska House Democratic Campaign Committee, and NEA-Alaska, the public teachers union. He also gave $4,000 in non-monetary contributions to his own campaign in printed materials, signs and associated hardware.
Costello raised more than $23,700 by the week before the election. Individual donors as well as the Anchorage Republican Women’s Club, and the Alaska Cabaret, Hotel, Restaurant and Retailers Association political action committee. 
Other notable races
On the Kenai Peninsula, in the House District 7 and House District 8 races, Republican incumbents landed first place in the primary elections, even though Democratic and independent challengers raised more in campaign donations so far this year. 
In the race for House District 7, which includes Kenai and Soldotna, Democratic challenger Kate Veh is running against Republican incumbent Justin Ruffridge who was first elected to the seat in 2022. 
Veh raised over $6,700, which was bolstered by a $3,000 donation from the Alaska Democratic Party. Ruffridge raised over $3,800 in donations this year, with roughly $6,200 held over from last year. This year Ruffridge had just a handful of donations, including $1,000 from the Laborers Local 341 construction union and $1,000 from the Pacific Seafood Processors political action committee. 
In the August primary, Ruffridge won nearly 74% of the vote, while Veh won 26% of votes cast in the district. 
Ruffridge said he’s not surprised at the Democratic and independent fundraising efforts. 
“I feel like in my four years of being in elected office, that has generally seemed to be the case. I think there’s a bit of a more national fundraising effort in this state on behalf of folks in that particular party alignment, and you don’t see that necessarily from folks on the Republican side, I think ours is a little more grassroots, typically,” he said.
He said his campaign has not had support from the Alaska Republican Party. 
The Alaska Republican Party did grant an interview to the Alaska Beacon for this story.
Ruffridge said he doesn’t see the fundraising numbers as evidence of a pushback against Republican policies or the Trump administration, but said support for the party in power usually lapses during midterm elections. 
In House District 8, which encompasses the northern Kenai Peninsula from Hope in the north to Seward in the southeast, independents Nissa Savage and Frank Quinn are challenging incumbent Republican Bill Elam, who was elected in 2025. 
Elam had a strong lead in the primary, despite raising only $50 since February. Quinn raised $139 before the primary elections. Savage, a certified public accountant based in Soldotna, raised more than $9,700, including a $3,000 donation from the Alaska Democratic Party. 
In the primary, Elam won by 72.5% of the vote, while Savage landed 17.1%, and Quinn won 10.3% of votes.  
In Southeast Alaska’s House District 1, which encompasses communities from Metlakatla and Ketchikan to Wrangell, Republican incumbent Jeremy Bynum is running for re-election against independent challenger Grant Echohawk. He led the primary vote and has outraised Echohawk, in part because of a $10,000 donation to his own campaign.
Bynum said in an interview he sees running for re-election as first doing the job of a legislator. He said he provided his own funding as a backstop since he was involved in three special sessions this summer as a member of the House Finance Committee, and could not campaign according to state law. He said he’s not surprised to hear Democrats and independents are out-fundraising Republicans this year. 
“There’s people that run as nonpartisan, but they’re strongly supported by the Democrat Party and the apparatus,” he said. “The Democratic Party in the state has made sure that they’re putting funding into those races not only this year but even last year if a candidate was filed, you know, so they’re very motivated. That’s for sure.”
All Alaska candidates are required to file new financial disclosure reports ahead of the November general election. The next disclosures are due October 3.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Cameron the Capitol Cat statue effort revised after commission skepticism of ‘whimsical’ idea
description: LINCOLN — An effort to create a permanent sculpture honoring the Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot has been scaled back after a commission expressed skepticism last month over the “whimsical” idea. State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward and former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln will again present the idea to honor Cameron the […]
text:
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, at the podium, to the left, and former state Sen. Anna Wishart, at the podium, to the right, testify before the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — An effort to create a permanent sculpture honoring the Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot has been scaled back after a commission expressed skepticism last month over the “whimsical” idea.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward and former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln will again present the idea to honor Cameron the “Capitol Cat” to the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission this Friday. The commission is not yet voting on whether to greenlight the statue.
Until this spring, 11-year-old Cameron had made a home away from home at the Capitol near his former downtown Lincoln residence with his owner, Dianna McGinnis, for nearly a decade. In May, Cameron and McGinnis moved into assisted living.
“We have incorporated the feedback provided to us by the committee as well as community members (many who are part of Cameron’s growing fan club) and are excited about the updated proposal we are coming to Friday’s meeting with,” Wishart said in a Wednesday text.
A ‘whimsical’ proposal
The idea has been revised slightly from an original proposal, which called for a life-size, 18- to 20-inch-tall bronze statue of Cameron on a limestone pedestal about 28-32 inches in height. 
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward. Sept. 22, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The sculpture is now proposed to move slightly east, closer to the state parking lot at the same intersection of H Street and Goodhue Boulevard as before, Hughes confirmed. Cameron’s statue would sit atop a limestone slab that could also serve as a bench.
“There would also be room around that area that some of the school field trips could spread out and eat their sack lunches in that area, which I think would be cool,” Hughes said.
Wishart told commissioners that honoring animals has been a tradition throughout history, such as the case of Fala, the Scottish terrier of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Both are now honored in bronze at Roosevelt’s presidential memorial in Washington, D.C. 
“These animals become a part of the human story of our institutions, and we think Cameron should be a part of Nebraska’s Capitol,” Wishart said last month.
Commissioner Kile Johnson at a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission, which Johnson chairs, on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Moving Cameron’s statue a little east would transfer maintenance responsibilities from the City of Lincoln to the State of Nebraska. Hughes and Wishart are fundraising to pay for the statue and any ongoing costs. No public dollars would go toward the effort.
Commissioner Kile Johnson, chair of the commission, had summed up last month’s skepticism as whether the commission should allow something so “whimsical.” He appeared the most open to the idea, while some commissioners asked about what precedent the sculpture would set.
“This is whimsical, but on the other hand, it looks like it’s done in a very, very high-quality manner,” Johnson said.
Historical significance?
Former state Sen. David Landis, who served 28 years in the Legislature, from 1979 to 2007, and now serves on the Environs Commission, said in August that just as on the floor of the Legislature, sometimes policymakers disagree.
“And this is a place where I don’t agree,” Landis said.
Commissioner David Landis, a former Lincoln state senator, at a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Landis described figures in the Capitol Environs District, such as statues honoring Ponca Chief Standing Bear and Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte on Lincoln Mall to the north of the Capitol, as meant to honor people whom history has perhaps forgotten but who deserve to be remembered. 
He said Cameron didn’t rise to that.
“This is a well-loved cat, but when that time runs out that those of you who love this cat have passed by, what is the historical significance of Cameron?” Landis asked. “I think it pales, other than whatever we carry around in our hearts for the cat.”
Defining ‘public art’
Benjamin Victor of Boise, Idaho, the artist who sculpted the Standing Bear and Picotte statues, has agreed to sculpt Cameron’s statue, too. Victor has also sculpted four statues currently in Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol, including another Chief Standing Bear statue for Nebraska.
Then-state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln attends a public listening forum on property taxes in Lincoln. July 22, 2024. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Collin Christopher, a staff planner for the Lincoln-Lancaster County Planning Department, who assists the committee, had advised the commission that he thought it was “very unfair” to compare a Cameron sculpture to Standing Bear or Picotte. Under commission regulations, the revised Cameron statue would be closer to public art than a memorial or monument.
Commissioners include a mix of Lincoln mayoral and Nebraska governor appointees, plus four nonvoting members. Christopher is one of those nonvoting members on behalf of Lincoln.
“From staff’s perspective, there should be room within the environs for a fun, engaging piece like this, and Goodhue Boulevard and the space identified near the state parking lot seems like a logical place for it to be located,” Friday meeting materials state.
Cameron’s ‘gravitas’
Speaking against the statue effort in August was Bob Ripley, who served as the State Capitol administrator from 1975 until 2023. Ripley said he and his wife, who have been married for 52 years, have always had at least one cat. He said he, too, loved seeing the “enchanting critter” Cameron come out of the building.
Former Nebraska State Capitol Administrator Bob Ripley during a meeting of the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
But Ripley questioned the “gravitas” of Cameron compared to Nebraska Hall of Fame members, including Standing Bear and, as of this summer, Husker legend Tom Osborne. He said putting those inductees in one place is purposeful. 
Instead of the public statue near the Capitol, Ripley suggested placing a Cameron statue in the garden of the Nebraska Governor’s Mansion, which is regulated separately. Access to the mansion also fluctuates from one governor to the next.
“I hate to beat up on a cat that I thoroughly enjoy to this very day, but I think it’s more appropriate scale-wise in a smaller garden space,” Ripley said.
‘Small but meaningful symbol’
Courtney Wittstruck of Lincoln, a registered lobbyist at the Capitol, testified in favor of Cameron’s sculpture in her individual capacity. Wittstruck said the commission needs to separate Cameron the physical cat from what he represents and symbolizes.
“It’s not just remembering this cute cat,” Wittstruck told the commission. “It’s remembering and reminding people of what this cat represented to those who were in the state Capitol.”
‘So freaking cute’: Supporters pitch Cameron the Capitol Cat statue outside Nebraska State Capitol

Wittstruck said Cameron is a reminder that Nebraskans have more in common than their differences and offered a reprieve in hard legislative times. She said Cameron became a “dedicated public servant, and perhaps the most universally beloved figure around the Capitol.”
“In carrying out his unofficial duties comforting and consoling his constituents, Cameron became more than just a Capitol mascot,” Wittstruck continued. “He became a small but meaningful symbol of the best of Nebraska — kindness, friendliness, compassion and willingness to find common ground, which I think in this day and age is especially necessary.”
Commissioner Andrea Gebhart, while similarly voicing hesitation to the original idea, had said she might be able to support a smaller, more whimsical, even temporary statue. Gebhart had suggested that Hughes and Wishart lean away from the “pop icon” that is Cameron now to how the sculpture and an accompanying plaque represent his values, as Wittstruck outlined.
“I think if the plaque speaks to the kindness, the loyalty of the community, that changes the conversation quite a bit,” Gebhart said.
‘He’ll land on his feet’
Speaking with reporters after last month’s meeting, Wishart and Hughes agreed that placing the sculpture near the Governor’s Mansion, to the southwest of the Capitol, wouldn’t work — Hughes described it as a “cage” and “Fort Knox” — but the duo said they wouldn’t give up.
Wishart encouraged supporters of the “Cameron Fan Club” to show up, voice support or donate if possible.
“I think we do need a little whimsy in our lives, and it is quite unique for a cat to be that attached to a large population of people, in particular children,” Wishart said.
“He’ll land on his feet,” Hughes said with a laugh. “We just got to figure out where that is.”
The commission meets at 8:30 a.m. Friday in the Lincoln City Council chambers.

title: Alaska Beacon reporter recognized with national science journalism award
description: Alaska Beacon reporter Yereth Rosen’s award-winning story weaves together regional indigenous knowledge, scientific study findings and political influences to answer a freighted question about the future viability of village life in Western Alaska after ex-typhoon Halong.
text:
The village of Kipnuk, largely submerged by the remnants of Typhoon Halong, is seen from the air on Oct. 12, 2025. Alaska Air National Guard rescue personnel conducted search and rescue operations there, and the Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management has worked with the Alaska Organized Militia and the U.S. Coast Guard in the response. (Photo provided by the Alaska National Guard)After the latest catastrophic storm hit Western Alaska, displacing more than 1,500 people, killing at least one and leaving villages in ruins, residents face an existential crisis. 
Will the wide delta that fans out between the lower Yukon and Kuskokwim Rivers and has supported one of the circumpolar north’s largest Indigenous populations for millennia continue to be a place where Alaska’s Yupik people can live?
So begins Alaska Beacon reporter Yereth Rosen’s award-winning report from 2025, which weaves together regional indigenous knowledge, scientific study findings and political influences to answer a freighted question about the future viability of village life in Western Alaska after ex-typhoon Halong.    

Yereth Rosen
 

Her story, reported with help from Corinne Smith, was honored most recently with the American Geophysical Union’s Perlman Award for Excellence in Science Journalism. The award is a top honor for science reporting that makes information about science accessible and interesting to the general public.
The award is named for the former science editor of the San Francisco Chronicle.
Rosen’s story was selected as the anniversary of the devastating Western Alaska storms approaches, and as parts of the region are again under flood and storm warnings from ex-Typhoon Dujuan.
Typhoon disaster in Western Alaska raises questions around the region’s future

Her reporting did not stop with the one story — she followed the residents of the two villages hardest hit by the storms as they grappled with whether to leave their ancestral homelands or stay in areas that are vulnerable to catastrophic flooding and storms.
Ultimately, the residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok decided to relocate.
Rosen’s story is an example not just of national excellence in science journalism, but a realization of the Alaska Beacon’s mission to report fairly and independently on the people and interests that affect state policy, and to tell stories that aren’t being told, to bring fresh perspectives to state issues and to amplify the voices of Alaska communities that have been marginalized.

name: WyoFile
title: National Elk Refuge fields questions about what feeding elk could mean for Jackson Hole’s water
description:
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is weighing pros and cons of feeding wildlife, which could lead to more chronic wasting disease. That’s raising questions about health risks beyond the herd. 
The post National Elk Refuge fields questions about what feeding elk could mean for Jackson Hole’s water appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
JACKSON—As National Elk Refuge leaders laid out long-term options for managing elk and bison wintering on the edge of Jackson, a discussion Tuesday turned to the northwestern Wyoming town’s water supply.
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is weighing the pros and cons of feeding elk and bison, in part to keep the animals away from town and from damaging private property. But wildlife disease experts predict that continuing to concentrate animals around alfalfa pellets in the winter could lead to more elk infected with always-lethal chronic wasting disease, smaller populations and reduced hunting opportunities. 
Although there’s been long-standing discussions about what that could mean for the long-term health of the elk herd, scientific research is also probing what accumulating prions in the environment could mean for the soil, plants, water and even human health. (Chronic wasting disease has never been documented in humans, but the interspecies barrier is not considered absolute and public health officials advise against eating meat from infected animals.) Meanwhile, a new peer-reviewed study, published this summer in the journal “Environmental Science & Technology,” suggests prions that cause chronic wasting disease may pass through soil into surface waters or groundwater aquifers.
What that could mean in the future for the refuge and town of Jackson came up during questions from the public as Elk Refuge staff laid out four possible options for managing elk and bison — a decision expected to ultimately shape feeding operations, hunting opportunities and disease response. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is taking public comment on a draft environmental impact statement released Aug. 28 that studies the potential impacts of updating the elk and bison plan.
“Why does the new management plan not evaluate the risk CWD poses to the town of Jackson water supply?” asked Shane Moore, a wildlife filmmaker, who grew up on his family’s ranch south of Jackson. Moore has been following state and federal management responses to the disease for decades. The always fatal disease had been detected in wildlife in 36 states in the U.S. and four provinces in Canada as of April 2025, an increase from 26 states and three provinces in 2019, according to researchers.
“Do you intend to keep feeding elk directly over the town well that is located under the south end of the refuge with CWD known to be present?” Moore asked. 
The 33-ton elk crematory arrived at the National Elk Refuge, where it will be used to incinerate the remains of elk believed to be infected with chronic wasting disease. (Eric Cole/National Elk Refuge)
Three of Jackson’s drinking water wells are located on the 24,700-acre refuge. They draw water from 200 feet underground in the Snake River Aquifer, according to a town report.   
Above ground, an ailing elk was identified and euthanized April 15. Lab results later confirmed that case marked the first ever detection of the degenerative brain disease in an elk on the refuge. Refuge officials announced a second case in July.
“You would expect to find CWD prions in the soil first,” said Eric Cole, the refuge’s senior wildlife biologist, who told the audience that new research would be out soon on testing soil and water for prions. “We expect that prions will bind to soil and be less of a threat to groundwater supply. So it’s kind of a second-tier concern at this point until a firm human health risk is established.”
In parts of Wyoming where CWD infects a large percentage of mule deer, devastating populations like the Project Herd, consumption of meat from potentially infected animals is commonplace. The Wyoming Game and Fish Department encourages hunters to test their animals, but in most areas doesn’t require it. 
The refuge is working with the town of Jackson to start doing some water testing, Refuge Project Leader Frank Durbian said Tuesday at the Fish and Wildlife Service’s only in-person public meeting on the draft plan. Just a handful of people attended the meeting at the Teton County Library in Jackson where stakeholders from federal, state and local agencies answered questions. The service held a Sept. 15 virtual meeting. 
National Elk Refuge Project Leader Frank Durbian, left, and Senior Wildlife Biologist Eric Cole run through four possible long-term strategies for managing elk and bison during a meeting Tuesday at Teton County Library in Jackson. Alternatives range from feeding elk and bison indefinitely to ending feeding within five years. (Rebecca Huntington/WyoFile)
Researchers are investigating how chronic wasting disease moves through the environment but available testing is so far still experimental, Cole said Tuesday. “There’s no off-the-shelf assay for testing CWD, prions, in soil or water,” Cole said, adding that the refuge is working with the U.S. Geological Survey on testing. 
“Based on those preliminary results, we are not detecting CWD in soil on the refuge yet,” Cole said. 
Scientists wouldn’t expect to find it yet because prevalence is low since the disease has just been detected there, he said. Researchers also have been testing soil samples throughout Wyoming, including in areas with a very high prevalence of the disease, he said, adding “even in those situations, many of the samples, in a relatively small area, were negative.”
Jackson’s Ecosystem Stewardship Administrator Tanya Anderson also spoke at the meeting. 
“We communicate regularly with the Elk Refuge, our neighbor to the north,” Anderson said. “We definitely want to ensure safe drinking water for everyone.”
Anderson said she has been talking with the health department and reading scientific papers. 
“It is our understanding that those prions love absorbing to soil so much that they generally don’t go deeper than about a half a centimeter in the soil,” Anderson said. “That we have a groundwater supply, and not a surface water supply, should be a great relief to everyone who depends on that water supply.”
In June, Teton County Public Health Director Travis Riddell said he was exploring options to test the town’s water supply to get ahead of any potential concerns in an interview with KHOL 89.1.
“The chance that this could become an actual health threat to humans is quite low,” Riddell told KHOL. “But it’s a new and emerging problem.”
What about the elk?
The new preferred alternative for managing elk and bison marks a shift from focusing on feeding to curtail the elk herd’s size to leaning more heavily on hunting. 
Cole and Brad Hovinga, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s Jackson regional supervisor, both stressed plans to work closely to target short-distance migrants with hunters, and using GPS-collar data to do it. 
Managers split the Jackson Elk Herd into two buckets — those that migrate short distances, from areas like subdivisions along the Snake River corridor, and those that migrate long distances from summer ranges on the Bridger-Teton National Forest and Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks. By hunting short-distance migrants more heavily, the plan aims to reduce the number of elk wintering on the refuge, which could reduce conflicts on private land, reduce disease prevalence and improve habitat, including for other wildlife like birds, the analysis suggests. The draft study also says this approach would reduce impacts to hunters, guides and outfitters. 
The refuge plans to start working with Game and Fish this year to target those short-distance migrants and will adapt as necessary, Durbian said.
Snake River elk, which populate private lands, are seen in Jackson Hole in 2016. (Laura Thompson/USGS)
The proposal does not alter the Jackson Elk Herd’s overall population objective of 11,000 animals, a goal established and changed by Game and Fish. But about 7,500 elk on average winter on the refuge and the goal is to get that number down to 5,000. 
“What we would like to do is change the number of elk that use the National Elk Refuge,” Hovinga said. “We can do that from, not only just harvesting elk on the refuge, but the challenge is to be able to harvest the right elk.”
The short-distance migrants can be prolific and provide less of an ideal opportunity for hunters since they tend to migrate along private lands, officials explained. Changing the distribution of elk, through hunting, could mean more elk wintering on natural forage and fewer elk coming to the refuge, he said. 
The last plan failed to reduce the number of elk wintering on the Elk Refuge but did succeed in reducing the average feeding season length by 19%, Cole said. Refuge officials found through experience that starting feeding later proved difficult, but ending artificial feeding earlier in the spring worked. So all four alternatives call for shortening feeding seasons by ending about two weeks earlier on average. Shortening the overall feeding season would lower future chronic wasting disease prevalence and lead to healthier herds over the long-term, the service’s analysis suggests. 
During the presentation, federal wildlife managers stressed that all alternatives result in long-term elk population declines. Continuing feeding indefinitely, however, is expected to result in the worst outcome for herd size and hunting opportunity. 
Bison chow down on alfalfa pellets on the National Elk Refuge in March 2013. Elk, which are subordinate, wait for the chance to feed. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
In addition to continuing to feed elk, the Fish and Wildlife Service’s current preferred alternative, which officials said could change, also calls for continuing to feed bison on the northernmost portion of the refuge. Roughly 7,500 elk and 500 bison consume around 35 to 40 tons of alfalfa pellets per day. It’s not uncommon for the refuge to feed about 2,000 tons of pellets over a season, which has averaged 65 days and typically costs more than $1 million a year, Cole said. During mild winters, the refuge has not fed at all, which was the case last winter and has occurred 11 times in the refuge’s history, he said. Reducing elk on the refuge to 5,000 could reduce costs tied to labor-intensive feeding operations. 
The draft analysis contemplates scenarios that would phase out feeding for elk but continue it for bison, in part, to keep bison from heading into subdivisions bordering the refuge where they could pose a problem for people. Some meeting attendees questioned Tuesday whether that would work. Cole said feeding is a learned behavior and elk could learn over time that bison aren’t about to share any alfalfa pellets with the smaller ungulates. The pellets get gobbled up quickly and don’t remain on the landscape as an attractant, he said. 
The public has 45 days to review the new draft environmental impact statement and submit comments, which are due Oct. 13. 
Mike Koshmrl contributed reporting.

title: Federal judge denies request to block TN Highway Patrol traffic stops conducted in tandem with ICE
description: A federal judge on Wednesday denied a request for a preliminary injunction that would prevent the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting pretextual traffic stops in tandem with federal immigration agents. U.S. District Judge Aleta Trauger ruled the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition had not made a “clear showing” it was entitled to the injuncti[...]
text:
A federal judge in Nashville on Wednesday denied a motion to enjoin the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting traffic stops in tandem with ICE. Pictured: a Tennessee Highway Patrol officer and two Homeland Security Investigations officers search a vehicle during a traffic stop on Lamar Ave. in Memphis, Tennessee on Oct. 7, 2025.(Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A federal judge on Wednesday denied a request for a preliminary injunction that would prevent the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting pretextual traffic stops in tandem with federal immigration agents.
U.S. District Judge Aleta Trauger ruled the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition had not made a “clear showing” it was entitled to the injunction at this stage of the litigation.
The coalition had sought the injunction as part of its ongoing challenge to the constitutionality of state troopers conducting traffic stops of motorists suspected of being noncitizens and then allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — riding along or stationed nearby — to demand immigration papers and detain drivers.
The coalition, which filed suit in May against the Tennessee Highway Patrol, or THP, and its oversight agency, the Tennessee Department of Safety and Homeland Security, is alleging the practice violates motorists’ rights under the 4th and 14th Amendments. Seven Tennessee residents joined as plaintiffs.
In a swift ruling, issued one day after a court hearing to consider arguments over the injunction, Trauger expressed deep skepticism that the immigrant coalition could ultimately demonstrate that the cooperative traffic stops violated motorists’ rights under the 4th Amendment, which protects individuals against unreasonable searches and seizures.
Immigrant advocates seek immediate halt to highway patrol traffic stops conducted in tandem with ICE

Trauger wrote the immigrant advocates had “no likelihood of success” on the claim “even if the court accepts as true that the THP troopers, pursuant to a policy, are pretextually pulling over non-White motorists in Memphis for the purpose of aiding ICE agents to investigate the motorists’ immigration status.”
“Supreme Court precedent is clear: a pretextual traffic stop supported by probable cause to believe a traffic violation has occurred does not violate the Fourth Amendment, irrespective of the arresting officers’ subjective intent.”
Trauger gave more weight to the immigrant organization’s allegation that the traffic stops violated drivers’ 14th Amendment rights against discrimination, signalling the argument may have merit if supported by more evidence.
The evidence introduced thus far in the ongoing litigation “though not robust” is “sufficient to establish some likelihood of success on the merits” of the Fourteenth Amendment challenge to the traffic stop as “motivated by a discriminatory purpose” or having a “discriminatory effect,” she wrote.
Trauger noted that data and evidence submitted to support allegations of discriminatory traffic stops conducted in tandem with ICE focuses heavily on a weeklong operation in Nashville in May 2025 that resulted in scores of immigration arrests. That operation has formally ended and Trauger indicated she needed more evidence of ongoing constitutional violations in the state, specifically in Memphis where the THP is part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, a multi-agency effort including federal immigration enforcement, convened last fall by President Donald Trump. 
Trauger also ruled the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition had a right to sue on behalf of its members, dismissing arguments by state lawyers that the organization lacked standing to pursue legal action.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont Yankee decommissioning is nearly complete
description:
Almost all of the $602 million decommissioning trust fund has been spent on demolishing the reactor and its affiliated structures and shipping the debris thousands of miles away.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Yankee decommissioning is nearly complete.
text:
A worker cuts apart a beam during the deconstruction of the former Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant in Vernon in October 2023. The salvaged metal from the plant, which is not radioactive, is being recycled. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Susan Smallheer was first published in the Brattleboro Reformer on Sept. 21, 2026.
VERNON — The sound of jackhammering has largely stopped. And the view of the Connecticut River is frankly astonishing: Gone is the large, five-story pale green reactor building that has dominated the site for close to 50 years. There are no more giant industrial buildings at the former Vermont Yankee nuclear power plant, just what looks like an ordinary construction yard.
Decommissioning or demolition work at the reactor, which was shut down in 2016 by its then-owner Entergy Nuclear because it was losing money in the “deregulated” New England energy market, is fast approaching completion. Almost all of the $602 million decommissioning trust fund has been spent on demolishing the reactor and its affiliated structures and shipping the debris thousands of miles away.
During a tour last week of the site, Scott State, who until recently was the CEO of NorthStar Group Services, the owner of the 140-acre Yankee site, said the 10-year project was “99 percent done.”
State stepped down as NorthStar’s CEO in July to become its executive chairman and chief nuclear officer.
Along on the tour was NorthStar’s new CEO, Jeffrey Adix, who was promoted from his position at NorthStar as chief financial officer.
State said the project has used up almost all of the $602 million in the decommissioning trust fund NorthStar inherited when it bought Yankee in 2019.
State said there is $8.5 million left to complete what needs to be done in the next several months. There is another fund for site restoration. Final work will be completed in 2027, three years ahead of NorthStar’s promised deadline of 2030.
Although construction and cleanup may soon be completed by NorthStar, in the parlance of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission the site can’t be “released” for potential reuse until it has reviewed NorthStar’s work — a review that State expects will take a couple of years.
All the concrete from the reactor building’s foundation and above-ground building, approximately 28,000 cubic yards, was shipped out of Vermont to Waste Control Specialists’ disposal site in Andrews, Texas, at the low-level radioactive waste site operated for Texas, Vermont and other waste generators.
The reactor’s foundation and walls were in some places 12 feet thick, and NorthStar has agreed to remove any concrete 4 feet below the surface.
During negotiations with the state over the sale of Yankee to NorthStar, it was agreed that the concrete would not be pulverized and used as fill on site, State said.
“Consistent with its obligations under the MOU (memorandum of understanding) entered into during the Public Utility Commission Certificate of Public Good process, NorthStar shipped all the concrete generated from excavating the reactor building superstructure, totaling approximately 28,000 cubic yards, to Waste Control Specialists’ disposal site in Andrews, Texas,” State said in a follow-up exchange.
NorthStar sourced the clean fill for the reactor building basement from a local Vermont quarry, State said. When excavation and fill of the reactor building site is completed to the 4-foot-below-grade-structure standard, NorthStar anticipates that it will have used approximately 28,000 cubic yards of locally sourced clean fill to restore the reactor building site.
Last week, there were still dozens of construction workers at the Vernon site, with NorthStar manager Corey Daniels estimating there were between 50 and 80 people on site.
One of the remaining projects that won’t be tackled until early next year is dismantling the plant’s water discharge structure, a non-nuclear concrete structure that would release the heated but not radioactive cooling water from Yankee’s cooling towers, and indirectly its reactor, back to the Connecticut River.
NorthStar anticipates completing physical decommissioning in 2027, State said.
“Following physical decommissioning, NorthStar’s team will work efficiently to satisfy all Nuclear Regulatory Commission requirements for partial site release,” he said.
The NRC typically hires a consultant to evaluate the work done by a decommissioning firm, and NorthStar anticipates completing both physical and regulatory decommissioning and site restoration by 2030. State anticipates the NRC will hire the Oak Ridge Institute for Science and Education, and that will be paid for by NorthStar.
“We pay for everything,” he said.
NorthStar largely won over the state’s support of its purchase in 2018-19 by promising to dismantle Yankee as soon as possible. Previously, the plan under Entergy was to put the plant into cold shutdown, a process the NRC called SAFSTOR, and start demolition and cleanup in about 60 years. The time would have allowed the decommissioning trust fund, which was invested in government bonds, to grow and radiation to decay. State said that none of the nuclear reactors shut down in recent years has gone into SAFSTOR.
NorthStar in 2018 said the $602 million was adequate to do the job, and it provided guarantees to the state in case it wasn’t. Those guarantees won’t be necessary, State said.
Back in 2016, the natural gas market made generating electricity in a nuclear power plant too expensive, State said, and Entergy eventually shut down and sold its reactors to get out of the business.
State said Entergy still operates nuclear power plants in the South, where the energy market is regulated.
Workers have already tackled the intake structure, which drew millions of gallons of river water to indirectly cool the reactor. In both cases, the river bank will be recontoured to its original slope, NorthStar officials said. “It’s not a rad thing,” State said, pointing out both structures had no exposure to radioactivity.
As a condition of last week’s tour, State and other NorthStar officials wouldn’t talk about the future use or development of the site or PowerTransitions, the Texas-based company that has a lease with NorthStar to study the site for potential future use. PowerTransitions is said to be exploring a battery storage facility, to take advantage of the adjoining power substation, owned by VELCO (Vermont Electric Power Co., which is a joint operation of Vermont utilities). PowerTransitions is also considering a data center and even a small modular nuclear reactor, although Vernon town officials have said that its focus is on a battery storage facility.
Although the large industrial buildings are gone, the large collection of giant steel and concrete casks — about 20 feet tall and containing the 42-plus years of spent nuclear fuel — remains at the north edge of the property. The casks will remain there for the foreseeable future until the federal Department of Energy creates a national repository and takes them away.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Rhode Island rural health projects take shape with $156M federal award
description: The federal government infused $50 billion into rural healthcare last July when President Donald Trump signed into law H.R. 1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. How Rhode Island will spend its $156.17 million share of the nationwide Rural Health Transformation Program awards is now taking shape ahead of the federal Oct. […]
text:
Dr. Milton J. Liu treats a dental patient at Wood River Health in Hopkinton. The health center serves several of Rhode Island’s state-designated rural communities and operates a twice-monthly dental clinic on Block Island, where access to routine dental care can require off-island travel. (Photo by Seth Jacobson/Seth Jacobson Photography)The federal government infused $50 billion into rural healthcare last July when President Donald Trump signed into law H.R. 1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
How Rhode Island will spend its $156.17 million share of the nationwide Rural Health Transformation Program awards is now taking shape ahead of the federal Oct. 1 deadline to obligate the funds for the first year. 
“How do we do that in places that don’t have doctors right now, that don’t have a physical doctor’s office to put people?” Christopher Ausura, the Executive Office of Health and Human Services’ director of policy and community investment, said during a virtual meeting Wednesday morning of the Rural Stakeholder Advisory Council.
The meeting brought together state officials and providers to focus on the 18 of the state’s 39 municipalities that fall under the Ocean State’s own version of the “rural” label. One common federal standard is to base rurality on census data, largely how far a particular community sits outside a metropolitan area — so most of Rhode Island is considered metropolitan because few municipalities are far away from a city, leaving only Block Island and Westerly federally designated as rural. Rhode Island, meanwhile, defines a rural community as having fewer than 25,000 residents and fewer than 1,000 people per square mile. 
The 18 municipalities are home to about 195,800 residents, or 17.9% of the state population. The transformation program is meant to improve access to healthcare in communities facing primary care shortages, or a dearth of specialists, dentists or behavioral health providers — even if the communities may appear different from the outside.
Ausura noted that eight of the 18 communities have no healthcare providers, while another three or four have a very small pool of practitioners or infrastructure. 
But the state is not advocating merely throwing money at places with poor infrastructure, Ausura noted.
“One, there’s going to be an upper limit of how much they’re going to be able to take, how much practice transformation is sustainable in those practices with the patient populations that they have,” Ausura said. “And secondly, if we collectively as a state only invest in the places where there’s existing infrastructure, we’re not transforming healthcare. We’re just piling onto the places where it currently exists.” 
 

  What’s ‘rural’ in Rhode Island?

The municipalities eligible for Rural Health Transformation Program money include:

Burrillville
Charlestown
East Greenwich
Exeter
Foster
Glocester
Hopkinton
Jamestown
Little Compton
New Shoreham (Block Island)
North Smithfield
Portsmouth
Richmond
Scituate
Smithfield
Tiverton
West Greenwich
Westerly




The options discussed by the advisory council — its full membership, officials said, is not online but is expected to be soon — to provide healthcare in hard-to-reach places included mobile clinics, community-based care and telehealth. 
State health officials stressed during the meeting that they are open to feedback about the best ways to implement the state’s intended slate of 13 programs. The federal grant application and subsequent state budget amendment detailed the various buckets into which the funds will ideally flow, such as mobile dental care, nutrition programs, maternal and child health services and improved telemedicine capacity in schools.
But like the various definitions of rurality, stakeholders also had different ideas about what some of these initiatives would mean in practice. Alison Croke, president and CEO of Wood River Health — which has a main office in the village of Hope Valley in northern Hopkinton and a satellite in Westerly and offers services at least twice a month on Block Island — wondered during the meeting what “mobile” treatment would actually look like. It sounded to her like a traveling vehicle. 
“Trying to achieve having a vehicle and expecting people to go and seek their healthcare on said vehicle is probably not realistic,” Croke said, “and [it] might not achieve the program goals that you’re looking to achieve.”
Croke said in a follow-up email to questions from Rhode Island Current, “Conceptually, bringing health care into the local community is a great idea.” But she added, “Expecting patients to want to be seen for primary care in a vehicle is less realistic.”
Mobile treatment works better in urban areas, where pedestrians and public transportation make getting to the vehicle itself a more viable option, Croke said. In the towns Wood River Health serves, the coverage area is too large and lacks public transportation, she said. She suggested a nurse practitioner-led team and home delivery of care for chronic issues or behavioral health, plus some additional funding for services like Wood River’s health center van.
Wood River operates a dental clinic at the Block Island Health Center twice a month for patients of all ages, including those on Medicaid. Croke said appointments are always fully booked, although the service’s waiting list remains short.
Wood River Health Services in Hope Valley in northern Hopkinton. (Photo by Harold Hanka/The Westerly Sun)
Before the clinic, Croke wrote, “Medicaid patients, including kids, would need to take a full day and travel off-island to seek routine care. Not all families are able to do this, which causes delay in routine care and can lead to oral disease and decay.”
But figuring out the most effective — and fiscally shrewd — ways to deliver crucial healthcare to rural Rhode Island with the new grant money is exactly what the advisory council exists to discuss. 
Jessica Patalano, a contractor and physical therapist who is leading the mobile health project for the state health department, said officials are open to different design options that would allow more complete coverage of the state’s rural areas. Block Island, she noted, was excluded from initial plans for the mobile unit because of “the challenges of getting on a ferry.”
Still, psychotherapist and counselor Kerri Gaffett, who runs her practice out of Wickford and was invited to speak at the meeting, thought that mobile services could uniquely benefit Block Islanders.
“A lot of my Block Island clients will come to Wickford for the privacy aspect of it,” Gaffett said. 
But not every medical visit requires such privacy: “It takes a whole day to go to the dentist or to go to seek mental health or behavioral health or any kind of care, right?” Gaffett said. “We have a small community, so a mobile health team makes a lot of sense for Block Island.” 
“If we need to pivot, then we will pivot,” Patalano said.
Christina Angelone-Gatteri, a licensed mental health counselor and outpatient director of Gateway Healthcare’s Washington County region, noted to Croke’s point that “mobile… really implies a vehicle bringing the treatment team around.” She added that a community-based treatment model can involve the same care team traveling to homes or other community venues without having to lug a van around.
About $5.6 million was allocated in the budget to rural community-based and mobile health services, one of the 13 initiatives funded for the first year through Rhode Island’s federal grant. 
Other investments include workforce development, behavioral health services, health information technology, hospital-at-home care and expanded EMS services. The state has until Sept. 30, 2027, to spend the first-year grant money.
The Rural Stakeholder Advisory Council is scheduled to meet again on Oct. 28, with plans to discuss the program’s data infrastructure.

title: Lock up your guns. It could prevent a suicide.
description:
Nearly two-thirds of Vermont suicide deaths involve a firearm. Secure storage and Extreme Risk Protection Orders can buy a person in crisis the time they need.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Lock up your guns. It could prevent a suicide..
text:
This commentary is by Seton McIlroy, the executive director of GunSense Vermont.
September is Suicide Prevention Month. Last year, 140 Vermonters died by suicide, and nearly two-thirds of these deaths involved a firearm. This is why GunSense Vermont promotes Vermont’s secure storage laws. Not only does secure storage prevent children from accessing firearms in the home, but it also helps to prevent or delay a suicidal person from accessing a gun.
In the most recent Vermont Youth Risk Behavior Survey, almost 40% of high schoolers said they could access a loaded gun from their home without their parents knowing.
According to the State of Vermont, secure storage involves a sturdy gun safe, a locked chest or a trigger or cable lock. There are places throughout our state that offer free gun locks, including public libraries, police departments and county sheriffs’ offices. 
In addition to securing guns, it’s important to recognize when a friend or family member is in crisis and needs help. Mental health professionals, teachers, counselors and trusted religious clergy are all good places to start. When a person is in crisis and is at risk of hurting themselves or others, an Extreme Risk Protection Order (ERPO) can temporarily remove their access to buy, have or receive guns or explosives until the crisis is over.
An ERPO can be initiated by a family member, healthcare professional or law enforcement. The request is decided by a judge and reviewed 14 days later to decide if it needs to be extended. There are no charges filed, and nothing is recorded on a criminal record. 
In 2025, 28 ERPO petitions were filed, 13 of which were granted because the person threatened or attempted to harm themselves. Temporarily removing access to guns gives a person in crisis time to calm down and get the help they need.

READ MORE

People without easy access to a gun do not necessarily find other ways to end their life. Nine out of 10 people who attempt suicide do not go on to die by suicide. Giving a person in crisis the gift of time can be the difference between life and death.
Hopelessness and despair are potent emotions, but secure storage and ERPOs can be effective deterrents. This month, GunSense Vermont encourages all gun owners to make sure they have a safe, secure way to store their firearms. It could save a life.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Voters to decide fate of state taxes this fall
description: This fall, voters in at least nine states will decide whether to cut, cap or raise taxes through ballot measures that will give them a direct hand in steering state tax policy in a conservative or progressive direction. Some states, such as California, will weigh whether to tax — or untax — their wealthiest residents. […]
text:
Canvassers in Denver received petition packets as they prepared to gather signatures in support of a graduated income tax measure that will appear on the Colorado ballot in November. Colorado is one of at least nine states that will decide whether to cut, cap or raise taxes this fall. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)This fall, voters in at least nine states will decide whether to cut, cap or raise taxes through ballot measures that will give them a direct hand in steering state tax policy in a conservative or progressive direction.
Some states, such as California, will weigh whether to tax — or untax — their wealthiest residents. Others, such as  Florida, are considering a myriad of mostly conservative-backed measures to cut property or income taxes.
“The California wealth tax is part of a broader conversation regarding the wealthy having to pay their fair share,” said Janelle Fritts, senior policy analyst at the Tax Foundation, a nonpartisan tax analysis and research organization. “Florida is reflecting the broader conversation about property taxes right now.
“Any kind of tax elimination is going to require a lot of tradeoffs.”
Below is a rundown on the states where tax measures are on the ballot, and how they could reshape the money available for communities to spend on public services.
Taxing the rich
California voters in November will weigh a measure no other state has tried: a one-time wealth tax on billionaires.
Proposition 40 would take 5% of billionaires’ net worth in order to raise tens of billions to close budget holes the state’s Medicaid, food assistance, education and other programs. The measure is largely a response to the loss of federal funding from President Donald Trump’s 2025 budget law, the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
California’s 250 billionaires are collectively worth $2.3 trillion, equal to the entire income of all 20 million California taxpayers, according to a September letter written in support of Proposition 40 by a group of six Nobel Prize-winning economists.
A billionaire wealth tax in California, they said, could “kickstart a movement to tax ultra-high-net-worth individuals in other states.”
A handful of other states, including Maine, Massachusetts, New York and Washington, already have a so-called millionaire tax that taxes earnings above the $1 million mark at higher rates, Earlier this year, Hawaii joined the group by passing a law that added a 13% income tax bracket for joint filers earning more than $1 million, while also preserving some income tax cuts for lower-income filers.
But California is going further with its one-time 5% tax.
The state’s Democratic leaders are divided. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, is against the proposal, as are some state education and medical associations.
Critics say the tax could push billionaires to leave the state entirely, leading to a dramatic loss in future income tax revenues and fewer business investments. Some say it would face myriad legal challenges. And because the tax is earmarked, some groups oppose it because the funds couldn’t be used to support programs including affordable housing and subsidized child care.
The state Democratic Party has narrowly endorsed it. Other supporters include some labor organizations, as well as California U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna, a Democrat.
Billionaire opponents, including Google cofounder Sergey Brin, have funneled enormous sums into opposing the tax and supporting competing ballot measures. Two constitutional amendments also on the ballot, Propositions 41 and 42, could undo parts or all of Proposition 40, as long as they receive more “yes” votes, according to California’s Legislative Analyst’s Office.
One new poll found that just 45% of likely voters approve of taxing California’s wealthiest residents, according to polling from Politico and the University of California, Berkeley.
California voters also will consider another measure, Proposition 3, that would extend higher tax rates for the state’s three highest income brackets. Those rates contribute $10 billion a year to state coffers, according to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a tax policy nonprofit.
In Colorado, voters will decide on a similar measure, which would raise taxes on the state’s highest-income households and cut taxes for nearly everyone else by replacing the state’s flat tax. But like in California, a competing ballot measure could undo this one if it receives more “yes” votes.
In Washington state, a ballot measure would repeal that state’s new millionaire tax. Earlier this year, the Democratic-led state legislature created a 9.9% tax on incomes above $1 million per year, but a “yes” vote on the new ballot measure would repeal it. Complicating the issue are new findings from the state that the tax — if voters keep it in place — will bring in more than previously expected, about $3.1 billion the first fiscal year and about $8.3 billion from 2029-2031.
Unpopular property taxes
The Florida legislature is asking Floridians to make one of the most significant changes to their property taxes in decades. A constitutional amendment, if passed, would gradually reduce any property taxes that don’t benefit school districts by increasing the state’s homestead exemption.
“Property taxes are always unpopular, but they’re especially unpopular this year,” Fritts said.
That’s partly because they’re among the most “visible” taxes, she said. Most people don’t know how much they paid in sales tax last year, but they almost certainly know the total on their property tax bill.
And Florida doesn’t have a personal state income tax, meaning property taxes are more squarely in the crosshairs for those wanting to cut taxes.
While the state GOP endorses the proposed amendment, other groups — including law enforcement, child welfare advocates and municipal government officials — say it would blow a massive hole in local governments’ budgets. State and local coffers could take a hit of up to $12 billion each year beginning in 2031, according to state projections.
And yet, in a poll conducted earlier this month of more than 900 Florida voters, fewer than half said they supported it.
In August, a Florida circuit court judge ruled that much of the proposal’s ballot language — which was initially drafted by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis’ administration and later amended by GOP legislators — was “akin to a political slogan” and violated state law because it was misleading. The judge ordered Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier to rewrite it.
In North Carolina, a proposed ballot measure that would cap how much cities and other local governments can grow their revenue sailed through the House and Senate. It was a priority for Republican leadership focused on addressing constituent complaints over rising property taxes.
“Property taxes are out of control,” said North Carolina state House Speaker Destin Hall, a Republican, in a March post on social media.
“Levy limits will stop runaway property tax hikes and protect NC taxpayers.”
The amendment would require the state legislature to pass a law limiting how much local governments can grow their revenue through property taxes every year.
Critics say North Carolina’s proposal could torpedo local budgets: Property taxes are the largest single source of revenue for local services including public school buildings, libraries, parks and emergency services, according to the North Carolina Budget & Tax Center.
Fritts of the Tax Foundation said such levy limits, which a number of states already have, are one of the most effective ways to limit property tax increases.
In Wyoming, voters will decide whether to cut state property taxes through a new program that would exempt half of a primary residence’s assessed value from being taxed.
And Oklahoma voters will decide whether to reduce annual increases in property tax values.
Reining in legislators
Earlier this year, Missourians overwhelmingly rejected a ballot proposal — supported by Missouri Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe — that would have required state lawmakers to eliminate the state’s income tax.
“We already saw a big income tax cut go down in flames in Missouri because voters weren’t happy about the tradeoffs it would require, namely higher sales taxes and worse public services,” said Aidan Davis, state policy director at the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, said in a statement to Stateline.
“It remains to be seen if voters in other states are going to view those tradeoffs the same way.”
Other states are targeting income taxes through ballot measures. And some are looking to rein in the power of lawmakers to push taxes higher.
In North Carolina, voters will consider a constitutional amendment to cap state income taxes at 3.5%, which is half of the current maximum rate of 7%. Critics say it would cement tax cuts that mainly benefit the wealthy and corporations.
It’s similar to a proposed Colorado measure that would cap that state’s flat 4.4% corporate and personal income tax rate.
Both would prevent lawmakers from enacting higher taxes on higher earners to generate funds for public services.
An Iowa ballot initiative also would  make it harder for legislators to tinker with taxes: it would require a two-thirds supermajority of state lawmakers to raise personal or corporate income taxes.
Iowa’s Republican-led legislature voted the proposal onto the ballot as a “common sense” way to rein in taxes. But critics say it benefits wealthier households and could push the state to raise other taxes when it needs revenue, such as sales tax increases that have a bigger impact on low- and middle-income families.
An August poll showed Iowa voters split on the issue, with about a third of likely voters planning to vote in favor, 36% planning to vote against, and another 30% undecided.
Finally in Massachusetts, a “yes” vote on Question 5 would change how the state’s tax revenue limit is calculated. Currently, state law caps how much tax revenue the state can keep annually, and any extra beyond the cap must be refunded to taxpayers as credits. But if voters approve changing how the state calculates tax collections, taxpayers would be more likely to get money back in a given year. Proponents say it would slow down state spending, while opponents say it leaves less money available for public services.

Stateline reporter Anna Claire Vollers can be reached at avollers@stateline.org.

title: For laid off St Albans Creamery workers, health insurance benefits run out next week. The union representing them is asking the courts to intervene
description:
The union says many members have serious medical issues and it would be “stunningly cruel” for Dairy Farmers of America, the co-op that owns the creamery, to stop contributing to workers’ health care plan.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  For laid off St Albans Creamery workers, health insurance benefits run out next week. The union representing them is as[...]
text:
The St. Albans Co-op Creamery in St. Albans in August 2019. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Teamsters Local 597, which represents employees at St. Albans Creamery, filed a motion with the Vermont District Court on Tuesday, hoping to force their employer to continue making health insurance contributions while the dairy processing plant remains closed.
Without action from the court, the union’s insurance is set to expire at the end of the month. 
The dairy plant, which is owned and operated by co-op Dairy Farmers of America, shuttered on August 17. The co-op described the plant as unviable, and labeled the closure a private-sector business decision. 
DFA covered 85% of their employees’ health insurance premiums, and nearly all the employees and many of their families are covered by the plan, according to the court filing.
This latest filing comes in a series of legal actions taken by the union, which alleges DFA illegally retaliated by closing the plant after the union went on strike late last year. The union secured a temporary restraining order to stop DFA from making irreversible changes to the plant, like selling it. The union argues that, because the parties haven’t gone through arbitration, the plant should remain in a condition that would allow it to reopen.
The court vacated the restraining order once DFA agreed it would not take any more steps to further close the plant and would expedite arbitration proceedings.
The union also says the employer is violating its commitment to expedite arbitration in the filing.
Both parties have not been able to agree on an arbitration date before early next year, which the union argues isn’t soon enough.
Tuesday’s filing describes seven employees, all of whom were laid off on August 17 with the plant’s closure, who would not be able to afford health insurance for themselves or their families without the employer’s contributions. The filing said the employees would lose coverage at the end of the month.
Dairy Farmers of America has not replied to a request for comment.
Nearly half of Vermonters are insured through their employers. Accessing health insurance through an employer tends to be more affordable. That’s because employers often cover the majority of health premium costs, according to KKF Health News.
“Many of our members and their families are dealing with serious medical issues, for which they will require extensive medication, treatment, and procedures in the coming weeks,” Teamsters attorney Jason Vazquez told VTDigger in an email. 
“Stripping their health insurance, particularly while the Union’s grievances related to the plant closure remain pending, would be stunningly cruel. It would cause many of our members immense pain, suffering, and hardship — and could result in catastrophe or tragedy,” he said.
The case is before Judge William K. Sessions III. Vazquez hopes the judge will set a hearing for next week. The union’s health insurance would expire on Wednesday.
