name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: ‘Let the little children come to me’: SC moms lack childcare options
description: I spent an afternoon calling more than 50 childcare centers in one Sumter ZIP code. I called every single one. A mother we were trying to help had an infant and a school-age child, whose father had been deployed. She needed care for both children on a schedule that didn’t align with 9 a.m. to […]
text:
According to a survey released in August 2025, childcare disruptions cost South Carolina an estimated $997 million annually in employer costs and lost tax revenue. (File photo by Vanessa Nunes/Getty Images)I spent an afternoon calling more than 50 childcare centers in one Sumter ZIP code. I called every single one.
A mother we were trying to help had an infant and a school-age child, whose father had been deployed. She needed care for both children on a schedule that didn’t align with 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.
Her job, like so many available to mothers here, needed her some evenings and weekends, not the typical daycare center’s hours.


To read more commentaries in this series, click here.


Fifty-plus calls. Not one center could take both children.
I hung up the phone feeling like a failure. One number at a time, I had personally confirmed that Sumter did not have a place for her children to be cared for while she went to work.
For mothers raising children alone, work is an economic necessity, and for many families receiving public assistance, it is also a condition of receiving help.
Parents receiving temporary cash assistance must work, seek employment or participate in job training. Food assistance has similar requirements if their children are older than 13.
Even childcare assistance is largely tied to employment.
The logic makes sense: help families while parents work toward greater stability. But it creates an impossible equation when the childcare required to go to work is unaffordable or simply doesn’t exist. We can require a mother to work. We cannot require a childcare slot to appear.
I am a working mother of four. I have not worked full-time since we had children. Even with a spouse, grandparents and neighbors who help, a church preschool program, in-home daycare,
a stretch of years as a stay-at-home mom, and for a while, a part-time nanny, it has never stopped being a juggling act.
Today it’s afterschool care, summer camps, and backup plans stacked on backup plans. And I am, by any honest accounting, one of the fortunate ones.
If it takes that much outside support for someone with every advantage stacked in her favor, what does it mean that the mother I was calling on behalf of had almost none of it?
I’ve since learned that some local mothers are selling plasma to pay for childcare. I heard that at a listening session from a provider watching families leave her program after eligibility changes cost them the childcare scholarships that made care affordable. Nearly every child in her care depends on financial assistance.
Parents are scraping together tuition from grandparents, friends, and their own blood.
Everyone loses. Without subsidized care to fall back on, the mother often loses her job and with it, any stability she’s built for her family. The provider loses enrollment and may have to close her doors.
Childcare disruptions cost South Carolina an estimated $997 million annually in employer costs and lost tax revenue, according to a survey released in August 2025.
Childcare workers lose, too, earning an average $13.34 an hour as of May 2023. That’s far less than a living wage. Center-based care for two children now costs more than average rent in every state, and help is disappearing.
South Carolina has paused new and renewal applications for its Working Families childcare scholarship, citing insufficient funding.
Children lose the most of all.
High-quality early care strengthens language, social skills, and school readiness, particularly for children from low-income families. Statewide, fewer than 4 in 10 South Carolina kindergartners arrived ready for school in 2024, with children who lack access to quality early education facing the greatest barriers.
According to an often cited (but outdated) statistic from 2018, 42% of South Carolinians live in childcare deserts, where there are more than three young children for every licensed childcare slot. Availability could be worse today.
I didn’t need that statistic. I’d already experienced it.
When the disciples tried to turn children away, Jesus stopped them.
“Let the little children come to me,” he said.
Children belong first to their families, but they also grow up within communities.
What happens to them matters to all of us.
That conviction runs through the rest of Scripture too. Widows and orphans are named again and again as a community’s responsibility, not a private misfortune for one family to bear.
A single mother raising children alone occupies much the same place today. Yet, we often leave her to figure it out by herself.
We say we value families, yet we have built a system that makes it nearly impossible for many mothers to care for their children and hold down a job. The mother I called on behalf of is still cobbling something together out of friends, luck, and an employer’s patience that could run out any day. I don’t know how her story ends. Neither does she.
What would it look like if we meant “let the little children come” — not only as something we say, but as something our systems made possible?

name: Mississippi Today
title: 2nd man denied bond in death of Tasia Fortune, as Jackson police search for more suspects
description: Christy Spivey poses with a portrait of her late daughter Tasia Fortune, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Marion, Ky.
text:
A second man was denied bond Wednesday in connection with the killing of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother of four who was found last month hanging from a tree in west Jackson. 
Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney announced the arrest of Earnest Lloyd Jr., 25,  Tuesday at the Jackson City Council meeting. She said the Jackson Police Department is seeking help from the U.S. Marshals Service to arrest at least one other person. 
Last week, police charged Jarques Ratliff, 51, with Fortune’s killing. He pleaded not guilty and remains in custody after being denied bond. His attorney said a preliminary hearing is scheduled for Friday.
“I will guarantee you, there are actually more arrests to come in this incident,” Brackney said at the meeting.
Fortune’s death became national news, as the story of a Black woman found hanging harkened back to the Mississippi’s dark history of racist terror lynchings. Both Lloyd and Ratliff are also Black.
On Aug. 3, Fortune’s body was found hanging from a tree outside a vacant house on the 500 block of Road of Remembrance. She was 29 years old.
Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, was at the meeting when the police chief announced the latest arrest. She and her husband traveled from Kentucky to be in Jackson this week to attend the court dates of the two suspects and to visit Fortune’s children. 
She held a press conference with Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes before the Tuesday council meeting. Stokes is trying to schedule a meeting with the U.S. Attorney and the FBI.
“You know, she didn’t have a lot to give, she was struggling,” Spivey said at the press conference. “But she would do anything to help anybody.”
Spivey told Mississippi Today that the recent arrests, after a “brutal silence,” have given her hope that authorities are now more aggressively seeking justice for her daughter. She said the family is anxious about any additional arrests.
Spivey also visited the crime scene for the first time on Tuesday. 
“It was hard, but I felt like I owed it to Tasia,” she said.
Spivey described seeing cardinals flying, and she took pictures of her daughter’s memorial, a small mound of flowers, balloons, teddy bears and pinwheels surrounding a framed picture of her.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington nears final step in joining California-Quebec carbon market
description: Taking the stage at Climate Week in New York City Wednesday morning, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced his authorization to move forward with linking Washington into its carbon market that’s shared with Quebec, Canada, the next-to-last step in California’s process to complete the merger.  On the same day, Washington state officials completed the rulemak[...]
text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announces his authorization to link Washington state in its carbon market during Climate Week in New York City on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo courtesy of Washington State Department of Ecology)Taking the stage at Climate Week in New York City Wednesday morning, California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced his authorization to move forward with linking Washington into its carbon market that’s shared with Quebec, Canada, the next-to-last step in California’s process to complete the merger. 
On the same day, Washington state officials completed the rulemaking process to allow the linkage. California and Quebec will still need to complete regulatory changes, the final step, before merging can occur.
In June, the three jurisdictions signed a linkage agreement to fully join operations in 2027. Washington hopes that joining the older and well-established carbon market will stabilize prices for businesses, which have swung wildly in recent years on the state’s 5-year-old market.
“By joining forces with our partner in Washington state, we will build a stronger, more durable carbon market that will drive investment, cut pollution and power the clean economy of the future,” Newsom said. 
For more than a decade, California’s carbon market has sought to cut climate pollution by setting a cap on greenhouse gas emissions and requiring major polluters to buy allowances to cover their share of emissions. In 2014, its market linked with Quebec. 
Former Gov. Jay Inslee signed Washington’s carbon market into law in 2021 under the Climate Commitment Act. Since the state’s first auction in 2023, it has raised just over $5 billion in revenue.
A Washington-California-Quebec carbon market will put the same price on greenhouse gas emissions across an economy that ranks as the third largest in the world, said Caroline Halter, communications manager at Washington’s Department of Ecology. 
“Linkage isn’t just good climate policy — it’s smart economics,” said Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson in a press release. “Linking will unlock greater emissions reductions, lower the cost of clean technologies, and create good‑paying jobs in high‑growth industries.”
Both supporters and critics of Washington’s carbon market say that linking would stabilize prices and cut costs for polluters who have navigated an uncertain market with widely fluctuating allowance prices.
Large polluters covered under Washington’s carbon market are required to obtain allowances for each metric ton of greenhouse gases they emit. 
In Washington’s first year of auctions, the highest allowance cost soared to $63 per metric ton of emissions, and the state raised nearly $2 billion in revenue. In 2024, amid the campaign for an initiative to eliminate the Climate Commitment Act, allowance prices dropped dramatically. When that measure failed, the market bounced back. 
In December of 2025 Washington’s allowance prices hit a peak of $70 per ton. During its most recent auction earlier this month, allowances were $39. 
Meanwhile, allowances in the California-Quebec market have been comparatively stable and hover around $30. Its most recent price was $32. 
Newsom added that the linkage would create “more reliable pollution reductions and local investments, no matter what happens in DC,” in a post on X.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Collins, King urge feds to release heating oil supply amid price surge
description: U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King of Maine are calling on the federal government to release reserve heating oil as fuel prices continue to surge while temperatures drop.  In a letter to President Donald Trump Tuesday, the senators urged him to release supply from the ​​Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to “protect Mainers from […]
text:
Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. (Photo by gmnicholas/ Getty Images)U.S. Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King of Maine are calling on the federal government to release reserve heating oil as fuel prices continue to surge while temperatures drop. 
In a letter to President Donald Trump Tuesday, the senators urged him to release supply from the ​​Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to “protect Mainers from the very high prices that are imposing a difficult financial burden.” 
The reserve holds 1 million barrels of ultra low sulfur diesel, designated for heating oil, to protect the Northeast if there is a disruption in the heating oil supply. 
The Maine Department of Energy Resources reported last week that the average statewide price of heating oil was $5.77 per gallon, a 74% increase from this time last year. The department estimated that it will now cost nearly $675 more this year to fill a standard 275-gallon oil tank. 
“As the most heating oil-reliant state in the country, Maine people are particularly exposed to oil market price spikes,” Celina Cunningham, department acting commissioner, said in a press release. “Rising global energy prices driven by conflicts abroad are putting added pressure on households as we head into the winter heating season.”
Everyday increases cost Maine households $4,300 since Trump returned to office

Roughly half of Maine households use heating oil as their primary heating source. That number is down from 70% of households in 2010, according to the department. 
The Natural Resources Council of Maine on Monday released an analysis of heating oil costs, estimating that this winter Maine households will pay an additional $319 million to heat their homes, compared to last year. 
On average, that would mean a household could pay $1,262 more for heating oil this winter. 
In their letter, Collins and King noted that earlier this year the president ordered a release from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and said the “same urgency now applies” to the heating oil reserve. 
They also said the wars in Iran and Ukraine have prevented additional supplies from reaching the global market. 
“Maine is particularly vulnerable to global supply shocks because our state imports much of our home heating oil,” Collins and King wrote. “With both domestic and international supplies running low, a release from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve would help ease these prices.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Warnock urges greater federal oversight of automatic license plate readers
description: U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock is calling for federal guardrails around the use of automatic license plate readers, citing multiple cases of law enforcement misusing the cameras to stalk and harass U.S. citizens. Warnock, a Democrat, is teaming up with U.S. Sen. Katie Britt, an Alabama Republican, to urge the U.S. Department of Justice to issue […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock called for greater federal guidance around the use of automatic license plate readers. Alander Rocha/Georgia RecorderU.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock is calling for federal guardrails around the use of automatic license plate readers, citing multiple cases of law enforcement misusing the cameras to stalk and harass U.S. citizens.
Warnock, a Democrat, is teaming up with U.S. Sen. Katie Britt, an Alabama Republican, to urge the U.S. Department of Justice to issue guidance on the subject. Earlier this week, the two sent a letter to U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche urging the department to issue guidelines for state and local law enforcement and disclose how much federal funding has gone toward purchasing license plate readers. The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
GOP lawmakers call for more oversight of license plate cameras after string of misuses in Georgia

“We are deeply concerned about the misuse of ALPR systems and believe that appropriate safeguards are necessary to protect against unauthorized access and abuse,” the letter states. “We also want to ensure that funding of these technologies is paired with appropriate oversight to ensure that the funding is not used to facilitate such abuse.”
Automatic license plate readers, such as the ones made by Atlanta-based Flock, work by capturing license plate data, along with other information like a car’s make and color, and storing that information in a searchable database. Law enforcement agencies that contract with Flock can use the database to track down stolen vehicles, locate missing people and solve other crimes.
But the cameras have also drawn controversy after a number of law enforcement officials across the country have been found searching the databases for personal uses. According to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation, at least 19 people who work in law enforcement or emergency services have been arrested and charged this year for misusing a state law that restricts use of the cameras to only official law enforcement purposes. 
Flock did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“Right now, there are no federal policies to punish or even track when one of the 140,000 law enforcement officers across the country with access to license plate tracking data misuses that information,” Warnock said in a press conference Wednesday. “Unfortunately, we’ve seen dozens of cases of women being stalked by ex-boyfriends or husbands who have been given unrestrained access as law enforcement officers to this surveillance technology.”
Sen. John Albers. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Last month, two Republican members of the Georgia Senate called for greater oversight over the cameras, with Roswell Republican Sen. John Albers announcing plans to collaborate with law enforcement associations to address misuse of the technology. 
Warnock condemned the lack of national guidance, noting that many municipalities have purchased license plate readers with federal funds. In the absence of clear guidelines, he said, state and local governments are left with a “patchwork system” that undermines public trust in the technology.
“The technology can’t be trusted to manage itself,” he said. “And right now there are no guardrails at all.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Bipartisan bills would allow 17-year-olds in Michigan to receive EMT license with parent permission
description: As Michigan reckons with a shortage of emergency medical personnel, a pair of lawmakers are looking to help grow the number of emergency medical technicians by tweaking the age requirements for an EMT license. Members of the House Health Policy Committee met on Wednesday to consider House Bills 5488 and 5489, introduced by Reps. Angela […]
text:
Getty ImagesAs Michigan reckons with a shortage of emergency medical personnel, a pair of lawmakers are looking to help grow the number of emergency medical technicians by tweaking the age requirements for an EMT license.
Members of the House Health Policy Committee met on Wednesday to consider House Bills 5488 and 5489, introduced by Reps. Angela Witwer (D-Delta Township) and David Prestin (R-Cedar River). If signed into law, the policies would allow 17-year-olds to obtain their EMT or medical first responder license, if a parent signs off on the application. 
Prestin, himself a licensed paramedic, explained that these bills focus on the two entry level licenses for emergency medicine, noting that a first responder can be trained in 60 hours, while an EMT can be trained over the course of a semester.
EMT’s must have a minimum of 32 hours of clinical experience, including direct patient care in hospital emergency departments.
“By the time a student completes an approved EMT program and passes the national registry exam, they have already been exposed profoundly to real life emergencies,” Prestin said. “Community colleges have long provided these programs, and high schools across the state have increasingly embraced them through career and technical education.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Students are generally 17 or 18 when they graduate high school, Prestin noted, with the state’s current rules around licensure forcing some graduates to wait several months before they can begin working in their trained profession.
“For students who, like my younger self, don’t have their heart set on a certain career path and are seeking opportunity, whenever and wherever it appears, these artificial barriers can push them into a different career path and we lose them forever,” Prestin said. “These bills allow graduates to enter the workforce sooner, support both full-time and volunteer ambulance services, and give high school career technical programs a clear pathway to employment.”
For those with concerns about whether 17-year-olds are emotionally ready to work as an EMT, Prestin stressed that the real world experiences students gain through the training programs vet out those who are not ready. 
Additionally, these students will not be driving ambulances, Prestin noted, explaining that drivers must be 18 or 21 depending on the agency, and must undergo additional training in order to drive.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Johnston and Grimes join dozens of cities suing fire truck manufacturers
description: The cities of Johnston and Grimes are joining Des Moines and dozens of other municipalities in suing the some of the nation’s biggest providers of fire trucks over alleged parasitic pricing. Johnston and Grimes, as members of the Johnston-Grimes Metropolitan Fire District, are suing REV Group and more than a dozen of its affiliates in […]
text:
The cities of Johnston and Grimes are joining Des Moines and dozens of other municipalities in suing the some of the nation’s biggest providers of fire trucks. (Stock photo by Perry Gerenday via Getty Images)The cities of Johnston and Grimes are joining Des Moines and dozens of other municipalities in suing the some of the nation’s biggest providers of fire trucks over alleged parasitic pricing.
Johnston and Grimes, as members of the Johnston-Grimes Metropolitan Fire District, are suing REV Group and more than a dozen of its affiliates in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa. Other defendants include American Industrial Partners and its affiliates, Oshkosh Corporation, Pierce Manufacturing and Boise Mobile Equipment.
The lawsuit challenges what it calls “the defendants’ multi-year, anticompetitive schemes to consolidate and ‘roll up’ markets for critical lifesaving apparatuses — fire trucks and the chassis on which they are built — and exclusionary restraints in the markets for replacement parts for their apparatuses.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The lawsuit claims the defendants have methodically acquired industry competitors, as well as key companies in the apparatus supply chain, and that Oshkosh and Pierce have restricted fire departments’ ability to replace parts — all with the intent of lessening competition.
Through these “illegal schemes,” the lawsuit alleges, the defendants have “reaped extraordinary profits on the backs of fire departments, taxpayers, cities, and counties.” This has resulted in Johnston and Grimes paying “substantial overcharges” and reduced  equipment value, the lawsuit claims.
Specifically, that lawsuit claims that in November 2024, the Johnston-Grimes Metropolitan Fire District purchased a Pierce firefighting truck for $1.7 million. In October 2025, the district purchased a Pierce pumper truck for roughly $1 million. Those prices, the lawsuit alleges, include “hundreds of thousands of dollars in anticompetitive overcharges.”
In addition, the lawsuit claims, the defendants have drastically extended the delivery dates for purchased equipment, with Johnston-Grimes’ wait time to receive the pumper purchased in October 2025 now estimated to be more than three years.
The lawsuit claims that beginning in 2008, AIP embarked on a decade-long strategy to consolidate the markets for fire apparatus and chassis manufacturing with its acquisition of E ONE, then one of the largest fire apparatus manufacturers in the United States.
In 2015, AIP allegedly accelerated its consolidation strategy under the REV Group of companies, and acquired Kovatch Mobile Equipment Corp. In 2017, AIP and REV Group acquired Ferrara Fire Apparatus and three years later acquired Spartan Emergency Response.



Quotation







The markets for fire apparatuses, chassis, and Pierce replacement parts are no longer competitive. They are markets dominated by powerful behemoths.


– Lawsuit filed by the cities of Johnston and Grimes


Eventually, the lawsuit asserts, nearly a dozen once-independent companies were rolled into a single corporation, and the REV Group began shutting down manufacturing plants, causing significant price increases as well as product-order backlogs estimated at $4.2 billion in value.
“The markets for fire apparatuses, chassis, and Pierce replacement parts are no longer competitive,” the lawsuit claims. “They are markets dominated by powerful behemoths. These manufacturers bought their way to dominance, and they are now in full extraction mode, deliberately suppressing output, withholding supply, delaying deliveries, restricting competitive options, and charging supra-competitive prices without consequence … Our fire departments do not deserve this. Our firefighters do not deserve this. The taxpayers those firefighters swear an oath to protect do not deserve this. The extraction of excessive private rents from the public must stop, and it must stop now.”
In April, a federal court consolidated the claims of more than 60 cities into a trio of antitrust class action lawsuits to be tried in a Wisconsin court.
In June, the City of Des Moines sued the REV Group, 14 of its affiliates and 11 other companies that produce firefighting trucks, parts and equipment. The claims in that lawsuit are virtually identical to those in the newly filed Johnston-Grimes case.
As part of its lawsuit, Des Moines claims it has ordered firefighting apparatus with a delivery date 42 to 45 months away — although the equipment’s useful life is no more than 10 to 20 years.
The lawsuits filed in Iowa and elsewhere allege private equity has played a pivotal role in the alleged reduction of competition. In 2018, the lawsuits claim, REV Group’s then-CEO Tim Sullivan told investors, “We like backlog, we love backlog.”
The lawsuits seek not only unspecified financial damages to recover money lost to the allegedly illegal anticompetitive actions of the defendants, but also an injunction that would prohibit any such conduct in the future.
In various court filings, the REV Group and other defendants have denied any wrongdoing and asserted the COVID-19 pandemic “prompted skyrocketing demand and disrupted supply chains, causing price increases and longer wait times.”
By some estimates, three manufacturers now control 70-80% of the U.S. fire truck market, and according to the International Association of Fire Fighters, fire engine prices have nearly doubled since 2020, from about $589,000 to more than $1 million.
Last fall, at a U.S. Senate hearing on the consolidation of fire equipment providers, Dennis Rubin, the fire chief in Kansas City, Kansas, told federal lawmakers, “There must come a day of reckoning when the manufacturers of our most important tools are held accountable for runaway pricing and extended delivery times.”
In July, U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, along with Democratic Rep. Becca Balint of Vermont and Republican Rep. Ben Cline of Virginia, filed a resolution directing the Federal Trade Commission to investigate the consolidation in the fire truck manufacturing industry.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Florida sues NY Times over alleged anti-Israel bias; demands internal records
description: The state of Florida filed a shareholder lawsuit Wednesday against The New York Times in a Manhattan state trial court, arguing its coverage of the Israel-Hamas conflict would harm shareholder value for the state’s agencies and public sector retirees. The named plaintiff is the Florida State Board of Administration (SBA), which oversees more than $276 […]
text:
Photo of copy of NY Times on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)The state of Florida filed a shareholder lawsuit Wednesday against The New York Times in a Manhattan state trial court, arguing its coverage of the Israel-Hamas conflict would harm shareholder value for the state’s agencies and public sector retirees.
The named plaintiff is the Florida State Board of Administration (SBA), which oversees more than $276 billion in assets for state and local government entities. Along with the National Center for Public Policy Research, the suit asks a judge to force the Times’ board of directors to hand over internal records pertaining to the paper’s coverage of the events.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, via Department of Legal Affairs
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier said during a press conference in Miami-Dade County that the state was not suing the Times because of a specific news article or editorial discretion, but over corporate governance, saying that as a publicly traded company the newspaper holds “legal responsibilities and duties to your shareholders.”
The Florida SBA invests and administers its assets and owes fiduciary duties to more than 1.2 million members and beneficiaries. It holds 161, 375 shares of Times stock.
A spokesperson for the paper said it would fight the request for internal records.
“This lawsuit has no merit and was brought for an improper purpose,” said Charlie Stadtlander, executive director for media relations and communications for the Times.
“Although it is positioned as a corporate governance petition to inspect the company’s books and records, it is a transparent attempt to exert agenda-driven pressure against an independent media organization, level false allegations of bias and chill journalism protected by the First Amendment. We will defend against the suit vigorously.”

The lawsuit comes about six weeks after the attorney general sent a 28-page letter to Times executives, questioning the accuracy of news articles going back several years, declaring they were “publicly documented failures.”
He requested records showing whether and how the paper’s board of directors have been briefed about specific news stories, most notably a May column by Nicholas Kristof alleging Israel used dogs to rape Palestinian prisoners.
The Times never sent those documents. Attorneys for the paper said on Aug. 21 that the request “does not serve a proper purpose and violates the First Amendment” while constituting “coordinated harassment,” according to the lawsuit.
Records sought
In a press release, the attorney general’s office says that the SBA narrowed its request on Aug. 26 to board-level governance records from 2020 going forward, including:

Any charter provision, escalation protocol, or reporting line by which editorial-standards compliance, journalistic accuracy, corrections practice, or defamation exposure reaches the board or a board committee.
Board and committee agendas and calendars sufficient to show whether those subjects have appeared as agenda items.
Versions of the audit committee charter and the company’s editorial standards, and documents showing who approved them.
The reporting line of the standards editor.

“The company’s repeated publication of materially false or baseless factual assertions, many later admitted internally or disproven externally, supports a reasonable inference that the Board has not only failed in its obligation to monitor the Company’s internal controls, but it has allowed such flagrantly selective application of the internal controls to support the conclusion that in the absence of any Board-level oversight, journalistic standards have been weaponized within the Company to serve the personal agendas of unchecked editors,” the lawsuit says.
As a publicly traded company, Uthmeier said, the Times bears legal duties to its shareholders.
“And we saw some very dangerous trends that appeared to call into credibility the sound business sense of what that company is doing,” he said. “We counted 72 recent errors where the company admitted in its own correction column in a very single coverage area in just eight months.  All pro-Hamas-style reporting that had to be clawed back as incorrect.”
Uthmeier added at one point that the Times had “retracted” the Kristof column, but there are no reports of the paper having done that. On May 21, Kathleen Kingsbury, the opinion editor of the Times, declared that the paper stood by the column.
Whistleblower
The lawsuit relies on information from a whistleblower who raised concerns about the reporting of “many instances of anti-Israel bias.” The suit says the whistleblower on at least 15 occasions raised concerns about broken editorial standards between 2019 and March 2026, when she left the paper.
That whistleblower went on to say that “the staffers who engaged in public advocacy on the war in favor of Palestine, which she reported through the same channels, received, so far as she is aware, no such request to edit or delete their support,” the lawsuit says.
The lawsuit also notes the Times last month suffered its first defamation lawsuit loss in more than 50 years. That’s when the U.S. District Court for the Northern Division of Alabama awarded $9.25 million dollars to a former University of Alabama basketball player named Kai Spears, because the paper had mistakenly placed him as a passenger in a car that was at the scene of a shooting death.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Colorado River stewardship begins in often dry tributaries like Little Badger Wash
description: Diné writer Alastair Lee Bitsóí considers a tributary that runs through his land amid unprecedented September monsoons in New Mexico, and how stewardship for the Colorado River begins with such arroyos.
text:
Protecting tributaries like the Little Badger Wash on his land is part of the larger stewardship of the Colorado River, Alastair Lee Bitsóí (Diné) writes. (Photo courtesy Alastair Lee Bitsóí)Between the September monsoon storms, I waited for a clear stretch of weather before walking into the dry wash that runs through our farm in Naschitti, Navajo Nation, New Mexico. On my daily task to achieve 10,000 steps, I followed it toward the foothills of the Chooshgai Mountains with a question in mind: Where does the water — tó — that floods my cornfield begin?
I was only beginning to explore the wash’s headwaters, which begins on top of the nearly 9,000-foot Chooshgai Mountains. Walking upstream from my 11-acre farm, Near The Water Farms, also meant walking toward dormant farms shaped by a harder history. Colonization in part disrupted Diné relationships to land, while economic pressures and land disputes have left farms in my family’s clan territory dormant. Not just my family, but other families across the Navajo Nation, too. Following the ditch channel made me think about what it would take to care for those farms and grow food there again. This valley could be a place where Indigenous food crops grow in abundance once again.  
Monsoon flooding across the Navajo Nation this season has taken lives, cost damage and shown the possibility of bringing farmland back into food production, the author writes. (Photo courtesy Alastair Lee Bitsóí)
My family’s farm sits below dry channels that can appear empty for much of the year. This summer, floodwater reached the field a historic 10 times between July and September. In an ordinary monsoon season, we might see two or three floods along it. Ten flood events is insane. They bent corn, reshaped the ground and damaged our fence that needed immediate repair from livestock interference. Still, white, yellow and blue Diné corn stands among squash, watermelons, a Hopi sunflower and wild tea. Drought-tolerant Four Corners spuds, an 11,000-year-old food species, have been reintroduced and naturally growing here again. An October harvest lies ahead before the first frost comes.
I asked my mother, who is Tó’áhaní (Near The Water People), whether she remembered a summer like this. She did not. 
The latest storms had cut Little Badger Wash deeper. Pools of water remained along its path, with green forage grasses growing nearby and through the dormant farms. Standing there between storms, I could see that this was not an empty ditch. The water had changed the land, and the land was responding.
When the monsoon arrives, the wash carries more than water. It can carry waste dumped in its channel, along with the sediment it moves across the land. At our farm, I watch where the water spreads and what it leaves behind as I learn how to grow food here again. Waste like a plastic chair from the mountains or an illegal trash dump stop by my farm once the floods recede. Sometimes it is big logs, manure from livestock or pine cones and needles. 
Writing this piece from my car at the farm, I called my dad to ask what locals call the wash in Diné Bizaad (in the Navajo tongue). He told me, it is known as Nahashch’id Yázh – Little Badger Wash. In fact, Naschitti, geographically as a community, is known as Nahashch’idí or “Badger Springs.”  



Quotation







We need to reconnect with arroyos as allies, not treat them as waste dumps.


My family’s knowledge of the land and virtual maps on my iPhone help me trace the drainage downstream. Three earthen dams attempt to interrupt its flow, including a water basin in my cornfield. From there, it connects to Chaco Wash just east of Naschitti, the San Juan River near Shiprock and, ultimately, the Colorado River at Lake Powell. We talk about the Colorado River’s low flows as if the solutions begin at the big dams, or create new rules by the Bureau of Reclamation for reservoirs along its 1,450-mile path. But here in the San Juan Basin of the Navajo Nation, I am seeing what it means to care for the water before it reaches the river: reconnecting with the arroyos that bring moisture and sediment to our land, and giving our food systems a chance to grow again.
KQRE Chief Meteorologist Grant Tosterud estimated that nearly three trillion gallons of rain fell across New Mexico over seven days, from Sept. 13 to 19. That statewide figure is difficult to picture, but it also is not because of the number of floods I recorded on my iPhone. I can picture the water that came through Little Badger Wash: where it spread across the cornfield, tore through the fence and left sediment behind. It is also just out of habit to document to share with the Bureau of Indian Affairs that my farm is active and beneficially used to prevent any threat of revocation of the legal farm permit. This new week, Tosterud estimates more heavy flooding across the state at least through Thursday.
The floods across the Navajo Nation have since caused damage including the unfortunate drownings of three lives, washed out roads, and water and power outages, but they have also shown the possibility of bringing dormant farmland back into food production with water harvesting methods. Little Badger Wash is part of that work. Its water and sediment shape the field where our crops are growing, particularly as climate and drought tolerant seeds. The waste carried through a channel like this matters, too. What is left in an arroyo does not simply disappear when it dries.
We need to reconnect with arroyos as allies, not treat them as waste dumps. That shift begins with local people caring for the channels, observing where water flows and having resources to clean up waste and repair flood damage. It can help protect local surface water and the land through which water may reach groundwater. It also belongs in the broader work of caring for the Colorado River Basin and the communities downstream.
For the Navajo Nation, that work is an exercise of sovereignty. People who know these washes and farm along them should help decide how they are protected and how water supports local food systems. A river basin map can show where Little Badger Wash leads. It cannot show the work of bringing a field back into production, or the knowledge gained by watching ten floods pass through it.
Now, with flood watches across much of New Mexico, I will stay out of Little Badger Wash. A dry arroyo can fill quickly, even when rain is falling upstream rather than overhead. No walk or photograph is worth entering a channel when flooding is possible. Caring for these waterways begins with respecting their power, and recognizing what they make possible. And the teaching of Indigenous Peoples of New Mexico that Water Is Life.

name: National
title: More Americans lose SNAP as Congress weighs food stamps’ future
description: Tens of thousands of Americans continue to lose access to food assistance each month, even as Congress debates slowing down major cuts to federal food stamps. New data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture shows more than 330,000 Americans lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, between May and June, the latest […]
text:
A sign noting the acceptance of electronic benefit transfer cards for food aid is displayed at a grocery store in California. New data shows millions of Americans have lost food stamps since the passage of a major law last year. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Tens of thousands of Americans continue to lose access to food assistance each month, even as Congress debates slowing down major cuts to federal food stamps.
New data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture shows more than 330,000 Americans lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, between May and June, the latest numbers available. 
More than 5 million people have lost food stamps since the enactment last July of the One Big Beautiful BIll Act, which cut taxes and federal safety net programs. The law changed SNAP eligibility rules, ended certain work requirement exemptions and shifted new costs to states that administer the federal program.
An analysis by the anti-hunger nonprofit Food Research and Action Center shows SNAP participation has decreased since the new law in every state except Alaska. State leaders there cited unique geographic and economic conditions, including higher food prices and high seasonal unemployment specific to Alaska. 
SNAP cuts could lead to kids losing free school breakfast and lunch

In Arizona, SNAP participation dropped by more than half since July 2025, with about 421,000 people receiving assistance this June, the center’s data shows. Louisiana’s enrollment dropped by more than 173,000 — a decrease of about 22%. Participation in Illinois dropped by more than 368,000 — a drop of about 20%.
Those numbers come as advocates pressure Congress to reverse the SNAP cuts they say will exacerbate growing hunger across the country as grocery prices continue to soar.
While nonprofits and many local, state and federal political leaders have pushed for a complete rescission of those cuts, Republicans in control of Congress have so far only signed off on delaying some of their impact.
For months, the Senate has been debating details of the farm bill, a major piece of legislation that funds SNAP, farm subsidies and rural development programs. Earlier this month, the Republican-led Senate Agriculture Committee approved on party lines a farm bill proposal that would delay for one year impending SNAP cost shifts to states. Democrats had pushed for a two-year extension.
That legislation awaits debate by the full Senate before the current legislation’s Sept. 30 expiration.
Last year’s tax and spending law requires states to cover more of SNAP’s administrative costs, and beginning in fall 2027, states for the first time will fund some benefits themselves. The new law will penalize states depending on their payment error rates — a technical calculation by the feds of SNAP overpayments and underpayments, not fraud. That change could cost states billions of dollars, raising fears about the future of the program. 
If the version of the farm bill that advanced this month is passed, states would have until October 2028 to lower their error rates before they are required to shoulder part of the costs. 
Citing a hunger ‘crisis,’ US mayors call for end to federal SNAP cuts

Aside from coming up with the funds, states will likely need to implement new IT and budgeting processes. Historically, SNAP benefits were not a budget line item for states because federal funds flowed directly to recipients’ benefit cards, Lauren Kallins, a senior legislative director for the National Conference of State Legislatures, told lawmakers in July. 
“There are lots of questions about how and when the cost share will be paid,” Kallins said. “Will this be in real time as benefits are issued? Will it be reconciled at a later date? We don’t know.”
Republicans, including Arkansas U.S. Sen. John Boozman who leads the agriculture committee, have argued that error rates are evidence that improvements are needed in state administration of the program.
Anti-hunger advocacy groups say the one-year delay is insufficient to protect states and people relying on SNAP.
“We urge Senators to speak out against this flawed Farm Bill and to stop it from advancing to the floor for a vote,” Crystal FitzSimons, president of the Food Research and Action Center, said in a statement last week. “Congress must use any other legislative vehicle to reverse the SNAP cuts and address the cost shifts to states to provide meaningful assistance to both families and farmers.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Ex-Capitol Police officers on trial on manslaughter charge
description: Special Assistant Attorney General Luke Williamson and Assistant Attorney General Brandon Ogburn talk during a break in the trial of Steven Frederick Jr. and Michael Lamar Rhinewalt, who are charged with manslaughter in the 2022 death of Jaylen Lewis.
text:
The trial began Wednesday for two former Capitol Police officers charged with manslaughter in the shooting death of a 25-year-old Jackson man.
Steven Frederick Jr. and Michael Lamar Rhinewalt, who are both white, were part of the crime suppression Flex Unit of the Capitol Police involved in the death of a Black man, Jaylen Lewis, on Sept. 25, 2022.
According to the indictment, the men said one of them shot Lewis because it “was necessary to protect himself from great bodily harm or death at the hands of Lewis,” but the indictment concluded that was “not a reasonable belief under the circumstances.”
Frederick, the son-in-law of Rankin County Sheriff Bryan Bailey, and Rhinewalt have pleaded not guilty to the criminal charge.
At the time of the fatal shooting, Frederick and Rhinewalt were conducting a drug narcotics operation when they saw a white Jeep Grand Cherokee turn north on West Street in Jackson driven by Lewis, who had a female passenger.
After the officers saw the Cherokee run a red light at Stonewall Street, they turned on their police lights and pulled Lewis over and blocked him from going forward with his car.
Lewis wound up reversing his car and bumping into the police cruiser behind his vehicle. 
Jaylen Lewis Credit: Courtesy of Arkela Lewis
“Jaylen does not brandish a weapon, reach for a weapon, make any violent gestures, threaten anyone, or take any other actions that could be reasonably perceived as endangering officers or others,” according to a lawsuit filed by Lewis’ mother, Arkela.
After this, Frederick and Rhinewalt opened fire into the Cherokee, shooting Lewis in the head and killing him, according to the lawsuit. 
But the former officers have maintained they faced harm from Lewis. “Officers fired into the vehicle to stop Lewis from harming or killing them or others, because Lewis was driving the vehicle toward the officers,” wrote J. Scott Gilbert, a Jackson lawyer representing Rhinewalt.
In his opening statement to the jury, Special Assistant Attorney General Luke Williamson said Lewis’ death was “not a justified killing. It was not self-defense. We will ask that you find the defendants guilty of manslaughter.”
Jackson lawyer Merrida Coxwell Jr. told the jury — made up of nine Black jurors and three white jurors — that officers blocked Lewis in with their car and called on him to show his hands. “Suddenly and without warning, Jaylen Lewis slammed into the back of the police car behind and came right at the officers,” he said.
In response to the 707-horsepower engine Cherokee heading toward them, Coxwell said Rhinewalt shot Lewis in self-defense.
In Lewis’ car, officers found Glock pistols, an assault weapon and bags of marijuana, Coxwell said. “We’re not trying to paint a negative picture, but it’s the truth.”
Lewis decided to run “probably because of the drugs and weapons,” Coxwell said. “That’s never a safe thing to do with officers standing in front of you.”
Lt. Kevin Swinney of Capitol Police testified that he was present when the shooting took place. He said he didn’t see where Frederick and Rhinewalt were standing when they fired their guns.
Asked if the officers had done anything that fell outside police practice, Swinney replied no.
If there had been, Gilbert asked, “you would have reported it, right?”
Swinney responded yes. “I ain’t going to jail for nobody.”
Capt. Dennis Weaver of the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation testified that the passenger in Lewis’ vehicle, Selena Hayes, told agents that she yelled out, “Stop, stop, stop” when Lewis tried to speed off.
“As best you could tell, he (Frederick) was telling the truth?” Coxwell asked.
Weaver replied yes.
Arkela Lewis, bottom right, mother of Jaylen Lewis, who was shot to death during an encounter with officers of the Mississippi Capitol Police department, testifies before members of the Jackson delegation of the Mississippi Legislature at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson, Monday, March 6, 2023. Lewis was one of several witnesses who spoke against a bill that would increase state involvement in the Hinds County court system and expand the jurisdiction of Capitol Police inside the city of Jackson. The hearing drew a large number of spectators. (AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis)
Lewis’ mother said hearing all the justifications for killing her son angers her. Any time an officer kills someone, “it’s always self-defense,” she said. “It’s something I have already been prepared for.”
She’s not optimistic the officers will be convicted, she said. “I’ve been praying and leaving it in God’s hands. That’s all I can do.”
In 2022, the state Legislature expanded the jurisdiction of Capitol Police beyond the state Capitol in Jackson. Within that year, officers shot at least four people.
A month before Lewis was killed, Rhinewalt and former Flex Unit officer Jeffery Walker opened fire on a car, striking a passenger in the head. That victim, Sherita Harris, was taken to the hospital where she had surgery to remove bullet fragments from her head. She survived but now has “permanent neurological and facial injuries,” according to her lawsuit.
A grand jury indicted Rhinewalt and Walker for aggravated assault in that case. According to the lawsuit, no weapon was recovered from the car.
Walker also faces federal charges for allegedly violating the civil rights of a handcuffed man by slamming his head into the hood of a car and kicking him in the head and face in July 2022. 
Earlier this year, he pleaded guilty to the charge. He is now seeking to withdraw that plea, claiming ineffective assistance of counsel, according to court documents.
On March 12, 2023, Frederick totaled his Capitol Police Ford F-150 on U.S. 49 South in Covington County. He flunked the DUI field test with a .15 score, nearly twice the legal limit of .08. He was handcuffed and arrested. He was released without bond into Bailey’s custody.
Steven Frederick with two unidentified state troopers on March 12, 2023, in Covington County.  Credit: Courtesy: of the Mississippi Highway Patrol
Five months later, Frederick dodged conviction when a state trooper failed to appear for the court hearing, and the judge dismissed the DUI charge.
Frederick resigned three days after the wreck “to prevent termination,” according to his certification records. He had worked for Capitol Police less than eight months and paid nothing toward the cost of the Ford F-150 he totaled.
A year and a half after Frederick demolished his Capitol Police truck, he wrecked another patrol vehicle, this time as a deputy for Scott County. Bailey picked up Frederick before the arrival of a state trooper, who interviewed Frederick at the hospital. The Rankin County Sheriff’s Department released a statement that Bailey responded to the accident as a Scott County deputy.
In September 2025, Lewis’ mother filed a federal lawsuit against the Capitol Police officers who shot him to death in 2022, accusing them of “willful, reckless and malicious conduct.” 
The lawsuit also accuses the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, which oversees the Capitol Police, of permitting “officers who have engaged in excessive force or unreasonable violence toward citizens to avoid the consequences of discipline.”
The Mississippi Department of Public Safety denied the litigation’s claims, saying there is no proof the agency did anything that was “the moving force behind the alleged injuries to Plaintiff.”
U.S. District Judge Kristi H. Johnson has since dismissed the department from the case, which remains pending against the former officers. They have asked for the lawsuit to be dismissed. 
This is a developing story.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Democrats propose revamped consumer protection, digital safety laws
description: New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, state Rep. Linda Serrato (D-Santa Fe) and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland on Wednesday announced their plans to modernize the state’s consumer protection law and to craft new regulations for kids on the internet. Their proposed bills would increase the maximum penalties for consumer protection violations[...]
text:
Left to right: state Rep. Linda Serrato (D-Santa Fe), New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland, on Sept. 23, 2026, announce plans to modernize the state’s consumer protection law and to create an Online Safety and Accountability Act in the 2027 legislative session. (Joshua Bowling/Source NM)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, state Rep. Linda Serrato (D-Santa Fe) and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland on Wednesday announced their plans to modernize the state’s consumer protection law and to craft new regulations for kids on the internet.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
They said they intend to introduce a bill during next year’s legislative session called the Consumer Protection and Fair Pricing Act that would update the penalties and regulations under the state’s decades-old consumer protection law. A proposed Online Safety and Accountability Act would more closely regulate online content aimed at children, in particular.
Torrez has invoked the late-1960s Unfair Practices Act when suing the social media giant Meta and retailers he’s accused of marketing vaping products to underage youth. The state Legislature last updated the consumer protection law in 1970, Torrez said, setting a maximum penalty of $5,000 per violation of the law.
Earlier this year, a Santa Fe jury ordered Meta to pay the state $375 million in damages after Torrez’s New Mexico Department of Justice argued the company had misled the public regarding child exploitation and adverse mental health effects. If the maximum penalty had been adjusted for inflation, Torrez said at a Wednesday Albuquerque news conference, that judgment would have been around $3 billion.
“The penalty that we have, while meaningful and important…is simply not enough on its own to change behavior at the corporate level,” he told reporters. “New Mexico needs to update its penalties to match the scale of the harm and match the scale of the resources that are brought to bear by these companies.”
Torrez said he hopes to see the Legislature take up a bill that establishes tiered penalties depending on the level of harm. The proposed bill would increase penalties to $50,000 per violation, and could increase further when companies target children, people with disabilities or people under a guardianship.
Torrez and Serrato, the Santa Fe Democrat who said she plans to sponsor the legislation, said the bill would also update the consumer protection law to account for modern technology. It would more closely regulate “personalized pricing,” the practice by which companies use artificial intelligence to offer differing prices on goods and services depending on who the customer is.
It would also ban “manipulative” design elements, such as a ticking clock on an online shopping cart.
And, Haaland said, the law would take the step of prohibiting landlords from using AI to “rent fix” by giving different rates to different prospective tenants.
She cited a range of issues, “from digital price tags that can raise prices on shoppers in real time to subscription services that make it nearly impossible to cancel to corporate landlords using AI to coordinate and drive rents higher and higher,” as areas the legislation would meaningfully address.
Serrato also said she’d sponsor legislation to create an Online Safety and Accountability Act, which would specifically focus on digital content aimed at children, including AI companion chatbots and “addictive design features.” It would mandate safety precautions for young users, such as requiring developers to disclose that AI programs do not “represent or mimic” how real people act.
It would also require that developers make products with youth-specific features, including a chronological feed; a two-hour daily default; silenced notifications overnight and during school hours; and automatic blocks on profiles that exhibit sexual extortion or grooming behaviors. 
Under the law, AI chatbots could not sexualize minors, pose as licensed professionals or discourage minors from seeking behavioral healthcare. A new Office of the Online Safety Monitor within the New Mexico Department of Justice would be responsible for investigating potential violations, which could carry penalties up to $150,000 for repeat offenders.
Serrato cited her recent work in calling on the state Public Education Department to work more closely with parents after it implemented a controversial AI program in classrooms across the state.
“In so many ways, New Mexicans are unprotected,” Serrato said. “Our data is out there and we are flailing in this system that our federal government has no protections for.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Public intoxication charge dismissed against Oklahoma secretary of state
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A misdemeanor charge of public intoxication against Oklahoma’s secretary of state has been dismissed with costs, the City of Edmond said Wednesday. A dismissal notice states Benjamin Michael Lepak is “verifiably engaged in services more appropriate than those provided through the (municipal) Court,” city spokesperson Emily Ward said.  Oklahom[...]
text:
Oklahoma Secretary of State Benjamin Michael Lepak attends a news conference announcing details of the Fiscal Year 2027 state budget on April 1 at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A misdemeanor charge of public intoxication against Oklahoma’s secretary of state has been dismissed with costs, the City of Edmond said Wednesday.
A dismissal notice states Benjamin Michael Lepak is “verifiably engaged in services more appropriate than those provided through the (municipal) Court,” city spokesperson Emily Ward said. 
Oklahoma Voice filed an open records request Wednesday seeking a copy of the dismissal notice, but the city had not yet provided it as of publication. Ward said she had no further details beyond what is in the notice.
Lepak, 42, said Wednesday he had no comment on the services or the dismissal. He said he did not know how much he paid in court costs.
City records show Lepak would have owed $280 on the date of his arraignment, which had been scheduled for Thursday.
He was arrested and booked into the Edmond city jail the night of Aug. 14 on a complaint of public intoxication. Police officers were called to a McDonald’s at 10:45 p.m. where Lepak was standing outside.
Benjamin Lepak (Photo provided by the Edmond Police Department)
Lepak had “extremely slurred speech,” the odor of alcohol on his breath and was unable to maintain a coherent train of thought while answering questions, according to a police report of the arrest. He told police he had arrived from a church gathering, and though he initially denied consuming alcohol, he later said he had a beer but didn’t finish it, the arresting officer reported.
His vehicle was parked at the restaurant, and “it was apparent that Lepak drove to the location,” the report states. He was not charged with driving under the influence.
Lepak has faced alcohol-related charges twice before, records show.
Edmond police arrested him in 2022 on a public intoxication complaint after finding Lepak’s car stopped on East Danforth Road with a damaged front tire, according to a police report.
The officer discovered Lepak had slurred speech and swayed where he stood, the report states. Lepak told the officer someone had run him off the road and he swerved to avoid them. He said he was almost home from a “work thing” where he drank a beer, according to the report.
Municipal court records show Lepak pleaded no contest to the 2022 charge.
In 2021, he pleaded guilty in Oklahoma County District Court to misdemeanor charges of having actual physical control of a vehicle while intoxicated and transporting an open container of beer, according to court records. 
He received a one-year deferred sentence, probation and a six-month requirement to have an interlock device installed in his vehicle, records show.
A police officer in The Village had found him asleep behind the wheel of a pickup truck parked by the side of Plymouth Lane, records show. He failed both a field sobriety test and a breathalyzer test, according to the officer’s report.
Gov. Kevin Stitt appointed Lepak as secretary of state in October 2025. He previously served as Stitt’s general counsel.
Senior reporter Barbara Hoberock contributed to this report.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Supreme Court hears appeal of school library ‘explicit sexual material’ law
description: The Missouri Supreme Court is weighing whether a 2022 law making it a crime for school employees to provide students with “explicit sexual material” violates constitutional free speech protections.  The law, which a Jackson County Circuit Court judge struck down last November, “sowed great confusion across Missouri school districts” and spurred school librar[...]
text:
The Missouri Supreme Court heard oral arguments Wednesday debating whether a state law criminalizing school librarians who stock "explicit sexual content" violates their free speech rights (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).The Missouri Supreme Court is weighing whether a 2022 law making it a crime for school employees to provide students with “explicit sexual material” violates constitutional free speech protections. 
The law, which a Jackson County Circuit Court judge struck down last November, “sowed great confusion across Missouri school districts” and spurred school librarians to remove books from shelves when it was passed, attorneys representing the Missouri Association of School Librarians and Missouri Library Association wrote in their brief.
In oral arguments Wednesday morning, much of the discussion focused on a decades-old U.S. Supreme Court precedent that determines what content can be considered obscenity — which is outside the bounds of what the First Amendment protects as free speech rights.
The three-pronged Miller Test used to determine whether material is obscene considers whether content as a whole appeals to a “prurient,” or lewd, interest and depicts sexual conduct in a “patently offensive way” based on “contemporary community standards.” Obscenity restrictions must also consider if the entire book or other work lacks literary, artistic, political or scientific value.
The language approved by lawmakers in 2022 restricts explicit sexual material, with exceptions for “works of art, when taken as a whole, that have serious artistic significance, or works of anthropological significance, or materials used in science courses.”
The Missouri Attorney General’s Office contends that the law falls within constitutional limits, asking the judges to overturn the circuit court’s decision and allow the case to go to trial. But David Thoreson, an attorney representing the librarians, told the judges that the law sweeps much more broadly than obscenity restrictions and therefore is unconstitutional.
“Any time that a state legislature or Congress decides to depart from that standard, or jettison any part of it, or substantively modify any part of it, it is playing with constitutional fire and very likely to get burned,” he said.
Judges zeroed in on the differences between the law and the controlling precedent Wednesday. Judge Mary Russell asked how the law addresses the first prong of the Miller test, which considers whether the material as a whole appeals to a prurient interest.
“It appears the statute completely omits that first standard,” she said, adding that there is no mention of community standards.
Since the law concerns material given to minors, Deputy Solicitor General Graham Miller responded, the requirement to consider the work as a whole is not applicable.
“Minors possess a more restrictive right to judge and determine for themselves what sexual material they may read or see,” he said. “They don’t have the ability to judge the work in relation to its whole as compared to a normal adult, so the determination is made under community standards.”
His answer opened up additional questions. The law overlaps with an existing statute that criminalizes “furnishing pornographic material to a minor.”
A first offense under the existing law, like an offense under the 2022 school library law, is a Class A misdemeanor. But the key difference is how the two laws define prohibited material. The existing law bars “pornographic material to a minor,” which is defined using a near verbatim copy of the Miller Test.
The Missouri Supreme Court, pictured during a separate set of oral arguments Sept. 2, heard debate Wednesday on a law that pulled “hundreds of books” off of school library shelves (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Chief Justice W. Brent Powell asked why the 2022 law didn’t adopt the same definition.
“The state is allowed to have overlapping criminal statutes,” Miller said. “Just because the state has criminalized the distribution of pornographic materials to minors, it doesn’t mean it cannot again criminalize the distribution of pornographic materials to minors in the school setting.”
“So do you think it is just banning the same material?” Powell asked.
“Correct,” Miller said.
When the law was passed, schools interpreted it to be broader than the existing restrictions. Attorneys for the librarians wrote in their brief that hundreds of books were removed from the shelves.
“Ultimately, (the law) resulted in the widespread removal of books previously deemed appropriate solely to avoid the possibility of criminal prosecution,” they wrote.
The state argues those removals were unnecessary, writing in its filing that the law only criminalizes books that are obscene and in violation of the existing law.
“There is no avalanche of banned books which exist outside these categories,” the state’s attorneys wrote.
The attorney general’s brief included pictures from three books with sexual content that were in high school libraries. This caught Russell’s attention.
“Are those actually on the shelves at our public school libraries?” she asked Thoreson.
Those books were some of those removed from libraries, he said, adding the books do not meet the definition of obscenity.
The images are “mere components of single scenes in multifaceted narratives with richly developed characters in which sex is merely an element in some storylines,” librarians’ brief states.
“The fact that the state appears to believe it must be removed” and schools’ decisions to stop distributing the books are proof that the law is too vague, Thoreson said.
 School-sponsored speech

Even if the court finds that the law’s definition goes beyond just barring obscenity, judges could still conclude that it does not violate constitutional free speech protections.
A second tier of the state’s argument claims that the law falls under government or school-sponsored speech and does not restrict private speech.
“Government officials have no right to use official powers for their own expressive activities,“ Miller said Wednesday. “Librarians selecting or removing books from a library is not conveying their own message, but is rather conveying the school’s message,” 
He cited an 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals decision from April that found that schools have a “legitimate pedagogical interest in prohibiting speech involving sexual content” when considering a similar law in Iowa.
Missouri’s law differs from Iowa’s in a couple ways. Missouri’s law carries criminal penalties, while Iowa’s is limited to professional consequences, like written warnings and license suspensions.
Iowa’s law is also confined to public schools, whereas Missouri’s applies to “public or private elementary or secondary schools.”
Judge Ginger Gooch asked about this distinction, saying the state is “asking the court to construe it in a way to only have the statute apply to public school settings, even though it goes beyond that.”
If the law only bars obscenity, this piece does not matter, Miller responded. He also suggested removing the language including private schools and allowing the law to move forward only for public schools.
“Severing the private schools would be in accordance with the legislature’s wishes in this case,” he said. “Then at that point, the government speech or the school-sponsored speech doctrines would apply.”
A piece of the debate not covered Wednesday but included in attorney’s briefs is whether the law could restrict school employees outside their work at school.
The state argues that the law is limited to school staff’s work on school grounds, pointing to the statute’s language applying to those “affiliated with a public or private elementary or secondary school in an official capacity.”
But the librarians’ counsel argued that, grammatically, the phrase “in an official capacity” applies to those impacted by the law but doesn’t limit its bounds to when a school official provides the material.
“The second clause defining the prohibited conduct contains no time or place limitations whatsoever,” the attorneys wrote.
The court did not immediately issue its decision Wednesday.

title: Kansas school superintendent charged; community ‘resilient in working through the chaos’
description: TOPEKA — Former Ness County school superintendent Jeff Jones has been charged with 19 felonies and misdemeanors, including multiple financial crimes and two felonies involving a minor.  Jones, superintendent of USD 106 in south-central Kansas, was arrested in August. Official charges filed Friday range from theft valued between $25,000 and $100,000 to misuse[...]
text:
Former USD 106 superintendent Jeff M. Jones has been charged with 19 felonies and misdemeanors, mostly financial crimes. (Booking photo from Ness County Sheriff) TOPEKA — Former Ness County school superintendent Jeff Jones has been charged with 19 felonies and misdemeanors, including multiple financial crimes and two felonies involving a minor. 
Jones, superintendent of USD 106 in south-central Kansas, was arrested in August. Official charges filed Friday range from theft valued between $25,000 and $100,000 to misuse of public funds and making or participating in prohibited contracts. 
The two charges involving a minor are aggravated intimidation of a witness or victim and contributing to a child’s misconduct or deprivation.
The second charge means to “unlawfully, feloniously, and knowingly” encourage a child to commit an act that, if committed by an adult, would be a felony, according to the charges filed in Ness County District Court.  
Details of the case haven’t been released. Ness County Sheriff Brandon Mitchell wrote in an email that an investigation was opened after a USD 106 school board meeting where an allegation of potential misuse of school funds or equipment was made. 
“Situations like this are especially difficult where students, teachers and neighbors often have longstanding relationships,” Mitchell said. “My primary concern is making sure the investigation is handled professionally and fairly while protecting the integrity of the case and all the people involved.”
Mitchell said students and staff in the school district have been “extremely resilient in working through the chaos.”
He said moving forward for the community doesn’t mean ignoring what happened. 
“It means acknowledging the seriousness of the situation, supporting the USD 106, and continuing to work together to make sure our students and staff have a safe environment to teach and learn,” Mitchell said.
At an Aug. 14 special meeting of the school board, member Brent Schreiber made a motion to terminate Jones’ employment, according to board minutes. The motion failed after receiving no second.
Board member Lowell Foos made a motion to accept Jones’ resignation as high school golf head coach, co-high school Scholar’s Bowl sponsor and summer weights supplemental contracts, effective immediately, and resignation as high school boys head basketball coach at the end of the 2026-2027 season, the minutes said.
At a second special meeting Aug. 18, Jones was placed on administrative leave. At subsequent meetings, according to minutes, the board removed Jones’ name from a bank account and appointed Cherie Nicholson to serve as interim superintendent through Dec. 31. 
In a phone call, Nicholson said Jones no longer works for the district. 
The charges filed against Jones include: 

Interference with the judicial process
Making false information
Unlawful acts concerning computers
Official misconduct
Interference with law enforcement
Presenting a false claim
Misuse of public funds
Four counts of making or participating in prohibited contracts

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Gov. Armstrong announces new department to streamline North Dakota workforce efforts
description: Gov. Kelly Armstrong announced Wednesday the creation of the Department of Workforce Development to streamline workforce programs under one roof. The department will combine staff and resources from the Department of Commerce’s Workforce Development Division and Job Service North Dakota; the Department of Public Instruction’s adult education program; and the[...]
text:
Gov. Kelly Armstrong, left, speaks next to Workforce Development Commissioner Katie Ralston Howe during the 2026 Governor's Workforce Summit at Bismarck State College on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Gov. Kelly Armstrong announced Wednesday the creation of the Department of Workforce Development to streamline workforce programs under one roof.
The department will combine staff and resources from the Department of Commerce’s Workforce Development Division and Job Service North Dakota; the Department of Public Instruction’s adult education program; and the Department of Health and Human Service’s vocational rehabilitation program and Office of Refugee Resettlement.
“One of the things we recognize is we need to better align the systems that North Dakota already has,” Armstrong said during the Governor’s Workforce Summit at Bismarck State College. “I think right now, anybody who is honest about it knows it’s too fragmented.”
The workforce environment is rapidly changing, he said, and the new department will be able to operate with the “speed and urgency” necessary to keep up with those changes.
The first commissioner of the new department will be Katie Ralston Howe, who serves as deputy commissioner of the Department of Commerce and director of the department’s workforce development division.
“The work starts today, and we are working with these partners starting now to build a framework for this agency,” Ralston Howe said.
She added a recent workforce ecosystem study the agency conducted with stakeholders last year led to the discussions that formed the new department.
“What we heard from that is that the system would benefit from a unified strategy and a single entry point,” Ralston Howe said.
North Dakota farmers increasingly rely on foreign labor

Armstrong said he plans to ask state lawmakers to formalize the agency during the 2027 legislative session.
“The people that are looking for work in those legislators’ communities are going to like this,” he said. “We can do some of this without the Legislature, but we really are going to need their help to get it set up the way where it will work the best.”
The combined agency is expected to operate with about 300 total staff members. Armstrong said he doesn’t anticipate any new hiring because staff are going to be moving from positions within other state agencies.
North Dakota’s unemployment rate reached 2.2% in August, second lowest in the nation behind South Dakota’s 2% rate, according to a preliminary report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The preliminary unemployment rate for August in the United States was 4.1%.
Armstrong said consolidating workforce programs under one agency will create a “front door” for all of the state’s workforce initiatives.
“If you are really busy, you don’t have time to negotiate seven different drop down tabs on nine different websites, trying to figure out how all of that works,” he said.
The state launched a new website called the North Dakota Workforce Information Network for job seekers, employers and other partners in support of the state agency.

text:
Children's Hospital Colorado is pictured on June 23, 2026, at the Anschutz Medical Campus in Aurora, Colorado. (Photo by Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)A Denver judge shut down a motion for contempt against Children’s Hospital Colorado that alleged it was not in compliance with an order that required the hospital to reinstate gender-affirming care for minors. 
Children’s Hospital Colorado stopped offering gender-affirming care to minors in January due to threats from the Trump administration. Four families sued Children’s Hospital after it initially stopped offering care to their children. The families are referred to by pseudonyms in the lawsuit due to safety concerns.
The Colorado Supreme Court ruled in May that the hospital violated the state’s anti-discrimination law when it stopped offering care like puberty blockers and hormone therapy to transgender patients under 18 but continued offering it to cisgender children for some hormonal conditions. The hospital has never provided gender-affirming surgeries for minors.
