The state’s highest court directed a lower court to issue a preliminary injunction against the hospital. The lower court in June issued the injunction, which required Children’s Hospital to resume gender-affirming care for patients under 18.
Denver District Court Judge Ericka Englert ruled Tuesday that the hospital complied with her order when it reinstated gender-affirming care into its scope of services. Her order did not instruct the hospital to provide medical gender-affirming care. Rather, it ordered the hospital to stop refusing to offer the care, which it did, she said. 
The doctors who offer care through the TRUE Center for Gender Diversity, after consulting their own legal counsel, independently refused to prescribe medications given federal threats to their ability to further practice medicine. TRUE Center doctors are employed by the University of Colorado’s School of Medicine, not Children’s Hospital, and are independent contractors through the hospital.



Quotation







This is an extremely difficult and emotional time for our clients and they are thankful for those who have shown support as we continue this fight to protect their rights.


– Paula Greisen, attorney for families that sued Children's Hospital Colorado


Still, the hospital’s actions complied with the order, and it cannot demand that medical providers prescribe any specific treatment, the hospital’s attorneys argued. Englert cited the Supreme Court’s ruling, which also said the hospital cannot force providers to prescribe gender-affirming care. 
“CHC did what the Court ordered: it stopped refusing to provide medically necessary gender affirming care,” Englert wrote. “CHC’s scope of services returned to the status quo, as requested by Plaintiffs.”
The providers are not parties in the court case and are not agents of Children’s Hospital, meaning they are not bound by her injunction, Englert said. Providers testified that the hospital had no influence on their decision to stop offering care. She said the hospital could face liability from providers and patients if it tried to control a medical provider’s professional judgment.
Families still unable to access care
In a statement, a spokesperson for Children’s Hospital said it appreciates the judge’s recognition that it has fully complied with all court orders. 
“Throughout this process, we have maintained that the hospital reinstated medical gender-affirming care for minors within our scope of services and that we have acted in accordance with our legal obligations,” the statement says. “We remain focused on complying with the law and serving the patients and families who rely on our care.”
Plaintiffs filed a motion for contempt at the end of June since patients are still unable to access care. Attorneys for the plaintiff families and the hospital laid out their arguments on the contempt charge over a three-day hearing earlier this month. Plaintiffs argued the hospital has a responsibility to ensure patients are actually able to receive gender-affirming care, while the hospital said it cannot control or interfere with a healthcare provider’s individual medical decisions. 
Paula Greisen, attorney for the plaintiffs, said she is disappointed that the hospital “continues to refuse to provide necessary medical care to transgender adolescents.” She said Colorado law that protects the right to healthcare cannot depend on a patient’s race, religion or gender identity. 
“Allowing the erosion of these laws for anyone, especially the most vulnerable, is a stain on our community,” Greisen said in a statement. “This is an extremely difficult and emotional time for our clients and they are thankful for those who have shown support as we continue this fight to protect their rights.”
A December declaration from U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy threatened to pull Medicaid and other federal funding from any facility that provided gender-affirming care to minors. Colorado joined several other Democratic-led states in suing over that policy, and an Oregon judge ruled the declaration was unlawful in March. 
While Colorado has shield laws that protect gender-affirming care providers and patients from criminal prosecution and subpoenas by other states, those protections don’t extend to the federal government, which has also threatened healthcare providers who prescribe gender-affirming medication. Colorado also passed a law that prohibits insurance plans from limiting or denying gender-affirming care that a doctor identifies as medically necessary.
A jury trial for the families’ lawsuit against Children’s Hospital is scheduled for early January.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Budget outline offers glimpse into potential price of adding trial work for state public defender
description: It could cost up to $697,000 a year for South Dakota’s state-level public defender to begin taking on trial-level cases in the state, an advisory committee heard on Wednesday. The Office of Indigent Legal Services opened in 2024 with the hiring of a director, and expanded the following year to add four additional attorneys and […]
text:
An equal justice statue stands outside the doors of the Minnehaha County Courthouse in Sioux Falls. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)It could cost up to $697,000 a year for South Dakota’s state-level public defender to begin taking on trial-level cases in the state, an advisory committee heard on Wednesday.
The Office of Indigent Legal Services opened in 2024 with the hiring of a director, and expanded the following year to add four additional attorneys and a paralegal. At the moment, the office handles appeals in criminal and abuse and neglect cases.
South Dakota was among the last states in the U.S. to saddle counties with the entire cost of providing lawyers to people who can’t afford one but are constitutionally entitled to representation in court. Counties remain responsible for trial-level legal fees, but handing off appeals to the state is expected to save them $2.1 million a year.

Chris Miles, South Dakota’s chief public defender. (Courtesy of Chris Miles)
 

Adding five more lawyers would allow the state office to begin taking on “resource-intensive” felony cases in counties that lack the funds or qualified attorneys needed to guarantee a fair trial to indigent defendants, according to Christopher Miles, the state’s public defender.
“This would be less of an overhaul of the system and more of us picking up some of the overflow,” Miles said Wednesday during a virtual meeting of the Commission on Indigent Legal Services, which has overseen the rollout of state-level public defense operations.
Trial-level staffing would add between $627,000 and $697,000 to the office’s current budget of $1.45 million a year, but Miles told commissioners the proposal is “not necessarily something” he’d propose to the Legislature in the 2027 session.
“The primary purpose is to put the information out there and get some feedback from some other stakeholders in terms of what we’d want in an expansion,” Miles said.
Joe Kippley, vice-chair of the commission, told Miles that the budget rough draft is a good start, but recommended refining it to give lawmakers a sense of how much pressure a state-level staff of five public defenders would relieve for counties. 
“You have to take this and quantify it in terms of the number of cases covered,” Kippley said.
The office would also need a framework for deciding which cases to accept, said commission member Larry Long, a former attorney general who retired as a circuit court judge. The attorney general’s office in South Dakota regularly steps in to assist in smaller counties with high-profile or time-intensive criminal investigations, Long said, but “a judge can’t appoint them” to prosecute a case the way judges appoint public defenders.
“At some point in time you need to have the ability to say no,” Long said. “I’m not sure how you want to do that or want to structure that, but there’ll come a point in time when you run out of money. And maybe for that reason, or maybe there is another series of reasons, you would want to say no.”
That’s part of the discussion, Miles said, noting that budget constraints would likely play a role. If the issue were more about workload for a trial team, Miles said, the office could look at contracting with trusted private attorneys.
Caseload increasing, staff needs
There are two more immediate staffing issues lawmakers could be asked to address in 2027, Miles said: another appellate attorney and a legal office assistant.
State public defenders deliver their first oral arguments to South Dakota Supreme Court

The office currently has 125 open appeal files, spread across 109 clients. About 25 of those are in the briefing phase, meaning the office’s attorneys are working through legal arguments at the state Supreme Court level. 
This summer saw a “flurry of cases,” Miles said.
“This is maybe the first time our attorneys are having some time crunch issues, having to think about what briefs to prioritize,” Miles said.
Another appellate attorney might be necessary, but Miles said the legal office assistant position would be the lightest lift as a budget request.
The office has five attorneys and one paralegal at the moment, and Miles said the office spends 95% of its personnel budget to fund those positions. 
The office is authorized to hire a legal office assistant, but hasn’t done so.
“Right now, it would be a salary that is just simply not appealing to anybody that’s looking to get into the workforce,” Miles said. “So if we are able to increase that ever so slightly — it would not need to be a big bump — that would give us enough room to fill that position.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: State asks Missouri Supreme Court to block award of 13 marijuana licenses
description: The Missouri Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday challenging an appeals court’s decision in March directing the state to award cannabis company Hippos LLC 13 facility licenses after finding the 2019 application scoring process was inconsistent. It’s been five years since the Missouri Administrative Hearing Commission denied Hippos’ appeal over its applic[...]
text:
In March — just weeks before the appellate judges’ unanimous ruling in favor of Hippos — Missouri State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick issued a scathing state audit of the Division of Cannabis Regulation (Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current).The Missouri Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday challenging an appeals court’s decision in March directing the state to award cannabis company Hippos LLC 13 facility licenses after finding the 2019 application scoring process was inconsistent.
It’s been five years since the Missouri Administrative Hearing Commission denied Hippos’ appeal over its applications for marijuana facility licenses, after the company argued identical applications received different scores from the same grader. 
That dispute has since worked its way through the state court system and landed Wednesday before the seven Missouri Supreme Court judges.
At issue is whether the commission acted properly when it rescored Hippos’ applications by selecting the most common score given to answers the company was challenging — or whether that approach was “completely flawed,” as three appellate judges found in March, because the grader left no notes explaining the scores.
The Missouri Department of Health and Senior Services, which oversees the state’s cannabis regulatory agency, argued Wednesday that the commission acted correctly and did a thorough investigation of the scores given to Hippos’ applications. The department also urged the court to focus on the commission’s decision and not to rehash the state’s controversial grading process of marijuana applications as part of the case.
“The Administrative Hearing Commission’s decision is under review here, not the department’s initial decision,” said Sean McDowell, an assistant attorney general representing the state.
However, Chief Justice W. Brent Powell challenged that distinction, saying state law requires the court to combine “how the agency acted” and the commission’s decision.
“Isn’t that how the statute indicates we should review this?” Powell asked McDowell.
McDowell agreed, saying the commission “steps into the shoes” of the department, conducts a review and “their decision becomes the agency decision.”
Audit finds flawed scoring cast ‘shadow’ over Missouri medical marijuana licensing

In March — just weeks before the appellate judges’ unanimous ruling in favor of Hippos — Missouri State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick issued a scathing state audit of the Division of Cannabis Regulation. The audit examined, among other issues, the state’s 2019 marijuana facility licensing process, citing erratic scoring, poor documentation and a process so opaque it cast doubt on the integrity of the results.
When the state was working in 2019 to build the framework of Missouri’s now multi-billion dollar industry, it hired Nevada-based company Wise Health Solutions to score the nearly 2,000 applications. 
“In each of Hippos’ applications, there were many instances in which identical answers to the same question received inconsistent scores,” wrote Missouri Court of Appeals Southern District Judge Jeffrey Bates in the March ruling. “That should never have occurred if Wise’s scorers had followed the instructions that they were given. Neither the department nor Wise did anything to correct this situation.”
The three appellate judges found the commission’s approach to rescoring was flawed “because there are no notes explaining why the scores were given,” the ruling states. 
“The conflict in these unexplained scores cannot be reconciled by simply assuming the more common score for a particular answer is the correct one,” it states.
Fitzpatrick’s audit found scorers were instructed by Wise Health Solutions to take limited notes while scoring applications in order to reduce the amount of documentation that could be produced in litigation. 
The appellate judges agreed with Hippos that the commission’s decisions affirming the state’s denial of the company’s applications were “arbitrary, capricious and unreasonable, and these decisions were not supported by competent and substantial evidence on the whole record.” 
McDowell argued Wednesday that the commission’s rescoring was valid because Hippos didn’t successfully “disprove the validity of the original scores.”
Two witnesses for Hippos testified that the applications should have received higher scores, and the appellate judges noted that the state did not present experts to rebut their testimony.
However, McDowell said the witnesses were cross-examined and one admitted that her interpretation of the grading system could be different than the graders. 
“It’s clear from the record the department contradicted Hippos’ expert witnesses,” McDowell said.
Hippos’ attorney Austin Preston argued Wednesday that “simply asking cross-examination questions” wasn’t enough to rebut the witnesses’ testimony, and that the commission was required to make a finding about whether the witnesses’ information was credible or not. 
Supreme Court Judge Zel Fischer pressed Preston on that argument.
 “When cases are tried to the trial court, we do it all the time,” he said. “The assumption is that all facts not specifically found were found in accordance with the judgment. Are you suggesting that the administrative context provides a different presumption?” 
Preston said he believes case law requires it. 
The judges asked if Hippos is asking the judges to remand the case back to the Administrative Hearing Commission or to make a finding themselves. 
“I’m asking this court to make findings as to the proper score for each of these applications, which has been laid out, would satisfy the minimum cutoff and order those licenses be issued,” Preston said.
McDowell responded that if the judges believe additional fact-finding is necessary, the case should go back to the commission.
“I think the proper remedy would probably be to remand to the Administrative Hearing Commission,” he said, “because they were the fact finder in this case.”
The court did not issue a ruling Wednesday.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska minimum wage will increase next year by 29 cents less than voters called for
description: LINCOLN — Legislative changes this year to annual bumps in Nebraska’s minimum wage mean workers’ increase next year will be 29 cents less than what voters approved in 2022. New data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released this month indicates a 3.6% annual rise in the Consumer Price Index for goods and services […]
text:
State Sen. Jane Raybould of Lincoln, center, talks with state Sens. Paul Strommen of Sidney and Kathleen Kauth of Omaha on May 28, 2025. Raybould sponsored a measure to slow down voter-approved minimum wage increases while Strommen sponsored a measure to water down voter-approved paid sick leave. Kauth chairs the Legislature's Business and Labor Committee that considered both bills. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Legislative changes this year to annual bumps in Nebraska’s minimum wage mean workers’ increase next year will be 29 cents less than what voters approved in 2022.
New data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics released this month indicates a 3.6% annual rise in the Consumer Price Index for goods and services between August 2025 and August 2026 for the Midwest region. That’s the indicator voters approved to calculate minimum wage bumps beginning in 2027, after Nebraska’s minimum wage hit $15 this year. 
Lawmakers this spring instead locked the annual increase at 1.75%.
State Sen. Jane Raybould of Lincoln talks with state Sen. Stan Clouse of Kearney before debate on her priority bill to amend voter-approved annual increases to the state’s minimum wage. March 31, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Over the past 25 years, inflation for the Midwest averaged 2.4% and was at or below 1.75% 11 times, as low as -1.8% between 2008 and 2009 and as high as 8.1% between 2021 and 2022, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics for the Midwest. Average inflation for the past five years was 4.1%, while over the past 10 years, it was 3.2%.
State Sen. Jane Raybould of Lincoln, who led the changes in Legislative Bill 258, and Sen. Stan Clouse of Kearney, who pushed for a consistent increase, said predictability was key. The bill passed 33-16, with Raybould, a Democrat, joining 32 of 33 Republicans in support of her bill.
Raybould’s law also created a “youth minimum wage,” allowing employers to pay teens ages 14 or 15 a lower wage, $13.50 hourly, beginning July 19.
Predictability was key consideration
Clouse said he always felt CPI was the wrong indicator because it fluctuates. In 2025, he said,  the debate should have been what the annual increase should be, not other issues.
State Sen. Stan Clouse of Kearney, center, leans back in his chair after voting against advancing a bill to alter voter-approved annual increases in the state’s minimum wage on April 1, 2025. Since that debate, he and the sponsor, state Sen. Jane Raybould of Lincoln, worked on a “compromise” to flip his vote to support. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“I’ve talked with numerous small businesses about the negative impact minimum wage is having and I think we see a negative impact on youth employment as well,” Clouse said in a text Tuesday. “It is just one topic of the myriad of issues facing us all right now, and it does present challenges from many views and opinions.”
Raybould said businesses have told her that no matter the economic circumstances, businesses want to budget and plan for the future. She said minimum-wage increases often have the largest negative impact on those who often have the hardest time finding employment, including those out of the job market for a while, young people and people with disabilities.
“I think that is clearly something that is unintended,” Raybould said.
‘Short-sighted decision’
But others, such as state Sen. Terrell McKinney of Omaha, a sponsor of the 2022 ballot measure that raised the state minimum wage from $9 to $15 this year, and which put in place the cost-of-living increases after, said the latest data proved why the Legislature was wrong.
“It was a short-sighted decision not for the people but for corporations and larger entities,” McKinney said Monday. “It wasn’t thoughtful about what’s actually going on in society, especially with an affordability crisis going on.”
State Sen. Terrell McKinney of Omaha, center, greets Gov. Jim Pillen ahead of the governor’s annual State of the State Address to the Legislature. Jan. 15, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln, who led opposition to Raybould’s measure, said the nation faces a “clear affordability crisis” that seems to worsen almost every month. She said when voters decided in 2022 whether to increase the minimum wage, they “smartly” tied increases to non-arbitrary, Midwest-specific factors.
“To have a cynical Legislature come in and undercut the will of the people so that working Nebraskans can’t keep their head above water against basic inflationary factors that are beyond their control, it just exacerbates this affordability crisis,” Conrad said.
She said lawmakers had heard “countless examples” of economic challenges facing Nebraskans but that the latest inflation figure is “much more negative and much more dramatic.”
“That’s real money for hundreds of thousands of minimum-wage workers,” Conrad said.
Legal battles continue
Under the legislative changes, Nebraska’s minimum wage will increase to $15.26 on Jan. 1, which is annual pay, before taxes, of $31,746, assuming 2,080 work hours in a year at 40 hours each week and no overtime. 
The voter-approved 2022 law would have increased the wage statewide to $15.55, with increases rounded up to the nearest 5 cents. Annually, that equates to $32,344, a difference of $598 between the two wages.



While Raybould achieved her legislative win after four years of trying, the fight barreled on in Omaha and Lincoln, Nebraska’s two most populous cities. This summer, city leaders in both cities passed local ordinances seeking to reinstate the 2022 law for cost-of-living increases, as well as prohibit the new lower wage based on age.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers leads a news conference at the Nebraska State Capitol on Sept. 14, 2026, detailing recent historic stops by the State Patrol. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers sued to block both ordinances, arguing they are a “matter of statewide concern” and that despite city charters, city leaders overstepped. Raybould and state Sen. Beau Ballard of Lincoln had requested Hilgers opine on the constitutionality of such ordinances.
Lancaster County District Judge Lori Maret blocked the Lincoln ordinance before it took effect in mid-July. Douglas County District Judge Timothy Burns has not yet ruled on the Omaha ordinance, which is set to take effect Oct. 1.
‘False sense of security’
State Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, who chairs the Legislature’s Business and Labor Committee, said the purpose was in part to allow slower minimum wage bumps and give businesses more time to absorb it. Kauth said that when the minimum wage increases, it leads other wages to increase, too, leading to wage compression or increased consumer costs.
State Sen. Kathleen Kauth of the Millard area. March 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
“A state or government-mandated increase in the minimum wage does nothing more than give you a false sense of security for about six months, and then all of a sudden all of those costs are going to catch up,” Kauth said.
She said the solution is for workers to ask their employers what they can do to earn a wage, get more skills or find a different job, rather than the government changing the baseline pay.
Of the minimum wage ordinance fights in Lincoln and Omaha, Kauth said it echoes what she called a “socialism push” nationwide. She said if the ordinances stand, it could lead employers to fire workers and expect more of employees, risking burnout, or to look toward automation.
Of the 16 senators who opposed Raybould’s law, McKinney led 15 in a letter supporting the Omaha ordinance. The lone exception was state Sen. Dave Wordekemper of Fremont, a Republican. 
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln, center, talks with state Sens. Carolyn Bosn of Lincoln, Kathleen Kauth of Omaha and Brad vonGillern of the Elkhorn area, from left. April 8, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Conrad said she appreciated city leaders for “standing in their power” and said it’s “undeniable” that residents in Omaha and Lincoln face higher costs of living than other parts of the state. She said voters should hold “cynical, out-of-touch politicians” accountable for their actions.
“I hope he (Hilgers) steps forward to voluntarily dismiss his frivolous political litigation,” Conrad said.
Raybould reiterated her concerns that the minimum wage increases have had detrimental effects on youth employment rates. She said policymakers will be watching whether the “youth” wage helps.
“Teenage youth being employed does help with family expenditures, particularly on things like clothing and entertainment, et cetera, and some save for their future education,” Raybould said. “But it’s sort of a moot point when young people are not getting employed.”

title: Nebraska US Sen. Pete Ricketts asks Trump to push China to buy more ag goods
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts sent a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, urging the Trump administration to push China for more market access for U.S. agricultural products and ensure it upholds existing commitments.
text:
Photos of a farmer-owned wind farm near Petersburg, Nebraska, in Boone County. (Courtesy of Nebraska Farmers Union)LINCOLN — Nebraska U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts sent a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, urging the Trump administration to push China for more market access for U.S. agricultural products and ensure it upholds existing commitments. 
Chinese leader Xi Jinping is in the U.S. this week to meet with President Donald Trump for a three-day summit. Issues including AI, trade and Taiwan will likely be top of mind for the two world leaders. Ricketts’ letter comes as China hasn’t met its May pledge to buy more American agricultural products. 
“While American producers have spent decades building markets in Communist China, they continue to face unfair trading practices and uncertainty from Beijing,” Ricketts’ letter reads. “The bilateral discussions provide another opportunity to make progress on restoring market access for American beef. Nebraska farmers and ranchers can compete with anyone in the world when given fair and reliable access to foreign markets.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Trump administration announced in May that China has agreed to buy at least $17 billion a year of U.S. farm goods through 2028, with the target prorated for 2026, according to The New York Times. The same report said that in the first seven months of 2026, China bought only $3.9 billion of U.S. agricultural products, excluding soybeans, according to the most recent USDA data.
Ricketts mentioned the “deal” between the Trump Administration and Beijing in the letter, saying, “It made notable progress toward restoring market access for U.S. beef, but there is still work to be done.” 
“Communist China restored some market access by renewing licenses they allowed to expire for more than 400 U.S. beef facilities,” Ricketts wrote. “Many facilities are still suspended. Under the Phase One agreement, Beijing agreed to accept food meeting international standards and provide a clear path towards resolution if a particular exporter demonstrated a pattern of failing to meet standards.” 
While a breakthrough is not expected during the three-day visit, Greer has said that the U.S. and China are still working through a trade truce extension, according to Bloomberg. The two countries entered a truce from trade escalations last year. The truce is set to expire in November. 
“More work remains, and I am committed to working with you to give our farmers and ranchers a stable, level playing field to compete and win on,” Ricketts wrote. 
Trade has been an issue in the senator’s heated race against registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn, who has criticized Trump’s trade wars as having hurt Nebraska farmers. He said he prefers more strategic tariffs rather than “blanket” tariffs.
Ricketts has defended the widespread tariffs imposed under the Trump administration, saying they help level the playing field between the U.S. and other nations. He said he wants to keep using tariffs to protect Nebraska agriculture. Osborn used Trump’s plan to import foreign beef in a new ad as he tries to make inroads with rural voters. 
Ricketts also has spoken out against the plan to import foreign beef. The Ricketts campaign said in a statement to Politico that the former governor has a record of standing for his state’s agriculture community “no matter who is president — from fighting Biden’s 30×30 plan to opposing this beef import plan.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nunn introduces bill to suspend Trump’s beef imports, bolster U.S. herd
description: U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn is calling for the suspension of President Donald Trump’s initiative allowing more foreign beef into the U.S. and for congressional oversight of future beef import decisions from the executive branch. Nunn announced a bipartisan bill Wednesday, with Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico, aimed at increasing domestic beef and lowering[...]
text:
A bipartisan bill would reverse a presidential decision to allow more foreign beef into the U.S. (Photo by Lance Cheung/USDA)U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn is calling for the suspension of President Donald Trump’s initiative allowing more foreign beef into the U.S. and for congressional oversight of future beef import decisions from the executive branch.
Nunn announced a bipartisan bill Wednesday, with Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez of New Mexico, aimed at increasing domestic beef and lowering consumer prices of the protein. 
The Banning External Entry of Foreign Beef, or BEEF Act, would also create a Beef Import and Domestic Supply Advisory Board, that would be tasked with developing a strategy for rebuilding the U.S. beef herd which has declined significantly in recent years. 
“Lowering beef prices for Iowa families and supporting our cattle producers should go hand-in-hand,” Nunn said in a news release. “If we want more affordable beef for the long term, we need more American beef being raised and produced here at home.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The bill follows a move from the Trump administration to suspend tariffs for 90 days to allow up to 300,000 metric tons of imported ground beef into the country, saying it would help lower the cost at the grocery store. 
Under the bill, this action from the president, and “any successor or substantially similar proclamation” would be null unless approved by Congress. 
“Cattlegrowers in New Mexico and across the nation have made it clear – they want to reverse the President’s foreign beef imports and they need more time, and more tools, to grow their herds and fix the domestic supply chain,” Vasquez said in the release. 
Growing domestic herd 
Shortly after the president’s announcement to import ground beef, the U.S. Department of Agriculture launched a “Ranchers First Initiative” with tools to support heifer retention, build up grazing land, revitalize local processing facilities, support new ranchers and prioritize U.S. raised beef in government food budgets. 
USDA said the plan would help to rebuild the U.S. cattle herd which it said is currently at a 75-year low. 
The beef advisory board that would be initiated under the BEEF Act, would “complement” the recent USDA initiative, according to the news release, by coalescing cattle producers, processors and industry experts as an advisory board to consult with the department and Congress. 
Per the bill text, the advisory board would be tasked with developing a plan to rebuild the U.S. cattle herd, increase domestic beef production, cut red tape for U.S. ranchers and keep beef affordable for consumers.
While the cattle herd has been shrinking with drought and consolidated markets, the price of ground beef has been on a steep increase since 2023. U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data show the price of ground chuck has not dropped below $6 per pound since April 2025. As of August, the average price was $6.77 per pound. 
A group of U.S. lawmakers, including Nunn, previously wrote a letter to Trump, urging him to consult with cattle producers and stakeholders before making policy changes that impact the industry.
“Our bipartisan bill puts producers at the table to develop a long-term plan to increase our domestic beef supply, while giving Congress a say before future decisions are made to expand foreign imports,” Nunn said. 
Nunn, a Republican, is facing a competitive race for reelection in Iowa’s 3rd District against Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott that national political forecasters have rated as a “toss-up.” It’s the second time in just over a week that Nunn has publicly broken with Trump — he was one of seven Republicans who supported a war powers resolution Sept. 16 that would require congressional approval for further military action in Iran.
Calls for Trump to hold China to ag deals
As Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House this week, agricultural groups have urged the president to hold China to trade agreements, particularly agreements to purchase U.S. soybeans. 
The American Soybean Association and National Sorghum Producers sent letters to the president urging trade negotiations to remove China’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural goods and to strengthen commitments to purchase agreements.
Previous meetings between the presidents have resulted in annual purchase agreements of U.S. soybeans and other agricultural products. A meeting last October resulted in a Chinese commitment to purchase 25 million metric tons of U.S. soybeans in 2026, 2027 and 2028. 
American Soybean Association President Scott Metzger said soybean producers need “consistency and predictability” in the Chinese export market. 
“That means ensuring China fulfills its purchase commitments, addressing barriers that put U.S. soybeans at a competitive disadvantage, and working toward a durable trading relationship,” Metzger said in a statement. 
In the letter, the association estimates China has ordered 15.5 million metric tons so far this season.
Nunn also called for Trump to use his “leverage” in the trade meetings with Xi to “demand real results for Iowa farmers and American workers.” 
In May, the White House announced that China had agreed to purchase an additional $17 billion in agricultural products, annually, over the same time frame as the soybean deal. USDA data from July show 2026 Chinese purchases of U.S. agricultural products, excluding soybeans, was less than $4 billion. 
“I pushed the administration to secure China’s commitment to reopen its market to American soybeans earlier this year, and that was an important win for Iowa farmers,” Nunn said in a statement. “But it’s clear we can’t take Beijing at its word. Any new trade agreement should be enforceable and open markets for American products without giving China more leverage over our farmers, manufacturers, or national security.”
Trump’s meetings with Xi are expected to begin Thursday.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel speaks during a Center for American Progress forum on the 2026 Midterm Elections on Sept. 23, 2026. (Screenshot)Federal threats to election processes in states where President Donald Trump lost in previous elections are top of mind for law enforcement officials and the clerks who run elections in Michigan’s 83 counties, Attorney General Dana Nessel said Wednesday during a voter forum held in Washington, D.C.
Nessel was one of the featured panelists during the Center for American Progress’ 2026 midterm elections presentation, which also included fellow Democrats Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and California Attorney General Rob Bonta. 
The forum centered on the preparations that officials in California, Maine and Michigan have made for the worst case scenarios of the upcoming November general election, and what assurances the states could offer voters that elections will run smoothly.
The Trump administration, aside from demanding state voter rolls and efforts to curtail vote by mail rules, have not ruled out the placement of federal monitors, law enforcement and even U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents at polling places to investigate alleged voting irregularities or immigration violations involving people who appear at polling places.
Nessel and Bonta have been allied in pushing back against the administration through various joint lawsuits, including President Donald Trump’s posturing on voting matters and election integrity, while Bellows has also dealt with threats and election denialism.
Nessel said Michigan is ready for threats against election officials
On the threats of federal agents showing up to Michigan polling places, Nessel said that her state was a sort of “ground zero” for Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election. She recalled emergency phone calls she had with her partners at the federal level and with Democratic attorneys general across the nation, discussing the “bizarre” circumstances that were occurring in real time.
Recording allegedly captures Trump pressuring Wayne Co. canvassers to reject 2020 election results

Among the 2020 actions Nessel mentioned were Trump pressuring Republican members of the Wayne County Board of Canvassers to reject election results; the state’s Senate majority leader and the House speaker being flown to the Oval Office for meetings with the president; Rudy Giuliani showing up in Michigan to host an election integrity hearing, later lampooned by Saturday Night Live, and the case of the alleged false electors for Trump, who were prosecuted but saw their charges dropped in connection with the president’s attempts to overturn the results.
“The list really goes on and on,” Nessel said. “I will say there’s nothing that I don’t think this president will try to do in his effort to keep majorities in the House of Representatives and in the Senate. I think Michigan will be at the heart of this again, but we’re kind of old hats at this now.”
Nessel emphasized that Michigan has decentralized election processes, run by each of the state’s 83 county clerks and thousands of local clerks across its cities, townships and villages. Still, Nessel said conspiracy theories about election officials persist. 
“Whenever I hear that there’s some sort of conspiracy, I just don’t know how that would ever work,” Nessel said. “But I will say that I feel really bad for our local clerks who … feel under threat.”
Clerks, Nessel said, also face harassment, including “swatting” and “doxing,” in which false emergency reports or the release of personal information can put officials at risk. Former U.S. Department of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, who lives in Michigan with his husband and children, was a victim of one of the most recent high-profile swatting events.
Nessel said her team set up a hate crimes and terrorism unit when she took office in 2019, and that unit has been at the forefront of investigations of threats to public officials and their families.
Other preparations have included advice to local law enforcement, stationing attorney general office agents in case there is a criminal incident or voting threat at polling locations, and making sure its assistant attorneys are prepared to do the same.
“We have briefs that we’ve prepared for virtually every set of circumstance we could think of, except the zombie apocalypse,” Nessel said. “I don’t have that down yet.”
Panelists speak during the Center for American Progress’ 2026 Midterm Elections forum. From left to right: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows and Ben Hovland, a senior fellow with Center for American Progress; former chair, U.S. Election Assistance Commission. Sept. 23, 2026. (Screenshot)
The breakdown of federal agencies tasked with voter protections is troubling, Nessel said
On Trump’s politicization of the U.S. Department of Justice, and his threats to use the agency to undermine confidence in voting, Nessel said it has been hard to watch her key federal allies be broken down in such a way.
“We’ve had federal monitors who have shown up at our elections every other year for as long as I can remember. But they’re usually there for the purpose of ensuring that no one is losing their right to vote, that voters are not being suppressed,” Nessel said. “Even though, for the purposes of the primary, we had monitors there, but they didn’t do anything wrong, they didn’t do anything illegal, they didn’t do anything differently than what they usually do. Now, in my mind, is this pre-litigation? Are they going to use that to manufacture something and to say, ‘ah, I saw this in the city of Detroit; I saw this in Lansing.’?”
Nessel said there is a very real scenario where federal actors could be poised to violate federal law, or at least have a willingness to do so, by tampering with state elections through brute force.
“Which, of course, is deeply concerning,” Nessel said. “But my hope is that at the end of the day, you have these people, they’ve sworn to take an oath, and that they will follow the law. … If you are going to do something illegal at the behest of a president who is 80 years old, and can only be expected to be in office another couple years, there’s a lengthy statute of limitations for any crimes that a federal agent might commit in the event that they violate a court order.”
Ballot cast by noncitizen in Michigan triggers an investigation, felony charges

Threats to voter confidence in Michigan’s elections was as big a threat, Nessel said, as federal agents potentially roughing up voter lines or smashing through the door. That’s why Nessel’s team in Michigan have also been focused on battling misinformation when they find it.
That was especially true regarding stories about noncitizen voting, which she said Republicans have weaponized in attempts to make residents feel like the system was rigged against them in favor of those who have no legal right to vote in the first place.
Nessel said the legal deterrents in place have helped curtail incidents of noncitizen voting, even as her office had attempted to prosecute a Chinese national who voted in 2024 but skipped the country and ultimately avoided state prosecution.
“We’re seeing people candidly who are trying to test the system, and the encouragement is, ‘If you are a noncitizen, why don’t you see if you can vote?’” Nessel said. “Well, we are catching people if they try to do that, and those people are getting prosecuted. And for any of the noncitizen voters, they’re getting deported.”
Echo chambers are driving the biggest wedge on confidence in elections
That said, the stories of noncitizens voting in Michigan elections — whether real or fabricated for social media outrage — have been difficult to combat, Nessel said. 
The attorney general said that’s why her team, as well as attorneys general in other states, have been reviewing election irregularities, which have shown that noncitizen voting is a rare occurrence.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Again, in the handful of cases where you had noncitizen voters who were able to cast a ballot, those people got prosecuted,” she said. “There are real consequences for those people.”
Nessel said there are also conspiratorial messages coming from federal agencies sowing mistrust in elections, and that her team has to push back against those claims to debunk them on behalf of the state’s voters. The best thing she can do, however, is to just show people “what the truth is and what has actually happened, versus what they’re hearing.”
“The problem is we’re in different echo chambers, and the media that I pay attention to might not be the media that people are watching, where they’re receiving this just flagrantly false information,” Nessel said. “So all we can do is try our best to combat that, and for people to understand again, who’s administering the election? It’s your local clerk that you elected. … She’s not trying to undermine the election.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Florida couple put on probation for submitting fake petition signatures for No Labels Kansas
description: wo Florida residents serving probation for felony crime of submitting fake petition signatures to help establish No Labels Kansas as a political party.
text:
The basic "vote here" sign directs Kansans to a polling center in Johnson County for the Aug. 4, 2026, primary election for local, state and federal candidates and a proposed Kansas constitutional amendment to require election of Kansas Supreme Court justices. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — The second of two Florida residents convicted of submitting bogus signatures on petitions to establish No Labels Kansas as an official political party has been ordered to serve 18 months on probation.
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, who is running for reelection against Democrat Chris Mann, said George Edward Andrews was found guilty of election forgery and perjury for his part in a 2023 petition drive that legitimized No Labels Kansas. The resolution of his case in Johnson County District Court followed that of accomplice Jamie Louise Johnson, also of Dade City, Florida. She was placed on probation for 18 months.
Originally, Andrews was arrested on 30 criminal counts, and Johnson was taken into custody in Nebraska on 19 criminal counts.
No Labels Kansas was approved by Secretary of State Scott Schwab as a political party in good standing in 2024 after party organizers presented petition signatures equal to 2% of total votes cast in the state’s gubernatorial general election in 2022. A portion of those signatures were forged.
Under Kansas law, a petition circulator may be criminally liable for falsely declaring they witnessed the signing of an election petition or aided the placement of forged names on a petition.
“Kansas law requires petition circulators to tell the truth under oath and to collect only genuine signatures of qualified electors,” Kobach said. “These defendants did neither. They submitted false affidavits and put other people’s names on official election petitions.”
In May, leadership of No Labels Kansas requested termination of the party’s recognition in Kansas, and Schwab agreed to do so. That converted the voter registration of about 7,000 party members to independent status.
In a bizarre episode, David Miller, a former chairman of the Kansas Republican Party, and Kris Van Meteren, owner of a Kansas political marketing firm, unsuccessfully tried to assume control of No Labels Kansas.
Kobach said the criminal case demonstrated the state’s commitment to prosecuting individuals who violated laws designed to maintain election integrity.
Andrews, 32, and Johnson, 49, entered guilty pleas in district court to one count of election perjury and two counts of election forgery. Both worked as petition circulators in Kansas and admitted to individually forging signatures of two people on the No Labels Kansas petition.
Andrews was sentenced Wednesday, while Johnson was sentenced in March. Their controlling penalty was 14 months in state prison on the nonperson felonies, but that was suspended by the judge for a punishment of probation.
Schwab, who will leave the office of secretary of state in January, said the Kansas offices of attorney general and secretary of state worked collaboratively on the case to advance a policy of “zero tolerance for election crime.”
Meanwhile, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement said in 2024 that Johnson and Andrews were arrested and accused of petition fraud in Sumter, Hernando, Pasco and Pinellas counties in Florida. While working as paid petition collectors, Florida law enforcement officials said, Johnson and Andrews allegedly submitted 133 invalid petitions on a state constitutional amendment.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Opponent alleges US Rep. Ezell violated campaign finance laws. Ezell camp calls it a ‘political stunt’
description: Jackson County Sheriff Mike Ezell, who is running for Congress, talks to a supporter during a campaign press conference at the Great Southern Club in Gulfport, Miss., on Thursday, June 9, 2022. (Hannah Ruhoff/The Sun Herald via AP)
text:
Carl Boyanton, an independent candidate running for the 4th Congressional District, filed a complaint with the Federal Election Commission alleging his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Mike Ezell, accepted more money from campaign donors than the law allows. 
Boyanton, a business owner, filed the report against Ezell in June and focuses on seven members of the Chouest family, which owns shipbuilding company Edison Chouest Offshore. They donated to Ezell, who chairs the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation. Congress awarded the company a $950 million contract.  
“This is a classic pay-to-play scheme where special interests and billionaires think they can buy a Mississippi Congressman,” Boyanton said in a statement. “South Mississippians deserve a representative who answers to them, not to wealthy campaign donors or defense contractors seeking special favors.”
Josh Gregory, Ezell’s campaign manager, said in a statement that the campaign complies with federal campaign finance law. 
“While Mr. Boyanton’s allegations are obviously a political stunt, making a false statement to a federal agency, such as the FEC, is illegal and we will be reporting him for doing that,” Gregory said. “In the meantime, voters will have their say when they defeat him for the fourth time on November 3.”

The complaint centers on a joint fundraising committee called the Ezell Victory Fund, which Ezell’s campaign formed with the National Republican Congressional Committee and his leadership PAC, New Sheriff PAC.
The complaint alleges that seven members of the Chouest family, in August 2025, each gave $3,500 to Ezell’s primary campaign and $3,500 to his general election campaign, maxing out the $7,000-per-cycle limit an individual can give directly to a candidate, totaling $49,000. 
The family also donated another $150,000 to the joint fundraising committee: $10,000 each from five family members and $50,000 each from Gary and Carolyn Chouest.
The complaint argues that when the Ezell Victory Fund later transferred $47,625 of that money to Ezell’s campaign committee on Sept. 18, 2025, it amounted to funneling additional Chouest family money to the campaign beyond federal limits. 
But it’s unclear if what Boyanton is alleging actually took place because FEC records don’t typically show a donor-by-donor breakdown when a joint fundraising committee transfers a lump sum into a candidate’s personal fundraising committee. 
Federal rules require a joint fundraising committee to divide each donor’s contribution among its participating committees so that no individual’s total contribution to any one committee, whether given directly or through a joint account, exceeds that donor’s limit for that committee.
Even if Ezell violated the law, he is unlikely to face penalties anytime soon because the FEC, which is supposed to regulate campaign finances, doesn’t even have enough confirmed members to meet, let alone consider complaints, according to a recent report from the New York Times. 
Boyanton also alleges that the contractor and Ezell broke the law because contractors who receive money from Congress are prohibited from directly donating money to candidates and committees. 
But federal law does not prohibit individuals who have an ownership stake in a contractor company from making individual donations. 
Ezell, Boyanton and Democratic nominee Jeffrey Hulum will compete against each other during the general election on Nov. 3.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: A federal lawsuit challenges new NC requirements for absentee ballot returns
description: Three North Carolina nonprofit organizations and two voters are suing over new absentee ballot requirements that put votes in jeopardy of being discarded.  The North Carolina Alliance for Retired Americans, North Carolina Asian Americans Together, Down Home North Carolina, and two voters filed a federal lawsuit on Tuesday against the state Board of Elections[...]
text:
Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images)Three North Carolina nonprofit organizations and two voters are suing over new absentee ballot requirements that put votes in jeopardy of being discarded. 
The North Carolina Alliance for Retired Americans, North Carolina Asian Americans Together, Down Home North Carolina, and two voters filed a federal lawsuit on Tuesday against the state Board of Elections and elections boards in Guilford and Durham over the directives the state board adopted earlier this month. 
The lawsuit asks the court to block the requirements for the November 2026 election and future elections. 
The state board adopted the new requirements in a 3-2 vote along party lines, with Democrats opposed, on the same day that the first absentee ballots of the 2026 general election were mailed out to voters.  
According to the new requirements, voters who don’t seal their ballots in an inner envelope inside the mailing envelope will have their ballots discarded. Those voters will be sent another ballot. 
But voters won’t have time to receive new ballots if problems are discovered on the Saturday before Election Day through Election Day, the lawsuit says. 
“The Board’s new Republican majority rushed to implement eleventh-hour absentee ballot restrictions that will inevitably disenfranchise scores of North Carolina voters,” the lawsuit says.  “They did so without meaningful public notice and over the fierce objections of dissenting members. The State Board’s new policies will require counties to invalidate absentee ballots for innocuous, technical errors unrelated to individuals’ eligibility to vote.”
At least some new NC voting rules may be delayed until after the midterms

Republicans had sued over the issue of absentee ballot return envelopes. As part of the legal settlement, the state board agreed to reconsider its policy of allowing ballots that were not sealed in the inner envelopes to count. 
The board adopted the change as a formal rule this year, which the state Rules Review Commission approved. But opponents blocked the rule from being implemented in time for the midterm election. So the board implemented it as a directive this year instead.
The lawsuit also opposes a new signature verification requirement that had previously been prohibited. 
The state board gave no clear standards or instructions to counties on how to verify signatures, the lawsuit says, and it doesn’t tell the counties what to do if they determine a signature can’t be verified. 
“This state-sanctioned free-for-all will inevitably subject ballots to varying scrutiny between and within counties—resulting in unequal treatment of voters and arbitrary disenfranchisement,” the lawsuit says. 
A spokesman for the state board said in an email it has no comment on the pending litigation. 
As of Wednesday, nearly 84,000 absentee ballots had been requested.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Democrats have been trying to nail Collins on corruption for years. Will this time be different?
description: As U.S. Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied odds to hold onto her seat by touting her ability to bring in federal money to Maine, Democrats have tried to target that defense by leveling corruption accusations, so far to no avail. Now, they see new reporting alleging the incumbent Republican’s involvement in a pay-for-play scheme […]
text:
Joined by former Maine CDC director Nirav Shah (left) and former state legislator Cathy Breen (right), Executive Director of the Maine Democratic Party Devon Murphy-Anderson discusses corruption allegations involving U.S. Sen. Susan Collins during a Portland press conference on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)As U.S. Sen. Susan Collins has repeatedly defied odds to hold onto her seat by touting her ability to bring in federal money to Maine, Democrats have tried to target that defense by leveling corruption accusations, so far to no avail.
Now, they see new reporting alleging the incumbent Republican’s involvement in a pay-for-play scheme as a turning point that could upend the nationally relevant race six weeks out from the election. 
“It appears that she has sold us out yet again and gotten bailed out of trouble by the president of the United States,” Devon Murphy-Anderson, executive director of the Maine Democratic Party, said at a press conference outside Collins’ Portland office on Wednesday. “It is not the first time that she has betrayed us. However, this November we have the opportunity to ensure that it is one of the last.”
The FBI anti-corruption squad was circling Susan Collins — until Trump got in the way

Collins’ office and FBI officials denied that the senator, who became chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee in 2025, was involved in any such scheme. Doubling down after the press conference Wednesday, Collins’ longtime Chief of Staff Steve Abbott called the allegations “not only false, I would say outrageous.” 
“We hear this every cycle that Susan Collins is corrupt,” Abbott said. “It’s the same thing over and over and over again. It’s their effort to discredit the work that she does on behalf of the people of Maine.”
This is far from a new tension. Questions about Collins’ ties to the donor at the center of the latest accusations were initially raised during her last re-election bid in 2020, but more has been brought to light in an in-depth investigation published by ProPublica on Tuesday. 
One of Collins’ top donors, Martin Kao, the former CEO of defense contractor Navatek, pleaded guilty in 2022 to illegal campaign contributions involving a pro-Collins super PAC. According to ProPublica, Kao said Collins’ team was aware of the scheme in which he made donations with the understanding that she would award contracts to his company.
ProPublica reported that as recently as 2024 the FBI sought to launch an investigation examining interactions between Collins and Kao, but after Donald Trump returned to office for a second term, the investigation died as part of his purge of the bureau. 
“At a very minimum, Senator Collins and every other elected official had an obligation to speak out, if not outright block the termination and the dismantling of this public integrity unit,” said Nirav Shah, former director of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention. “It also happens to mean that in this situation, we may never truly find out what is at the heart of these allegations because they will not get a chance to be vetted.”
The New York Times spoke with current and formal officials who confirmed that the inquiry was closed last year, because senior bureau officials questioned the veracity of Kao’s account. ProPublica’s report centers on previously undisclosed FBI interviews with Kao, who is serving a little over seven years in prison as the result of multiple convictions, but the investigative outlet said they independently corroborated much of Kao’s account, including through emailed communications and a cashed check.
Abbott denied several specific accusations in the story, including that the campaign required contributions for meetings and Kao’s claim that Collins told him, “You’ve seen me deliver.” 
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins’ Chief of Staff Steve Abbott addresses corruption allegations outside the senator’s Portland office on Sept. 23, 2026. (Photo by Emma Davis/ Maine Morning Star)
“None of that happened,” Abbott said. “That’s totally fiction from a guy who was facing sentencing for two federal convictions.”  
During the Democrats’ press conference Wednesday, they took the opportunity to highlight other accusations of corruption, including familiar criticisms of her husband’s lobbying work. 
When introducing his “corruption crackdown” agenda at the same location back in June, former Democratic nominee for Senate Graham Platner revived talking points also used by Collins’ 2020 challenger, Sara Gideon, alleging she used her office to benefit her husband’s former lobbying and consulting firm. They both centered the accusation in ads. While the firm could have been affected by legislation Collins worked on, there is no direct evidence showing Collins acted specifically to benefit her husband’s business. 
That accusation did not dent the senator’s campaign last cycle, when she defied polling and outsized spending to maintain her seat. Now, Collins is the one with massive funding behind her as Republicans hope to defy political headwinds in the midterms. 
Murphy-Anderson said the party’s volunteers are focused on speaking with voters about many ways “Collins has betrayed us here in Maine,” noting that the campaign had its largest organizing weekend yet last weekend, knocking 14,000 doors. 
“We will add this to the very long list,” she said of the ProPublica reporting.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT laws effective Oct. 1: AI, Flock cameras, ICE enforcement
description: Nearly 100 CT laws on a range of issues from Flock cameras to distracted driving will fully or partially take effect on Oct. 1.
text:
Nearly 100 Connecticut laws on a range of issues from immigration enforcement to distracted driving will fully or partially take effect on Oct. 1, 2026.
Connecticut laws are passed by the General Assembly during the legislative session each year — this year’s ran from Feb. 4 to May 6 — or in a special session. They typically take effect on Jan. 1, July 1 or Oct. 1.
Here is a look at some of the laws that will go into effect next week.
License plate readers
Automated license plate readers are often referred to as Flock cameras because one of the top sellers of these devices, which record data like a vehicle’s license plate number, make and model, is the company Flock Safety. 
With residents across the state raising data privacy concerns about the use of the data collected by the cameras, Connecticut lawmakers passed a law earlier this year restricting the use of the cameras, which entities the data can be shared with and how long the information captured can be kept.
The bill restricts the amount of time that data is retained to 21 days, and it bans the use of data for immigration enforcement, investigating people who have sought or received abortions or transgender care, or finding the identity of someone “engaged in an activity protected under the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.”
The state also restricts sharing of this data with out-of-state agencies outside of New York, Massachusetts or Rhode Island, unless the law enforcement agency or task force “provides a written declaration affirming that any data received will be used in compliance with the prohibitions set forth” in the state law.
Immigration enforcement
In response to concerns about U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement actions across the country, state lawmakers passed a law earlier this year that establishes “protected areas” — including schools, hospitals, social service agency facilities and houses of worship — where people may not be arrested solely on the basis of a civil offense, such as an immigration violation.
The bill also includes a section that allows state residents to sue federal law enforcement agents for violations of their constitutional rights.
Wage theft
Lawmakers revised a law this session that already allowed state officials to issue stop work orders to entities being investigated for wage theft. 
The revision gives the comptroller the power to temporarily halt payments to contractors working on state-funded projects if those contractors are being investigated for wage theft violations. The measure was previously introduced in 2025, but did not pass.
AI transparency
The Connecticut Artificial Intelligence Responsibility and Transparency Act, or CART, made significant progress on prior efforts to pass legislation related to artificial intelligence.
Among the law’s impact is new expectations for companies that offer AI chatbots to children. The act requires them to implement a protocol to detect and address chats indicating a risk of self-harm.
It also requires employers to provide a written notice when using AI to make decisions that impact employment statuses.
Distracted driving
New language was added to the state’s existing laws to clarify and expand what is considered distracted driving. Under the current law drivers engaged in a phone call or texting while on the road, without using the hands-free feature, are considered distracted.
Under the new law, anyone holding a phone while driving is considered distracted, a change meant to include activities like scrolling. There still remains an exception for emergency calls.
Separately, distracted driving in a highway work zone will now be considered reckless driving, currently it is considered a misdemeanor.
Female genital mutilation
In an effort to stop the ritual which is still performed in around 30 countries, Public Act 26-5 bans female genital mutilation in the state, making it a class D felony.
The law also allows girls 12 years old and under to testify via video recordings from outside the courtroom. 
Exempt from the new law are physicians or licensed professional who perform the procedure if it is medically necessary.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Rate of insured Arkansas children continues to grow, report shows
description: Action is needed to address the uninsured rate for Arkansas children, which remains at its highest level in a decade, according to an Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families report released Wednesday.  Nearly 57,000 kids — 7.7% of Arkansas children — were uninsured in 2024, according to the annual study, which found that children in […]
text:
A mother and her son hold hands on a swing set. (Photo by Troy Bennett/Maine Morning Star)Action is needed to address the uninsured rate for Arkansas children, which remains at its highest level in a decade, according to an Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families report released Wednesday. 
Nearly 57,000 kids — 7.7% of Arkansas children — were uninsured in 2024, according to the annual study, which found that children in low-income working families face the greatest risk of being uninsured. That’s 7,000 more uninsured children than the previous year. 
Hispanic, immigrant and non-English-speaking children continue to face major barriers to coverage. Hispanic children had the highest uninsured rate of any racial or ethnic group at nearly 14%, according to the study. Foreign-born children were more than seven times more likely to be uninsured than children born in the U.S.
Camille Richoux, the group’s health policy director and author of the report, said progress in covering Arkansas’ children and families has trended in the wrong direction since 2016.
Arkansas healthcare providers alarmed by potential end of state’s Medicaid expansion

“At the same time, families are facing a rapidly changing healthcare landscape,” Richoux said in a press release. “The passage of H.R. 1 and the largest cuts to Medicaid in the program’s history are expected to create new instability across the health system, with ripple effects that will impact children and families for years to come.”
H.R. 1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, was signed into law by President Donald Trump last year and is expected to reduce federal spending on Medicaid by about $1 trillion during the next decade to help pay for tax cuts that disproportionately benefit the wealthy. 
Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program faces an uncertain future. The state requested permission to continue the program through the end of 2028 after the Trump administration denied its request to renew the program, which provides health coverage to more than 200,000 low-income Arkansans. 
The report also found that access to health coverage for Arkansas adults remains deeply tied to income, education and employment. Many uninsured adults are working, including in low-wage, seasonal or gig-economy jobs that don’t offer affordable health insurance, the study found. 
Women of child-bearing age continue to experience significant coverage disparities with more than 13% of Arkansas women ages 15 to 45 uninsured in 2024. 
Arkansas, which has some of the nation’s highest maternal and infant mortality rates, remains the only state in the country that hasn’t extended postpartum Medicaid to 12 months after pregnancy.

title: Rate of uninsured Arkansas children continues to grow, report shows
description: Action is needed to address the uninsured rate for Arkansas children, which remains at its highest level in a decade, according to an Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families report released Wednesday.  Nearly 57,000 kids — 7.7% of Arkansas children — were uninsured in 2024, according to the annual study, which found that children in […]
text:
A mother and her son hold hands on a swing set. (Photo by Troy Bennett/Maine Morning Star)Action is needed to address the uninsured rate for Arkansas children, which remains at its highest level in a decade, according to an Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families report released Wednesday. 
Nearly 57,000 kids — 7.7% of Arkansas children — were uninsured in 2024, according to the annual study, which found that children in low-income working families face the greatest risk of being uninsured. That’s 7,000 more uninsured children than the previous year. 
Hispanic, immigrant and non-English-speaking children continue to face major barriers to coverage. Hispanic children had the highest uninsured rate of any racial or ethnic group at nearly 14%, according to the study. Foreign-born children were more than seven times more likely to be uninsured than children born in the U.S.
Camille Richoux, the group’s health policy director and author of the report, said progress in covering Arkansas’ children and families has trended in the wrong direction since 2016.
Arkansas healthcare providers alarmed by potential end of state’s Medicaid expansion

“At the same time, families are facing a rapidly changing healthcare landscape,” Richoux said in a press release. “The passage of H.R. 1 and the largest cuts to Medicaid in the program’s history are expected to create new instability across the health system, with ripple effects that will impact children and families for years to come.”
H.R. 1, also known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, was signed into law by President Donald Trump last year and is expected to reduce federal spending on Medicaid by about $1 trillion during the next decade to help pay for tax cuts that disproportionately benefit the wealthy. 
Arkansas’ Medicaid expansion program faces an uncertain future. The state requested permission to continue the program through the end of 2028 after the Trump administration denied its request to renew the program, which provides health coverage to more than 200,000 low-income Arkansans. 
The report also found that access to health coverage for Arkansas adults remains deeply tied to income, education and employment. Many uninsured adults are working, including in low-wage, seasonal or gig-economy jobs that don’t offer affordable health insurance, the study found. 
Women of child-bearing age continue to experience significant coverage disparities with more than 13% of Arkansas women ages 15 to 45 uninsured in 2024. 
Arkansas, which has some of the nation’s highest maternal and infant mortality rates, remains the only state in the country that hasn’t extended postpartum Medicaid to 12 months after pregnancy.
