name: Daily Montanan
title: Debate between US Senate candidates tips scales for audience members
description: MISSOULA — Democrat Alani Bankhead repeatedly jabbed independent Seth Bodnar with her own questions in a political debate for U.S. Senate. Bodnar mostly responded with answers to the audience, but at one point, he mulled the tactic aloud, to chuckles from the crowd. “I guess we’re going to ask questions to each other,” Bodnar said. […]
text:
Indivisible Missoula hosted a debate between U.S. Senate candidates Alani Bankhead, a Democrat, and independent Seth Bodnar. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)MISSOULA — Democrat Alani Bankhead repeatedly jabbed independent Seth Bodnar with her own questions in a political debate for U.S. Senate.
Bodnar mostly responded with answers to the audience, but at one point, he mulled the tactic aloud, to chuckles from the crowd.
“I guess we’re going to ask questions to each other,” Bodnar said.
For about a hour on Sunday, the candidates took questions at an event at the Missoula Public Library hosted by Indivisible Missoula, a civic engagement organization.
They talked about health care, immigration, and corruption in politics, among other topics, in front of an estimated 200 people a couple of weeks before absentee ballots are sent.
Bankhead greets audience members before a U.S. Senate debate in Missoula in September 2026. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)
Bankhead, of Helena, mentioned her law enforcement experience multiple times and stressed her existing connections in Washington, D.C.
Bankhead spent 21 years with the U.S. Air Force and retired as a lieutenant colonel. In the military, she worked in law enforcement and counterintelligence.
“I’m the only candidate who has the trusted relationships of the inspectors general up in D.C. who are already texting me to say, ‘Hurry up and get here so we can hold ICE (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement) and the Department of Justice accountable,’” Bankhead said.
Bodnar told the standing-room-only audience to stay focused on the goal to beat the Republican nominee in November.
The former president of the University of Montana stepped down in January after eight years and filed in March to run for the Senate.
Republican incumbent U.S. Sen. Steve Daines withdrew his candidacy at the last minute in March, U.S. Attorney Kurt Alme filed to run, and Daines threw his support behind Alme.
Neither Alme nor Libertarian Kyle Austin participated in the debate Sunday, but Indivisible scheduled other Senate candidate forums.
Austin said he participated in an event with Bankhead one week earlier. Alme could not be reached Tuesday.
“Kurt Alme is nothing more than a rubber stamp for Donald Trump,” Bodnar said.
Before the deadline to withdraw, powerful Democrats urged Bankhead to bow out to consolidate support for Bodnar, who has earned progressive endorsements.
At least a couple of audience members said the debate helped them choose between the two candidates.
Janet Fiero was undecided before the event, but immediately following she picked up a Bodnar yard sign from the back of the room.
Fiero, of Missoula, said Bodnar showed competence and offered strong policy positions. She said Bankhead’s digs at Bodnar turned her off.
“Alani was just very irritating with her clips, and it did not serve her well,” Fiero said.
Seth Bodnar, an independent, visits with crowd members at an Indivisible Missoula U.S. Senate candidate debate in September 2026. (Keila Szpaller/The Daily Montanan)
But Bankhead and Bodnar demonstrated similarities as well, including in their approach to the safeguards they would “insist on” before backing immigration enforcement funding.
Bankhead said the country needs comprehensive immigration reform, and it must uphold due process.
She said she comes from a family of retired law enforcement officers and supports law enforcement, but law enforcement isn’t respecting due process.
“They would get no funding from me until they were held accountable for what they were doing to our immigrant brothers and sisters,” Bankhead said.
Bodnar said the country needs strong borders, and it needs to enforce immigration laws, but it needs accountability.
“We need to do that without allowing a masked, untrained, unaccountable paramilitary force to run rampant through our cities, trampling on the individual liberties of American citizens,” Bodnar said.
He pointed to his experience as a platoon leader in Iraq with the 101st Airborne Division.
“We don’t violate due process rights. We don’t violate basic human rights,” Bodnar said. “We didn’t do that in Iraq. We should not allow that to happen on our soil to people here in this country.”
The candidates also addressed how they would modify the Affordable Care Act to ensure everyone in the country can access affordable health insurance.
The questions the moderator asked included ones based on questions audience members submitted in advance of the forum.
Bankhead said she’s the only candidate for universal health care, and the country is already set up for it through an existing program, the military health care system called TRICARE.
She said taxpayers already are spending the money, and a budget reallocation could help everyone get “great quality health care.”
“We can fund it using your taxpayer dollars,” Bankhead said. “It’s called the defense budget and the illegal war on Iran.”
Bodnar said health care is “a crisis” in the country, with premiums rising 26% year over year, and fixes are urgently needed.
He said he would restore ACA subsidies to be sure people can get health care; protect Medicaid expansion, important to rural hospitals; and reverse bureaucratic work requirement verifications that will lead to 30,000 Montanans losing access.
“I’m not about bumper stickers or slogans. I’m about getting things done,” Bodnar said.
Bankhead used her rebuttal to quiz Bodnar: “So you’re advocating to keep health insurance companies?”
Bodnar said tens of millions of Americans have a private-coverage option, and he’s interested in solutions. He said even under the Obama administration with Democrats in control of Congress, doing away with private options wasn’t realistic.
“I don’t think that … fighting for five years to rip the private options out of people’s hands is going to get us the type of change that Montanans so urgently demand,” Bodnar said. “I’m about getting results and getting them quickly.”
Bankhead addressed her opponent directly after the very first question.
After the moderator asked candidates to address the actions they would take as senators to dole out consequences when it’s clear federal officials have broken the law, Bankhead took a shot at Bodnar.
“Well, Seth, that was a whole lot of words to not answer the question,” Bankhead said.
She said she was the only candidate on stage who signed a pledge to impeach Trump and put him in jail, and she’s the only one who already has a record of holding government officials accountable.
Citizens’ Impeachment aims to remove Trump from office as a “tyrant” and “would-be king” whose crimes “meet the definition of tyranny.” It’s billed as a national volunteer organization intent on gathering support for Trump’s impeachment.
“I’ve arrested pedophiles and traffickers on six different continents,” Bankhead said. “A lot of them have been government officials, so I’m very familiar with this space.”
Asked if he wanted to use his rebuttal time, Bodnar said yes, to correct the record. He said he’s the only candidate endorsed by the anti-corruption organization End Citizens United, and he’s the only one that signed the Political Integrity Project pledge.
The organization is dedicated to getting big money out of politics and opposing corruption, and it gives him an A- grade. Bankhead isn’t graded or listed as a signatory.
“My duty is to the Constitution of the United States,” Bodnar said. “I want to be really clear about this: A U.S. senator? Their job is to be a juror. I will be a juror. I will hold the powerful accountable.”
After the debate, Jane Borish said she wished a Social Democrat was running, but she was leaning toward Bodnar before the debate.
“Alani made some good points, although not specific enough,” Borish said. “But I really was turned off by the mud slinging, so I’m more likely to vote for Seth Bodnar after that talk.”
Borish said she appreciated the way Bodnar “resisted the urge” to respond in kind because “sharp elbows” have been too much a part of politics. She said she thought Bodnar also could have offered more specifics, “but they were limited in time.”
Another audience member already in support of Bodnar described Bankhead’s approach as “snarky.”
“I was very turned off by the negativity in her replies and how she always had to attack him,” Mark Heyka said.
But Robbie Liben, of Missoula, said he was more likely to support Bankhead after the debate.
He said he walked into the debate slightly leaning toward Bankhead but also turned off “by her militarism.” He said in the debate, Bankhead supported particular policies, but Bodnar offered mostly platitudes.
“It struck me that really all he’s got to run on is stopping Alme,” Liben said.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Trone Garriott tours Epstein files ‘reading room,’ calls for Congress to act
description: Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott criticized Congress and the U.S. Department of Justice for not taking action to investigate the crimes of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and related parties as she visited a “reading room” traveling exhibit on the “Epstein files.” The exhibition, hosted at The Loft DSM, is an event staged by The Institute […]
text:
Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, running for Iowa's 3rd Congressional District, toured a traveling exhibition showcasing documents related to U.S. Department of Justice investigation documents of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein in Des Moines Sep. 22, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowa Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott criticized Congress and the U.S. Department of Justice for not taking action to investigate the crimes of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and related parties as she visited a “reading room” traveling exhibit on the “Epstein files.”
The exhibition, hosted at The Loft DSM, is an event staged by The Institute for Primary Facts and DEFIANCE.org, and includes books that contain excerpts of documents, released by the DOJ in 2025, stemming from the federal investigation into Epstein and his collaborators. Some of the information in the records has been redacted.
Some Republicans have called for the DOJ to publicly release more government documents related to Epstein, but much of the push for more information has come from Democrats who link President Donald Trump to Epstein.
At the “reading room” exhibition, Trone Garriott spoke with organizers who included family members of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, one of the most prominent accusers of Epstein’s sex trafficking crimes, as well as Sharlene Rochard, who said she is a victim of Epstein. Trone Garriott said she was moved by the stories told in the exhibit and called for Congress to take more action to prosecute and investigate people involved in these crimes.
“I’m so disappointed that Congress has been so weak on this issue, and that the Department of Justice has not done its job, and actively worked to prevent a real investigation from happening,” Trone Garriott said.
Trone Garriott, the Democratic candidate running for Iowa’s 3rd Congressional District, criticized her opponent, incumbent U.S. Rep. Zach Nunn, for not supporting measures to compel the DOJ to release more information. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, filed a discharge petition to have the House consider a bill that would allow state attorneys general, victims and members of Congress to sue the DOJ for not disclosing documents related to the Epstein investigation — a petition Nunn has not signed. Only three other Republicans, Reps. Nancy Mace, Ralph Norman and Brian Fitzpatrick have signed the discharge petition.
“We need elected leaders who will stand up for what’s right, and make sure the truth is told, and that powerful people are held accountable for their crimes,” Trone Garriott said.
A campaign spokesperson for Nunn’s campaign said Monday, “Zach Nunn has led to hold abusers accountable and fight human trafficking. He voted to release the Epstein Files to deliver transparency to the American people and justice for victims. Sarah Trone Garriott skipped votes in the Iowa Senate to strengthen sentencing for sex predators.”
In 2025, Nunn, alongside other members of Iowa’s all-GOP federal delegation, said they supported providing more public information about Epstein, but supported the Trump administration and DOJ approach to releasing information rather than Congress compelling another release.
“Transparency and accountability from our government isn’t optional, it’s a duty,” Nunn said in 2025. “Jeffrey Epstein is a disgusting human being who committed horrific crimes. Victims deserve justice, not DC politicians who want to use them to score political points.”
Nunn and other Republicans have also pointed to their votes in support of the Epstein Files Transparency Act in November 2025 to show their support to have more information released.
Scott Roberts, the brother of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, thanked Trone Garriott for attending the exhibition and “giving us the opportunity to share our stories with her.” He said he supported candidates like Trone Garriott, who he said are willing to stand up to “the most rich and powerful” in society.
“What we need is we need congressional leaders that are willing to have a backbone, and are willing to stand up for survivors that are willing to listen to our stories, that are willing to act,” Roberts said.
This story has been updated with a comment from Rep. Zach Nunn’s campaign.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Secretary of state announces new ‘Idaho Free Speech Summit’ in partnership with UI, BSU
description: A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for free speech and encourage civil discourse. The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State’s Office, the University of Idaho’s College of Law […]
text:
The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State's Office, the University of Idaho's College of Law and Boise State University's Institute for Advancing American Values. (Photo by Getty Images)A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for free speech and encourage civil discourse.
The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State’s Office, the University of Idaho’s College of Law and Boise State University’s Institute for Advancing American Values, according to a Secretary of State’s Office press release.
The keynote speaker for the event will be Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, who has championed Disagree Better, a national, nonpartisan initiative “designed to reduce inflammatory rhetoric and foster a culture of healthy debate,” according to its website.
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. (Photo courtesy of Phil McGrane)
“Free speech is fundamental to our system of government, but protecting it requires more than simply agreeing that it is important,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. “It means listening to people we disagree with, defending their right to speak, and being willing to have difficult conversations. That is what we hope to accomplish with the Idaho Free Speech Summit.”
Sessions at the summit will explore First Amendment issues “ranging from campaign finance and campus free speech to the broader challenges of maintaining civil discourse in an increasingly divided political environment,” the press release said.
Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (left) listens as Gov. Spencer Cox holds a press conference to present his budget proposal at the Salt Lake County Library in Kearns, Utah, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
Cox will talk about how Americans can disagree without abandoning strongly held beliefs, a theme he explores in his new book, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt,” according to the release.
“We are pleased to be part of a discussion centered on one of our nation’s most important constitutional freedoms,” said Brian Kane, University of Idaho College of Law dean, in the release. “The University of Idaho College of Law is a natural partner for this conversation. Law schools should be places where difficult constitutional questions are examined carefully and where people learn how to engage seriously with ideas they may not share.”
The daylong summit will have presentations and panel discussions, followed by an evening reception. A continuing legal education credit will also be available for participating attorneys.
“Universities have an important role to play in creating spaces where people can wrestle with difficult questions and hear perspectives different from their own,” said Boise State University’s Andrew Finstuen in the release. “The Summit provides an opportunity to model the kind of thoughtful, constructive dialogue that is essential to a healthy civic culture.”
Registration and additional information, including the Summit schedule and speaker lineup, are available at FreeSpeechIdaho.com.
“Our goal isn’t to bring together people who all agree,” McGrane said in the release. “It is to bring together people who recognize that our constitutional freedoms are strongest when we defend the right of others to speak, listen to one another, and engage in good faith.”

title: Iowa universities see US News & World Report rankings rise
description: The University of Northern Iowa has taken the top spot in the U.S. News & World Report’s rankings of public regional universities in the Midwest, joined by other public and private Iowa institutions that saw their rankings in the 2027 report climb. The Cedar Falls university attributed its graduation rates and “graduation rate performance” to […]
text:
The 2027 U.S. News & World Report rankings put the University of Northern Iowa in the top slot for public regional universities. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The University of Northern Iowa has taken the top spot in the U.S. News & World Report’s rankings of public regional universities in the Midwest, joined by other public and private Iowa institutions that saw their rankings in the 2027 report climb.
The Cedar Falls university attributed its graduation rates and “graduation rate performance” to the new ranking in a Tuesday news release, stating that they are two of the “most heavily weighted criteria” of the 17 factors U.S. News & World Report uses in determining its Best Colleges rankings.
“The University of Northern Iowa is honored to be recognized by U.S. News & World Report for our ongoing dedication to student success, our outstanding graduation rates and the exceptional value we offer to families across the Midwest,” said UNI Director of University Relations Pete Moris in the release.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Significant methodology changes” were introduced by U.S. News this year as concerns persist about the affordability and value of a college degree, the media company stated in an article announcing the rankings, including replacing its “graduate indebtedness factor” with “earnings by major,” which covers earnings of people four years after earning their degree.
“With families increasingly scrutinizing the true cost and return on investment of a college degree, our goal is to provide clear, actionable data,” said LaMont Jones, managing editor for Education at U.S. News, in the article. “The 2027 Best Colleges rankings serve as a vital decision-making tool for prospective students and parents, offering transparent metrics on outcomes, affordability and academic quality to help families make fully informed financial and educational investments.”
UNI tied for 13th place in the rankings of all Midwest regional universities and for 6th place in best value for in-state students, according to the rankings. The university stated in the release its four-year graduation rate is 25 percentage-points higher than its national peers, and average student debt falls below state and national averages.
The University of Iowa made it back into the top 100 national universities after falling to #102 in 2026, now tying at spot 100 with eight other universities across the U.S. The UI is the highest-ranked Iowa institution on the national universities list, followed by Iowa State University at #116 and Drake University at #191.
In the top public schools ranking, the UI took 46th place and ISU came in at #55.
Other top rankings for the UI include fourth in undergraduate nursing programs, eighth in insurance and 10th in “writing in the disciplines.” The university stated in a press release it “continues to build upon its strength in writing to support communication excellence across campus,” through initiatives like the Office of Writing and Communication and the “Writing Enriched Curriculum” pilot program to identify field-specific writing skills to instill in students.
“Iowa gives students access to nationally recognized programs in writing, health care, and business, along with the support they need to succeed,” said Kevin Kregel, executive vice president and provost, in the release. “Expanding writing across disciplines advances our academic mission, encourages innovation in teaching, and creates new ways to prepare students for a rapidly changing world.”
Iowa’s private colleges and universities also made it into the rankings, with Dordt University tying for sixth place for regional universities in the Midwest — a drop of one spot from last year. It is followed by UNI at #12 and St. Ambrose University at #32, with other Iowa institutions ranked below #50.
Grinnell College saw the highest ranking of Iowa liberal arts colleges on the national list, tied at #16 with two other colleges. No other Iowa colleges crack the top 100, the next highest being Luther College, tied at #111.
Wartburg College beat other Iowa colleges in its seventh-place ranking of Midwest regional colleges, with Simpson College in eighth place and Loras College in 10th.
“This recognition reflects the collaborative work happening across campus to help all our students thrive both on campus and after graduation,” said Wartburg College President Rebecca Ehretsman in a news release. “We continue to invest in the academic opportunities, relationships and experiences central to a Wartburg education. Our outstanding faculty and staff have sharpened their focus on student retention and strengthened the ways they identify and respond to students who may need additional support.”

title: New Mexico activates emergency center ahead of anticipated flooding
description: The New Mexico Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management announced on Tuesday afternoon it had activated the State Emergency Operation Center in anticipation of expected flash flooding.
text:
New Mexico communities that have experienced wildfire remain particularly vulnerable to flash flooding, such as Ruidoso, pictured above in July of 2024 after storms dumped rain into the burn scar of the South Fork and Salt fires and flash flooding closed roads. The state Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management on Sept. 22, 2026, activated its emergency operations center in anticipation of heavy rains and flash flooding. (Photo courtesy of City of Ruidoso)The New Mexico Department of Homeland Security and Emergency Management announced on Tuesday afternoon it had activated the State Emergency Operation Center ahead of of expected flash flooding. 
Forecasts from the National Weather Service in Albuquerque predict heavy rainfall through Thursday, putting New Mexico’s burn scars at high risks very for flooding.
 A news release says state agencies are coordinating with the Homeland Security agency to put people and equipment across the state with the New Mexico National Guard Swiftwater personnel  pre-positioned near Ruidoso and Las Vegas, and regional teams on standby in Doña Ana, Santa Fe, Sandoval and Valencia counties.
“Sudden, heavy rainfall can become dangerous – especially in burn scar areas – so we’re putting resources in place to respond to any flash flooding emergencies quickly and effectively,” Maj. Gen. Miguel Aguilar, Adjutant General of the NM National Guard and interim Cabinet secretary of DHSEM, said in a statement.
In addition, the agency says it has coordinated delivery of 5,000 sandbags across four different counties and a mechanical sandbagger to Sandoval County. 
DHSEM also issued recommendations to residents ahead of flooding, including evacuating immediately if told to do so, and otherwise sheltering in place at the highest point of your homes. In addition, avoid walking, swimming or driving through flood waters. More information on flood safety is available on DHSEM’s website.
PNM on Tuesday also issued a news release urging residents to take precautions during expected storms and prepare for possible weather-related outages, which can be tracked online.

title: Q&A: Louisiana Tech President Jim Henderson
description: After serving as president of the University of Louisiana System from 2017-23, Jim Henderson became president of Louisiana Tech University in Ruston. In a recent interview, he detailed his work returning to a student-facing role.  This transcript of the interview has been edited for length and clarity. The full interview can be heard on Episode […]
text:
Jim Henderson is the president of Louisiana Tech UniversityAfter serving as president of the University of Louisiana System from 2017-23, Jim Henderson became president of Louisiana Tech University in Ruston. In a recent interview, he detailed his work returning to a student-facing role. 
This transcript of the interview has been edited for length and clarity. The full interview can be heard on Episode 68 of “The Light Switch” podcast. 

Piper Hutchinson: One of your big goals when you were first going into the job is that you wanted to boost Louisiana Tech’s research profile and maybe even become an R1 university. How is progress coming along with that? 
Jim Henderson: To be a Carnegie R1 university, you have to produce 70 research-based doctorates a year, and have at least 50 million dollars in reportable research expenditures on what’s called the NSF HERD (National Science Foundation Higher Education Research and Development Survey) report. 
Being an R1 has never really been the goal itself, but we have wanted to produce more research, more meaningful, relevant research that solves real world problems, both novel and enduring problems. And to do that, you have to grow your doctorate programs, and you have to to expend more on research. So we’ve seen some remarkable growth. We’ve seen a significant growth in research expenditures. 
The Ph.D.s, the research doctorates, we’ve seen modest growth. We expect to see more over time as we’ve done very well in securing federal grants for public-private partnerships that lend themselves well to bringing doctoral students on and giving them research opportunities. 
Hutchinson: The state is looking at the higher education funding formula right now because a lot of people have been saying it doesn’t work for them. I recall back in the legislative hearing (where a higher education funding task force was proposed), it was a lot about how it didn’t work for Tech. Can you tell me about your concerns with the existing funding formula?
Henderson: I would suggest to you that the funding formula doesn’t work for Louisiana, nor has it ever. I’ve been complaining about the funding formula for over 21 years now, and I think it’s through six iterations of the formula. And that’s not a criticism or complaint about any of the individuals involved with it. It’s just that it is exceedingly difficult to create a single model for distributing funds to such varied institutions, we have very distinct missions. 
Over the years, the funding formula has emphasized different things. At first, it was solely about equity, and that’s the constitutional charge. Over the years, they tweaked it to add cost components to it and then outcomes components. 
I think if we if we take the right steps, we’ll have done something that’s that’s meaningful, that improves how the funding formula helps the state of Louisiana, as and as long again as it’s predictable, it’s transparent, distributes funds equitably, and aligns with a strategic intents, I think we can we have an opportunity to do something pretty important.
Hutchinson: Louisiana Tech had an eventful year in athletics. Y’all switched conferences. You got sued over switching conferences. Now things are settled a little bit. Tell us about that journey.
Henderson: It’s always a difficult journey anytime you have some significant change like this. For us, the change was vitally important. We looked at the health and well-being of student-athletes. We’re going to save an average of 66 hours of seat time in buses and airplanes for our student-athletes. That equates to more time in the study hall, more time in classes, more time asleep in their own beds, that makes sense for us. 
At the same time, we’re going to be bringing in opponents that have fan bases that are in driving distance, that are coming at a that our fans are interested in watching us compete against. So we know there’s going to be a revenue increase associated with this, a dramatic drop in travel expenses, at least a million dollars. 
Hutchinson: You are a former journalist and one of your goals when you took the job was to restart Tech’s student newspaper. How is that going? 
Henderson: Not as successful as I thought. But we do have a great communications professor who has gotten some wonderful students writing for her class and doing a digital version, albeit not beautifully designed. It’s not a full-fledged newspaper, but there is some student journalism occurring. That’s certainly going to be a point of emphasis for us going forward. 
I would love eventually to have a print paper. I don’t know if that’s just a pipe dream, and maybe it’s a little bit nostalgia. Maybe it’s not as necessary, but a robust digital minimum periodical newspaper, at least weekly, would be a great advantage for us. I think it’s essential to having a healthy institution. It’s a great way to keep students engaged, keep them informed, to elevate areas of controversy sometimes, which I think is also healthy. So we haven’t made as much progress as we’d like, but we have made some.

name: VTDigger
title: Rural Vermont Rising demands to be heard — now and in the future
description:
From fury over a regional land use plan to a new slate of legislative policy positions, the ascendant forum Rural Vermont Rising has been anything but dormant this summer.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Rural Vermont Rising demands to be heard — now and in the future.
text:
Several hundred demonstrators gather to protest Act 181 at the Statehouse in Montpelier in March 2026.  The law seeks to modernize Act 250, the land use law. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
TUNBRIDGE — Over the hubbub of music and corn dog vendors, Amanda Janoo addressed a standing crowd at the World’s Fair. She had no microphone, and her voice was fading after weeks on the campaign trail. But this conversation was too important to miss. 
“OK, everybody, come on in,” bellowed event moderator and TikTok-famous Peacham farmer Morgan Gold. “We’re gonna get friendly!” 
The dozens of listeners included farmers and landowners from across the state concerned with the economic sustainability of their communities — and political candidates who hoped to earn those citizens’ votes in November. They shuffled inward, closer to each other and to where Gold and Janoo sat beneath a large banner with the words adopted by a movement: Rural Vermont Rising.
It’s been just three months since Gov. Phil Scott signed into law a partial rollback of Act 181, tossing large sections of the 2024 statute that overhauled Vermont’s approach to land use permitting. A provision requiring complex reviews for nearly all new development in areas labelled the state’s most sensitive ecosystems (called “Tier 3”) and another requiring them for some new roads and driveways, were repealed. It also exempted some on-farm business ventures from such reviews.
In an unusual move, driven in large part by widespread advocacy from rural Vermonters who resented what they saw as restrictive, top-down reforms, the state’s Democrat-controlled Legislature ultimately reversed course on parts of its own initiative. Republican lawmakers and Scott — whose veto of Act 181 was overridden in 2024 — had long been opposed to the law.
That public backlash, which included a protest and critical testimony during the legislative session, began increasingly to flow through the growing Rural Vermont Rising Facebook page. And the online forum — now touting roughly 18,000 members — has been far from dormant after its policy wins earlier this year.
That movement has become a broad forum for organizing around issues affecting rural communities. In particular, the state’s efforts to balance conservation with rural housing and economic development — and indeed the role working lands should play in the state’s conception of conservation — remain at the center of the group’s debate. So too does the state’s ability, or lack thereof, to attract young people and families through robust land-based industry and financially feasible development.
“We’ve spent a decade setting policy as if we’re under this immense growth pressure, when it’s actually the opposite,” said Neil Ryan, a Corinth beef farmer and consultant who has become one of Rural Vermont Rising’s most visible members. “We’re facing a demographic cliff.”
The movement has continued to grow, and its wide variety of participants have a correspondingly broad set of priorities under the umbrella of rural prosperity. This summer, its members have rallied against a regional land use plan and helped ready a sweeping manifesto of policy recommendations for lawmakers to take up in January. 
Rep. Greg Burtt, R-Cabot, who was a primary advocate for repealing parts of Act 181 in the last legislative session and has become a celebrated figure for many in Rural Vermont Rising, said in an interview before Friday’s event that candidates across the political spectrum are urgently trying to connect with these newly engaged voters.
“What should our (land use) policies be in Vermont to create the culture and the lifestyle that we ultimately want?” he said. “I feel like everyone is having to answer that to some degree right now.”
Burtt faces a challenge in November from Democrat Eric Bach, whose platform includes reducing overregulation and “preserving rural Vermont for those who live there.”
Molly Gray, the Democratic candidate for lieutenant governor, also spoke at Friday’s event, calling the movement “probably one of the most impactful modern-day grassroots movements in Vermont.” Republicans Scott and Lt. Gov. John Rodgers conducted similar conversations at the booth over the weekend. 
The governor is “excited about the grassroots organization and putting party politics aside,” said Emma Shouldice, a spokesperson for Scott’s reelection campaign. “This could help shape policy, and help farmers, and help parts of Vermont truly be heard at the Statehouse.”
Ryan said he thought Friday’s event signaled promising seriousness from Democratic statewide candidates in their engagement with rural landowners. The GOP, including Scott and Rodgers, he said, has been “more consistently welcoming” of the movement since its inception. 
The mix of crowds and lawmakers who had stopped by throughout the fair demonstrated the movement’s desire to push issue-based discussion rather than partisan politics, he added.
Janoo agreed.
“I think it’s important that we are not writing off this movement as, you know, some fringe, extremist group or something,” she said in an interview, “but as really the reflection of — I think — some pretty legitimate demands for a voice in policymaking.”
Rural Vermont Rising
In recent months, the movement has begun assembling a more formal leadership structure as it seeks to strengthen internal communication and build its ability to advocate. 
At least 14 local chapters have formed to facilitate in-person political conversations. The movement’s new steering committee, which was formed by a charter approved by members earlier this month, will have duties that include policy strategy and public communications.
The document says the movement will not endorse particular political parties or organizations, and candidates are largely prohibited from campaigning directly on the Facebook group, according to Colleen Geddis of Newark, the page’s founder.
“Our political diversity does make election season tricky,” Megan Durling, a fellow Newark resident who sits on the movement’s new steering committee, said in an email. “Many, no doubt, are counting on us to fail that test and to splinter along party lines.”
Some critics of Act 181 were the target of a bipartisan rebuke from Vermont’s legislative leadership over “reprehensible” and allegedly threatening online language this spring. Geddis, who questioned elements of the lawmakers’ statement, said she has always sought to root out such attacks on the Rural Vermont Rising page. She posts near-daily reminders to keep discussion civil in the forum, where friction over particular candidates, events or positions is not uncommon.
“We remain entirely committed to fostering a productive, passionate, and respectful community page where rural Vermonters can voice their very real concerns,” Geddis said in a text message.
Though some members feel their advocacy will have a clear impact on this fall’s election season, many agree that electoral politics are only a small part of long-term efforts to educate and activate the state’s rural public.
“We’re too young a movement to hold (electoral politics) as our primary goal,” said Durling. “Elections are not a goal in themselves, but a means to an end. There are other means.”
One central path to reform, she said, will be ensuring rural voices can fully take part in the legislative process.
Rural Vermont Rising is positioned to fill a gap in advocating for a better-balanced approach to land use policy and support for working lands, according to Mary White, who leads the Vermont Farm Bureau. White’s organization has advocated for agricultural interests since 1915 but has recently encountered challenges in making farmers’ voices heard, she said. Some legislative leaders have been unreceptive to requests for individual testimony, she said, and it’s often been tough to convince the Farm Bureau’s member business owners that speaking to lawmakers is worthwhile.
“It’s been harder and harder year after year, because people felt like they weren’t being heard,” White said.
For her, Rural Vermont Rising has not only injected renewed energy into some of her organization’s central issues but also created a direct connection between lawmakers and a broad base of informed, active landowners. This kind of large-scale, “raw” advocacy that reaches Montpelier without a pass-through lobbying entity, she said, is difficult for policymakers to ignore.
For Ryan, the Corinth beef farmer, the movement has also reframed the political conversation in Vermont in recent months. 
“Almost everyone in the state involved in politics is watching that Facebook page,” he said.
“By and large, when people are talking about these issues of rural Vermont and land use,” he added, “They’re evoking what emerged out of this movement.”
Land use is a difficult subject for Democrats in particular, according to Ryan, who he believes are experiencing something like “growing pains” as a party after the consensus over Act 181 shifted suddenly this spring. Candidates are being asked to prove their understanding of the topic — and their openness to listen to rural voices — to a new depth, he added. 
“They’re unaccustomed to people asking substantive questions,” Ryan said, calling the new engagement “exciting and hopeful.”
Rep. Troy Headrick, a Burlington Progressive/Democrat-turned-Independent, shares Ryan’s concerns. In a much-discussed online essay aimed at Democrats, Headrick wrote last month about “the political cost of talking when we should be listening” in relation to rural issues. 
While it’s difficult to predict how such a movement might impact the November elections, he added in an interview, it’s clear to him that Democrats need to lend more credence to rural voices than they have in the past.
Todd Heyman, a Hartland sheep farmer and lodging business owner who participates often in the Rural Vermont Rising forum, said he believes there was evidence of the movement’s impact in the August primaries, where two Upper Valley House Democrats lost their seats. 
Such impacts are difficult to track. However, while this year’s primary turnout increased roughly 50% statewide from August 2024, the rural districts of defeated Reps. Jim Masland, D-Thetford, and John Bartholomew, D-Hartland, shot up far more, by nearly 70% and about 135% respectively.
Dylan Morse and John Tansey, the Democrats now running unopposed to represent Hartland, Windsor and West Windsor in the House, each said in interviews that finding a better balance between land conservation and rural economic prosperity was a central legislative priority for them. Morse added that the issue was a factor in choosing to launch his campaign in the first place, and that his engagement with local landowners on such reforms likely helped him succeed in the primary.
Two Rivers ‘tsunami’
Rather than coalescing around electoral politics as the general election approaches, many Rural Vermont Rising members have instead been galvanized in recent months by a bureaucratic land use planning process that’s underway on the state’s eastern side.
For a number of local landowners, the issue is intertwined with concerns over Act 181.
A regional development plan in the works at the Two Rivers-Ottauqueechee Regional Commission — which Rural Vermont Rising members say is both overly prescriptive and insulated from public input — has become central in the movement’s discourse. Heyman, one of the loudest voices on the issue, said Rural Vermont Rising’s platform has helped shine a light into a little-examined part of land use bureaucracy, creating an unprecedented level of interest.
Like all Vermont regional planning commissions, Two Rivers is tasked with creating a plan to guide future development and land use for the 30-town block it represents, which runs from Plymouth north to Topsham, and from Hancock east to Thetford. 
Tony O’Meara, who chairs the Newbury Planning Commission and is the town’s appointed representative on the Two Rivers board, said this year has stood in stark contrast with previous iterations of the regional planning process. Previously, he said, board discussion and public comments had essentially rubber-stamped the staff’s suggested plans, but this year has brought a “tsunami” of public criticism.
“As an organization, they’re just not used to dealing with this level of informed pushback,” he said of Two Rivers’ staff in an interview.
O’Meara believes the organization has been “dismissive” of legitimate questions posed in public hearings and has inappropriately cut local voices out of meetings in which they had a right to participate. Two Rivers acknowledged earlier this year that the organization had violated Vermont’s open meeting law in March by failing to allow appropriate public comment before a land use rules vote, but O’Meara said problematic efforts to close off discussion of the regional plan have continued in the months since. 
O’Meara also said that the regional plan “crossed a line” by introducing a large number of its own policies that would regulate future development, an argument Two Rivers Executive Director Peter Gregory firmly rejected in an interview. The board’s chair, Bill Emmons, did not respond to requests for comment.
The comprehensive regional plan, now in a more than 200-page draft form, includes maps categorizing swathes of land as more or less appropriate for different types of growth and places requirements on new development proposals that trigger the state’s land use review process. 
That Two Rivers proposal remains squarely within accepted practices under state law, and is not out of step with other regional commissions, Gregory said. The planning process has also gone “well beyond any statutory minimums as far as public engagement,” he added, including meeting with each town during the planning process.
But the Vermont Land Use Review Board, which oversees land use policy statewide, has expressed real concern about both the plan’s content and the process by which it was generated.
The state board said late last month that it questions whether “mandatory land use restrictions expressed throughout the plan infringe on constitutional property rights without adequate input from affected landowners.” It also said a number of the plan’s mandatory policies appeared overly restrictive, including a rule outlawing fossil fuel heating in some future buildings and another banning certain retail operations from ever opening in specific areas. Such rules, the body said, could be “at odds with removing barriers to housing development and rural enterprises.”
Two Rivers staff have expressed a willingness to consider some changes to the plan. But Gregory has argued that the Land Use Review Board’s response showed deep inconsistencies with the body’s approach to other regions’ plans.
At the very least, Two Rivers is an outlier when it comes to public interest in its hearings and planning steps — and the discourse has often been heated.
In one of a number of blog entries and social media posts on the subject, Ryan — who lives in the affected region — called the plan a “naked power grab” by the organization’s staff. Heyman said in an interview that the commission was “designed to be unaccountable.”
Heyman further argued that local residents have been rendered effectively powerless in the planning process, with statutory protections around community participation giving no concrete leverage to the public. It’s not that the regional plan is illegal, he said — it’s adhering to an inherently undemocratic regulatory process.
“The irony is, we are entirely dependent on the unelected Land Use Review Board to save us from the unelected regional planning commission,” he said.
The Two Rivers plan remains subject to change or rejection by the state land use panel. But for the first time, a host of local landowners will be watching the outcome closely and making their feelings known.
‘I just felt compelled’
Barbara Baumann, a Randolph resident who stopped by the Rural Vermont Rising booth — wearing the movement’s logo T-shirt — for much of Friday afternoon, said she never expected to become politically involved. Then, she found discussions of Act 181 online, and soon she was protesting the law in Montpelier.
“It’s never been my thing. It’s never been my style,” she said in an interview. “I just felt compelled from someplace deep inside to go.” 
Baumann isn’t a farmer. But she nonetheless began listening “obsessively” to House Environment Committee hearings, becoming more and more convinced that the state’s conservation laws constituted overreach.
“I would like more people to understand what’s happening, and I would like more people that voted for this to look deep within themselves and understand the impact on Vermonters,” she said. “They really need to stop partisan politics, stop listening to their higher-ups, check their morals.”
Rural leaders are looking to convert the grassroots momentum they’ve built this year into lasting, substantive policy change.
Last week, a website called “Grow What’s Good Here” went live, and with it a working slate of policy recommendations “crowdsourced from rural Vermonters of all politics and the community of Rural Vermont Rising.” 
The sweeping suggestions, which range from expanding the state’s local food purchasing incentives to changing the role of regional planning commissions, are largely aimed at supporting rural communities. One section of the site calls on lawmakers to publicly commit to nine rural policy priorities, including land use deregulation measures for farms and working forests, and major shifts in requirements and funding mechanisms for schools.
“Our work will continue regardless of who takes office in January,” wrote Durling, who helped develop some of the new proposals. That legislative involvement, she said, “is going to make for real change that recenters our state’s policies on sustaining the rural way of life that continues to serve as the substance — and not merely the appearance — of Vermont.”
Whether further organizational structures or funding are needed to bolster that effort, Ryan added, remains in question.
For Burtt, the Cabot Republican, Rural Vermont Rising’s strength — and indeed, its ability to survive — is impossible to separate from its bipartisan appeal. “It had nothing to do with politics, ultimately,” he said of the grassroots mobilization around land use this spring.
“I think so long as they focus on being nonpartisan, not advocating for individuals, and focusing on policy, on education and engagement,” he said of the movement, “I don’t see this ever going away.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Rural Vermont Rising demands to be heard — now and in the future.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Lawmakers divided on influence of newest Nebraska Economic Forecasting Board Pillen appointees
description: LINCOLN — As criticism clouds Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen’s latest appointments to a state advisory board predicting state tax revenues, lawmakers are divided on what influence the most well-known of those newest board members will have. The nine-member Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board will meet Oct. 30 and project whether Nebraska faces a budget sh[...]
text:
Gov. Jim Pillen hosts a news conference at the end of the Legislature's special session to address property taxes that begin almost one month prior. To his far left is State Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of the Elkhorn area, chair of the Legislature's Revenue Committee. Aug. 20, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — As criticism clouds Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen’s latest appointments to a state advisory board predicting state tax revenues, lawmakers are divided on what influence the most well-known of those newest board members will have.
The nine-member Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board will meet Oct. 30 and project whether Nebraska faces a budget shortfall through mid-2029, and at what scale. The meeting comes just days before the Nov. 3 general election, in which Pillen faces a tougher-than-usual four-way race to hold onto the governor’s seat.
Gov. Jim Pillen, left, hands State Treasurer Tom Briese one of three property-tax-related proposals that the Legislature passed earlier in the day on Aug. 20, 2024. Pillen said it was a ceremonial gesture for Briese’s seven years in the Legislature working on tax relief, from 2017 to 2023 when he became treasurer. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Two of Pillen’s newest appointees, former state Sens. Tom Briese of Albion and Lou Ann Linehan of Elkhorn, were key allies for Pillen in enacting major income tax cuts in 2023, as well as supporting multiple property tax proposals throughout 2024, which were significantly slimmed back.
In November 2023, Pillen elevated Briese to state treasurer, where he served for two years. And last year, Pillen appointed both Briese and Linehan as members of a new School Financing Review Commission to review state and local funding of K-12 schools, seeking to reduce property taxes.
Pillen last week said he believes new perspectives are always good, doesn’t play “goober politics” and believes Nebraska’s diverse economy “puts us in great shape” economically.
“I’m not a speculator,” Pillen said Friday when asked what he’s expecting next month. “I learned in my business if you speculated, you went broke, so I don’t speculate.”
‘A head-scratcher’
Pillen’s appointments have faced resistance, including from former state Sen. John Stinner of Gering, a six-year chair of the Legislature’s Appropriations Committee. He told the Omaha World-Herald that recent forecasting board appointments have been “too political.”
Then-state Sen. John Stinner of Gering listens to testimony during an Appropriations Committee hearing in the Nebraska State Capitol on Oct. 7, 2022. Behind Stinner, who chaired the committee at the time, the then-vice chair, former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln, watches in the background. (Photo by Zach Wendling)
Stinner told the Nebraska Examiner he worries the next forecast could be “rosier” than reality.
“It’s a head-scratcher for me why anybody would do this,” Stinner said this week. “It’s a distortion, and people need to understand that it’s all about politics with this current administration.”
State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, the outgoing four-year chair of the Appropriations Committee, disagreed. Clements was appointed to the Legislature in February 2017 and served out the next six years with Stinner, seven with Briese and eight with Linehan.
“Senators Briese and Linehan are independent thinkers, and I don’t know that there’s any political portion of that,” Clements said. He said he believes Briese and Linehan always acted in “good faith for Nebraska, not as rubber stamps of the governor.”
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen speaks with reporters after hosting a kickoff event where he confirmed he is sticking with his running mate, Lt. Gov. Joe Kelly, for another four years on Aug. 25, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The forecasting board was created in 1984 as a way to reduce politics in predicting state revenues. It replaced forecasts made by the Department of Revenue, which reports to the governor. Membership consists of four gubernatorial appointees and five appointees from the Legislature’s Executive Board.
The Omaha World-Herald and Flatwater Free Press first reported on the new appointments last week.
‘No preconceived notions’
Like Clements and Pillen, Linehan and Briese reject the idea that they’re in this for politics.
“I arrive really with no preconceived notions as to where they’ve been, where they should be going, other than look at the data, look at the numbers objectively and see where they lead us,” Briese told the Examiner.
Added Linehan: “I’m hoping, mostly, that I learn a lot and that we can get closer to what the actual numbers are versus what we forecast.”
State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood. April 10, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In addition to Briese and Linehan, Tim Wilson, a retired certified public accountant from Omaha, joins the board. Pillen reappointed Matt Miltenberger, who was campaign manager and chief of staff for former Gov. Pete Ricketts.
The three departing board members are:

Former state Sen. John Kuehn of Heartwell, a legislative ally of Ricketts. Ricketts had appointed Kuehn to the forecasting board shortly after Kuehn left office in January 2019.
Thomas Henning, a Kearney businessman who had been on the forecasting board since 2010.
Leslie Andersen, a banker from Bennington who had been on the board since 2002.

Despite their disagreements, Stinner, Clements, Linehan and Briese agree on the importance of an accurate forecast, which in part sets a ceiling for state spending. 
Missed revenue targets can lead to unexpected surpluses, or to the predicament Nebraska faces now: an approximately $208 million deficit through June 2027, which must be addressed next year.
The Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board meets for its April 2025 meeting to revise economic projections for the state. (Screenshot of Nebraska Public Media livestream)
If the shortfall isn’t fixed, it would grow to almost $847 million by July 2029, according to the latest state projections confirmed in July.
These figures will be revised at the Oct. 30 meeting and set the stage for the 2027 legislative session, where the budget, as it has for the past two years, will likely dominate debate. The figures will again be revised in February and April as the budget-writing process moves forward.
“I’m glad that the Appropriations Committee just can’t say, ‘I think we’ll just raise the forecast a little bit, that should make it a lot easier,’” Clements said. He said the forecasting board process is better than the Legislature deciding spending based on its own revenue forecasts.
What’s in a forecast?
State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, who faces reelection this fall, seeks to chair the Legislature’s Revenue Committee next year. He came to Pillen’s defense as he faced reporters’ questions Friday about the budget and forecasting board at an unrelated news conference.
State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, center, meets with, from left, state Sens. Dave Murman of Glenvil, Barry DeKay of Niobrara, Steve Halloran of Hastings, Steve Erdman of Bayard and Brian Hardin of Gering. Feb. 23, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Jacobson said the forecasting board had more “rose-colored glasses” and overforecasted revenue in part because of higher-than-expected tax refunds as a result of federal changes.
“I don’t think it’s a bad thing putting money into our residents’ pockets,” Jacobson said.
Pillen has long said that because Nebraska cut income taxes, it must cut spending as well.
After the news conference, Jacobson said Briese and Linehan will be a “welcome addition because they understand how the sausage is made.” 
Board members receive a plethora of data before each meeting and receive a briefing from economists from the Legislative Fiscal Office and Nebraska Department of Revenue. Jacobson called the forecasters the “boots on the ground” who add nuance to the economic picture.
Former state Sen. Lou Ann Linehan of the Elkhorn area, center, and Superintendent John Schwartz of Millard Public Schools, at right, during a meeting of the School Financing Review Commission. Aug. 12, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
All nine members anonymously write down their projections for tax revenues for the current fiscal year and each year of the following biennium. This is done four times, for sales and use taxes, individual income taxes, corporate income taxes and miscellaneous taxes.
Once estimates are submitted, an average is calculated. The board can remove outliers, if there are any, but is not required to. A board member can then motion to accept a projection as the board’s consensus. 
It takes a simple majority to accept a projection — five votes.
The state has seen revenues more closely match projections the past two months after multiple months where revenues missed the mark. Jacobson said he expects continued improvement. Clements said that while he’s seen improvements, he predicts an increase in Nebraska’s shortfall.
‘Cook the books’
But while Jacobson, Clements and the appointees are confident politics weren’t part of the appointments, others are more skeptical, including outgoing state Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha, who said they’re a “clear attempt” to impact the board’s decisions. 
State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha, right, hugs state Sen. Ashlei Spivey of Omaha, who gave Cavanaugh a tribute speech marking her eight years of legislative service. April 10, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
She pointed to a social media post from a colleague, state Sen. Ashlei Spivey of Omaha, who wrote: “As the saying goes, ‘It is easier to cook the books when you pick the chefs.’” Cavanaugh and Spivey serve on the Appropriations Committee with Clements.
Cavanaugh said she “1,000%” would agree that someone such as Linehan is her own person and won’t take marching orders, but she said the “catch” is how aligned Linehan is with Pillen.
“She was selected because she has the same objective, and that is to put more money to property tax relief, to keep the tax cuts that she implemented that have put us in this position … both that she was the architect of, to keep those in place and force the Legislature to cut funding to direct services as a result,” Cavanaugh said.
 But Linehan said the conversation with Pillen’s staff was whether she was willing to serve, “end of conversation.”
“There was no other additional ‘This is what we can do,’” Linehan said. “That is all just made up in people’s minds. And I don’t believe, after watching Tom Briese and Lou Ann Linehan, that anybody thinks we would do that.”
“Certainly no instructions, marching orders, even recommendations or suggestions,” Briese said.
‘There’s enough checks and balances’
Stinner, a Republican, also blamed Linehan’s legislation for repeated deficits, and he criticized Clements for more closely toeing the line on the governor’s budget proposal. He said lawmakers need to assert their independence on the governor’s recommendation, which he said is just that.
State Sens. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha, Ashlei Spivey of Omaha and Mike Jacobson of North Platte meet on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. Jan. 9, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Clements said that like Linehan and Briese, he was independent and did what he felt was best for the state. He and Jacobson said Linehan and Briese are also just two of nine votes.
“They can let their opinion be made, and they can make a motion for a rosier picture, but they would need five votes in agreement with what they’re proposing,” Clements said. “There’s enough checks and balances there that it isn’t likely to affect an outcome of the forecast.”
Linehan said her record in decades in public service, including with the U.S. State Department and as a chief of staff to former U.S. Sen. Chuck Hagel, speaks for itself: “I try to find the right answers. I ask tough questions, and I challenge information I don’t think is accurate.”
A different forecast?
In addition to pulling out outliers, there’s another caveat to the forecast: The Legislature is under no obligation to accept the forecast when drafting the next budget.
Stinner and Keisha Patent, who leads the Legislative Fiscal Office, confirmed that is an option. No Appropriations Committee chair has used that authority, Patent said, to her knowledge.
State Sen. Rob Clements of Elmwood, left, and Keisha Patent, director of the Legislative Fiscal Office, address lawmakers at a pre-session legislative retreat in Kearney on Friday, Dec. 13, 2024. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Stinner said he never felt a need to sidestep the board. He went to meetings, watched the board’s work and “had no problems with what the outcome was.” Clements, too, never used the authority. He said he didn’t know that was an option or that the board could remove outliers.
The budget shortfall also includes a legislatively estimated spending increase of about 2.4% in the next two years, nearly $400 million in total. The Legislative Fiscal Office, at the direction of the Legislature’s Appropriations and Revenue Committee, projected that figure.
Pillen, while he incorrectly blamed the forecasting board for the spending estimate, said a spending increase is “not happening as long as I’m your governor.” 
During his time in office, spending has increased each year, according to data from the Nebraska State Treasurer’s Office. Though reports on Nebraska’s “general fund,” the state’s main checking account, show decreases, that’s in part because of more spending of federal funds and across state cash funds. Some cash funds were swept to shore up the general fund.
The November election
Pillen’s Democratic opponent, former state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, said in a statement that Pillen had “stacked” the advisory board “with the same people who helped him write his tax plan and the reason we are in the budget crisis today.” Walz came in at the same time as Linehan and Briese in 2017, overlapping all six years with Stinner as Appropriations chair.
“Nebraskans deserve the truth about the state of their budget — not appointees who will project inaccurate numbers to make the governor look good before the election in November,” Walz said.
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen of Columbus, a Republican, top left, is running for reelection against former Democratic state Sen. Lynne Walz of Fremont, top right, Rick Beard of Omaha, the nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, bottom left, and former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, the nominee for the America First Party, bottom right. (Photos courtesy of the candidates/campaigns | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Stinner has added another quirk to this year’s governor’s race: He’s endorsed Walz. He said that decision wasn’t made lightly and came from a “realistic viewpoint” about the budget.
Pillen, too, has touted cross-partisan endorsements, such as former state Sen. Heath Mello of Omaha, leader of the Omaha Chamber of Commerce.
Multiple senators told the Examiner that by Oct. 30, many voters will have voted or made up their minds, regardless of the forecast, so they discounted the electoral stakes of Linehan and Briese joining the board.
The governor said the $400 million spending estimate is one quick area to solve. On top of a total $21 billion budget over the next three years, he said Friday, that’s something in the business world that he and Jacobson know “you solve that percentage before breakfast.”
“Only politicians who want their name in the paper are trying to make something of that, make sense?” Pillen said. “Not asking you to agree with it, but hopefully it makes sound, simple mathematic sense.”
‘Confidence in our result’
State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, the current Revenue Committee chair, also downplayed the roles of Linehan and Briese. He wrote in an opinion piece in the Omaha World-Herald that neither the governor nor any state senator is motivated to encourage a specific forecast.
“The fact that these two former senators are fiscal hawks should not in any way taint their reputations, their future efforts, nor predict any particular outcomes,” von Gillern wrote, saying the “worst thing” any forecaster could do is come to an inaccurate projection, politics aside.
State Sen. Brad von Gillern of the Elkhorn area, left, talks with state Sen. Jane Raybould of Lincoln on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. April 1, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Von Gillern faces his own tough reelection bid against Cindy Maxwell-Ostdiek, a registered nonpartisan whom von Gillern faced in 2022, a different time economically and politically. If von Gillern is not reelected, Jacobson said he would run for speaker of the Legislature and not Revenue chair, confirming months of speculation that von Gillern might seek the speakership.
While hopeful for an improved projection, von Gillern echoed Jacobson, Patent, Stinner and others: “The right number is the right number, and the Legislature will budget accordingly.”
Briese said he’s seen some of the negative comments on his appointment but is focused on doing his best and remaining objective. He said he has the utmost respect for outgoing members and believes it’s important that people have confidence in the forecasting process and result.
“It’s likewise important to conduct ourselves and conduct our work in a manner that generates that confidence in our process and confidence in our result.”
Nebraska Examiner reporter Erin Bamer contributed to this report.

title: North Dakota college enrollment stable
description: North Dakota’s 11 public colleges and universities reported 47,377 students for the fall semester, with enrollment leveling off after several years of growth. The University System had 47,522 students at this time last fall, 145 more than this year. The biggest decline in number of students came at North Dakota State University, which saw enrollment […]
text:
Students walk through the North Dakota State University campus in Fargo on Aug. 28, 2026. The college saw a 3% decline in enrollment from the previous fall. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)North Dakota’s 11 public colleges and universities reported 47,377 students for the fall semester, with enrollment leveling off after several years of growth.
The University System had 47,522 students at this time last fall, 145 more than this year.
The biggest decline in number of students came at North Dakota State University, which saw enrollment fall by 343 students to 11,609. 
After being hired in March, NDSU President Marshall Stewart set a goal of growing enrollment to more than 15,000 students.  
The University of North Dakota recorded its seventh straight year of enrollment growth. The state’s largest college has 15,908 students for the fall semester. 
Janelle Kilgore, UND vice provost for strategic enrollment management, said the freshman class could have been larger, but limited space in some programs meant a slightly smaller first-year class than 2025. 
She also pointed to strong retention from last year’s freshman class, with 82% of students returning for their sophomore year. 
Kilgore made her comments to the Legislature’s Higher Education Institution Committee that was met Tuesday in Grand Forks on the UND campus. 
North Dakota University System Commissioner Brent Sanford. (Photo provided by North Dakota University System)
Bismarck State College gained 119 students. Valley City State University and Dakota College at Bottineau also reported increases. 
University System Commissioner Brent Sanford, who presented to legislators Tuesday in Grand Forks, noted that enrollment growth or declines were small at most campuses. 
He said more high school students enrolled in dual-credit courses and slightly fewer international students in North Dakota colleges 
Sanford said nationwide college enrollment is down more 11.5% since 2011 while North Dakota is down 2.7%, though the state has been trending upward in recent years. 
Other states are experiencing an “enrollment cliff,” Sanford said, with states such as Minnesota and Iowa seeing a significant decline in high school graduates.

text:
A backyard chicken raised to lay eggs. (Photo by Jared Strong/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship confirmed a case of the highly pathogenic avian influenza in Boone County, marking the state’s seventh detection of the bird flu in 2026. 
The outbreak occurred in a backyard, mixed species flock of 138 birds, according to IDALS.
Iowa has not reported a case of the H5N1 bird flu since March, when it logged two backyard flock outbreaks. None of the 2026 outbreaks in Iowa have been in commercial poultry flocks. 
The current outbreak of the highly pathogenic avian flu started in February 2022 and since then has impacted more than 30 million birds in Iowa and more than 208 million birds nationally, according to the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service with the U.S. Department of Agriculture. 
IDALS urged poultry owners to continue “bolstering” their biosecurity practices and to contact their veterinarians immediately if they suspect birds are sick with the virus.
