name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Judge rules Chatham County data center can proceed despite moratorium
description: At least 30 local governments across North Carolina have passed moratoria on data center development in recent months.
text:
A server room in a data center. (Photo by Getty Images)A Chatham County data center project will move forward despite the county’s moratorium, following a court decision. 
In February, Chatham County commissioners enacted a year-long moratorium on new data centers. The ban remains in effect until Feb. 11, 2027, or until new zoning regulations are adopted — whichever comes first. 
But it won’t stop at least one new data center from getting underway. Data center developer Eco TIP West plans to build a 750-megawatt data center at the Triangle Innovation Point West business park near Moncure. 
The developer sued the county in April, arguing that its project was already in progress when county commissioners approved the moratorium, and therefore should have been exempted. 
Superior Court Judge John Morris ruled last week in favor of the developer.
“After careful consideration of the file, counsels’ legal briefs, Plaintiff’s motion for summary judgment, and the exhibits and arguments of counsel during the August 31 hearing, the Court finds that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that Plaintiff is entitled to a judgment in its favor as a matter of law,” Morris wrote. 
Three more NC localities weigh pauses on data centers as developer backs away from Raleigh project

The company spent $11 million on the project, according to its court filing. The developer noted in its lawsuit that the zoning of the intended site permitted its use for a data center, and said it had been working with the county in good faith before the moratorium was passed.
Morris ruled that Chatham County must pay damages to Eco TIP for trying to slow down work on the project. 
“The Moratorium, and the County’s refusal to recognize that Eco TIP’s existing data center project is exempt, has and continues to cause Eco TIP substantial financial and other losses,” the developer’s lawyers wrote in a brief. “The county did not simply make one mistake but violated almost every applicable statute and governing legal principle. In short, the Moratorium is a legal trainwreck that should have never been approved, and never been applied, to take away Eco TIP’s property rights in its project.”
At least 30 local governments across North Carolina have passed moratoria on data center development in recent months. It’s unclear how this lawsuit will affect other bans.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Electric cable manufacturer plans $400M expansion in SC
description: A company that makes high-voltage electrical cable is expanding its manufacturing plant in South Carolina.
text:
(Photo by Gregory Thomas/USDA)A company that makes high-voltage electrical cable for utilities, solar, rail and more is expanding its manufacturing plant in Orangeburg, with plans to hire more than 100 new employees.
The Okonite Company announced Tuesday it would invest $400 million in a new, 552,000-square-foot building on its existing site near the Orangeburg Municipal airport.
South Carolina will spend $1.5 million in grant funding on the site, building a rail spur, grading and constructing the plant.
The county approved a reduced property tax rate over the next 30 years. Laws passed in 2017 and 2021 effectively lowered the property tax rate on manufacturers from 10.5% to 6%. This proposed deal takes the rate even lower — to 4% — plus additional incentives to further buy down the company’s tax bill an average of 25% over the life of the deal. 
“We are truly grateful for Okonite and the commitment they have shown to Orangeburg County over the years,” Orangeburg County Council Chairman Johnnie Wright said in a statement.
He said Okonite’s pledge to expand means “more quality jobs right here at home.”
The company will pay an average wage of $33 per hour, “well above the state and local average,” said the county’s economic development director Ty Davenport. The state average is $28.50 per hour, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
“They’re one of the premier employers in the county,” Davenport said.
Construction on Okonite’s cable manufacturing plant will begin later this year and is expected to take two to three years to complete.
Founded in 1878, Okonite is one of the oldest electrical wire insulating companies in the United States, with 34 locations nationwide. The massive cable it makes even runs power to the Statue of Liberty.
The expansion comes amid major investments by utility companies to upgrade the country’s aging electric grid.
SC utility regulators set January deadline for decision on Dominion, NextEra merger

Analyses by industry groups and utility watchdogs of capital spending plans filed by 51 investor-owned utilities show an estimated $1.4 trillion investment through 2030, half of which will go to transmission and power lines. A little less than half that spending is concentrated in southern states.
Charlotte-headquartered Duke Energy is slated to be the top spender, with nearly $103 billion on the books. Florida-based NextEra and Virginia-based Dominion Energy, which are in talks for a $67 billion mega-merger, are both also in the top 10, planning to spend $94 billion and $65 billion respectively.

name: Delaware
title: Delaware Supreme Court upholds permanent absentee voting
description: Justices say voters must qualify for each election; challengers question how the state checks whether they still do DOVER, Del. — The Delaware Supreme Court upheld the state’s permanent absentee voting law Monday, clearing the way for qualified voters on the permanent absentee list to receive ballots for the Nov. 3 general election. The ruling leaves lawmake[...]
text:
The court drew a distinction between receiving a ballot and being legally entitled to cast it.  Today, permanent absentee voting procedures rely in part on voters reporting changes and affirming that they remain eligible. Hocker and Washington argued the checks are insufficient. The court said the Constitution leaves the choice of election safeguards to the General Assembly.
Justices say voters must qualify for each election; challengers question how the state checks whether they still do
DOVER, Del. — The Delaware Supreme Court upheld the state’s permanent absentee voting law Monday, clearing the way for qualified voters on the permanent absentee list to receive ballots for the Nov. 3 general election. The ruling leaves lawmakers with a policy question: How much should election officials do to verify that a voter’s reason for voting absentee still applies?
In a unanimous decision, the justices said the law does not expand absentee voting beyond the categories allowed by the Delaware Constitution. Permanent absentee status allows a voter to receive a ballot automatically, but it does not allow someone whose circumstances have changed to cast that ballot, the court said.
Why the law was challenged
State Sen. Gerald Hocker and fellow Senate candidate Steven Washington argued that a voter who qualified for one election could continue receiving ballots years later without election officials adequately confirming that the original reason still applied.
The Constitution permits absentee voting when a registered voter cannot appear at a polling place for a specified reason, including illness, physical disability, certain work or public service obligations, vacation or religious observance. The permanent absentee law applies to a narrower group, including voters with qualifying illnesses or disabilities, military service obligations or jobs that require constant care for a relative.
Must voters qualify again?
Hocker and Washington focused on the Constitution’s language about a voter’s inability to appear at a particular election. An illness can end, a caregiving responsibility can change and public service can conclude. They argued that automatically sending another ballot places too much weight on an earlier application and on the voter’s willingness to report a change.
The justices agreed that a voter must qualify to vote absentee in each election. They rejected the argument that the Constitution requires the state to recertify each permanent absentee voter before every election.
How the state checks eligibility
The court drew a distinction between receiving a ballot and being legally entitled to cast it. The law requires permanent absentee voters to report changes affecting their eligibility. The Department of Elections sends reminders before election cycles, removes voters from the permanent absentee list in specified circumstances and requires voters to affirm their eligibility when returning each ballot.
Those procedures rely in part on voters reporting changes and affirming that they remain eligible. Hocker and Washington argued the checks are insufficient. The court said the Constitution leaves the choice of election safeguards to the General Assembly.
The challengers sought to invalidate the law in all its applications. To prevail, they had to show it could not operate constitutionally. Imperfect procedures do not meet that standard when eligible voters can use the law, the justices said.
What the ruling means for voters
Voting rights advocates emphasized the law’s value to people whose qualifying circumstances persist. In a statement after the ruling, the Delaware Voting Rights Coalition said permanent absentee voting helps eligible voters with disabilities, illnesses, caregiving duties and other qualifying obligations participate without submitting a new application for every election.
The ruling differs from the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision striking down Delaware’s no-excuse vote-by-mail law. That law allowed people outside the Constitution’s absentee voting categories to vote by mail. The permanent absentee law, the justices found, serves only a subset of voters within those categories.
A Superior Court judge ruled against permanent absentee voting in 2024, but the Supreme Court vacated that decision because the plaintiffs lacked standing. Monday’s decision reached the constitutional issue and upheld the law. The Department of Elections says it is sending permanent absentee voters their general election ballots.
TO GO

Who: Delaware voters who qualify for permanent absentee voting.
What: Voters already on the permanent absentee list will automatically receive a ballot for the Nov. 3 general election. They must still qualify to vote absentee when they cast it.
Check your status: Visit iVote.de.gov. “Indefinite” means you are on the permanent absentee list.
Request a ballot: Eligible voters can apply through iVote.de.gov or contact their county elections office.
Deadline: Completed absentee ballots must reach the county elections office by 8 p.m. on Election Day.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: You’ll do anything for your baby. The algorithm knows how to exploit that.
description: This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th. Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. This piece was published in coordination with The Washington Post. The madness unfolded in a familiar pattern: Ellen FitzGerald would wake in the dead of night to nurse her baby for […]
text:
Bringing home a bundle of joy in America today unleashes a digital onslaught of advertisements pushing products, services and apps that target mothers most fiercely, with a clear promise: The gadget that will solve all your parenting puzzles is just a click away. (Tara Anand for the 19th)
This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th.  Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
This piece was published in coordination with The Washington Post.
The madness unfolded in a familiar pattern: Ellen FitzGerald would wake in the dead of night to nurse her baby for about a half hour, then hand him off to Dad to rock another half hour. Carefully, ever so gently, Dad would lay little Rowan back in his bassinet.
Instantly, Rowan’s body would stiffen, his mouth splitting open in a roar that restarted the rocking process. This would happen sometimes three, even four times a night until the FitzGeralds wanted to scream at each other, the heavens and anyone they knew who didn’t tell them what having a newborn would be like.
But there was no one there to hear them — except the algorithm.
As she scrolled to keep herself awake, FitzGerald’s phone responded with a stream of solutions. Teach your baby to sleep with this $179 course. Keep your baby asleep with this $1,995 smart baby bed. Track your baby’s breathing and chest movements while he sleeps with this $289.99 baby monitor.
A handful of times in the middle of the night, FitzGerald and her husband debated buying these purported miracle products in strained whispers. They purchased at least a dozen different types of swaddles in the hopes that Rowan — who like a baby Houdini would pop his arms out of every enclosure, waking himself and his parents — would finally rest in the bassinet instead of their arms.
FitzGerald felt like the algorithm knew she was struggling. It knew she was not as prepared for parenting as she thought.
“The algorithm completely clocks that,” she said.
Bringing home a bundle of joy in America today unleashes a digital onslaught of advertisements pushing products, services and apps that target mothers most fiercely, with a clear promise: The gadget that will solve all your parenting puzzles is just a click away.
That proposition is enticing for a generation that is raising kids unlike any other. Parents today lack community. They are less likely to be living near family who could help them through those early sleep-deprived months. They are having kids later in life and having fewer of them. And most American moms have just weeks with their infants before they’re back at work.
In these conditions, the $60 billion baby product market has found its stride. Parents are made to believe that if they have the right things — the things all their friends are buying or the ones that mom on Instagram suggested — their babies will sleep. They will eat. They will be safe.
And the parents, in turn, will have done it all right. They will be the perfect parents to the perfect baby.

Moms’ phones respond with a stream of solutions for their newborns: Teach your baby to sleep with a $179 course. Keep your baby asleep with a $1,995 smart baby bed. Track your baby’s breathing and chest movements while he sleeps with a $289.99 baby monitor. (Tara Anand for The 19th)
It’s a quest that can start to feel like a trap. FitzGerald spent much of Rowan’s first year tracking every wake up, every feed and every diaper change on an app, hoping the data would help her understand why her baby wouldn’t sleep. It felt like a digital timeline of her motherhood — all the gaps in his sleep examples of where she may have failed.
“I thought I could get an ‘A’ in parenting a newborn,” said FitzGerald, 38, a retired ballet dancer and “recovering perfectionist.”
Emily Oster, an economist and the author of several best-selling parenting books, said the pressure on moms to chase perfection — particularly in a society that is having fewer kids — is omnipresent. For moms who are having kids older, when their life or career may be more established, having a child may feel like another thing they’re being assessed on.
“Doing it ‘really good’ means doing all the best stuff. That makes you very susceptible to the marketing pitch of, ‘Thing X is the best,’” Oster said. “We sort of get into a situation where you kind of feel like you have to do these things because they’re the best, and if you don’t do them, then you have ruined your child forever.”
Moms know that the world stands ready to judge them for any minor misstep; that part isn’t new. The internet has just gotten smarter about capitalizing on those insecurities, making moms believe that they need to project good parenting through good purchases, even when they can’t afford it.
Nina Bandelj, author of “Overinvested: The Emotional Economy of Modern Parenting,” said that for mothers, every little buying decision can feel like a reflection of who they are as parents. “These moves and purchases are entangled in both: We do something for our children, but aren’t we also thinking, ‘What will make me a good parent? What should a good parent do? What will others say? What do others do?’” she said. “The industry is good at emphasizing and playing on all of those.”
And the marketing starts in the most fragile, tender period for a young family.
Many of the more than a dozen mothers The 19th spoke to described the newborn days as the most disorienting of their lives. They felt disconnected from the instincts they were told they should have. They were lost. They were exhausted. And these products and services promised to save them.
“What’s the replacement for real, actual support?” FitzGerald said. “It’s things. It’s products.”
Of course she hit “add to cart.”
At the Prego Expo in Orlando, Florida, this spring, a conference center ballroom was stuffed with strollers, pacifiers, baby bottles and a few items the attending parents had likely never considered: a silicone tether that keeps tiny utensils from tumbling to the floor, a “dad bag.”
Lines of expectant parents formed for anything free, the day’s soundtrack the rattle of a perpetually spinning raffle wheel.
The parents at Prego Expo were navigating a baby product market that only keeps growing, driven in part by shoppers seeking more premium products. But as big-box baby retailers have disappeared, so has the experience of pushing a stroller or buckling a car seat at a store. So some parents flock to events like the Prego Expo, which by the end of the year will have hit seven major cities, to answer a critical question: What do I actually need to have a baby?
But, much like online, the options at such expos are endless, expensive and, if you don’t pick the right one, it “makes you feel like you’re a bad mom,” said Rachel Riling, who visited the Orlando convention from Savannah, Georgia, a four-hour drive away.
We got here, to this mega-consumption, maximum-guilt stage of parenting because of big cultural shifts that changed the way Americans raise kids.
In the baby boom after World War II, new parents felt an enormous pressure to raise the generation that would marshal the country’s post-war prosperity. To get there, an idea in the scientific community began to go culturally mainstream: Beyond just caring for children, parents should shape them. Investing in them from the time they were infants could set them up for success later.
In 1946, pediatrician Dr. Benjamin Spock published “The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care,” the first guide that encouraged a style of parenting that centered children’s feelings rather than the more authoritarian approach that had long been the norm. (In 1929, the experts at the U.S. government’s Children’s Bureau offered this tip: A baby should learn that “habitual crying will only cause his parents to ignore him.”)
Spock’s advice — that children be hugged, told they’re special and loved, fed when they’re hungry and disciplined with words — was radical. His book went on to sell more than 50 million copies. Publishers dubbed it the “child-rearing Bible,” and it displaced other sources of advice — including the government — as the top authority on parenting.
And what did this new generation of doting, nurturing parents do? They spent money on their children.
In the 1950s, the baby product market experienced a growth spurt. Disposable diapers were developed, the baby food market exploded and infant formula popularity ballooned. By the 1980s the country was going through another baby boom, and the industry bounded into an era of designer-brand infant clothing, stylish nursery furniture and increasingly intricate baby exercise gyms.
“Out of the millions and millions of things available for adults, multiply that by five or six times and that’s what you’ve got available for your children,” one dad told The Los Angeles Times in 1987.
By that time, parents, both high- and low-income ones, were convinced that they could give their children the biggest head start possible by buying them the right things.
At the turn of this century, as the birth rate began its freefall, parents having fewer kids started to feel more anxiety about getting it exactly right each time. By then, the amount parents spent on their kids was rising, and everything lined up: The market responded by offering even more premium products, more solves, more options.
And the internet gave a platform to the people best positioned to shepherd advice-hungry mothers into the new parenting age. Enter the mommy bloggers.
Candor was the super power of the first wave of mommy bloggers in the early 2000s. They gave women permission to talk about the difficult, even ugly sides of parenting. They also gave them permission to rely on one another. “Admitting that this job isn’t always easy doesn’t make somebody a bad mother. At least, it shouldn’t. We’re all on this ride together,” wrote the late Jill Smokler, the founder of “Scary Mommy,” one of the most influential mommy blogs of the aughts.
Their relatability turned them into authorities on all things babies. In addition to offering tips on sleep training and feeding, they also became powerful product pushers. Eventually, mommy bloggers began to capitalize on the relationship they built with readers, monetizing their advice by working with brands to review products and share their favorites.
Instagram’s rollout in 2010 birthed the curated, edited reboot of mommy bloggers — momfluencers. They seemed to have it more together, more figured out. And they wanted to sell you their secret.
As the platform evolved, its algorithm only became better and better at ensuring these momfluencers got on your screen as soon as it detected you were pregnant. Maybe it was the pregnancy announcement photo you posted or the gender reveal video you lingered on for more than a few seconds; it’s enough to indicate to the algorithm that it should start pulling up more nursery videos, more momfluencers and more baby products.
This year, NielsenIQ and baby product brand Momcozy did a survey of 1,240 mothers and expectant first-time mothers in the United States. Fifty-eight percent said information overload was creating pressure when purchasing baby products. Moms’ top source for information on these products? Social media.
But we can’t just blame the internet. America created the conditions for this mass consumption —  where moms stand bump to bump in stuffy conference centers comparing pacifier models — because of a policy decision.

When moms go back to work after parental leave, their babies are still waking multiple times a night. Moms are often still figuring out feeding, nap schedules, developmental milestones and just about everything else. To achieve a life that doesn’t feel like a 24-hour circus, working parents lean on solutions they can access from their phones. (Tara Anand for The 19th)
By the 2000s, nearly every industrialized nation had developed a paid leave policy that allowed parents to stay home for months — up to a year in some places — with their infants, giving them more room to adjust to parenting, learn their children’s needs and troubleshoot the tough stuff. The United States is the only outlier. To this day, it remains the only industrialized nation to offer no such policy.
That means most U.S. mothers return to work within two months of giving birth. That’s no time at all in baby world. Two-month-olds are still waking multiple times a night, their parents are still in the throes of sleep deprivation. Moms are often still figuring out feeding, nap schedules, developmental milestones and just about everything else.
To achieve a life that doesn’t feel like a 24-hour circus, working parents lean on solutions they can access from their phones. The United States accounts for roughly 10 percent of all global baby product revenue, though it’s home to just 4 percent of the world population. Only China draws in a larger share of the global revenue (14 percent), but with a population four times the size of the United States. By 2033, the U.S. market is expected to grow another 40 percent, and the fastest growth will be in one sector: online purchases.
Raena Boston, a mom of three who founded the Working Momtras, an online community for mothers, said the only time she didn’t experience postpartum depression was with her third child, the only one with whom she had six months of paid leave. “The bottom line is we do not have enough time with our infants, period,” she said.
“We wait longer, we have less children, everything feels compressed and like you have only one opportunity to get it right,” said Boston, 38. “There is a market for people to prey upon that, to seize upon those anxieties and fears of, ‘Here, just buy this thing. You just need this product, and you’re gonna have an optimal kid.’”
In the eyes of these moms, “good parents put their children first,” Bandelj wrote in her book. “And good parents show how much they love their children by how they spend, save, invest or borrow for them.”
Bandelj interviewed 120 parents for her book, and she heard over and over again from moms that “children are at the center of their universe,” she said.
None of these words came from dads.
Like many new parents, Rachel Martin took a class at her local hospital in St. Louis, Missouri, before the birth of her son. It touched on how to prepare for labor and feed the baby. But on sleep, she got only a warning: “It’s a war zone, good luck.”
A class couldn’t have adequately prepared her for the fear that seeps in for many parents once the sun begins to set, the baby edition of Russian roulette. Will your baby refuse to sleep, plunging you deeper into a state of insurmountable sleep deprivation — or, totally randomly, sleep for hours?
It’s here where the baby marketing industry swoops in most effectively. Parents told The 19th that sleep products felt the most predatory because so much of the marketing banked on people’s inexperience and exhaustion.
The products and courses are also some of the most expensive on the market. The Snoo, a robotic bassinet that can detect crying or fussing, soothing babies to sleep with automated rocking and white noise, costs $1,995. You can also rent it, starting at $159 a month. Influencer Cara Dumaplin’s Taking Cara Babies course, which promises to teach parents how to train their infants to sleep independently from as early as five months, costs $179. She has 2.8 million Instagram followers.
For some parents, these products and courses improved their postpartum lives.
But Martin felt like she was being bamboozled. So many of the Instagram posts she saw showed tips on each slide, but when she scrolled to the last one there was almost always an upsell: “But for my No. 1 tip, you gotta buy this.”
“They have the secrets and I need them — that’s what it felt like,” Martin said.
Three months into new parenthood, Martin was still getting only a couple of hours of sleep every night. She was willing to consider anything that would help her and her son sleep better.
Martin opted for a $57 course that promised to establish good sleep habits and gradually teach the baby —  with minimal crying — to sleep independently. But shortly after she started watching the videos that came with it, she realized she wasn’t learning anything she didn’t already know. Bedtime routines, red night-lights that won’t overstimulate the baby — she knew this from other (free) parenting advice she read. “I was frustrated with myself,” said Martin, 34. “I was influenced to spend money on services to not have my baby cry.”
She unfollowed the creator, a mom and sleep consultant certified through the Institute of Pediatric Sleep and Parenting, an online accreditor that is not recognized by the U.S. Department of Education.
On Long Island, Sarah Moeller was influenced to buy many items when she had her first daughter, who is now 8. Maybe the most outlandish was a vibrating paddle that slipped under the mattress to lull her baby to sleep. But rather than a gentle rocking, it shook the crib so violently that it tapdanced across her laminate floor.
“Before having children, everybody thinks that they remember or that they know what it’s like to be tired,” said Moeller, 41. “We all think we know what it is to go without sleep for a little while, but I have not ever experienced something comparable.” The algorithm responded to that. In those first months with a newborn, Moeller said she “felt very wronged” by advertising and messages online.
“Sleep deprivation is a form of torture, and I think that really plays into our spending habits,” said Dr. Leah Rappaport, a Boston pediatrician who is also a content creator. Rappaport had her children while she and her husband were still in their medical residency, and she found herself buying every major sleep product out there: the Snoo, the Taking Cara Babies course, the swaddles. “I was a pediatrician, and I was absolutely floored by having a child,” said Rappaport, 41.

In those first unmooring months of life with their newborns, moms are sucked into the online world of algorithms not just because they’re desperate, but because they need community. (Tara Anand for The 19th)
In those first unmooring months, moms are sucked into the online world of algorithms not just because they’re desperate, but because they need community.
“You’re alone by yourself in the middle of the night with a baby, and there’s someone else who is experiencing that,” Rappaport said. “And I think that that’s where that power is for the product placement.”
To get these courses and products in front of expectant parents at just the right time — before their brand loyalties are cemented and when they’re more likely to buy impulsively — companies have mined customer data for years.
More than a decade ago, Target started identifying which shoppers may be pregnant by analyzing changes in their spending habits. Target learned that pregnant people were more likely to buy unscented lotions and vitamin supplements in the second trimester. Those insights allowed them to assign a pregnancy prediction score to customers. By 2012, that system was already so advanced that Target could predict a customer’s due date window and send coupons and ads to match their stage of pregnancy.
On other sites, any pregnancy data that moms share — like the date of their last period, often put into a due date calculator — can be sold to advertisers. Pregnancy sites like BabyCenter have turned this into something of a science. Moms come for the handy calculator, stay for the newsletter on developmental milestones and the forums, and get their data packaged for the website’s sponsors who can then use it to send personalized ads. One of the most popular options for advertisers: slapping ads for baby products onto articles listing baby name ideas, where moms spend more time perusing, historian Lara Freidenfelds found in her book “The Myth of the Perfect Pregnancy.”
“In featuring baby name articles so early, BabyCenter is trading on women’s excitement, encouraging them to be highly involved and emotionally attached to their pregnancies, and bringing them into contact with a panoply of advertisers at an early stage of pregnancy,” she wrote.
Christine Mattheis, the vice president of content and brand solutions at BabyCenter, said the site does collect information from users, including their due dates, “and uses it to deliver stage-tailored content and relevant advertising.”
“We disclose our practices transparently in onboarding and our privacy policy, and we provide tools for users to manage their advertising preferences,” she said.
However, several of the major baby websites, including BabyCenter, Babylist and The Bump, have been accused of allegedly sharing user data without consent. A lawsuit against Babylist filed last year claims the website allowed third parties including Meta and Google to access user data input during the sign-up process “to help Babylist assist its marketing, advertising, and data analytics efforts.” Attorneys are still investigating allegations against Babylist; affected parents who file a claim may be entitled to as much as $10,000.
On social media, creators have gotten more sophisticated about converting viewers to buyers through applications like Manychat. A creator may put something in the caption of a video like, “Comment sleep and I’ll send you my top sleep tips!” Manychat runs the back end, and when that comment comes in, the user immediately gets a link in their DMs with the tips, course or products being promoted. The company said it sends billions of these messages a year.
Those sometimes include what are known as “deep links” for, say, Amazon. Clicking those takes prospective buyers not just to the Amazon website but directly to the Amazon app where they’re already signed in, making the conversion to a purchase as simple as possible.
The DM links also give brands a channel to contact you — they can follow up with more messages and more items, said Paige Connell, a content creator who specializes in talking about the mental load of motherhood.
Connell said all of this targeted marketing is deeply gendered. Women control about 85 percent of household purchases and for decades have been the object of advertisers’ affections. They’ve been targeted through daytime TV ads, magazines and, now, social media, where content is fed on a continuous loop.
“The second I became pregnant, my Instagram feed became heavily about pregnancy and babies, and my husband’s remained about woodworking and golf,” Connell said.
No wonder Mom feels like she’s on a “perfect mom hamster wheel,” she said. “We are marketed to so heavily and then criticized for following through.”
In the quest for perfect parenting, it’s easy to find yourself drowning under a pile of Amazon boxes. But what we buy our kids actually matters very little.
In the United States, where babies have more access than those in other places to the really important stuff — enough to eat, a stable environment and someone who loves them — parents are already giving their kids just about everything they need to succeed. To give it a number, they’re about 95 percent of the way there, Oster said. So it actually doesn’t matter which toy subscription box you sign up for (or if you sign up for one at all).
“It’s such a funny conversation, because there is a set of people who are obsessively trying to optimize on the last 5 percent, or maybe 2 percent or 1 percent … when there is vast space for improving the lives of kids that has kind of nothing to do with the conversations that we’re having over here. That’s a real tension in this space. Most of the time, when people ask me, ‘How do I do blah optimally?’ the answer is, ‘It does not matter.’”
Bandelj, the sociologist, lands in a similar place. “This whole idea of, ‘We can do all of this for our kids, and then they will be perfect,’ that parents influence children the most — that’s a prevalent idea, but the research shows it’s not that much,” she said. We don’t have as much control as we think we do, “and it’s very hard to hear that.”

In the United States, where babies have more access than those in other places to the really important stuff — enough to eat, a stable environment and someone who loves them — parents are already giving their kids just about everything they need to succeed. (Tara Anand for The 19th)
It wasn’t until the newborn fog lifted that FitzGerald started to realize how predatory all the baby product marketing felt. By six months, Rowan was waking only once or twice a night. At 3, he sleeps soundly until the morning. FitzGerald doesn’t track sleep anymore with her second son, Ciaran, who is almost 1. She doesn’t obsessively scroll in the night. Most of the products Ciaran has are secondhand.
“I have so much grace for her,” FitzGerald said of the version of herself who tracked poops and naps in an app.
If she could go back, she would tell her past self that how Rowan slept had nothing to do with her value as a mom. And that she probably didn’t need so many swaddles.
“I think I just would tell her, ‘You don’t have to worry so much,’” she said. “‘If Rowan only napped in your arms today, it’s not going to ruin him for life. He’s a really smart, really thoughtful, really cool kid, and how he slept when he was eight weeks old had no impact to the cool kid he has become.’”
She would try to tell her something that would undo the guilt and shame she felt when her baby acted differently than the others. Something helpful, so that she wouldn’t place that blame on herself.
But, actually, thinking back on it now, would she even have believed herself if she’d heard it firsthand? When everything else around her told her she was failing if she didn’t buy all the things?
The truth, FitzGerald said with a chuckle, is “absolutely not.”

name: National
title: False birth control claims are proliferating, survey says
description: More than half of women of reproductive age have seen or heard the false claim that hormones in contraceptives are harmful, and about 4 in 10 have been exposed to the false idea that hormones in contraceptives limit your ability to get pregnant in the future, according to a new survey. The survey by KFF, […]
text:
More than half of women of reproductive age have seen or heard the false claim that hormones in contraceptives are harmful, according to a new KFF survey. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline)More than half of women of reproductive age have seen or heard the false claim that hormones in contraceptives are harmful, and about 4 in 10 have been exposed to the false idea that hormones in contraceptives limit your ability to get pregnant in the future, according to a new survey.
The survey by KFF, a nonprofit health research organization, also found that about a third of women between the ages of 18 and 49 have seen or heard the inaccurate assertion that natural family planning methods are just as effective as hormonal birth control, and a similar percentage have been exposed to the erroneous idea that emergency contraceptive pills cause abortions.
According to the American College of Obstetricians & Gynecologists, long-acting reversible contraception and hormonal birth control are much more effective at preventing pregnancy than fertility awareness-based methods such as menstrual cycle tracking.
Feds have a new teen pregnancy prevention plan: Fertility and ‘reproductive goals’

A large majority of reproductive age women said health care providers are their most trusted source for reliable health care information, with 85% saying they trust them a great deal or a fair amount. In contrast, only 26% said they trust U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for reliable health information, and 48% said they trust federal health agencies. About 25% said they trust AI tools and chatbots, and 14% said they trust  social media and social media influencers.
Kennedy has made several statements related to reproductive and sexual health that contradict the medical consensus, including that prenatal exposure to Tylenol and COVID vaccines may be linked to autism. Under Kennedy, HHS has shifted the focus of federal family planning and pregnancy prevention grants away from expanding contraceptive services and toward promoting childbearing or what’s known as restorative reproductive medicine.
As Republicans spar over IVF, some turn to obscure MAHA-backed alternative

The KFF survey found that among 3,538 women of reproductive age, about 35% said they saw or heard something about contraception on social media in the past 12 months.
Of those who saw social media posts about contraception, 78% said they had used contraception in the past 12 months, with 62% using hormonal methods. Of those, 8% stopped and 9% started a new method because of something they saw or heard on social media.
But for a larger share of this group, contraception-related posts led to further consultation, either with a doctor (19%) or online or from AI (36%). Women ages 18 to 25 were more likely to consult AI or the internet (46%) compared with women ages 36 to 49 (29%).

title: The FBI anti-corruption squad was circling Susan Collins — until Trump got in the way
authors: William Turton, ProPublica, Avi Asher-Schapiro, ProPublica, Molly Redden, ProPublica, Kirsten Berg, ProPublica
description: This story was originally published by ProPublica.  In the final weeks of 2019, a top fundraiser for Sen. Susan Collins walked into a perilous meeting at a Corner Bakery in Washington, D.C. For the first time in her two-decade Senate career, the Republican lawmaker from Maine was in danger of losing her seat. President Donald […]
text:
Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins walks in the annual Moxie Day Parade on July 11, 2026, in Lisbon, Maine. (Photo by Scott Eisen/Getty Images)This story was originally published by ProPublica. 
In the final weeks of 2019, a top fundraiser for Sen. Susan Collins walked into a perilous meeting at a Corner Bakery in Washington, D.C.
For the first time in her two-decade Senate career, the Republican lawmaker from Maine was in danger of losing her seat. President Donald Trump’s dismal approval ratings were dragging her down in the polls, and she was falling behind her likely 2020 Democratic challenger in fundraising.
Scott Reed, head of the Collins super PAC, was on a mission to close that gap. Reed was meeting that day with three executives from a Hawaiian defense contractor, Navatek. A year earlier, Collins had helped their company land a multimillion-dollar Navy research contract in Maine. Now, seated at a coffee shop not far from the U.S. Capitol, Reed asked them for a $500,000 donation.
Government contractors are banned from making political contributions. More consequentially, for the company to offer donations to Collins in exchange for an official action, or for Collins to accept, would constitute criminal bribery.
But the company did have such a proposal: Navatek was hungry for more government contracts in Maine. If they cut a big check, the CEO told Reed, Navatek wanted Collins to guarantee tens of millions of dollars in additional federal funding.
To skirt campaign finance laws and conceal the source of the funds, Navatek planned to funnel the donation through a shell company. The CEO wanted assurance that Collins would know where the money came from. Reed confirmed that she would, the executive said — and that Navatek would get its government contracts.
After the Corner Bakery meeting, Navatek’s CEO, Martin Kao, sent an initial $150,000 to the Collins super PAC using the shell company. Two months later, he told Navatek executives that Collins committed to getting the company $32 million in naval contracts, according to an internal company email reviewed by ProPublica.
Three years later, Kao holed up in a conference room to recount the Corner Bakery meeting to a group of four FBI agents and federal prosecutors. The FBI had seen through his shell company ruse, and in 2022 a grand jury indicted him for making illegal campaign contributions. No one working for Collins was charged.
Facing years in prison, Kao hoped to do less time by revealing the entire scheme.
What he told them has never before become public. The Corner Bakery meeting, he asserted, was just one episode in a sprawling pay-to-play operation that embroiled some of the most powerful figures in Congress.
Over three days at the U.S. attorney’s office in Honolulu, Kao laid out in devastating detail how his operation worked. He gave agents a 50-page document naming dozens of lobbyists, congressional staffers and members of Congress who he said helped him trade cash for contracts. Kao and his close associates had donated nearly $900,000 to dozens of politicians, allowing Navatek to establish operations in half a dozen states with over $40 million a year in government funding.
Most damningly, Kao told FBI agents and prosecutors, the company’s work for the government was of no real value. Navatek’s research under his stewardship never resulted in products the military wanted to buy, ProPublica found.
Kao’s tell-all interviews with the FBI lasted into late 2024. His confessions opened up an entirely new phase of the investigation. Agents sifted through hundreds of thousands of records seized during Kao’s arrest and found that many were consistent with his account of widespread influence peddling.
Kao had credibility issues. He was now a felon trying to avoid a lengthy prison sentence. And there were other challenges. Building a corruption case against elected officials requires extraordinary proof of a quid pro quo arrangement, in part because the Supreme Court has narrowed what counts as bribery.
Even so, by the end of 2024, the agents had enough evidence to pursue a sweeping bribery probe that could ensnare top lawmakers of both political parties. They asked their supervisors to approve a new investigation and contemplated using undercover operatives to gather more evidence. Although their effort was in its early stages, and it was unclear where it would lead, FBI agents asked Kao extensive questions about his dealings with Collins and her office.
Then Trump returned to the White House. Consumed by a campaign of vengeance, he stacked the Department of Justice with his personal lawyers and demanded a purge of anyone who had ever investigated him.
The specialized FBI and DOJ teams handling public corruption investigations, some of which were involved in Trump-related cases, were eviscerated. One of the agents who had taken Kao’s confession was pushed out as retribution for her role in investigating Trump’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election. Dozens of agents and prosecutors quit amid the department’s destruction, including the career attorney assigned to Kao’s case.
Trump’s Justice Department no longer takes on public corruption in any meaningful fashion, former officials said. The investigation sparked by Kao’s revelations is dead. And the government is no longer talking to an informant who had offered a road map to corruption in Congress.
