title: ‘Drive them into hell’: Trump ponders destruction of Iran at United Nations
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump faces a “big decision” to make a deal with Iran or “annihilate” the country, he told the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. During a 37-minute speech to his international counterparts including Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, in New York City, Trump asked, “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?“Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly … Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he said Speaking at the annual gathering aimed at promoting multilateral discussion among 193 member nations, Trump suggested Iranian leaders were waiting to see the results of the approaching midterm elections for control of Congress before any major negotiating decision.“I believe we'll make a deal right after the election because it doesn't make sense for them not to,” he said. “They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election. What they don't realize is that I'm not running.”Iran tied to GOP midterm woesRepublicans running to maintain the majority in Congress in November face a difficult task amid sinking public support for Trump’s costly, months-long war in Iran. The Pentagon has confirmed 19 U.S. troops have died in the conflict, though The Washington Post has reported a more accurate count is either 22 or 23. Roughly 830 service members have been injured.And the war has spiked the price of fuel to record levels.Trump’s approval rating hit a record low of 32%, according to the latest polling figures published Monday by Reuters/Ipsos.Diesel hit a new high Tuesday, reaching a national average of $6.52 per gallon, according to AAA. Gasoline hovered at $4.47 a gallon. The cost of energy commodities and services, a main driver of current inflation, is up 16.3% over last year, according to the latest U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics consumer price index.Iran maintains its stranglehold of the Strait of Hormuz, a major global petroleum trade passageway, amid a U.S. naval blockade. And Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are now targeting the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for Saudi Arabian oil exports.The U.S. Senate is expected to vote on yet another War Powers Resolution this week aimed at curbing Trump’s military actions in Iran. Seven House Republicans joined Democrats Sept. 16 in passing a measure to stop Trump’s unilateral decision-making in Iran.‘They want to talk’Trump told reporters just before 2 p.m. Eastern that U.S. officials had met with Iranian leaders after his speech for what he described as “a very good meeting.” He did not provide further detail, according to reporters who traveled with him to New York City.Speaking to reporters just before 1 p.m. Eastern, Trump said he believed “a settlement is going to be reached.” “They want to talk to us,” Trump said. “They have been talking to us even today. They've been talking to us. The relationship is developing, I'd say. But we can't let them (have a nuclear weapon). They understand that. … And there's a price to pay for that.”White House poolTrump’s trip to New York City also comes as major U.S. media organizations refused to distribute video, audio or photos of the president after he banned CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. The three organizations have sued on First Amendment grounds.He told reporters Tuesday he has a right “to clean out fake news,” which he also described as “dangerous.”When pressed by a reporter on how the media outlets are “dangerous,” Trump responded: “When they make statements about the war, when they make false statements, false stories, and they don’t have sources but they say they do, it’s very dangerous for our country.”Iran’s Permanent Mission to the UN did not immediately respond to States Newsroom’s request for comment. An email address listed for Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs appeared to be inoperable.Upon arrival at the United Nations this week, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araqchi criticized what he called a “cowardly” war launched by the U.S. in conjunction with Israel on Feb. 28, according to a translation posted on his ministry’s website.“This year, after the war that took place, it is natural that this rostrum will be a place to express the oppression of the Iranian people, the martyrs of Iran, the martyrs of Minab School, and at the head of them, our martyred leader and leader,” Abbas Araqchi said, referring to early strikes during the war that killed Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, his family members and over 100 elementary school children. Iranian security forces killed thousands of Iranians in January as part of a crackdown on protests against the current government, according to Human Rights Watch and other advocates and observers.Threat repeatedTrump’s speech Tuesday was not the first time he’s threatened a choice between striking peace with or heavily attacking Iran. Just before a short-lived ceasefire between Iran and the U.S. took effect in April, Trump threatened “a whole civilization will die” if Iran did not cooperate with U.S. demands.The comment drummed up vocal opposition from some Republicans. Speaking about another military conflict, Trump said his Board of Peace was working to stabilize the Palestinian territory of the Gaza Strip following three years of bombardment by the Israeli government. When listing the countries involved in that effort, he twice mispronounced Kazakhstan.The board claimed in a statement in July it reached an agreement for the “COMPLETE DISARMAMENT” of Hamas, the militant organization that attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, though the conflict remains ongoing.Trump highlighted in his Tuesday remarks to global leaders the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, and claimed the U.S. “is stronger today than ever before.” He repeated familiar refrains on domestic policies, including his immigration agenda and crime statistics in the nation’s capital. He also briefly mentioned he would require federal documents to use the term “super intelligence” in place of “artificial intelligence.” Trump has ardently defended the use of AI without guardrails in recent weeks after tech leaders issued a warning to slow its development.The White House pointed States Newsroom to Trump’s comments to the press following the speech.

name: VTDigger
title: Westmore residents persist in fight against proposed telecommunications tower
description:
The resident leading the opposition to the tower said the state’s approval process “is unjust, unfair, stilted and does not protect Vermont.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Westmore residents persist in fight against proposed telecommunications tower.
text:
Balloons show where the top of proposed Westmore telecommunications tower would be. Photo courtesy of Donna Dzugas-Smith.

A group of Westmore residents is continuing in their multi-year fight over a 140-foot telecommunications tower proposed to be installed just northwest of Lake Willoughby, a national natural landmark.
The residents have said they do not believe the Public Utility Commission gave proper consideration to comments from the town’s planning commission, select board, town plan or nearby neighbors’ views of the tower.
Their belief persists in spite of the Vermont Supreme Court’s affirmation on Sept. 4 of the Public Utility Commission’s decision allowing the tower’s construction, stating the commission did its job correctly. 
The Public Utility Commission is a three-member quasi-judicial body that regulates Vermont’s utilities and the siting of energy projects through a formal process. The commission’s purpose, according to a guide to the process, is to “determine whether a proposal will serve the long-term public good of the State of Vermont and its citizens.”
But in the Westmore case at least, residents say the commission’s process has failed to serve its purpose. Last Wednesday, the appellants — a group of seven residents fronted by Donna Dzugas-Smith — filed a motion asking the court to grant reargument of the case.
The Public Utility Commission process “is unjust, unfair, stilted and does not protect Vermont. That is the problem,” Dzugas-Smith said in an interview. “What we’ve experienced is unbelievable and I know we’re not the only town. This is about all of Vermont.”

A photo of Lake Willoughby in Westmore shows the location proposed for a 140-foot tall telecommunications tower. Photo courtesy of Donna Dzugas-Smith.

Massachusetts-based Industrial Tower and Wireless filed an application for the tower’s construction in June of 2024, which the Public Utility Commission approved in September 2025. According to the final order issued by the commission, the hearing officer concluded that the project “is consistent with State telecommunications policy and the goal of providing improved access to telecommunications services in the regional plan.”
The group of residents filed the notice of appeal of that decision to the Vermont Supreme Court at the end of November 2025.
According to commission documents, an antenna serving the Glover Emergency Medical Services will be placed at the top of the tower. The project will also “provide the needed coverage and capacity” for Industrial Tower and Wireless subscribers living in, working in or passing through the Westmore area, “something that is impossible at present.”
But, the appellants argue, the commission’s approval process is notoriously difficult for the public and even for municipalities to participate in.
The process “is not friendly to the Vermont resident,” Dzugas-Smith said. “It is not friendly to municipalities.”
Michael Swain, special counsel to the Department of Public Service, told VTDigger earlier this year the commission’s process includes procedures and formalities that “may make participation as a party to a proceeding challenging for non-lawyers.”
Earlier this year, the Legislature extended the use of the Public Utility Commission process for three more years. If it had not done so, energy project siting would have gone through the Act 250 process, which is longer and has more avenues for public participation. In its extension, the Legislature made the preapplication public hearing mandatory for the municipality, applicant and Department of Public Service.
According to Ryan Clark, an external affairs regional director at AT&T, the company’s ability to invest and expand coverage in Vermont efficiently is a direct result of the commission process.
“Without [the commission process], we would expect the process of permitting a cell tower to take at least double the amount of time as it does today,” Clark said in his testimony to the legislature. “This would significantly reduce our ability to invest and improve wireless communications for the state of Vermont.”
Rep. Lauren Sibilia, I-Dover, who sponsored the bill extending the use of the commissions’ process, said Tuesday that the legislature heard more testimony than they had expected on the legislation.
“We’ve got some pretty strong opinions on all sides,” she said. “It would not surprise me were we to move to look at this determination again, whether it’s [the commission process] or [Act] 250.”
In Westmore, the group of about a half-dozen residents decided to ask for a reargument of the case because the Vermont Supreme Court decision “still has the same errors that the PUC made their decision on,” Dzugas-Smith said.
Appellants argue that the town plan as well as letters from the Westmore planning commission and select board that express opposition to the tower were not adequately considered. They add that the Public Utility Commission did not consider nearby neighbors’ views of the proposed tower in its aesthetic analysis.
According to Dzugas-Smith, the group of residents fighting the project has spent about $50,000 so far.
“This isn’t over,” she said Friday.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Westmore residents persist in fight against proposed telecommunications tower.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: As mail ballots begin to go out, Pa.’s top election official says midterms will be business as usual
description: As it stands, Schmidt said roughly 986,000 mail ballot applications have been approved in Pennsylvania — roughly 95% of those received. And 20 counties have already begun to send mail ballots to voters who requested them.
text:
A Pennsylvania mail-in ballot for a Bucks County voter (Photo by Tom Sofield)Following the defeat of the Trump administration’s push to implement new United States Postal Service rules that could have limited mail voting, Pennsylvania’s top election official Al Schmidt wants to assure voters that this election will work like any other.
“Having been a county election commissioner for 10 years, I know first hand how much preparation goes into every election, no matter what cycle or what’s going on in the political world outside of election administration,” he said. “I’m confident that eligible voters in Pa. can and should approach this election like they always do, which means voting by whichever method works best for them.”
The update was provided in a press conference  six weeks before election day.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
As it stands, Schmidt said roughly 986,000 mail ballot applications have been approved in Pennsylvania — roughly 95% of those received. And 20 counties have already begun to send mail ballots to voters who requested them.
Schmidt also urged voters seeking to cast mail ballots in person to check the Department of State’s website which lists what counties currently have the service available.
On-demand mail ballot voting is the closest thing Pennsylvania has to more traditional early voting, yet it’s been marked by challenges. Voters can go to a county election office or designated satellite office, request a mail ballot, fill it out on the spot and then return it to an election worker. But the system — and voter expectations that it function like an in-person polling place — caused some issues in the 2024 election cycle.
But Schmidt says the Department of State has made some administrative changes intended to ease the process. He said they follow the success of a redesigned mail ballot envelope, and a year-long education push, he credited with reducing rejections due to errors by nearly 60%. 
The department has also issued a new toolkit counties can use to serve voters who seek to cast mail ballots in person, including a streamlined mail ballot application. It includes a declaration that voters wish to receive a mail ballot at their county election office.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“This application will make it easier for counties to assist voters who choose to apply for, receive, mark and return their mail ballot all in one visit,” he said.
Schmidt said at this point in the election, his office is working with county election staff. 
“We continue to be focused on ensuring that all county election staff, including the many new directors preparing for their first general election, are given training and the support they need,” he said. “In Pennsylvania, it’s at the county level where elections are run, closest to home.”
Pennsylvanians interested in becoming poll workers can apply at vote.pa.gov.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: States file new lawsuits against Trump’s payouts stopping offshore wind
description: An 8-state coalition filed lawsuits Tuesday challenging Trump administration’s payments to private companies to cancel offshore wind leases.
text:
An eight-state coalition filed lawsuits Tuesday challenging the Trump administration’s payments to private companies to cancel offshore wind leases, escalating an ongoing legal battle over the government spending billions of dollars to block wind projects. 
Attorneys general from eight East Coast states are suing the feds over the buyouts of two offshore wind leases, under which the Trump administration pledged to pay developers Bluepoint Wind and Invenergy $1.4 billion to abandon their projects. Those projects were slated to be built off the coast of New York and New Jersey. 
Under the agreements with federal agencies, the companies will reinvest the funds into oil and gas projects elsewhere in the country.
The lawsuits were joined by the attorneys general of Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Vermont. 
Many of the states are already part of an existing lawsuit, filed in June, challenging the buyout of a separate project, also in waters off New York and New Jersey.
California has filed its own pair of lawsuits, one last month and one Tuesday, contesting the buyout of leases off the state’s Pacific coast. 
In total, the Trump administration has agreed to pay more than $4 billion to energy companies in exchange for relinquishing a dozen leases for offshore wind projects. 
“This Administration is paying developers to abandon building new sources of energy at a time when our grid needs more power to meet demand and residents need relief from high electricity prices,” New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, a Democrat, said in a statement. “Wind energy creates well-paid jobs and reduces our reliance on fossil fuels. The president cannot redirect public funds to make unauthorized investments in oil and gas simply because he favors the fossil fuel industry.”
The lawsuits take aim at the Trump administration’s use of the Judgment Fund, a permanent appropriation created by Congress for the payment of court judgments in cases won against the federal government, to buy out the leases. The taxpayer-funded account, Davenport said, is “meant to settle genuine claims arising from actual or imminent litigation against the federal government.”
The attorneys general argue that the settlements violate multiple federal laws, including the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Judgment Fund Act. The states are asking the court to strike down the settlements and restore the leases. 
One lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York. The other was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine.
Many East Coast states have set ambitious goals for offshore wind, and they’ve been counting on pending projects to meet their fast-growing power demands. Some state leaders say it will be nearly impossible to meet clean energy targets without a robust offshore wind sector. 
President Donald Trump has long been a critic of wind power, and offshore wind in particular. He has used nearly every tool at his disposal to block new projects and stop work on existing projects. 
This story was first published Sept. 22, 2026 by Stateline.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nearly half of Center for Intellectual Freedom advisory council members resign
description: Nearly half of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa’s advisory council membership have resigned from their roles after issues were voiced about the Iowa Board of Regents’ dismissal of their concerns relating to control of the center and finding its permanent leader. The Iowa Board of Regents Tuesday stated in a […]
text:
Eleven of the 26 advisory council members for the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa have resigned this week. Panelists speaking Dec. 6, 2025, at the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa, from left, are center Interim Director Luciano de Castro, U.S. Assistant Secretary for Postsecondary Education David Barker, state Rep. Taylor Collins, state Sen. Kerry Gruenhagen and Regent Christine Hensley. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Nearly half of the Center for Intellectual Freedom at the University of Iowa’s advisory council membership have resigned from their roles after issues were voiced about the Iowa Board of Regents’ dismissal of their concerns relating to control of the center and finding its permanent leader.
The Iowa Board of Regents Tuesday stated in a news release that it accepted the resignation of 11 members of the advisory council, including executive committee chair Richard Lowery and other professors and academics from universities across the U.S.
According to a letter sent to Board President Robert Cramer, the resignation was the group’s expression of its “vote of no confidence in the Board of Regents and in the Board’s Center for Intellectual Freedom (CIF) Supervisory Committee.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Regent Christine Hensley, who chairs the advisory council and leads the board committee overseeing the center, said in the release that the board appreciates “the work these individuals have put into the Center for Intellectual Freedom.”
“The Board of Regents looks forward to working with the remaining 15 members of the CIF Advisory Council to keep the Center moving forward in a positive direction,” Hensley said in the release. “The Board and the Advisory Council fully support helping CIF achieve its stated goals of providing scholarship on the intellectual foundation of free societies, the principles, ideals and institutions of the American constitutional order, and the foundations of responsible leadership and informed citizenship.”
Other resigning members include Thomas Gallanis, Dorian Abbot, Daniel Bonevac, Carlos Carvalho, Joshua Katz, Sergiu Klainerman, Ivan Marinovic, Nicola Persico, Joshua Rauh and Herald Uhlig.
The advisory council is now down to 15 members, having started with 26. The center advisory council moving forward includes Hensley, Cramer, Regent Steve Lacy, former Regents Jim Lindenmayer and Mike Richards, Fareway CEO Reynolds Cramer, Iowans for Tax Relief Foundation Policy Director John Hendrickson, former lawmakers Greg Ganske and Liz Mathis, former Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad, philanthropist Norman Johnson, Heart of America Group CEO Mike Whalen, UI Senior Advisor to the President Peter Matthes and professors Wilfred McClay and Mark Bauerlein.
Emails show friction on how to move forward 
Advisory council members have bristled at the amount of control the board of regents has exercised over the center’s staff and planning. They expressed concerns in a September meeting about restrictions on director travel and the UI’s involvement with figuring out required curriculum for civics education.
The main focus of the advisory council currently is to select a permanent director, and the board of regents last week approved a timeline for candidate interviews and finalist visits to campus. At the board meeting, Hensley said she would set up a council meeting this week to discuss candidates and tackle interviews and other steps throughout the month of October, but “some members of the executive committee” won’t be “pleased with us moving forward.”
Hensley shared the timeline with advisory council executive committee members in a Sept. 16 email, according to records provided by the board of regents, but Lowery responded saying “that is not the timeline we will follow.”
Cramer emailed Lowery Sept. 17 asking him to “get on board” with Hensley and work with her or step down to let someone else lead the search process, saying he appreciates Lowery’s work but “it appears we are going down different paths.” Gov. Kim Reynolds and Rep. Taylor Collins, chair of the Iowa House Higher Education Committee, were copied in the email.
Lowery seems to “want to run the center” his way and isn’t respecting board of regent decisions, Cramer said in his email, and while the board “covets and appreciates” the council’s thoughts, the board of regents is the body responsible for the center and any final decisions relating to it.
Rather than an “island of disgruntled nonconformists,” Cramer said he and other board members want the center to stretch its engagement across the UI campus and change university culture through their shared goal of teaching civics, debate and American history.
“Instead of fighting each step of the way, we want the permanent executive director and the Advisory Council to set a new course by working in partnership with the Board and the University,” Cramer said in his email. “CIF will maintain its independence and ensure its courses are taught in a fair and balanced way that matches the legislative intent. But we don’t have to do everything in isolation.”
Lowery responded Sept. 19, saying in an email it’s been made clear to him that the UI and board of regents “will never allow the Center for Intellectual Freedom to be a success and will never allow the Center to operate in accordance with the law,” and the center won’t receive the external support it needs to succeed. He said under Cramer’s leadership, “no serious academics with an interest in higher education reform” would want to stay with the center.
“Your message demonstrates clearly that you have complete contempt for those academics who do not adhere to the dominant, leftist ideology on university campus, describing us contemptuously as ‘disgruntled nonconformists,’” Lowery said in his email. “That is not an environment that can possibly lead to a vibrant Center for Intellectual Freedom.”
The pair exchanged one more email each Sept. 19, with Cramer saying he’s not interested in in-fighting but wants to “change hearts and minds.” Lowery said the board gave an ultimatum rather than accept the advice of the council and hasn’t answered questions of “hiring authority, independence, and tenure protections we raised months ago.”
“My colleagues and I gave our time to this in good faith, and the Board gave us no reason to keep giving it,” Lowery said in his email.

name: Mississippi Today
title: No ransoms paid in cyberattacks on UMMC and IHL, officials say
description: University of Mississippi Medical Center Vice Chancellor Dr. LouAnn Woodward, center, speaks at a press conference in Jackson shortly after cyber-attackers disrupted the hospital's computer systems on Feb. 19, 2026.
text:
No ransoms were paid to hackers during the cyberattacks that hit the University of Mississippi Medical Center or Institutes of Higher Learning this year, officials confirmed to Mississippi Today. 
“No state taxpayer dollars were used” to pay the perpetrators of either attack, said Sen. Nicole Boyd, a Republican from Oxford and the chair of the Senate Universities and Colleges Committee.
A cyberattack struck the Mississippi Institutions of Higher Learning offices on Sep. 7, temporarily rendering the Mississippi Office of Student Financial Aid unable to process student applications and payments. IHL officials are working with federal law enforcement and cybersecurity professionals to determine what happened and whether confidential or sensitive data was accessed or compromised.
IHL spokesperson John Sewell said the agency did not pay a ransom connected to the attack. He said he could not yet share an update on the agency’s recovery process. 
In February, a ransomware attack targeted the University of Mississippi Medical Center, compromising the health care system’s IT network and leading officials to shut down affected systems to contain the threat. As a result, the state’s only academic medical center closed clinics across the state and canceled elective procedures for nine days. IHL oversees the state’s public universities, including UMMC. 
Ransomware, or malicious software that holds computer systems or data hostage in demand for payment, has increasingly targeted healthcare organizations with the aim of garnering large payouts by disrupting critical infrastructure. 
Marc Rolph, a spokesperson for UMMC, said Friday the medical center did not pay a ransom to the hackers. 
Officials told Mississippi Today in April the medical center was conducting a detailed forensic analysis with support from the FBI and cybersecurity experts to determine what data was accessed or exfiltrated during the cyberattack. 
Ransomware group Medusa claimed credit for the cyberattack in March, nearly a month after the initial attack that shut down UMMC’s network. The group demanded payment to prevent the publication of stolen data, cybersecurity news outlet The Record reported. A UMMC spokesperson declined to confirm whether Medusa was the organization that attacked the medical center. In an April blog post, Louann Woodward said the perpetrator is well known to the FBI.
On Monday, State Auditor Shad White sent a letter to IHL Commissioner Al Rankins Jr. seeking more information about the agency’s response to both attacks. White requested information about the nature and scope of the incident, whether a ransom or extortion payment was requested, information about any such payments and copies of and plans for remediation. 
“Taxpayers deserve to know what happens to their money and the IHL should be transparent with what happened here,” White wrote in the letter.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Raccoon boot camp in Mississippi teaches survival skills to abandoned kits
description: A raccoon kit digs through water and mud at Woodside Wildlife Rescue in Pass Christian, Miss. on Sept. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Sophie Bates)
text:
PASS CHRISTIAN — Muddy, sweat-soaked and occasionally bloody, the dedicated staff at a Mississippi wildlife center are drill sergeants. And their soldiers? Baby raccoons.
Welcome to raccoon boot camp, where the goal is to help sick or injured animals learn to survive in the south Mississippi wilderness — a skill set they would have learned from their mothers, most of whom died or were separated from their kits by storms, traffic accidents or other traumatic events.
A raccoon kit peers through an enclosure at Woodside Wildlife Rescue on Sept. 1, 2026 in Pass Christian, Miss. (AP Photo/Sophie Bates) Credit: AP Photo/Sophie Bates
It’s a challenge that’s left Woodside Wildlife Rescue’s founder, Paula Woodside, with cuts from scared, defensive raccoons and their sharp claws, and when she isn’t able to save a kit, emotional scars too.
“When these babies come in, and they’re so desperate, it’s heartbreaking,” said Woodside, who most days is covered in sweat from caring for the animals in the Mississippi heat, and dirt from curious kits crawling up her legs and onto her shoulders. “It’s really important for them to get a little bit of a head start.”
After being weaned, the young troops get a taste off the wild
Woodside, a former U.S. merchant mariner, opened the rescue in 2019 after she helped rehabilitate a baby raccoon found aboard her ship. The rescue in the coastal city of Pass Christian typically raises dozens of kits each year, 76 so far this year, alongside other indigenous wildlife.
Raquel Priest, the director of Woodside Wildlife Rescue, holds a raccoon kit over her shoulder on Sept. 1, 2026 in Pass Christian, Miss. (AP Photo/Sophie Bates) Credit: AP Photo/Sophie Bates
City animal control and citizens call Woodside, or the rescue’s director, Raquel Priest, when they find a raccoon in need of saving. Together, they attempt to reunite the kits with their mothers, if they can find them, or bring the kits to the rescue.
The youngest raccoons will spend a few weeks mostly indoors being bottle-fed by rehabbers until they’re vaccinated for diseases carried by cat colonies and dogs and are ready to move to outdoor pens.
Though the kits stay close to their adoptive human parents, they’re eventually allowed to roam free during the day on the rescue’s rural 20-acre property, a sprawling mix of meadows and thick forest spotted with ponds and a nearby river. Thanks to that setting, Woodside and Priest can take their troops on learning excursions, a luxury many wildlife rescues don’t have, Woodside said.
Teaching by example: digging for worms and cracking acorns
Woodside and Priest teach by example. They hide worms in the dirt to show the kits how to dig for food, and break open pine cones or acorns to reveal the seeds inside. The raccoons’ eyes light up when they encounter a new tasty food, and they run to show their discovery to their rehabbers before hurrying back to fend off other kits who might try to steal their find.
Where a drill sergeant might yell, ‘Attention!,’ Priest and Woodside give a shrill trilling sound, mimicking the raccoon call for danger, that sends the kits running up trees to safety. A short whistle lets the troops know the coast is clear.
The kits also practice fishing in shallow pools, their uncoordinated paws tentatively patting the water until they’re quick enough to snag a snack. A live quail hunt provides hunting experience. While these are skills raccoons would likely learn on their own, Woodside’s staff hopes the training gives the kits a greater chance of survival.
A raccoon kit practices swimming, while supported by Woodside Wildlife Rescue Director Raquel Priest, on Sept. 1, 2026 in Pass Christian, Miss. (AP Photo/Sophie Bates) Credit: AP Photo/Sophie Bates
On the property’s pond, the raccoons learn to swim, a critical skill in hurricane-prone south Mississippi. The rehabbers take to kayaks and encourage the kits to swim back and forth. They also take trips to the deep woods, where kits learn to run from tree to tree to avoid being seen by birds of prey and to have a quick escape route from snakes or other dangers on the ground.
Raccoons graduate to ‘Pomp and Circumstance Marches’
For their final lesson, a volunteer — who isn’t Woodside or Priest — traps the raccoons in cages, scaring them enough to encourage them to avoid traps and humans. The experience helps the young raccoons wean themselves from their human rescuers, a process Priest said naturally occurs as they mature.
When a group of kits is ready for release, about six months after their rescue, Woodside and Priest host a graduation ceremony. They play Edward Elgar’s “Pomp and Circumstance Marches,” and read a roll call of each graduating kit’s name.
A reverend then blesses their journey as they’re released onto a different section of the rescue’s forest-covered property. For kits that die in care, the staff holds a second ceremony to bless and scatter their ashes.
“It’s like watching your children leave home,” Priest said. “It’s important to see them prosper and go and be the mischievous creatures they were meant to be.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Nolan Wells may have drowned, but questions remain: How? And why?
description: A person holds a picture of Nolan Xavier Wells during a news conference at National Action Network headquarters, Friday, July 10, 2026, in New York.
text:
The parents of Nolan Xavier Wells say they will continue to push for answers about his death, after a Jackson County grand jury concluded that he likely drowned and no one would face criminal charges.
Their attorney Ben Crump and the Rev. Al Sharpton said that the grand jury report doesn’t close the book on Wells’ death or answer lingering questions about what led to it or how the 18-year-old died. 
His mother, Christine Wonsley, said she received a text message from Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath Monday evening, not long before McIlrath posted the grand jury’s redacted report and a video explaining its findings on Facebook. 
Monday was Wonsley’s birthday. 
“Last night was a reminder that our son’s life does not matter to those who hold positions that are supposed to serve and protect the public,” Christine Wonsley said Tuesday during an online news conference at New Birth Missionary Baptist Church in Georgia. 
Christine Wonsley smiles as she is presented with a birthday cake for her son during a vigil for Nolan Wells at Greater St. John AME Church in Biloxi on Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026. Credit: Jackson Ranger/The Sun Herald
Wells, who was Black, traveled from Ocean Springs to Horn Island on the Fourth of July with friends. His body was found in the water off the Mississippi Gulf Coast barrier island two days later. 
While the grand jury heard evidence that he likely drowned, both the state medical examiner and a pathologist who completed an independent autopsy ruled Wells’ death as undetermined. In a preliminary report, Dr. Roger Mitchell, the pathologist hired by the family, said all other causes must be ruled out to conclude a death was by drowning. 
Mitchell also wrote that the record and examination doesn’t establish whether Wells entered the water on his own or was forced into it, and whether he was conscious when it happened. 
Because of lingering questions and Mitchell’s findings, the family’s legal team called for the district attorney to keep the death investigation open and to look further into blunt force injuries documented on the back of Wells’ head and neck, including whether they contributed to his death.
Attorney Ben Crump, who represents Wells’ parents, released Mitchell’s final autopsy report Tuesday, which the pathologist was able to complete after traveling to Mississippi and gaining access to reports from the state medical examiner. 
Mitchell concluded that two red discoloration marks were blood. The state examiner identified them as contusions early in the investigation, but did not explain where they came from, he wrote. 
“That is not nothing,” attorney Liza Park, a member of the family’s legal team, said about Mitchell’s updated findings. “That is where we begin to begin to understand what happened to Nolan Wells.” 
If new evidence is uncovered relating to his death, a grand jury can meet again to consider it and decide whether to charge anyone. Mississippi does not have a statute of limitations for murder charges. 
The family’s legal team and the NAACP are calling for McIlrath’s office to release the state’s autopsy report and the investigative file. They also continue to ask the U.S. Department of
Justice to complete a federal review as requested by the Congressional Black Caucus in August.
Forensic experts are examining Wells’ cellphone, and Crump said they will talk about what they found in an upcoming news conference. 
Crump asked the public not to attack Wells’ parents for continuing to seek answers. 
The case gathered national attention and sparked discussion about Mississippi’s history of  investigators not examining the deaths of Black people with the same rigor as the deaths of white people. 
This summer, at least three out-of-state people have been charged with threatening to kill or hurt witnesses in the investigation, including Wells’ friends and their family members. 
Friends of Wells have said they faced death threats from their names, pictures and personal information being shared online. 
Attorney Russ Latino, who is representing a former teammate of Wells, sent a cease-and-desist letter to at least one content creator, the Sun Herald reported. Attorneys representing the three friends who traveled to Horn Island with Wells threatened to sue Sharpton, Mississippi Today has reported. This week, the same attorneys also said they would sue “The View” co-host Sunny Hostin for comments she made, the Clarion Ledger reported.
On Monday, attorneys representing the friends acknowledged the grand jury’s decision not to indict, including one who demanded that Crump apologize to three of Wells’ friends. 
“We still have a First Amendment right here, and we still have the right to ask questions when our children are unalived in inexplicable ways,” Crump said at the Tuesday news conference. “We won’t stay silent, we won’t let it be swept under the rug and we won’t go quietly into the night because Nolan deserves better than that.”

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Donalds might retain Joseph Ladapo as surgeon general — Jolly says he’d fire him
description: Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds reiterated Tuesday that he remains open to reappointing Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo if he wins the Nov. 3 election. That marks a clear distinction with Democrat David Jolly, who has vowed to fire Ladapo on his first day in office. Ladapo has served as the state’s surgeon general since […]
text:
Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo during a news conference with Gov. Ron DeSantis on Sept. 7, 2023. (Screenshot/DeSantis Facebook)Republican gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds reiterated Tuesday that he remains open to reappointing Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo if he wins the Nov. 3 election.
That marks a clear distinction with Democrat David Jolly, who has vowed to fire Ladapo on his first day in office.
Ladapo has served as the state’s surgeon general since September 2021, when he was already known as a skeptic of COVID-19 vaccines.  He also opposed mask mandates and advised against COVID vaccinations for healthy children in 2022.
It was a little over a year ago that Ladapo and Gov. Ron DeSantis announced their plan to drop all required vaccine mandates for children, including those required for school attendance such as polio, diphtheria, measles, mumps, and chickenpox. The Republican-led Legislature opted to retain most vaccine requirements established in state law, but Ladapo does hold the authority to remove four vaccine requirements by rule changes.
Those proposed rule changes were finally released by the Florida Department of Health last month. The rule proposes to remove hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox), haemophilus influenza Type b (Hib), and pneumococcal conjugate virus vaccines for public school attendance.
Speaking in Daytona Beach Shores, Donalds said he agreed with those proposed rule changes.
“We’re going to leave those vaccines as informed consent,” he said. “The last set of vaccines that are now required for kids are now MMR, polio, and a handful of others that were passed by state law. For those vaccines, we’re going to conduct a full review and analysis with all parties at the table.”
Donalds added that neither he nor his family took a COVID vaccine, although he acknowledged, “There are a lot of people who did for various reasons.”
Ladapo told the Florida Voice last month that he “would be honored to continue serving under a Byron Donalds administration.”
The two Republicans did have a difference of opinion this summer in response to the measles outbreak in Florida. Donalds has said it might be happening because “of rampant illegal immigration into the United States from the previous [Biden] administration. “
Ladapo suggested the outbreak was related to abortion opposition.
The Phoenix previously reported that the Florida Chapter of the American College of Physicians wants a formal hearing regarding the state’s proposal to weaken vaccine requirements for Florida schoolchildren.
“The Chapter requests that the Department take note of its interest in this issue and to accept this correspondence as part of the official record,” Jacksonville health care attorney Christopher Nuland wrote on behalf of the association and its 10,000 members.
“Numerous scientifically vetted studies have demonstrated the safety and efficacy of these immunizations, while the Chapter is unaware of any substantial competent evidence that would indicate otherwise.”
Polls taken a year ago showed that removing all vaccine requirements in Florida schools was not a popular idea.
A James Madison Institute survey released in September 2025 of 1,200 registered Florida voters found 62% against elimination of all vaccine requirements, with just 29% in support. And a survey of 631 registered Florida voters, also conducted in September by Bendixen & Amandi International, found 60% opposed ending vaccine mandates and just 37% supporting it.
The DeSantis administration would not have to go through the rulemaking process had members of the Legislature gone along with its proposal to eliminate the mandates. While a proposal (SB 1756) did get through the Senate, it died because there was no companion bill in the House.
For more than a year, Jolly has received standing ovations on the campaign trail when he tells audiences his first order of business if elected would be to fire Ladapo. “We’re going to bring back science, data, math, vaccines, and public health and all the other things that contribute to human progress,” he has said.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Audit into public health contract process sparks outrage from Michigan House Oversight members
description: Michigan Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) called the results of an audit from the Michigan Office of the Auditor General into the work of the Michigan Public Health Institute “unbelievable” in a hearing on Tuesday morning. The Michigan Public Health Institute is a nonprofit established in 1990 by the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services […]
text:
Representatives on the House Oversight Committee question staff from the Office of the Auditor General on their report on the Michigan Public Health Institute on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)Michigan Rep. Jay DeBoyer (R-Clay) called the results of an audit from the Michigan Office of the Auditor General into the work of the Michigan Public Health Institute “unbelievable” in a hearing on Tuesday morning.
The Michigan Public Health Institute is a nonprofit established in 1990 by the Michigan Department of Health and Human Services to coordinate and promote health research with the state’s public universities. The audit report, which was released in early September, showed insufficiencies in the department’s efforts to monitor the institute’s contracts and grants and provide the Legislature with information about projects and deliverables. The audit also found only partial compliance with state law and policy in the department’s awarding of contracts and grants to the institute. 
“This just absolutely breaks my heart because we had so many opportunities here. We have some of the best educational institutions in the world, and we’ve robbed them of financing,” said Rep. Jamie Greene (R-Richmond), while Rep. Josh Schriver (R-Oxford) called the outcomes of the report “ridiculous” and Rep. Denise Mentzer (D-Mt. Clements) referred to the response from the department in the report as “a disappointment.”
The department disagreed or partially disagreed with all of the audit’s findings. Lynn Sutfin, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said in a statement to the Michigan Advance that the “information from the audit will be used to help inform future processes and department approaches.”
The findings of the report covered a period in which Elizabeth Hertel served as director of the department, a position from which she has since stepped down. She was replaced by Acting Director Amy Epkey. 
Yvonne Benn, audit division administrator, Ivy Jaroche, audit manager, and Chad Monger, principal audit supervisor (left to right) answer questions on their report on the Michigan Public Health Institute in the House Oversight Committee on Sept. 22, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)
In response to questions from committee members, Benn noted that conversations with Epkey since she was sent the audit have been both productive and cordial, and that Epkey is “open to our recommendations.” However, the official final responses from the department, which were submitted after Epkey took over the department, do indicate disagreement with the auditor general’s report.
Sutfin noted that collaborations between the department and the Michigan Public Health Institute have included responses to public health issues “including combatting disease outbreaks such as COVID-19 and cyclosporiasis; ensuring medical professionals and others receive needed information during a rapid rise in youth suicide; and addressing emerging threats like community violence.”
“The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) works with the Michigan Public Health Institute (MPHI) to develop and implement projects that advance community health, strengthen the public health system and support programs across the department. The nearly 40-year partnership was designed with a focus on improving public health for Michigan residents,” she wrote.
Yvonne Benn, the audit division administrator, explained that the audit focused on fiscal years 2024 and 2025, during which, “the state’s appropriations act authorized the department to use one-year agreements with MPHI, and during that two-year time, it established and awarded nine high-level agreements and 857 project-level agreements totaling $435 million.”
Ivy Jaroche, an audit manager for the office, explained that for many agreements with contractors that individually exceeded $50,000, the statements of work submitted only supported half of the nearly $17 million in subcontracted services within the agreement or final project budget. 
“The absence of information to fully support the project budgets limits the department’s ability to monitor the propriety of MPHI reimbursement requests related to subcontractor costs,” Jaroche said.
Chad Monger, the principal audit supervisor, also noted that around 80% of contracts had no deliverable information and submissions frequently “lack sufficient information to effectively monitor the progress of agreements and fully support payments made.”
Nearly 70% of Financial Status Reports lacked any underlying support for the cost, and work plans were frequently submitted late and reviewed after payments had already been made to the Michigan Public Health Institute. 
“We noted MDHS did not report any project information for two projects totaling 10.6 million dollars, did not provide detailed descriptions or appropriation line item fundings for almost 30 percent of the 18 projects it did include in the report, and did not identify subgrantees for the two projects with subgrantees,” Monger added. “Our review of these agreements noted that they included over 100 subgrantees who were allocated $11.8 million for fiscal year 24 and 25.”

name: National
title: States file new lawsuits against Trump’s payouts stopping offshore wind
description: An eight-state coalition filed lawsuits Tuesday challenging the Trump administration’s payments to private companies to cancel offshore wind leases, escalating an ongoing legal battle over the government spending billions of dollars to block wind projects.  Attorneys general from eight East Coast states are suing the feds over the buyouts of two offshore win[...]
text:
Wind turbines generate electricity at the Block Island Wind Farm off Rhode Island. President Donald Trump’s administration has pledged billions of dollars to persuade developers to abandon offshore wind leases. (Photo by John Moore/Getty Images)An eight-state coalition filed lawsuits Tuesday challenging the Trump administration’s payments to private companies to cancel offshore wind leases, escalating an ongoing legal battle over the government spending billions of dollars to block wind projects. 
Attorneys general from eight East Coast states are suing the feds over the buyouts of two offshore wind leases, under which the Trump administration pledged to pay developers Bluepoint Wind and Invenergy $1.4 billion to abandon their projects. Those projects were slated to be built off the coast of New York and New Jersey. 
Under the agreements with federal agencies, the companies will reinvest the funds into oil and gas projects elsewhere in the country.
The lawsuits were joined by the attorneys general of Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Vermont. 
Many of the states are already part of an existing lawsuit, filed in June, challenging the buyout of a separate project, also in waters off New York and New Jersey.
California has filed its own pair of lawsuits, one last month and one Tuesday, contesting the buyout of leases off the state’s Pacific coast. 
In total, the Trump administration has agreed to pay more than $4 billion to energy companies in exchange for relinquishing a dozen leases for offshore wind projects. 
As Trump buyouts shake offshore wind industry, states hope developers stay in the game

“This Administration is paying developers to abandon building new sources of energy at a time when our grid needs more power to meet demand and residents need relief from high electricity prices,” New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport, a Democrat, said in a statement. “Wind energy creates well-paid jobs and reduces our reliance on fossil fuels. The president cannot redirect public funds to make unauthorized investments in oil and gas simply because he favors the fossil fuel industry.”
The lawsuits take aim at the Trump administration’s use of the Judgment Fund, a permanent appropriation created by Congress for the payment of court judgments in cases won against the federal government, to buy out the leases. The taxpayer-funded account, Davenport said, is “meant to settle genuine claims arising from actual or imminent litigation against the federal government.”
The attorneys general argue that the settlements violate multiple federal laws, including the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Judgment Fund Act. The states are asking the court to strike down the settlements and restore the leases. 
One lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York. The other was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine.
Many East Coast states have set ambitious goals for offshore wind, and they’ve been counting on pending projects to meet their fast-growing power demands. Some state leaders say it will be nearly impossible to meet clean energy targets without a robust offshore wind sector. 
President Donald Trump has long been a critic of wind power, and offshore wind in particular. He has used nearly every tool at his disposal to block new projects and stop work on existing projects. 
Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: When a candidate won’t debate, should the voters lose their forum?
description: Tennesseans are preparing to elect a governor and members of Congress this November, but before Election Day arrives, news organizations need to answer a question of their own: When one candidate refuses to debate, why should the voters lose the forum? Campaign advertisements are not accountability. They are advertisements, carefully scripted, edited and fin[...]
text:
Pictured, a debate between 2022 Democratic gubernatorial candidates. No debates or forums have been scheduled in the 2026 gubernatorial race. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennesseans are preparing to elect a governor and members of Congress this November, but before Election Day arrives, news organizations need to answer a question of their own: When one candidate refuses to debate, why should the voters lose the forum?
Campaign advertisements are not accountability. They are advertisements, carefully scripted, edited and financed presentations designed to tell voters exactly what a campaign wants them to hear. Candidates get to select the images, highlight the statistics, emphasize their preferred issues and avoid the questions they would rather not answer. 
Debates create the possibility of the unexpected question, the follow-up, the contradiction and the policy proposal that sounds good until somebody asks what it costs, who pays for it or whether the office being sought by the candidate even has the authority to implement it.
Citizens deserve that distinction, and news organizations ought to defend it.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
Consider Tennessee’s gubernatorial race. Republican nominee Marsha Blackburn declined NewsChannel 5’s invitation to participate in a Republican primary debate in July. The station reported that Blackburn cited Senate votes, that it asked whether another date would work, and that it did not receive a response. U.S. Rep. John Rose then declined to participate without Blackburn, and the station canceled the debate.
Now Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jerri Green has proposed general-election debates with Blackburn, and Blackburn has declined. Whatever voters ultimately think about either candidate, the larger issue remains: one candidate’s decision not to participate should not automatically determine whether the public receives a serious forum in which someone is questioned about the job they are asking us to give them.
Media executives have been far too accommodating.
The answer should be simple. Invite every qualified candidate. Set the date. Establish the format. Give them a reasonable deadline to respond. If both candidates show up, host the debate. If only one shows up, convert the event into a rigorous town hall or extended interview with the candidate who accepted. Tell the audience exactly who was invited, who agreed to participate and who declined.
That participating candidate should not get a free campaign commercial. Put them under the lights. Bring in experienced journalists. Take questions from voters. Challenge weak answers. Fact-check claims. Ask follow-ups. Make them explain how their policies would actually work.
But do not allow a candidate who refuses to participate to effectively cancel the public’s opportunity for scrutiny.
That gives politicians too much control over journalism.
State Sen. Brent Taylor, the Republican nominee for the 9th Congressional District , has said he will not debate state Rep. Justin Pearson, the Democratic nominee. (Photos: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
The same concern applies to Tennessee’s newly redrawn 9th Congressional District, where Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor and Democratic state Rep. Justin J. Pearson are competing for a seat that spans portions of Memphis and other parts of West and Middle Tennessee. 
Voters deserve to hear these candidates questioned in real time about the issues that will confront whoever represents the district, particularly after a redistricting process that substantially changed the political geography of Memphis. 
What should federal policy toward artificial-intelligence data centers look like? What responsibility does Washington have regarding their energy demands, environmental impacts and effects on surrounding communities? What should Congress do about health-care costs, wages, inflation, education, war and energy prices? Which promises are actually within the authority of a member of Congress, and which ones are merely campaign rhetoric?
Those questions deserve more than competing thirty-second advertisements.
This issue feels even more urgent considering what we are seeing nationally. Just this weekend, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied access to the White House after President Donald Trump announced that those outlets would be barred because of coverage he characterized as false. The affected news organizations filed a lawsuit Monday.This is precisely the kind of moment that calls for more courage from the press, not less. Political leaders already possess extraordinary privilege, visibility and access to platforms that allow them to shape their own narratives. News organizations should be especially wary of helping them avoid the one thing campaign advertising cannot provide: sustained, unscripted exposure to difficult questions.
And when media executives simply accept a candidate’s refusal without creating another meaningful forum, they risk becoming complicit in the very avoidance they are supposed to interrogate.
Journalism is not supposed to exist merely to transmit whatever politicians are comfortable saying. Its democratic value is most apparent when it creates spaces where public officials and candidates must confront questions they did not write for themselves.
The public needs to hear more than slogans about inflation. Ask candidates exactly what they would do about grocery costs, gasoline prices and wages. Ask how they would improve access to health care. Ask what their education proposals would mean for public schools. Ask congressional candidates what wars they would support, oppose or attempt to end.
And when they answer with talking points, ask again.
There are legitimate legal and regulatory considerations for broadcasters, particularly around candidate appearances and equal-opportunities rules. Those issues should be handled seriously. But they should not become a convenient excuse for surrendering the public forum altogether.
Newsrooms solve complicated legal, technical and editorial problems every day. Surely, they can figure out how to ask candidates for governor and Congress some damn questions.
A debate requires multiple candidates. Accountability does not.
At a moment when political leaders are increasingly attempting to control when, where and by whom they are questioned, media executives should not hand them additional leverage by allowing one candidate’s refusal to collapse an entire public forum. Invite them. Set the date. Turn on the cameras. If both candidates come, let them debate. If one refuses, put the other one in front of the people and start asking questions.
Political candidates may have the privilege of declining a debate. They should not have the power to cancel the public’s right to a forum.

description: Teams from Georgia, Kentucky, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina are being deployed to Arkansas to assist in battling wildfires that have burned thousands of acres, the state Department of Agriculture said Tuesday. The department said in a news release that the state has activated the South Central Interstate Forest Fire Protection Compact to sup[...]
text:
An Oklahoma National Guard CH-47 Chinook  dumps water on a wildfire in Calhoun County, Arkansas on Friday, September 18, 2026. (Courtesy Arkansas National Guard)Teams from Georgia, Kentucky, Mississippi, North Carolina and South Carolina are being deployed to Arkansas to assist in battling wildfires that have burned thousands of acres, the state Department of Agriculture said Tuesday.
The department said in a news release that the state has activated the South Central Interstate Forest Fire Protection Compact to support firefighting efforts. 
“Arkansas has seen a string of wildfires across our state these past few months, and we’re grateful to our friends across the South for the support they’re providing us in the fight,” Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders said in the news release. “The resources our partners provide will be instrumental as our foresters, rangers, and National Guardsmen work long days and nights to protect Arkansans’ homes and businesses.”
The teams being deployed to Arkansas consist of bulldozers, engines and additional personnel.
The state has responded to more than 500 wildfires since Aug. 1 that have affected more than 11,000 acres. 
The Oklahoma National Guard and Mississippi National Guard provided helicopters last week to assist battling a wildfire near a Camden industrial park where several defense contractors are located. That fire is 90% contained as of Monday, according to the state’s online wildfire dashboard.
Helicopter crews have dumped 406,920 gallons of water on the fire, according to the Arkansas National Guard. There have been no reports of injuries or buildings damaged from the blaze.
“I’m incredibly proud of the entire team that has worked tirelessly to contain this wildfire and protect the people and critical defense capabilities at Highland Industrial Park,” Brig. Gen. Chad Bridges, Arkansas’ adjutant general, said in a news release.
All of Arkansas’ 75 counties are at high risk of wildfire, according to a state Department of Agriculture map. There are burn bans in 68 counties. 
Arkansas has responded to more than 1,400 wildfires since the beginning of the year, the department said.
