name: VTDigger
title: Migration doesn’t follow the climate script Vermonters might expect
description:
If tax policy debates rest on assumptions about where people move, the actual numbers deserve a closer look.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Migration doesn’t follow the climate script Vermonters might expect.
text:
Dear Editor,
In a recent commentary for VTDigger regarding tax loopholes for the wealthy, author Dan Jones said, “As I watch the South become insufferably hot and the West burn up, Vermont’s moderate climate looks more and more attractive. I’m pretty sure that, even with increased taxes, our well-to-do property owners won’t be going anywhere as the larger climate collapses.”
Climate change is not a new factor in 2026. The U.S. South and Southwest have been heating up for well over a generation to what seems to me, a longtime Vermonter, unbearable temperatures much of the year. Despite that, parts of the South and Southwest are experiencing the largest net domestic migration in the country, relative to their population. Ranked by net domestic migration rate per 1,000 residents between 2020 and 2024, the top 10 states include Nevada, Arizona and Florida. Ranks 11 to 20 include Texas, Alabama, Arkansas, Oklahoma and Georgia. Vermont ranked 20th.

READ MORE

I do not have answers to the incredibly complex question of what our state’s tax policy should be, but if the conversation is based on how the country’s population moves around, how our population actually moves is a critical piece to understand.
Joe Connelly,Burlington, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Migration doesn’t follow the climate script Vermonters might expect.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Amid opposition, Clearfield County commissioners approve ICE contract extension
description: The Moshannon Valley Processing Center, with beds for about 1,800 people, is the largest ICE detention center on the east coast. The county serves as a pass-through for about $5 million a month in federal money that ICE pays private prison operator The GEO Group to run the center. The county receives $200,000 a year.
text:
The Moshannon Valley Processing Center, with beds for about 1,800 people, is the largest ICE detention center on the east coast. Clearfield County serves as a pass-through for about $5 million a month in federal money that ICE pays private prison operator The GEO Group to run the center. The county receives $200,000 a year. (Photo by Ian Karbal/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)The Clearfield County commissioners voted Tuesday to extend a contract to operate the Moshannon Valley Processing Center on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after hearing strong public pushback.
Speakers called on the board to reject the six-month extension, citing three deaths and complaints about physical and psychological abuse, unfit food, lack of access to adequate health care, and retaliation for protesting the conditions.
The Moshannon Valley Processing Center, with beds for about 1,800 people, is the largest ICE detention center on the east coast. The county serves as a pass-through for about $5 million a month in federal money that ICE pays private prison operator The GEO Group to run the center. The county receives $200,000 a year.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Those gathered here today represent community members who refuse to stand by,” said Clearfield County resident Sam Mosier, the first of nine speakers. “We stand against these practices, including the use of the Moshannon facility and the inhuman treatment of individuals who are seeking nothing more than a better life for themselves and their families.”
Mosier added the county’s continued involvement would leave a stain on its legacy. 
“When history looks back on these times, … this will demonstrate to the world that human dignity matters more to our community and financial gain,” he said.
Clearfield County District Attorney Ryan Sayers was the only speaker in support of continuing the county’s relationship with ICE. He said that as the county’s chief law enforcement officer, he believes immigration laws should be enforced. 
“The citizens of Clearfield County deserve leaders and civil servants who will help uphold those laws and support those that do this work each and every day,” Sayers said, noting both of his parents work in the center. “That is why I stand here today with ICE, with the men and women, … that work hard every day to take care of those at the GEO institution and carry out their lawful responsibilities.”
The board voted 2-1 to accept the contract extension. Democratic Commissioner Dave Glass cast the dissenting vote. After the vote, the meeting room erupted in shouts and a chant of “Shame on you.” Absent an affirmative vote, the county’s contract with ICE was set to expire Sept. 28.
Advocates call on Clearfield County commissioners to vote ‘no’ on ICE contract extension

Glass said that he doesn’t fault those in the community who have taken well-paid jobs at the center, but he doesn’t believe the county should be involved in federal immigration policy.
“There’s a right way and a wrong way to do things. This is the wrong way,” he said “We’re in the middle of it. We shouldn’t be in the middle of it. I don’t want to even tangentially support this, and I think there’s a better way.”
Commissioner John Sobel said he didn’t doubt the sincerity of the speakers’ beliefs, but added  he doesn’t share their concerns that the facility is poorly or inhumanely run.
“In my many contacts with the folks at GEO, and particularly the director, I have not found evidence of a consistent policy or pattern of behavior of intentional abuse or improper behavior,” Sobel said.
Sobel added that while opponents are concerned about the county taking an administrative fee, which some speakers described as “blood money,” the center provides tax revenue to Decatur Township and the Phillipsburg-Osceola School District.
“If we reject the contract, that makes it easier for GEO to go away, and in the long run, that could impact monies that these other entities are probably dependent on. I’m very uncomfortable doing that,” he said.
Sobel also encouraged those opposed to the agreement with ICE to lobby their U.S. representatives and senators to change federal policy. Several members of Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation have been allowed to visit Moshannon Valley this year, after being denied access in the past. 
Democratic U.S. Sen. John Fetterman’s office earlier this month published a letter to acting ICE Director David J. Venturella urging him to ensure the agency paid a local emergency medical clinic for services provided to detainees and staff at Moshannon Valley. 
Moshannon Valley Emergency Medical Services is owed more than $230,000 by ICE, Fetterman’s office said, as a result of a lapse in an agreement between the agency and the Veterans Administration, which had handled medical payment processing related to immigration detention.
“We do try to intervene and see if there’s something we can do to help folks there at the institution,” Sobel said. “But in the end, this is ultimately a decision that has to be made at the federal level, and that’s really who you need to be making your argument to.”
More than 10,000 people were processed through Moshannon Valley between January and August, Commissioner Tim Winters noted. The center held 1,711 people on Tuesday, he said, adding that he believes immigration reform is needed.
“This transcends party lines completely. We need comprehensive immigration reform in the United States,” Winter said. “Unfortunately, the situation we are in now involves various federal policies, federal agencies, and I want to be very clear on this: A ‘no’ vote today will have absolutely no effect on the operations of the Moshannon Valley Processing Center. It will continue to operate tomorrow the same as it did yesterday.”
He said a vote against extending the contract would mean the county no longer has the ability to investigate claims of poor conditions, which he said had not been proven.
“Both Commissioner Sobel and myself have went there unannounced, eaten the same food. The claims are overblown,” he said. 
Moshannon Valley was built as a privately operated federal prison that opened in 2006 and closed in 2021, after the Biden administration banned new federal contracts with for-profit prison operators. 
It reopened later in 2021 as an ICE facility operated by GEO Group under contract with the county, in an arrangement that skirted the private prison ban. The Trump administration reversed the ban in 2025.
Immigration rights advocates note that there’s now evidence that the U.S. Department of Homeland Security intends to buy the facility. The agency issued a request for proposals last month for turnkey detention sites including one in its “Philadelphia Area of Responsibility. According to ICE, that includes all of Pennsylvania, Delaware and West Virginia. DHS said it intends to award 10-year contracts that would allow it to expand operations in the facilities.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
And The GEO Group’s CEO, George C. Zoley, told investors in an earnings call in August that the company is in an “active process” to sell some of its facilities, which the company hopes to continue managing under a long-term contract. 
Jasmine Rivera, executive director of the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition, said in a call with reporters last week that she believes the six month contract extension is needed for the parties to complete their due diligence before a sale. 
At Tuesday’s meeting, speakers strongly condemned ICE’s policies and practices, comparing it to a concentration camp
Sean Inlow, a retired state police detective, urged the commissioners to reject the contract on “legal, moral and personal grounds.” 
Inlow suggested that the arrest and detention of people awaiting due process in the immigration system is criminal. 
“If the county commissioners are going to accept this contract and they’re going to support this program, then you are participating in a criminal enterprise,” he said. “In my view, as a state trooper, I could not make those arrests.”
He added that the county’s involvement in the Trump administration’s mass deportation plan reflects badly on its people. 
“Personally speaking, I’m sick of this creeping Trumpist intimidation,” Inlow said. “I’m not hopeful, but I hope that you guys decline this contract because what we’re doing is morally wrong, criminally wrong, personally wrong.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Scholar seeks to correct the record on death of Rutgers student Tyler Clementi
description: A forthcoming book by an LGBTQ+ scholar seeks to correct the public record on the death of Tyler Clementi, a Rutgers freshman who died by suicide in 2010.
text:
Rutgers University freshman Tyler Clementi died by suicide 16 years ago. A new book out next year explores the aftermath of his death. (Rutgers photo by Daniella Heminghaus)When Rutgers University freshman Tyler Clementi died by suicide 16 years ago, reporters from around the world rushed to tell the story, a narrative that often suggested the university was negligent or uncaring and that his roommate’s actions caused his death.  
But independent LGBTQ+ scholar Judy Farmer Jarvis, a Lawrenceville resident, said the media coverage of Clementi’s death was incomplete, oversimplified, and polarizing. She hopes to correct the record with her book, “Untold Stories: Tyler Clementi’s Death and Crisis Leadership in Higher Education,” scheduled to be published by Rutgers University Press in May 2027.  
Independent LGBTQ+ scholar Judy Jarvis (Photo courtesy of Tori Repp/Fotobuddy)
“Tyler’s death and all the crisis response work that followed was well known but poorly understood,” Jarvis told the New Jersey Monitor.
Jarvis, a student affairs leader at the University of Pennsylvania, said she will donate all book proceeds to organizations that support LGBTQ+ youth.
She interviewed 16 people for the book, including members of Clementi’s family and Rutgers staff who had never spoken publicly about the incident, and explores themes that didn’t get press coverage at the time.  
Clementi died Sept. 22, 2010, when he jumped from the George Washington Bridge several days after his dormmate livestreamed and viewed an intimate encounter Clementi shared with another man. The dormmate and others then ridiculed Clementi about his sexuality on social media, conversations they later tried to distort or cover up. The dormmate pleaded guilty in 2016 to a single privacy invasion charge, paid a fine, and spent 20 days in jail.
Jarvis said one of the biggest misconceptions about the incident was that Rutgers was a homophobic institution that failed to support Clementi or his family following his death. While her book is focused on the aftermath of his suicide, Jarvis said the college had quickly responded to concerns Clementi raised about his dormmate, and it has long supported gay students.  
The work done in the aftermath of Clementi’s death by crisis response teams and advocates led by the Rutgers LGBTQ+ student resource center, founded in 1992, is part of the reason there were no copycat suicides, Jarvis said, something she called “just remarkable.” The university also held multiple vigils and forums on antibullying and inclusion.
“On the ground, Rutgers was doing some really important and best-practice supported work. However, one of their greatest failures is they were not able to well express that to the media,” she said.  
Jarvis said her research, personal experiences, and past work at an LGBTQ+ student center have shown her the critical role on-campus support services can play in the lives of gay and transgender students, including helping to reduce suicidality and other self-harm.  
“To have hubs where people can go for education, support, empowerment, those are really essential, and having visibility and clear names is very essential. I think we just still have a lot of work to do as a nation around empathy for identities that we don’t have,” she said. 

While some media coverage portrayed Clementi’s family as at odds with Rutgers, Jarvis said that wasn’t the case. Although they filed a legal notice allowing them to sue the school, they never did, and Tyler’s mother, Jane Clementi, told Jarvis the family felt well supported by the university. While the Clementi family wanted his dormmate and others held accountable for bias intimidation and bullying, Jarvis said Jane Clementi also understands many factors contribute to a suicide. 
“In her mind, and in the mental health professionals’ minds, suicide is so complicated. There can be things that bubble up, like depression and anxiety, but it’s usually never a single cause,” Jarvis said.  


Clementi’s death prompted New Jersey to strengthen its antibullying laws, already considered some of the toughest in the country. In 2011, then-Gov. Chris Christie expanded the existing statute to require colleges and universities have clear policies on harassment, intimidation, and bullying, protections that had previously existed in K-12 schools.  
Clementi’s family also founded the Tyler Clementi Foundation, which works with schools, sports teams, workplaces, and churches to reduce and respond to harassment. The foundation is also advocating for national antibullying legislation in Clementi’s name that would require higher education programs to have clear policies on harassment, like under New Jersey’s law.  
Rutgers created the Tyler Clementi Center, which highlights his story, describing him as a gifted musician excited for his freshman year, and hosts programs to diminish harassment, reduce bias, and help people from different backgrounds better connect.  
Jane Clementi, the foundation’s president and CEO, was not available to comment. At a media event in November with the Rutgers center named for her son, she said the work to reduce bullying remains critical. 
“I am still hopeful that we will see and create a possible shift where kindness, respect, and compassion prevail, and where it’s not just the cultural exception but rather where kindness becomes the cultural norm,” she said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Appeals court hears arguments over Arkansas’ Ten Commandments in classrooms mandate
description: A federal appeals panel is considering whether to allow six Arkansas school districts to enforce a 2025 state law requiring Ten Commandments displays in all public school classrooms. A three-judge 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel heard arguments Tuesday in St. Louis in a federal lawsuit challenging Act 573 of 2025, which requires public […]
text:
The Ten Commandments were on display in a classroom in the Conway School District in August 2025 in adherence to a state law requiring the religious display in  taxpayer-funded public buildings, including school classrooms. A federal judge ordered them to be removed. (Screenshot from court documents)A federal appeals panel is considering whether to allow six Arkansas school districts to enforce a 2025 state law requiring Ten Commandments displays in all public school classrooms.
A three-judge 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals panel heard arguments Tuesday in St. Louis in a federal lawsuit challenging Act 573 of 2025, which requires public schools and public institutions of higher education to “prominently” display a “historical representation” of the Ten Commandments in classrooms and libraries. 
The statute also applies to public buildings or facilities maintained or operated by taxpayer funds. 
The lawsuit involves ten Arkansas families of varying religious and nonreligious backgrounds who are suing the state and the districts their children attend — Bentonville, Conway, Fayetteville, Lakeside (Garland County), Siloam Springs and Springdale. 
U.S. District Judge Timothy Brooks in March said the law violated the families’ First Amendment rights, declared the statute unconstitutional and blocked it from being enforced in the six challenged districts. The state appealed the ruling.
Federal judge blocks Arkansas’ Ten Commandments law

During Tuesday’s oral arguments, Autumn Hamit Patterson, solicitor general for the Arkansas attorney general’s office, said Brooks’ decision was flawed and should be reversed. 
Patterson said the seven families who filed the original lawsuit lacked standing because their challenge was based on speculation that Ten Commandments posters would be donated and hung at their children’s schools, and “offend or coerce” them in some way.
Three families that were added to the lawsuit later joined after displays were hung in their kids’ classrooms. 
Patterson also said the displays have historical significance and are not coercive because the law doesn’t require them to be incorporated into the public school curriculum. Therefore, the statute doesn’t burden plaintiffs’ free exercise rights, Patterson said. 
“There’s no requirement for teachers, school officials or students to interact with, bring attention to or even acknowledge the posters in any way,” she said. 
Patterson made her arguments to Judges Bobby E. Shepherd, L. Steven Grasz and David R. Stras. Shepherd, who is from El Dorado, was appointed to the bench by George W. Bush. President Donald Trump nominated Grasz and Stras.
Brooks, who issued the ruling against the displays, was nominated to the bench by Barack Obama.
The panel said challenges to the Free Exercise Clause often focus on limiting religious activity, but this case is about religious activity coming into the classroom, and questioned how neutrality works in this case. 
“There’s nothing neutral about it,” said Jonathan Youngwood, an attorney for the plaintiffs, who noted the law mandates a Judeo-Christian version of the Ten Commandments that’s inconsistent with the beliefs of an atheist family or any faith tradition with multiple gods. 
The panel questioned if plaintiffs objected to the displays’ directives to not steal or kill or simply to the commandments as a whole. Youngwood said the displays also command belief in one God.
“Schools use their limited classroom walls to teach,” he said. “This is instruction. These are, after all, commandments, and they are directly religious.” 
Following the conclusion of arguments, the judges said the case had been submitted and they would render a decision “as soon as possible.”
Similar Ten Commandments laws have been challenged in Louisiana and Texas. Following rulings from the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals earlier this year that both laws could go into effect, a Louisiana teacher and Texas families asked the U.S. Supreme Court to hear challenges to their state’s laws.
The Alabama Legislature this year approved a law requiring Ten Commandments displays in schools that goes into effect Oct. 1.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Landry’s proposed 90-day pause on diesel exports ruffles industry group
description: Gov. Jeff Landry’s idea to pause U.S. diesel exports for 90 days to help bring down prices at the pump is a “misguided proposal,” according to a leading Louisiana’s fossil fuel industry group. Landry used social media Friday to pitch the Trump administration and Congress on his diesel export embargo. He appeared on CNBC Monday […]
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry wants Congress and the Trump administration to pause diesel exports for 90 days. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)Gov. Jeff Landry’s idea to pause U.S. diesel exports for 90 days to help bring down prices at the pump is a “misguided proposal,” according to a leading Louisiana’s fossil fuel industry group.
Landry used social media Friday to pitch the Trump administration and Congress on his diesel export embargo. He appeared on CNBC Monday morning to discuss his proposal, saying that Americans are subsidizing the cost of diesel in Europe. The limited fuel supply and higher costs there are connected to “issues in Iran” and Russia’s war against Ukraine, the governor said.
“Europe has done nothing to help America in either one of those two positions, but yet they’re sucking the energy out of America and making American citizens pay for it,” Landry said.
The U.S. average price for diesel reached a record $6.51 a gallon Monday, according to AAA, a nearly $1 increase from last month and approaching $3 higher than a year ago.
A 90-day halt to U.S. diesel exports would lower domestic fuel prices in the short term while Congress and the White House take steps to address lasting policy, the governor said.

Tommy Faucheux, president of the Louisiana Mid-Continent Oil and Gas Association, issued a statement Monday against Landry’s idea. His 103-year-old organization represents all sectors of the industry doing business in the state and the Gulf of Mexico.
“Pipelines for domestic diesel transportation are already at max capacity. Without available capacity to redirect supply, halting the export of American diesel would force refineries to reduce production which would also decrease the production of gasoline,” Faucheux said. “This is a misguided proposal that would cause more harm and increase, not decrease, costs for American families and businesses.”
Fuel market analysts have said restricting diesel exports would most likely lead refineries to cut back production and fail to alleviate high prices, which are influenced by global demand. As long as overseas shortages linger, the cost per gallon in the U.S. isn’t expected to drop.
Every day, U.S. refineries produce more than 5 million barrels of distillate, which primarily consists of diesel fuel, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Historically, about a quarter of that amount has been exported, but the Iran war and sanctions against Russia for its aggression against Ukraine have elevated foreign shipments to more than 35% of the supply.
Until this year, Mexico and Brazil were the top destinations for U.S. distillate. World events have since steered more shipments to Europe. Although domestic fuel prices have increased, the U.S. has not typically seen diesel shortages because it produces more of the fuel than it consumes.
The American Fuel and Petrochemical Manufacturers, a trade group representing refineries, has said this excess diesel is helping address demand in regions that rely more on the fuel,  especially Europe.
“Instead of cutting prices for consumers, it would result in less U.S. fuel production, tighter supplies, greater energy security risks and higher prices,” the group said Monday in response to proposals to ban fuel exports.
Landry’s call for an embargo echoes appeals from U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, to President Trump over the weekend to turn off the flow of diesel to foreign markets. He has stressed the harsh impact of high fuel prices on farmers in his agriculture-rooted state.
“If our govt can embargo chips to China it can embargo diesel to help American farmers & truckers,” Grassley wrote Sunday on X. “We need our family farmers who feed & fuel the world (to be) on the strongest footing possible no matter what’s happening across the globe.”
The White House has been cold to the idea of a fuel shipment stoppage. In an interview with The Daily Caller last week, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said exporting less diesel fuel would lead to a corresponding decrease in refining, sending gasoline prices higher in the process.
“The thing we need when the prices are high is more supply. We need to do everything we can to grow supply,” Wright said. “If you start putting barriers on flows, pretty quickly you’ll reduce the production, and you’ll have less supply.”
Along with a 90-day export halt, Landry also wants the Trump administration to give small refineries a permanent exemption from meeting federal renewable fuel standards. Starting in 2007, refineries that process fewer than 75,000 barrels of crude daily were not required to produce blended fuels. The blanket exemption was pulled in 2011, when small refineries had to start applying for it and justify their reasons.
In 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency granted the exemption to 34 small refineries, including three in Louisiana.
The EPA has already issued an emergency waiver for refineries to end production of summer blend gasoline slightly earlier than usual to boost fuel supplies. As of Sept. 1, facilities were allowed to switch to winter blends, which are cheaper for refineries to produce but create more harmful emissions. The summer-winter switch typically takes place in mid-September, though states like California can require summer blend production through October.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Trump administration’s WA voter roll lawsuit dismissed
description: SEATTLE — A federal judge in Seattle on Tuesday tossed the Trump administration’s lawsuit against Washington seeking the state’s voter rolls, in line with many rulings across the country. This marks the 25th case that the U.S. Department of Justice has lost in its push to access sensitive voter information. The Justice Department has sued […]
text:
Ballot envelopes sit in the Thurston County elections center. (Photo by Laurel Demkovich/Washington State Standard)SEATTLE — A federal judge in Seattle on Tuesday tossed the Trump administration’s lawsuit against Washington seeking the state’s voter rolls, in line with many rulings across the country.
This marks the 25th case that the U.S. Department of Justice has lost in its push to access sensitive voter information. The Justice Department has sued many states for voter rolls, and has yet to have a judge rule in its favor. An appeals court has also ruled against it in a lawsuit against Michigan. The federal government has appealed many of its other losses, as well. 
Both sides had been waiting for weeks for a decision from U.S. District Court Judge Kymberly Evanson after an early August hearing in federal court in Seattle.
In her order Tuesday, Evanson, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, said the Trump administration’s argument is “not persuasive as a matter of statutory interpretation, nor is it consistent with the purpose” of federal law.
Washington Attorney General Nick Brown called the decision “the likeliest of victories for democracy.”
“Trump’s DOJ is now 0 for 25 nationwide in efforts to plunder the private information of states’ voters,” he continued in a statement. “We should not have to spend election season defending voters from their president, but victory after victory reminds us there is hope for the rule of law.”
Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said the decision “reaffirms that my office has every right to protect voter’s private data.”
“These baseless demands for state voter rolls are part of a broader pattern of federal overreach in states’ elections,” he added. “The DOJ does not have the authority or any reason to interfere with state election administration.”
Since that hearing, the Justice Department has threatened Hobbs over election records, directing him early this month to preserve documents from the 2024 election. Failing to do so “may constitute spoliation of evidence, which may subject you to civil and criminal sanctions,” according to the letter to Hobbs.
The conflict here began last September when Hobbs refused to provide the Trump administration with the personal information contained in the state’s voter rolls. 
Hobbs reported he’d be willing to provide voter names, addresses, genders, years of birth, voting records, registration dates and registration numbers. But he wouldn’t give dates of birth, driver license numbers and the last four digits of social security numbers, since that information is protected under Washington law.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In the hearing last month, Tera Heintz, of the Washington state attorney general’s office, called the demand “unprecedented and dangerous.”
“There is simply no authority for DOJ’s claim that they should be able to superintend on a line-by-line, individual-by-individual basis who is allowed to register and vote in state and federal elections,” she said. “That is not DOJ’s authority. It usurps the constitutional authority.”
Hobbs, a Democrat, feared the information would be shared with immigration authorities to fuel President Donald Trump’s crackdown, or that it could be used as pretext to remove voters from the rolls. Trump has repeatedly claimed massive voter fraud without evidence. Federal officials insisted the request was to ensure the state was properly updating its voter list under federal law. 
The federal government filed the litigation in December, but the case was delayed for months as the Justice Department’s attorneys failed to serve Washington state officials with the suit. 
The Trump administration alleges the records are needed to ensure states are complying with National Voter Registration Act requirements to remove voters who are ineligible from their voter rolls and the Help America Vote Act prohibition on processing voter registration applications without verifying the applicants’ identity. Also the Civil Rights Act of 1960, which federal attorneys claim forces election officials to provide this voter information to the U.S. attorney general if it is demanded. 
The state counters that this argument is wrong, that these federal laws don’t authorize the voter roll demand. The Civil Rights Act provision was meant to help prevent racial discrimination in elections in the segregated South.
In the hearing, Evanson noted many other courts have decided similar cases across the country. 
“Is there any meaningful basis on which to distinguish this case?” Evanson asked Justice Department attorney Raymond Yang. 
He responded that the cases are mostly identical, but other judges have “misconstrued” federal law.
The Department of Justice didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling.
At least 16 states led by Republicans have provided or said they would provide their full voter registration lists, according to the Brennan Center for Justice.
This is just one of the state’s flashpoints with the Trump administration over elections. Washington has also been at odds with the president over his unsuccessful efforts to restrict mail-in voting.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Remember: You might be wrong
description: Remember: You might be wrong. That was an admonition that Federal Judge Russell Smith bestowed on those who entered his chambers.  He was a scholar and an exemplary judge.  The federal courthouse in Missoula is named after him. Remember: You might be wrong. Words to be remembered by every prosecutor, officer and juror. Sometimes we are wrong. […]
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Remember: You might be wrong.
That was an admonition that Federal Judge Russell Smith bestowed on those who entered his chambers.  He was a scholar and an exemplary judge.  The federal courthouse in Missoula is named after him. Remember: You might be wrong.
Words to be remembered by every prosecutor, officer and juror. Sometimes we are wrong. And, the consequences are intolerable. Innocent people jailed.
The presumption of innocence means that it is better for a guilty man to go free than to send an innocent man to jail.
Those values are pillars of our democracy.
I grew up in a family of prosecutors. My great, great-grandfather was the U.S. Attorney for Montana.  My grandfather was Attorney General of Montana. My father was the County Attorney of Cascade County. Two of my children are prosecutors.
My family embraced those values.
In law school, we studied “In Re Winship,” in which Justice John Harlan wrote that “it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”
Reality check: Our system isn’t perfect;  sometimes we get it wrong.  Innocent people do go to jail.
The National Exoneration Registry tracks exonerations.  Check it out.
Consider this: The Registry identifies 3,847 people who have been exonerated since 1989. Innocent people sent to prison. They served more than 36,004 years in prison. And they were innocent. That is equivalent to sending every person in Dillon to prison. A moral alarm should be going off. This is every prosecutor’s nightmare. It is America’s failure.
Remember the Judge’s admonition: You might be wrong. Turns out: Eyewitness testimony is some of the least reliable evidence possible. Sixty-one percent of the people exonerated by DNA evidence were convicted by mistaken eyewitness testimony.  In robbery exonerations, 86% were convicted by mistaken eyewitness testimony. For sexual assault exonerations, 79% were convicted by mistaken eyewitness testimony.
Crime victims step forward to do their civil duty. Good people. Honest people. And, many times, their testimony and memory are wrong. Today, DNA evidence proves that.
Memory is complex. Someone suffers a traumatic incident. They are questioned, shown photographs, questioned more. Sometimes, the investigative process shapes and changes memories.  Real to the victim, but still mistaken. The result? An innocent person is convicted and goes to jail. And, just as importantly, a victim is revictimized when they learn that their testimony sent an innocent person to prison.
Sometimes there is a juror who isn’t convinced the defendant is guilty. Reasonable doubt. They question if the prosecutor and the witnesses could be wrong. When that happens, the jury room becomes a pressure cooker to get a unanimous guilty verdict.
We should celebrate those who doubt. They keep innocent people from going to prison. Those are the values upon which our democracy is built. As Justice Harlan counseled us: It is better — far better — for a guilty person to go free than it is to convict an innocent person. Let us recognize and honor those who doubt and who stand by their honest convictions when guilt is not proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
Three-thousand eight hundred and forty seven innocent people exonerated. Two hundred and two people on death row. They spent more than 13 million days in jail. Ponder that for a minute.  Millions of days. It is constitutionally intolerable. Consider the cost to taxpayers —  more than $2 billion.  Add to that the cost of compensating the wrongfully incarcerated. But there is more. How many children were wrongfully separated from a parent? Imagine the trauma.
This is part of our America. Part of Montana, where 16 have been exonerated.  Collectively, they served 144.8 years.  In Montana.
We must ask: How can we make our criminal justice system fairer?  What can we do to prevent innocent people from going to jail?
When someone isn’t convinced that a criminal defendant is guilty, appreciate and respect their doubt.  Their doubt is the only safeguard between freedom and prison. Their doubt is the only thing that prevents an innocent person from going to jail.
There are innocent people in prison today. Our justice isn’t perfect.  We must do better.
Remember the judge’s admonition: Remember, you might be wrong.  Too often we are.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Task force: Regional ambulance hubs for South Dakota will take years to establish
description: Regionalizing ambulance services would preserve them for rural areas and allow the state to guarantee a basic level of coverage, but the state would still need to pick up some of the cost of that guarantee, members of a legislative task force said this week.  What regional service looks like and what the state might […]
text:
Ambulances are parked in a Spearfish Emergency Ambulance Service facility earlier this year. A task force of South Dakota lawmakers is meeting this summer to discuss ideas for supporting local ambulance service providers. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)Regionalizing ambulance services would preserve them for rural areas and allow the state to guarantee a basic level of coverage, but the state would still need to pick up some of the cost of that guarantee, members of a legislative task force said this week. 
What regional service looks like and what the state might have to pay to prop it up are still open questions.
Those were the takeaways from Monday’s meeting of the Emergency Medical Services Funding Task Force in Pierre, where 11 lawmakers gathered for the third of four scheduled meetings. They also concluded that fixing the system will be a multi-year commitment requiring a permanent advisory board.
The task force is the second study group formed in as many years to address ambulance service sustainability in South Dakota in the face of Medicare and Medicaid reimbursements too low to pay for the service, particularly in sparsely populated parts of the state.
Much of the state relies on a dwindling pool of volunteer labor, as well as fewer young people willing or financially able to commit to the hundreds of training hours required for emergency medical technician certification.
South Dakota lawmakers not ready to call emergency medical services ‘essential’

In February, lawmakers passed bills to create legal protections for nurses who care for patients in an ambulance and to let police officers and firefighters drive ambulances if local providers deem that necessary. Those bills were recommended by the first task force.
Sen. Tim Reed has chaired both task forces. After Monday’s meeting, which ended with votes creating subcommittees to study regionalization needs and potential revenue models in collaboration with the governor’s office, the Brookings Republican said he sees a path forward during the 2027 legislative session.
The first step will be to create an advisory council of stakeholders in and out of government to oversee the regionalization process.
“We know it’s going to be a big lift to get this done,” Reed said. “So it’s going to take an ongoing group.”
Josie Harms, spokeswoman for Gov. Larry Rhoden, said the governor’s office looks forward to working with the task force “to establish a sustainable EMS system for South Dakota.”
Regionalization remains focus
The work of reforming rural ambulance services got an injection of federal support over the summer.
The state Department of Health signed a contract in August worth up to $719,000 with the South Dakota Foundation for Medical Care for “statewide planning, development, implementation, and oversight of Regional EMS Hub models.” The money comes from a $189 million pool of federal funding awarded to the state for use over the next five years through 2025’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. 
That Rural Health Transformation Program money can’t be used to supplant funding for existing projects, needs a “transformative” element, and must be used for “sustainable” projects, Department of Health Secretary Melissa Magstadt told the task force members on Monday.
“Anything that we bring forward has to come through that sort of lens,” Magstadt said.
Magstadt said her department is prepared to work with lawmakers and an advisory council on other proposals to help shepherd through a regional hub system.
Regionalization should save money through efficiencies, said Rep. Drew Peterson, R-Salem, though it will take time to figure out how much. Even so, he said, the state will need a long-term revenue source to guarantee a minimum level of service.
If the state sets those standards, Peterson said, counties and cities can’t be the ones forced to pay for them.
“I do not want to have an unfunded mandate being sent down to these local governments,” Peterson said. 
Ambulance services are funded through a mix of reimbursements for services through private insurance and public insurance like Medicare and Medicaid, limited local government funding in some jurisdictions, fundraising and grant money.
Possible revenue sources
Sen. Ernie Otten, R-Tea, hopes the state can get creative with its federal rural health dollars to ease the transition to a regional model, and that the savings from regionalization make rural ambulance service more affordable. 
The committee also discussed more treatment on-site and updating state law to make sure rural ambulance services can bill for doing it, and mandating a certain level of reimbursement from private insurers for out-of-network ambulance services.
Even so, Otten said the task force needs to come to Pierre next year prepared to talk about new income sources to “backfill” gaps that remain after regionalization.
Lawmakers look for ways to deliver on support for ‘essential’ ambulance service

Otten asked the state Department of Tourism to prepare a revenue estimate for a $1 nightly fee on lodging, short-term rentals and campground stays, with the fee applied for up to five nights. Such fees would raise around $7.1 million, according to a document shared at Monday’s task force meeting.
A fee that small wouldn’t be “onerous,” Otten said. Even if people look at their hotel bill and get “a little miffed” about an ambulance fee, Otten said he wouldn’t expect people to balk at paying “a lousy dollar.”
He also mentioned a tax on vapor products like e-cigarettes. Those are taxed at the standard 4.2% state sales tax rate now, but lawmakers passed a bill to license vape retailers this year.
A tax on those products could “easily generate $3 million,” Otten said.
“At the end of the day, we’re going to have to just come to the realization that the state has to pick up a lot of this,” said Otten, who later told South Dakota Searchlight that guaranteeing ambulance service in rural areas is “more than a necessity.” 
Other revenue sources
Rep. John Hughes said the state needs to be willing to engage with the state’s three major healthcare systems — Sanford, Avera and Monument — on financial support.
“I can’t think of any entities with more of a vested interest in this,” said Hughes, who argued that supporting ambulance services would be a better use of revenue for the systems than “building another building” or marketing.
Patients wary of government, companies pushing AI as a rural healthcare solution

“That would be improving the human condition, in my opinion,” said Hughes, referencing marketing language used by Sanford Health.
Hughes had similar comments at a previous task force meeting, prompting an appearance on Monday from Tim Rave, the president and CEO of the South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations. In remarks prepared as a response to Hughes’ August remarks, Rave told the task force that hospital revenues in much of the state are razor thin, that hospitals already cover millions in charity care, and that many of the patients transported by ambulances struggle to pay their bills.
Subsidizing ambulance services with hospital dollars would ultimately hurt patient care, Rave said.
“Hospitals are not an unlimited piggy bank,” Rave said.
Hughes said he doesn’t want a mandate, but rather “a conversation” about the role health systems might play in making sure people who fall ill or experience an emergency in a far-flung area can get help in time.
Hospitals already offer some support for emergency medical services in parts of the state, said Rep. Nick Fosness, R-Britton. Fosness is a healthcare administrator, and said one healthcare system in his district pays nurses double their hourly rate to ride along on ambulance calls when the ambulance operator doesn’t have an available volunteer with advanced lifesaving skills. That same system “does the laundry” for the ambulance service, helps recruit new EMS volunteers and offers training.
Such steps are “just a necessity” to serve patients in some places, Fosness said.
“It’s a practical thing, to keep the service and to keep patient safety number one,” he said. “That’s what we all are doing across this great state, trying to keep patients safe and move the right patient to the right services.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Dana Nessel says she’ll vote for Abdul El-Sayed, ending potential Michigan Democratic Party rift
description: As Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed continues to court some of his biggest intraparty detractors, Attorney General Dana Nessel on Tuesday said that she is no longer one of them. Nessel and El-Sayed appeared together on the latest episode of the “For the Sake of the Argument with Lori Goldman” podcast, a production of […]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel appear together on the “For the Sake of the Argument with Lori Goldman” podcast, a production of Distill Social. (Screenshot)
As Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed continues to court some of his biggest intraparty detractors, Attorney General Dana Nessel on Tuesday said that she is no longer one of them.
Nessel and El-Sayed appeared together on the latest episode of the “For the Sake of the Argument with Lori Goldman” podcast, a production of the activist organization and social media outfit Distill Social.


 










View this post on Instagram






















 
A post shared by For the Sake of the Argument with Lori Goldman (@forthesakeoftheargument)



On the podcast, Nessel said she can’t be true to her values if she “even considers” voting for Republican nominee Mike Rogers, who has been endorsed by President Donald Trump.
“Yes, I’ll be voting for Abdul,” Nessel said. “We have one candidate that I know is going to fight against the Trump administration; who is going to fight to protect both our physical security, our safety, our health and our futures.”
Rogers, on the other hand, would “not do any of that,” Nessel said. She argued that Rogers “only cared about self-enrichment, and how many pats on the back he can get from Donald Trump. So, for me, I don’t want to say the choice is easy. But I am going to say that there is no choice, and that’s why I’m supporting Abdul for the U.S. Senate.”
El-Sayed, seated next to Nessel, said he was glad to have the attorney general’s support.
“I’m particularly grateful for it because I know we haven’t always agreed on everything,” El-Sayed said. “I know we won’t always agree on everything, but I also know that you care about my kids and have fought for them. I know you know that I care about your kids, and have fought for them and will fight for them. That’s the thing that we can do together.”
In video clips circulated of the exchange, El-Sayed and Nessel firmly shake hands just after they gave each other praise.
The attorney general, who is Jewish, had originally backed the senatorial primary campaign of U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham). Following a tense Michigan Democratic Party spring endorsement convention, in which some Jewish Democrats said they were harassed by pro-Palestine party delegates, Nessel said she no longer felt safe attending the party’s summer convention, and that Michigan Jews were having a tough feeling at home in the party.
That unease has led some Michigan Jews to say they were also unsure if they would be voting for El-Sayed, as others announced that they would be voting for Rogers instead.
Nessel started to turn the tide on El-Sayed, however, when she told Jewish Democrats this summer that they may need to put “the needs of the world” ahead of their own personal feelings on the race, a not-so-veiled jab at Republicans and their figurehead in Trump.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Takeaways from former Gov. Mark Dayton’s book stop in Northfield
description: Former Gov. Mark Dayton recently began a book tour following the release of “Perseverance,” a memoir reflecting on his nearly five decades in Minnesota politics. Dayton has rarely been seen in public after retiring from office in 2019. In revisiting the people and experiences that influenced his career, however, he’s sought to offer some insight […]
text:
Gov. Mark Dayton, appearing at Content Bookstore in Northfield, compared his activism against the Vietnam War to Operation Metro Surge during a recent book talk:  “Vietnam was so appalling because you saw these innocent people being maimed, attacked,” he said. “But, you know, that was Americans attacking people in another country. These were Americans attacking Americans.” (Photo by Maya Betti/Minnesota Reformer)Former Gov. Mark Dayton recently began a book tour following the release of “Perseverance,” a memoir reflecting on his nearly five decades in Minnesota politics.
Dayton has rarely been seen in public after retiring from office in 2019. In revisiting the people and experiences that influenced his career, however, he’s sought to offer some insight into the current political landscape ahead of November’s elections. 
Dayton recently joined longtime friend and semi-retired Minnesota Star Tribune columnist Lori Sturdevant, editor of his memoir, for a conversation hosted by Content Bookstore in Northfield. 
Here are some key takeaways. 
Why now? 
As Dayton approaches 80, the “L” word is hanging over him: legacy, especially how future generations — including his five grandchildren — view his public life. 
“I wanted to write something that they could remember me by, and something that hopefully the next generation will take to heart,” he said. 
The book’s title draws from advice Dayton said he received early in his career from late U.S. Sen. Ted Kennedy: “Perseverance is the prerequisite for success in politics.”
Dayton has survived multiple losing campaigns, mental illness, addiction and myriad health problems. 
The two-term governor added: “I hope if people reading this get nothing else out of it, they’ll think, ‘Yeah, I’ve got to persevere.’”
Echoes of Nixon era felt today
Dayton was involved in the anti-Vietnam War movement in college at Yale, which he describes in the book. His activism eventually put him under federal scrutiny. He was investigated by the IRS, had his phone tapped and was called before a grand jury. 
He was also, quite proudly, on former President Richard Nixon’s “enemies list.” 
“Back then, Richard Nixon had all the power,” Dayton said. “They were harassing people and imprisoning people unfairly.” 
During Operation Metro Surge, Dayton, who spends his winters in Arizona, began to draw parallels as he watched what was happening in his home state. 
 “Vietnam was so appalling because you saw these innocent people being maimed, attacked,” he said. “But, you know, that was Americans attacking people in another country. These were Americans attacking Americans.” 
Nixon’s career ended in the disgrace of Watergate, which revealed widespread corruption that had permeated his administration. 
“I’m hoping that parallel continues today, starting with the election in November,” Dayton said. 
Minnesota’s next leaders will face hard choices
Dayton said Minnesota’s next leaders will face a tougher economic climate than he did as governor. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During his eight-year tenure, Minnesota was coming out of the Great Recession, the farm economy was strong and employment rates were rising. Today, however, 47% of Minnesotans reported that their personal finances have worsened over the past year, according to a Chamber of Commerce poll. Minnesota’s population is aging, and both population and economic growth have slowed. 
“The choices are going to be much more difficult,” Dayton said. “Setting priorities can be much more important.”
His suggestions? A continued focus on education and an assurance that the state government’s fraud epidemic is finally squashed. 
“The checkpoints in state government were just not set up for that kind of onslaught. Now, they are,” he said. “Setting up the guardrails, making early detection, and responding immediately when there’s the first sign of any misdemeanors is going to be crucial.”
What makes a good politician?
The November election features races in each of the state’s constitutional offices including governor and attorney general, as well as contests for U.S. Senate, eight congressional seats and all 201 legislative districts, with voters preparing to make key decisions about the state’s future. 
“I think we’re going to turn this country around. To do that, you got to lead upward,” Dayton said.
The government and its leaders can and should recognize differences among people, but instead of deepening divisions, Dayton said, a good leader looks for a common cause and asks: “What matters that unite us?”
“I say there’s no saints in politics; they’re only shades of sinners,” he said. “But, there are shades.” (Dayton won over many crowds with his self-deprecation and wit.) 
For Dayton, that distinction between shades comes down to intent — whether leaders are serving themselves or the public.
And, in the end, we’ll need something new — or something old again. 
“It’s going to take a new brand of leadership, or an old brand reestablished,” he said.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Why the Colorado School of Mines is falling short in sustainability
description: In May I earned my undergraduate degree in environmental engineering from Colorado School of Mines in Golden. I was elated as any student might be, proud to carry the oath of an engineer to better our world. My pride was dampened when, just two months after graduating, I found out that a department integral to […]
text:
The historic 1905 Guggenheim Hall with its golden dome is part of the Colorado School of Mines campus in Golden, Colorado. (Getty Images)In May I earned my undergraduate degree in environmental engineering from Colorado School of Mines in Golden. I was elated as any student might be, proud to carry the oath of an engineer to better our world.
My pride was dampened when, just two months after graduating, I found out that a department integral to my experience at Colorado School of Mines was quietly dismantled: the sustainability department, know as Mines Sus. No public statement was given, only a LinkedIn post from the former department head.
Meanwhile, the website cannot be reached and the department is virtually untraceable. The department that embodied the principles that motivated me to become an environmental engineer, using resources in a way that enables the flourishing of future generations, was abolished within minutes.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mines Sus held the academic institution — which produces thousands of engineers per year — accountable by monitoring production of recyclables, landfill waste, and compost across the university. From 2022 to 2023, waste-to-landfill decreased by 1,500 tons, coinciding with expanded recycling education from a new Mines Sus program.
It also created carbon dioxide emission, energy and water consumption targets. It reported the status of Mines sustainability via the STARS program and publicly accessible reports. Not to mention, it guided senior year capstone projects focused on increasing sustainability at Mines, such as using local geothermal energy. It additionally created a green labs program to reduce emissions associated with fume hoods, which can consume 3.5 times the energy of an average home, as well as reduce lab waste via recycling pipette tips and latex gloves. I might add, at a university with a serious civil engineering reputation, that Mines Sus helped accredit buildings with LEED rankings. Most importantly, it ultimately was a one-stop-shop for sustainability awareness at Mines. 
School of Mines is a large academic and research institution that hosts thousands of students, not an average household. Without a department that ensures School of Mines is responsibly consuming water and energy and producing reasonable quantities of waste, how will the school be held accountable? It is likely that unless there is a paid position, departments left to themselves will be forced to direct their limited time and resources elsewhere. Not to mention, this may put Mines at a disadvantage for enrollment, considering that many students look at sustainability rankings when making their decision to commit. School of Mines will likely no longer have a sustainability ranking in the absence of the department. 
If the very institution students attend to learn to be an engineer is not held accountable to sustainable principles, how will those students walk into this world? Departments can certainly teach sustainability, but what is teaching without practice? As engineers, we swear to uphold an “obligation to serve humanity by making the best use of the Earth’s precious wealth.”
A school like Mines, one of the most renowned engineering schools in the country, should be walking the walk. 
Here is my recommendation: Mines alumni, students, staff and Golden community members should make their voices heard. They should email the board of trustees that they are unsettled by news of the discontinuation of the Mines sustainability department. They should demand accountability and transparency.
Let us create better engineers and ensure academic institutions keep the bar high, especially our own.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Proposal could boost FEMA’s response to domestic violence after disasters
description: After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, a study found intimate partner violence was nearly three times higher the year after the storm among people who were displaced and living in trailer parks in Louisiana and Mississippi.
text:
Tarps cover the damage Hurricane Laura inflicted in 2020 upon a home in Lake Charles. (Photo by Chris Vinn for Louisiana Illuminator)
This story was originally reported by Jessica Kutz of The 19th.  Meet Jessica and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
After a deadly wildfire tore through Maui in August 2023, community organizer Khara Jabola-Carolus set out to ask women how they were faring after the disaster. She teamed up with fellow community organizer Nadine Ortega to co-found Tagnawa, a grassroots recovery organization to meet the needs of Filipinos and other marginalized groups on the island.
There are plenty of statistics and anecdotes documenting the abuse and violence women have had to endure following natural disasters. Still, what Jabola-Carolus learned was startling: Of the 70 Filipino women Tagnawa surveyed, one in six said they felt forced to engage in “survival sex,” which involves the exchange of sexual acts for food, housing and other basic necessities.
Mental health experts also shared stories of child sexual abuse going unreported to keep a family unit together amid the uncertainty and instability caused by the fires. At Women Helping Women, a local domestic violence organization, the number of calls doubled to 550 per month in the first two months after the disaster.
“We tried to gather as much as we could in that short window of time in order to generate action,” said Jabola-Carolus, a former executive director of the Hawai’i State Commission on the Status of Women whose family is from the Philippines, where hurricanes and typhoons have been linked to increased violence against women.
Three years later, Reps. Laurel Lee, a Florida Republican, and Lucy McBath, a Georgia Democrat, have introduced legislation directing the Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, to strengthen safety at evacuation shelters and establish reporting protocols for issues like domestic violence and sexual assault.
The bill also requires training for FEMA personnel in how to identify and support survivors of gender-based violence, as well as changes to how the agency conducts household check-ins after a disaster. Currently, FEMA workers meet only with the head of household, typically a man. If the bill becomes law, they would have to meet with all adults in the family, something that advocates say could help women report abuse post-disaster.
The Federal Emergency Management Agency building in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 25, 2024. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)
In an email to The 19th, McBath said that FEMA’s own advisory council found in a 2024 report that the agency should do more to address gender-based violence and exploitation, and to stop human trafficking in the wake of disasters. “Our bill turns that expert recommendation into law.”
She added: “Our legislation addresses gaps in disaster response that impact survivors of natural disasters the most — being without their homes and their support systems. As a survivor of gun violence myself, the journey to recovery from any trauma is already incredibly difficult. This is our way of doing our part to ensure that every survivor is seen, heard, and protected.”
Lee has previously worked on legislation aimed at tackling human trafficking; Florida ranks third for human trafficking among U.S. states — and it faces the threat of hurricanes every year. She could not be reached for comment.
Though limited in scope, Tagnawa’s survey, “Equality in Flames,” echoed longstanding patterns of abuse following natural disasters. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, one study found that women in Mississippi who had live-in partners were twice as likely to report physical abuse after the hurricane; a separate survey found that intimate partner violence was nearly three times higher the year after the storm among people who were displaced and living in trailer parks in Louisiana and Mississippi.
More recently, after a severe winter storm impacted Texas in 2021, domestic violence calls went up. One national organization that provides cash assistance to survivors of gender-based violence noted that for one in four applicants, the abuse either began or worsened during the disaster, The Texas Tribune reported.
Under the Trump administration, the domestic violence services infrastructure has been destabilized through delayed and canceled grants and shifting priorities, forcing a number of organizations to lay off workers and reduce services, like hotlines that were previously available 24/7.
President Trump’s budget for fiscal year 2027, released in April and not yet approved by Congress, includes significant cuts to housing and legal assistance programs under the Office on Violence Against Women. In a statement at the time, the National Network to End Domestic Violence called federal funding “the backbone of our nation’s response to violence and our commitment to survivors’ safety, stability, and recovery.” Any reduction, the statement added, “jeopardizes vital services and risks the lives of victims and their children.”
It is against this backdrop that the bill was introduced, though it remains unclear whether it will advance to a committee hearing during a final sprint to end the legislative session after the midterms recess. Regardless of whether the legislation moves forward this time, Yasmin Vafa, co-founder and executive director of Rights4Girls, an advocacy organization that helped raise awareness among lawmakers on Capitol Hill, said there’s value in bringing the topic of gender violence and natural disasters into the national conversation. “That’s one of the important principles of doing federal policy advocacy is that even the mere introduction of a bill at the federal level can get states thinking about it,” she said.
She provided an example of another bill introduced in the House, and for which she lobbied, that would allow for shorter minimum sentences in cases where victims are convicted of harming their abusers: It has yet to pass in Congress, but it has led to similar laws at the state level in California, Hawaii, Illinois, Oklahoma, Tennessee and Virginia.
Jennifer Horney, a professor at the University of Delaware who has researched disasters and gender-based violence, said the FEMA bill has some of the same recommendations made in reports she has co-authored. One of the findings “was to think about ways that people whose primary job is in emergency response and emergency management could be more aware of the increased risk for violence post-disaster,” she said. “The fact that the legislation calls out the importance of trauma-informed care is really critical to providing these services.”
Beyond passing the legislation, Horney said the federal and state governments could allocate more money to domestic violence organizations, which would, in turn, increase support for survivors after disasters.
The Trump administration has moved in the opposite direction, though: It has slashed funding to these same organizations, which has already led to reduced services.
Globally, there is widespread recognition that disasters lead to an increase in gender-based violence, with most research and policy-making on the topic being produced abroad. Still, the U.S. State Department has recognized this is an issue, at least internationally, said Vafa, of Rights4Girls. In 2022, in its annual “Trafficking in Persons” report, the department acknowledged that climate change and extreme weather displace populations and can lead to an increase in trafficking of women and children.
The National Science Foundation, the federal government’s most prominent scientific agency, also released a report in 2024 finding that public health emergencies, like natural disasters, are associated with an increase in the severity and frequency of intimate partner violence.
Jabola-Carolus said that if the FEMA legislation passes, the United States would at least come closer to other countries that are already dealing with the impacts of climate disasters. Countries like the one her family is from. “Filipinos are essentially people from the climate future,” she said. They are already confronting the ways women are affected by climate disasters.
In 2016, the Philippines passed disaster reform legislation that integrated sex trafficking response and prevention into disaster recovery and planning. The United States, she said, can learn from them.

title: New ads feature young Hoosiers encouraging their peers to vote
description: A six-week advertising campaign launched Tuesday by the nonprofit group ReCenter Indiana features young Hoosiers going to vote and sharing their experience. It’s directed specifically at residents of Marion, Hamilton and Boone counties between the ages of 18 and 24. The videos were recorded in Lawrence, Carmel and Zionsville during Indiana primary voting in[...]
text:
ReCenter Indiana's YouTube page features the new ads. (Screenshot)A six-week advertising campaign launched Tuesday by the nonprofit group ReCenter Indiana features young Hoosiers going to vote and sharing their experience.
It’s directed specifically at residents of Marion, Hamilton and Boone counties between the ages of 18 and 24.
The videos were recorded in Lawrence, Carmel and Zionsville during Indiana primary voting in May. Outside their respective polling places, the young adult voters are shown sharing their personal feelings about the voting process and what the experience means to them. The videos do not mention candidates or political parties.
In one of them, a young woman votes for the first time in Indiana since moving here. She describes the process as easy and the staff as friendly and helpful.
“I’m advocating for what I feel is right. I’m also advocating for the community,” she said. “It’s always a good feeling when you vote and your voice can be heard.”
The nonpartisan group’s campaign will run through Election Day, Nov. 3, on YouTube, Instagram and connected TV services including Netflix, HBO and Peacock. The video ads are projected to generate more than 1.5 million impressions. A $50,000 grant from Glick Fund made the campaign possible.
ReCenter Indiana has made young adult voters a special focus of its work to strengthen civic engagement and voter participation. In the 2024 general election, only 39% of Hoosier young adults voted, according to Tufts CIRCLE 2024 youth voting report. That compares to the national young adult turnout rate of 47%. For eligible voters of all ages, Indiana is perennially among the states with the lowest turnouts.
“Instead of actors reading scripts, our videos feature authentic, young Hoosier voters — saying in their own words — why they’re enthusiastic about voting,” said Jocelyn Vare, executive director of ReCenter Indiana. “And, importantly, these voting experiences are built around the invitation, ‘Hey, can I vote with you?’”
The news release said research supports this peer-to-peer approach. In the Turnout Nation 2019 study, registered voters steadily encouraged by someone they knew were 13.2 percentage points more likely to actually cast a ballot. In two decades of studies, researchers reported, this approach proved more effective than any other.
ReCenter Indiana is asking Hoosiers to share the videos with young adults and then ask, “Hey,  can I vote with you?” The group says an invitation from a friend, relative, classmate or co-worker can make voting feel more comfortable, especially for a first-time voter.
