name: Washington State Standard
title: Coast Guard icebreaker Healy cancels fall voyage to Arctic Ocean after mechanical problem
description: The Coast Guard icebreaker Healy will not sail to the Arctic Ocean this year. The Healy is one of only two active Arctic icebreakers in the Coast Guard’s fleet and had been scheduled to return to service this year and sail to the Arctic after an overhaul, but during a post-shipyard voyage in July, it […]
text:
The U.S. Coast Guard icebreaker Healy is seen on Nov. 7, 2022, in Juneau, Alaska. (Photo by James Brooks/Alaska Beacon)

The Coast Guard icebreaker Healy will not sail to the Arctic Ocean this year.
The Healy is one of only two active Arctic icebreakers in the Coast Guard’s fleet and had been scheduled to return to service this year and sail to the Arctic after an overhaul, but during a post-shipyard voyage in July, it suffered a severe mechanical breakdown off the coast of Washington state.
The website gCaptain, which reported on the incident at the time, cited unnamed sources who said one of the ship’s crankcases had exploded.
In July and again this week, the Coast Guard declined to answer questions from the Beacon asking to confirm that account.
In a written statement, a Coast Guard spokesman said only, “The Coast Guard continues investigating the cause of the engineering casualty onboard Coast Guard Cutter (CGC) Healy. CGC Healy will not complete its planned 2026 high-latitude summer mission. However, the Coast Guard is developing repair plans and evaluating the feasibility of additional operations.”
The Coast Guard did not answer multiple followup questions, including how long the Healy’s repair will take and whether the Coast Guard will seek to have another icebreaker take the Healy’s place.
This is the second major problem aboard the Healy in two years. In 2024, an electrical fire aboard the ship canceled its fall voyage into the Arctic.
Without the Healy, the Coast Guard’s sole Arctic icebreaker is the former oilfield services ship Storis, which was commissioned into Coast Guard service last year and is not yet fully operational to Coast Guard standards.
The heavy icebreaker Polar Star is operational but is committed to service in Antarctica and is thus unavailable for Arctic service.
The Storis is less effective in ice than the Healy, which has reached the North Pole several times, and does not have dedicated science lab space, as the Healy does.
Earlier this year, the Coast Guard awarded construction contracts for 11 new icebreakers of two different designs. The first four ships — two from each design — are being built in Finland and are scheduled for delivery by 2028.
In the meantime, the Coast Guard has been using non-icebreaker ships in the Arctic. This summer, the CGC Munro monitored two Chinese research ships operating in the Arctic off Alaska.


This story was originally produced by Alaska Beacon, which is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network which includes Washington State Standard, and is supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Safe drinking water is human right, UN says, despite 5th Circuit ruling in Jackson case
description: Members of the Mississippi National Guard distribute bottled water to Jackson residents at the Mississippi Trade Mart in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, Sept. 1, 2022.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here. 

Although the federal 5th Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed a lawsuit from Mississippi residents related to lead-contaminated water earlier this month, the right to safe drinking water has been recognized by the United Nations as a universal human right since 2010.
The United Nations General Assembly adopted a historic resolution in 2010 recognizing “the right to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation as a human right that is essential for the full enjoyment of  life and all human rights” (A/RES/64/292). To advocate for these rights, the UN appointed a special rapporteur on the rights to safe drinking water and sanitation.
Such access to safe drinking water is considered a vital asset for the survival and coexistence of human societies. The criteria for such access are simple: water must be available, accessible, affordable, safe and acceptable. Most importantly, water is not a product to be traded and should never be considered an “economic commodity.”
Why did the United Nations adopt a human-rights based approach to safe drinking water? Access to safe water is considered by many to be the foundation of a healthy, educated and economically strong community. The right to a dignified life includes the right of everyone to the enjoyment of the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. For Americans, the basic rights defined in the Declaration of Independence as “Life, Liberty and the Pursuit of Happiness” are impossible without safe drinking water.
Emma Gilligan Credit: Sarah J. Slover
Unsafe water spreads diseases such as diarrhea, cholera and typhoid, compromising the physical health of any community. Safe water allows for gender equality and dignity by allowing us to maintain our personal hygiene and prevents women and girls in many countries from walking long distances to fetch water, compromising their safety and depriving them of the time they might be in school or at work. 
Safe water also makes it possible for young people, who might otherwise be incapacitated by waterborne illnesses, to attend school.
We are now in the eighth year of the United Nations Water Action Decade (2018-2028) and the World Economic Forum continues to rank the water crisis in the top three global risks. Given the enormity of that threat, the Forum named 2026 the “Year of Water.” 
Many Americans take clean water for granted. However, there are 2.1 billion people worldwide still living without access to safe drinking water, and far more drastic actions need to be taken to protect watersheds, design more resilient cities, and improve efficiency to conserve the clean water that exists for consumption and agriculture.
Protecting our natural resources for the sake of the common good, known simply as the “commons,” is central to the sustainability of our shared resources. The stewardship of those resources should not be driven by personal interest, economic gain or political ambition, but by a spirit of shared responsibility and accountability.
The water crisis for those who live in Jackson, Mississippi was avoidable. The actions that led to the contamination of public drinking water was not only a failure of governance but a staggering display of indifference to the health of its inhabitants, the region’s collective natural resources and utilities.
Unlike Montana, Pennsylvania or New York, there is no “Green Amendment” in Mississippi – an amendment to a state constitution’s Bill of Rights that recognizes and protects “the inalienable rights of all people to clean water and air, a stable climate and healthy environments.”
Nevertheless, managing the commons that houses our water supply requires transparent and publicly accountable management – a failure that looms large in the Sterling v. City of Jackson case.
Unlike the case in Flint, Michigan, Mississippi’s 5th Circuit Court rejected the claim that government officials had violated the residents’ right to bodily integrity, as protected under the 14th amendment. Equally egregious was the 5th Circuit’s conclusion that “we find no deeply rooted history or tradition establishing a constitutional right to truthful information from officials during a public health crisis” 
The question then remains; who exactly is responsible for the commons and the truth about its condition in the state of Mississippi? 

Emma Gilligan is the author of “The Future and You” and a leading expert in international human rights. With over 30 years of experience in the field, she currently serves as a professor of human rights at Indiana University and is co-founder of the Atrocity Crimes Advisory Group for Ukraine.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis’ commerce secretary approved as Pensacola State College president
description: Former deputy chief of staff to Gov. Ron DeSantis and sitting Secretary of Commerce Alex Kelly will take over as president of Pensacola State College next month — months before the two-term governor exits office. Pensacola State College trustees voted unanimously Monday that Kelly will succeed Edward Meadows, who has been president there since 2008. […]
text:
Alex Kelly takes a walk around campus before during his visit in which he was approved as Pensacola State College president. (Photo courtesy PSC)Former deputy chief of staff to Gov. Ron DeSantis and sitting Secretary of Commerce Alex Kelly will take over as president of Pensacola State College next month — months before the two-term governor exits office.
Pensacola State College trustees voted unanimously Monday that Kelly will succeed Edward Meadows, who has been president there since 2008.
Former Secretary of Commerce and now President of Pensacola State College Alex Kelly. (Photo courtesy of PSC)
“I have spent my career working to connect people with opportunity, and few institutions do that more directly than colleges like Pensacola State. Our students will be the workforce, entrepreneurs and leaders who shape Northwest Florida’s future,” Kelly, who is expected to begin Oct. 19, said in a news release.
His experience as commerce secretary “closely aligns with Pensacola State College’s role in creating opportunities for students, meeting regional workforce needs and supporting communities across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties,” the college said in a news release.
Kelly has been secretary of commerce since 2023. Earlier, he was deputy chief of staff to DeSantis and chief of staff in the Florida Department of Education. Before joining the DeSantis administration, he had a lengthy history working in the legislative process, including as a staffer and legislative affairs director for executive agencies, as well as in political campaigns.
“Alex understands, as well as anyone in Florida, how education and economic opportunity are connected,” Board of Trustees Chair Zack Smith said in a news release. “Throughout this process, we have seen a leader who listens, understands what employers and communities need and recognizes the extraordinary role Pensacola State plays in creating opportunity for our students and our region. The Board is confident he is the right person to lead PSC into its next chapter.”
Among the ranks of DeSantis officials to leave the administration for college leadership jobs are Eric Hall, former secretary of the Department of Juvenile Justice who is now president of Pasco-Hernando State College; and Anastasios Kamoutsas, former education commissioner and now president of Polk State College.
According to the college, 107 qualified candidates applied.
Pensacola State College is one of 28 state colleges.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: ‘A lot less bad’: Wake commissioners approve updated deal to combine WakeMed and Atrium
description: The Wake County Board of Commissioners voted 5-2 late Monday to approve a controversial merger between WakeMed and Atrium Health. The vote came after a five-hour public hearing during which deputies cleared protesters from the chambers as commissioners were preparing to vote on the transfer agreement. Atrium has pledged $2 billion in hospital improvements. W[...]
text:
Rev. Rob Stephens and members of The Patients Union cheer as Wake County Commissioner Tara Waters says that she will not support the WakeMed Atrium merger. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)  The Wake County Board of Commissioners voted 5-2 late Monday to approve a controversial merger between WakeMed and Atrium Health.
The vote came after a five-hour public hearing during which deputies cleared protesters from the chambers as commissioners were preparing to vote on the transfer agreement.
Atrium has pledged $2 billion in hospital improvements. WakeMed President and CEO Donald Gintzig has said that funding is vital as the county continues to grow.
WakeMed is the largest health system in the state’s largest county. The taxpayer-funded community hospital has served Wake County residents since 1961. In contrast, Atrium Health is a massive healthcare system with over 70,000 employees across 40 hospitals serving the Carolinas, Georgia and Alabama.
Longtime county residents, health advocates, and state employees voiced opposition to the merger, saying it would lead to higher healthcare costs, less charity care, and a likely reduction in hospital staffing, based on Atrium’s practices in other communities where it operates.
Governor Josh Stein, who voiced early reservations about the merger, entered the negotiation process over the weekend and by Sunday announced he would not stand in the way of the deal because Atrium had agreed to changes Stein said he requested.
Stein said improvements to the initial proposal included a sizable increase in charity care, a $150 million community benefit fund for Wake County, and a clarification that Atrium would make the $2 billion investment from its own assets, not WakeMed’s, over a 15-year period.
Stein said Atrium also agreed not to increase prices at WakeMed more than 1.5 times the annual increase in Medicare costs for the next five years.
After the commission voted, Stein invited Attorney General Jeff Jackson to provide an independent assessment.
“Since my time as Attorney General, I have been urging the General Assembly to give the Attorney General’s Office more authority to review hospital transactions,” Stein said in a statement. “Health care costs are too high, and additional oversight and authority would better protect patients.”
Commissioner Vickie Adamson said the proposed deal left her with many unanswered questions. (Photo: Wake.gov livestream)
Wake County Attorney Roger Askew said the final deal  agreement increases the indigent care WakeMed can provide from 4.8% in the initial offer to at least 8% of total adjusted revenues.
Askew said the new board of directors will be made up of eight Wake County appointees and six Atrium appointees. For institutional continuity, five of the appointees would be current WakeMed board members.
Commissioner Vickie Adamson said it was troubling that the legally binding documents they were being asked to approve during the meeting did not contain the commitments announced by the governor a day earlier.
Askew said in some cases the final language had not been drafted. But he assured commissioners that the language regarding the price cap and the $2 billion commitment would be fully scrutinized before the deal was finalized.
“And we don’t know what happens [with the price cap] at the end of five years?” asked Adamson.
“No,” acknowledged Askew.
Adamson said the deal was “a lot less bad” than what was presented in May, but she could not support it.
Commissioner Safiyah Jackson said she had to consider WakeMed’s long-term sustainability.
For two years, the WakeMed board studied whether the community hospital could survive alone and sustain its mission.
“They considered Duke, UNC, Novant and Atrium. They unanimously and still today unanimously maintain that Atrium was the best strategic fit,” said Jackson.
Jackson said while her vote would certainly make some angry, her decision was to try to protect the safety net for future generations.
“Every year, WakeMed provides over $100 million in free care to the most vulnerable families,’ said Jackson. “But standing alone in a changing world is getting harder every day.”
SEANC President Wendell Powell spoke against the merger during a September 21, 2026 rally in Nash Square. Powell said the merger would cost state employees more over time. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)
Commissioner Cheryl Stallings said federal cuts under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act were leading to more uninsured patients coming to WakeMed. Those financial pressures would only increase without a partnership, she said.
Nearly 100 critics of the merger gathered in Raleigh’s Nash Square Monday before the meeting to urge the commission to vote against combining WakeMed and Atrium Health.
Commissioner Tara Waters stood with opponents under a century-old oak tree and said she could not bring herself to vote for a deal that lacked transparency from the start.
“I represent a district where people tonight will sleep in their cars. I represent a district where people don’t know where their next meal is coming from,” said Waters. “I’ll magnify the needs of the least among us. That is the call that we are all charged to do.”
Waters said the deal deserved more public engagement, not last-minute changes made over the weekend, followed by a rushed vote.
Merger oversight out, but whistleblower protections and CEO pay caps remain in NC hospital bill

Rebecca Cerese with the N.C. Justice Center’s Health Advocacy Project agreed the public deserved a much better process.
“The price cap is only for five years.That goes by in the blink of an eye,” said Cerese.”What are the protections after that? Atrium is a much more expensive hospital system.”
Members of the State Employees Association of North Carolina (SEANC) estimate a combined WakeMed-Atrium would raise healthcare premiums for state employees another $10 a month.
Faith leaders also criticized Monday’s vote falling on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year in Judaism, preventing many from being present at the hearing.
Chairman Don Mial along with commissioners Cheryl Stallings, Safiyah Jackson, Shinica Thomas, and Susan Evans voted for the proposed merger Monday evening with Tara Waters and Vickie Adamson voting against.
The Federal Trade Commission and the U.S. Department of Justice will have to approve the deal before it can proceed.
Nikki Williams of Raleigh was among WakeMed’s patients opposed to the merger. Signs attached to her rollator reminded citizens to register to vote this November. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)

title: Spanberger presses Congress for AI guardrails as states forge ahead
description: Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday called on Congress to set national rules for artificial intelligence, warning that its rapid development could threaten jobs, privacy and public resources if oversight remains largely in the hands of the companies building it. In a letter to congressional leaders, the Virginia Democrat urged federal action while pledging to[...]
text:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger, shown signing an executive order establishing a state AI task force on Sept. 18, called on Congress Tuesday to set federal safeguards for the technology. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Gov. Abigail Spanberger on Tuesday called on Congress to set national rules for artificial intelligence, warning that its rapid development could threaten jobs, privacy and public resources if oversight remains largely in the hands of the companies building it.
In a letter to congressional leaders, the Virginia Democrat urged federal action while pledging to pursue measures within the state’s authority. She sent the letter to House Speaker Mike Johnson, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. 
“The potential impacts of AI are too great to leave the regulation of this technology solely in the hands of private entities, especially when the CEOs of those same companies are also sounding the alarm on the significant risks presented by uncoordinated regulation,” Spanberger wrote.
Her appeal comes as Washington remains divided over how aggressively the federal government should rein in the technology. 
Johnson told NBC’s “Meet the Press” earlier this month that Congress should not rush to regulate AI, warning that poorly considered rules could put the United States at a competitive disadvantage against China. He said the issue called for guardrails but would not commit to bringing the House back before the Nov. 3 election to pass them. 
Johnson’s remarks came amid calls to slow AI development, something Spanberger did not ask for in her letter. Instead, she argued that federal oversight and continued technological development need not come at the expense of one another. 
“The notion that the United States must choose between AI safety and AI leadership is a false dichotomy,” she wrote. “America can do both, but we need federal-state collaboration to advance thoughtful AI regulations that safeguard the public while supporting technological progress.”
Spanberger, who served three terms in Congress before leaving to run for governor, also stopped short of proposing specific federal legislation. Instead, she called on lawmakers to consider AI’s effect on Americans’ safety, livelihoods and well-being and establish “guardrails that achieve meaningful AI accountability.”
Amid the concerns she identified were data privacy, the technology’s potential effects on workers and the resources consumed by the infrastructure required to run increasingly powerful AI systems. 
Congress has already confronted one piece of the federal-state divide over artificial intelligence. 
Last year, the Senate voted 99-1 to strip a provision aimed at deterring states from regulating AI from a federal spending and tax bill. First proposed as a 10-year ban, it was later tied to federal funding for states. 
Advocates for a national approach had argued that differing state laws could hamper innovation and weaken U.S. competition with China. Its removal left states free to pursue their own rules while Congress continued debating federal oversight. 
Few states have as much at stake in AI’s physical infrastructure as Virginia, home to the world’s largest concentration of data centers. 
The facilities require enormous amounts of electricity and other resources, and proposals for new development have fueled disputes over utility costs, environmental effects and how much information the public receives before projects are approved. 
Spanberger moved on that front last week, announcing a data center accountability framework that includes proposed changes to environmental oversight, public disclosure and how industry costs are allocated. 
She also signed Executive Order 22 creating an AI task force to examine workforce displacement, data privacy and cybersecurity. Those actions fall within the state’s authority but do not provide the national standards that Spanberger is asking Congress to consider. 
“In the absence of federal action, states are leading within their more limited areas of jurisdiction,” Spanberger wrote. However, her letter did not give a timetable for its recommendations or identify specific federal requirements she wants lawmakers to adopt. 
Spanberger isn’t the only Virginia official pressing Washington to act. 
U.S. Rep. Don Beyer, D-Alexandria, co-chair of Congress’ bipartisan Caucus on Artificial Intelligence, led a bipartisan group of 10 House members in a letter last week urging Johnson and Jeffries to advance legislation on AI oversight, security and transparency. 
Citing recent incidents involving advanced AI systems, the lawmakers warned that future failures could threaten critical infrastructure and financial institutions.
“The Congress may not receive another warning shot,” they wrote. 
Some of the warnings about AI have come from the industry itself, although developers and researchers disagree over the severity of the risks and how governments should respond. 
Anthropic has published accounts of attempts to misuse its models and steps the company took to counter them. 
The company has also recently revealed that its Claude model is helping researchers develop its successor under human supervision, adding another dimension to the debate over how rapidly AI capabilities are advancing and what developers should be required to disclose. 
But Americans are increasingly skeptical that AI companies can handle those questions on their own, according to a Reuters/lpsos poll released Tuesday. 
According to the survey, 73% of respondents said that AI companies had not done enough to prevent serious societal harm. Most also said federal officials should have a major role in setting safety standards. 
The poll also captured the tension surrounding the technology, with 55% saying that slowing AI development would be a good thing, compared with 13% who said it would be bad. The remainder were unsure or did not answer. 
At the same time, AI continues to attract enormous investment and has been promoted as a tool that could boost productivity and accelerate scientific research. Its longer-term effects on employment remain uncertain.
In her letter, Spanberger did not ask Congress to halt that development. She instead argues that lawmakers should play a larger role in determining the rules under which it proceeds. 
“Our country cannot afford for the federal government to abdicate its oversight responsibility,” she wrote. “Congress must immediately and seriously consider how to best grapple with how AI’s emergence creates opportunities and challenges for our safety, well-being, and collective future.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas State agricultural economist predicts diesel prices remain high through 2027
description: Photos by Dan Donnert/K-State Extension.
text:
Gregg Ibendahl, farm management specialist with Kansas State University, says diesel prices paid by Kansas farmers and truckers will remain elevated into 2027 and beyond due to rising crude costs, limits on refining capacity and transport bottlenecks. In this image, the price of diesel in Kansas stands at $6.29 per gallon. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector) TOPEKA — Diesel costs are likely to remain elevated through next year to the detriment of farmers struggling to turn a profit and consumers grappling with food inflation, a Kansas State University agricultural economist says.
Gregg Ibendahl, farm management specialist with KSU’s Extension Service, said the diesel market was influenced by soaring crude prices, limited refining capacity and supply system interruptions. Consequences of international conflict may sustain those conditions and hold prices at $6 to $7 per gallon into 2027 or beyond, he said.
Shipping in the Gulf region and the Strait of Hormuz has been undermined since February by the United States’ war with Iran. In addition, diesel exports by Russia weakened since its full-scale military assault of Ukraine began in 2022. The only means of addressing pump prices would be to resolve global tensions and resume the regular international flow of fuel, Ibendahl said.
“Even in a best-case scenario, where the war in Ukraine winds down quickly and shipments through the Gulf normalize, it could easily take six months for the market to adjust,” Ibendahl said. “To see prices return to what we had earlier this year could take up to two years, even if everything goes right.”
Ibendahl said diesel costs in Kansas climbed approximately $2.25 per gallon during 2026. In Lawrence on Tuesday, the pump price of diesel stood at $6.29 per gallon. The national average for diesel climbed to $6.51 a gallon, according to AAA.
About one-third of escalation in domestic price was associated with crude oil costs, Ibendahl said.
“The price of oil has gone from the low to mid-$70s to more than $100 a barrel, and that probably explains about 70 cents of the increase per gallon,” he said. “The rest is really because there just isn’t enough diesel fuel in the world right now.”
The bulk of the ballooning cost should be attributed to supply disruptions at the refinery level and transit issues, he said.
“Russia is still producing oil but can’t get it refined easily because of damage to its refineries,” Ibendahl said. “They’ve essentially shut off diesel exports to Europe, and there’s not much moving through the Gulf, either. That’s created a very real shortage.”
U.S. refineries have operated at about 98% capacity, Ibendahl said, but overseas demand has drawn U.S. supplies offshore. An estimated 30% of diesel produced in the United States was destined for export and the tighter domestic supply was reflected in pricing, he said.
Ibendahl said many Midwest farmers returned to fields in the fall on tractors fueled by diesel. A north-central Kansas farmer might use four gallons of diesel to grow one acre of corn, he said. Assuming diesel remained $2.25 above normal, which previously was below $4 per gallon, that extra cost per gallon would add $10 for each acre seeded. So, Ibendahl said, a corn farmer working 2,000 acres would see an instant input cost increase of $20,000.
“For many operations, that can be the difference between having a profitable year and not making anything at all,” Ibendahl said.
Higher diesel prices hit the bottom line of transportation companies, and those costs eventually must be passed to consumers, he said.
“We move practically everything in this country by truck, and almost all of those trucks run on diesel,” he said. “They can’t eat those costs forever. Over time, consumers are going to feel higher diesel prices, even if they’re not buying diesel themselves.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: PFAS found in 43 water wells in Cieneguilla and La Cienega communities, new tests show
description: A total of 43 wells in the Cieneguilla and La Cienega communities in Santa Fe County showed ‘forever chemical’ contamination in recent tests, Santa Fe County announced on Monday. With the aquifer under the communities contaminated, state environmental officials and a not-for-profit company are examining alternate public water supply options for those impacte[...]
text:
A water plant in La Cienega, a community in Santa Fe County, captured on Sep. 21, 2026. New Mexico environment officials recently tested 116 wells in the communities and found 43 contained PFAS. (Matthew Mondschein/Source NM)A total of 43 wells in the Cieneguilla and La Cienega communities in Santa Fe County showed ‘forever chemical’ contamination in recent tests, Santa Fe County announced on Monday.
The well testing, which the New Mexico Environment Department undertook, follows a data-sharing agreement the state and county made earlier this year, which “gives opportunities for interaction between our scientists so they can learn from each other in real time,” NMED Special Project Coordinator Andrew Hautzinger said in a statement accompanying the news release announcing the test results. “This gives us the awareness of who is doing what, why they are doing it, and how we can learn together as we move forward.”
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl chemicals, or PFAS, were first found in the groundwater near the Army National Guard Aviation Support Facility by the Santa Fe Regional Airport in 2023. When the county subsequently tested wells in nearby La Cienega and La Cieneguilla, several wells were found to be contaminated.
Exposure through contaminated water and soil, as well as through the plants and animals, cause PFAS to build up in the human body. While still being studied, PFAS exposure is linked to increased cancer risks, fertility issues, low birth weights or fetal development issues and hormonal imbalances.
In the most recent round of testing, the state environment department found that of the 116 recently sampled wells in La Cieneguilla and La Cienega combined, 26 wells in Cieneguilla tested positive for PFAS contamination, as did 17 wells in La Cienega. 
With the aquifer below La Cieneguilla contaminated with PFAS, the news release said, a new public water supply for community members is being prospected by La Cieneguilla Water Company, a not-for-profit company that secured federal funds to assess potential options.  
NMED also provided free water filters for those affected by the contamination last November, a month after the department announced that approximately 100 homes in Curry County would be receiving a new water source due to PFAS water contamination from nearby Cannon Air Force Base. 
Santa Fe County Utilities Division Director Travis Soderquist said in a statement Monday the new data will help inform the county’s next steps. 
“We are trying to get a grasp on the extent and concentration of the contamination and how far it has spread throughout the community,” he said. “We want to know if the contamination is moving, if it’s stationary, or if there’s a continuous introduction of contaminants into the groundwater.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Where do Oklahoma universities rank among the nation’s best colleges?
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — An annual ranking of best U.S. colleges again rated the University of Oklahoma the highest in the state.  Despite falling six spots, OU led all Oklahoma-based higher education institutions in U.S. News & World Report’s 2027 Best Colleges rankings, which released Tuesday. It ranked No. 116 out of the 422 best national […]
text:
The University of Oklahoma and three other in-state higher education institutions made U.S. News & World Report's Best Colleges overall rankings. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — An annual ranking of best U.S. colleges again rated the University of Oklahoma the highest in the state. 
Despite falling six spots, OU led all Oklahoma-based higher education institutions in U.S. News & World Report’s 2027 Best Colleges rankings, which released Tuesday. It ranked No. 116 out of the 422 best national universities, tying with Brigham Young University, Iowa State University, the University of Oregon and the University of San Francisco.
In a statement through its communications office, OU said its trajectory “has never been stronger” with enrollment approaching 40,000 students, unprecedented philanthropic support and a rapidly expanding research enterprise. It also touted the “dramatic transformation” of the university’s health care system as it expands across the state.
“Together, these gains are strengthening OU’s ability to provide an exceptional and affordable education, drive discoveries that improve lives, and deliver greater impact for Oklahoma and beyond,” the university stated.
The University of Tulsa at No. 148 and Oklahoma State University at No. 191 each rose in the national university rankings this year, jumping 10 and seven spots respectively.
“These rankings reflect the strength and breadth of the academic experience at OSU and, more importantly, the work our faculty and staff do every day to help students succeed,” OSU Interim Provost Chris Francisco said in a statement.
The University of Science and Arts of Oklahoma was ranked in a separate category dedicated to the best liberal arts colleges. USAO, based in Chickasha, ranked No. 178 on that list.
Troutt Hall on the University of Science and Arts of Oklahoma campus pictured July 10, 2024, in Chickasha. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
U.S. News & World Report’s annual rankings put heavy emphasis on student outcomes, like graduation and retention rates, social mobility for low-income students and post-graduate earnings. The report also considers an academic peer assessment, faculty research, student-to-faculty ratios, financial resources and other factors when determining its ranking order.
Massachusetts Institute of Technology ranked as the top university in the country, ending Princeton University’s 15-year reign as No. 1. Princeton fell to No. 2, and Harvard University ranked No. 3 in the 2027 list.
Among the best public universities in the country, OU ranked No. 55 and OSU at No. 99.
Tulsa, followed by OSU and then OU, ranked highest of all Oklahoma institutions for best value, which organizes schools based on their academic quality and actual cost after need-based financial aid.
OSU led all Oklahoma schools for best value for in-state students, landing one spot ahead of OU.

name: VTDigger
title: A celebration of “maple-fired” punk highlights challenging times for Vermont’s live music
description:
Skunkfest’s co-organizer said that financial and personal challenges have gone into his decision to shut down his venue at the end of this year. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A celebration of “maple-fired” punk highlights challenging times for Vermont’s live music.
text:
Dead Street Dreamers performing at The Underground, courtesy of The Underground
For Dan O’Day, “there’s no better feeling” than performing live music for a crowd and feeling the energy go out and come back to you. 
“I think about these moments of just having people sing along to your songs, know your music, cheering you on,” he said. “I think I took a lot of it for granted — that stuff that normal people don’t get to ever experience is that feeling of that pure love of performing and getting that reaction from it.” 
O’Day is the lead songwriter for Steppin’ Razor Blades, a two-tone ska band formed of musicians from all over New England. Steppin’ Razor Blades is one of nine local punk and ska (an upbeat form of punk and reggae) bands slated to perform at “Skunkfest,” a brand-new festival that plans to celebrate both the music and the “do-it-yourself” ethos of punk. 
Skunkfest — a portmanteau of ska, punk and festival — is slated to take place Sept. 26 in Randolph, outside of The Underground, a local music venue, thanks to the combined efforts of The Underground and tattoo parlor Black Meadow Gallery and Tattoo. 
To the festival’s organizers and performers, the festival demonstrates the thriving punk ecosystem and deep connection between punk and Vermont culture. One band, Vallory Falls, proudly describes itself as “maple-fired punk rock.” 
But the festival also comes at a time of uncertainty for the future of punk in particular and live music in general. Venues across the state have been struggling, and The Underground is a part of that trend. In fact, owner Vincent Freeman said the club’s regular live shows will be going on an indefinite hiatus by the end of the year. 
The Underground began as a recording studio 15 years ago, offering a recording space and audio engineering to local musicians, Freeman said. But during the pandemic, he began hosting weekly livestreamed concerts in the basement. 
Freeman and Kate Branstetter, co-owner of Black Meadow, have been talking about organizing a festival for years, inspired in part by local punk flea markets and smaller concerts. 
Alongside the music, Branstetter has put together a punk-themed craft and makers’ market. “We’re looking at a flea market of band memorabilia, and homemade DIY crafts, and paintings that are asking intense questions, and graffiti art,” she said. 
The festival will also have a “fixer tent,” where visitors can see live demos of how to repair their own items. To Branstetter, that do-it-yourself attitude is one way that punk intersects with Vermont culture. 

McAsh performing at The Underground, courtesy of The Underground

“Vermont is a place for the nostalgia of the original punk and ska scene, because we’re just a little bit more removed from a lot of stuff, (so) we’re used to being DIY and crafty and scrappy,” she said. 
Vermont also influences the music of some of the bands coming to Skunkfest. Riley Rae Burridge, manager and drummer of Vallory Falls, said that the band’s latest EP, “Porchlights and Field Lights,” has songs like “Citronella” with lyrics that are partly based around life in Vermont: “At the base of this green ridge, Citronella candlelight / As the flames die down, I’ll hold you close.” 
But as passionate as she is about Vermont, Burridge is worried about some signs of a decline in the punk scene here, especially when it comes to places to see and hear bands. Radio Bean in Burlington closed earlier this year. Jim’s Basement and 242 Main, other popular Burlington punk venues, have both closed in the past 10 years. 
“A lot of folks tell me that Burlington used to be like the main scene for punk bands,” she said. “And right now, we’re kind of in a place where we’re trying to figure out what to do and what to go on with.”
Freeman said he’s been struggling with both his insurance costs and the cost of music licensing for song covers. With those expenses and others, he’s been barely breaking even on weekly shows.
“We were a (bring-your-own-booze) venue, and then yeah, my insurance company just dropped me overnight and said, ‘Hey, we’re not going to cover you anymore,’” he said. 
He’s also the father of a 14-month-old child and feels like he doesn’t have the capacity anymore to run a part-time venue.
“The other end of this DIY culture is … there aren’t these large organizations that are financially backed doing this; it’s all our musical creative community,” he said. “We have an idea and we want to roll with it and are super passionate about it, but eventually we burn out because we don’t see enough support.” 
These issues are part of national-level changes in the music industry, such as the increased concentration of venues into the hands of large corporations, and Freeman doesn’t know how Vermont will move forward with them. But he’s proud to support local businesses where he can, such as by using Seven Days’ ticketing platform rather than Ticketmaster. 
And he still believes that live music is “crucial” to human connection. 
“As an avid concert goer, it’s such a cathartic exercise physically and mentally to attend a concert,” he said. “You can just let out everything that’s weighing on you, any negative energy, and also celebrate the positive energy.”
Burridge said despite punk’s loud and prickly reputation, she’s found punk shows to be incredibly safe, and she’s felt very accepted as a trans person in the community. 
“A lot of people think punk and think like, ‘Oh, it’s scary. Oh, there’s a lot of folks that just look mean, look like they’re gonna hurt me.’ It is not like that. It is one of the most caring communities in the entire state,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: Dorothy (Dot) Naylor
description:
She was a lifelong learner, an innovator before innovation was cool, and generally a feisty woman who regarded obstacles as challenges to be overcome her whole life.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Dorothy (Dot) Naylor.
text:
Born: 01/24/1939
Newport, Rhode Island
Died: 09/07/2026
Berlin, Vermont
Details of service:
There will be a Celebration of Life on June 5, 2027 at Memorial Hall on Mirror Lake in Calais.
In lieu of flowers the family is asking you consider a donation to one of the following organizations:
Rural School Community Alliance or
North Calais Memorial Hall Association 207 G.A.R. Road, Calais Vermont

Dorothy (Openshaw) Naylor of Berlin, previously of Calais, passed away peacefully at Woodridge Nursing and Rehabilitation on September 7, 2026 after a long and well-lived life. 
Dorothy was born at Newport Hospital in Newport, Rhode Island on January 24, 1939, to James A. and Dorothy (Harvest) Openshaw. She moved with her family to Southampton, Massachusetts in 1941 where she attended the local elementary school and graduated from Northampton School for Girls in 1957.
Dorothy attended several universities including Cornell and New Mexico before landing at University of Massachusetts (Amherst) from which she graduated in 1961.  While at UMass she met and married her lifelong partner and love, Ben Naylor.  Together with their infant daughter (Sonja) they moved to Manhattan, Kansas in the summer of 1961. While there, Ben continued his studies and their family grew to include three sons. In 1967 Ben had completed his studies and they’d had enough of flat, featureless, windy land, so they moved the family back east and settled at Kents Corner in Calais before moving to Collar Hill in 1972 where they resided for over 50 years. 
Dorothy went by different names. Her father nicknamed her Lass when she was born because, as he said, “She was slow as molasses in January,” in a riff on her birthday and her tardy entrance to the world. Despite the nickname, she could never be considered sluggish, stagnant, or unproductive. For most of her adult life she was known as Dot (or Aunt Speck by some cheeky nieces and nephews). In her later years she was known as Dorothy at her request.
In addition to her several names, Dorothy wore many hats throughout her long and active life. She taught 5th & 6th grades at East Montpelier Elementary School for 20+ years, she served on multiple boards and committees, she partnered with Ben in homesteading their land and developing a thriving small business. She was a lifelong learner, an innovator before innovation was cool, and generally a feisty woman who regarded obstacles as challenges to be overcome her whole life.
Dorothy began her teaching career in the Four Corners (one room) School House. At the time it was an overflow building for the modern elementary school. She walked her students two-tenths of a mile to and from the main building several days a week for specialty classes such as PE, art, and the like. After a couple years overlooking the field across the road she envisioned a Nordic skiing program that would simultaneously teach winter survival skills, so she applied for a grant, bought cross-country ski sets and taught many generations of students how to ski and enjoy the winter.
Throughout her life Dorothy embraced serendipity. One day in 1976 she bought too many peaches from the co-op and turned them into a thriving boutique jam business now owned by son Kelt and his wife Kristina. In the beginning Dorothy hand wrote all the labels. Those labels are now digitally printed using her handwriting for the font. As the business grew, she delivered and managed, while Ben handled production and product development. Now this jam, and many other specialty food products, can be found on store shelves throughout New England.
Dorothy had a healthy respect for civic engagement and town service – she served on many boards – most related to education.  She and Ben were involved in the citizen committees that created the modern Calais Elementary School and U32; both built in the early 1970s.  She later served on the Calais School board during the contentious merger required by Act 46. She continued engaging in the fight to maintain local schools right up to the very end, attending school board meetings virtually from her nursing home.
Maybe it was immersion in a place where tourism is an economic staple, maybe it was just her personality; in any case Dorothy actively avoided crowds, mainstream tourism, and other “touristy” events. She and Ben took three very memorable vacations in their life. The first and most momentous in 1994 when they toured Antarctica on a retired Russian research vessel. They were caught up in international intrigue when the ship was impounded in the Falkland/Maldive Islands and Argentina refused to allow passage through their airspace to Tierra del Fuego in Chile!
Though she was always active, she was never too busy to wander their property in Calais or sit on the porch of their cottage on Lake Champlain with a gin & tonic.
Dorothy is survived by her three children: daughter, Sonja N. Andrews, (Ross), Calais, VT; son, Kelt M. Naylor, (Kristina), Dummerston, VT; son, Benjamin E. Naylor, (Jennifer), Petersburg, NY as well as 7 grandchildren: Lillian and John (Rebecca) Andrews, Caroline and Max Naylor, Aleana, Sophia (Lucas), and Eli Naylor, and one great grandson, Harvest Andrews. Dorothy was predeceased by her beloved husband, Ben Naylor, her infant son Kurt W. Naylor, her parents and siblings, Judy (Openshaw) Findeisen and James A. Openshaw, Jr.

title: Michigan Smart Trade Alliance tracker shows over $26 billion in tariff-driven costs paid statewide
description: The Michigan Smart Trade Alliance has launched a tracker estimating that Michigan households have incurred more than $26 billion in tariff-related costs since January 2025, or about $6,419 per household.  That number is based on the National Taxpayers Union Foundation’s state tariffs tracker, which uses import and duty data from Trade Partnership Worldwide a[...]
text:
U.S. Customs station at the Blue Water Bridge in Port Huron, Michigan. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)The Michigan Smart Trade Alliance has launched a tracker estimating that Michigan households have incurred more than $26 billion in tariff-related costs since January 2025, or about $6,419 per household. 
That number is based on the National Taxpayers Union Foundation’s state tariffs tracker, which uses import and duty data from Trade Partnership Worldwide and U.S. Census Bureau household counts. According to the alliance’s website, the tracker “reflects only the highest of several published, credible estimates of tariff costs to Michigan households.” The website also notes that other analysts and the White House put the number lower, while some dispute that tariffs impose any net cost after accounting for other economic effects. 
“The costs on Michigan families is taking a toll in the form of higher costs and frustration with trade policies and tariffs that are holding our economy back,” said Michigan Smart Trade Alliance spokesperson John Sellek in a press release. “It’s time to end the trade war with Canada, get both sides to the negotiation table, and find a solution that will end this affordability crisis in Michigan.”
Michigan Smart Trade Alliance tracker estimating Michigan household costs incurred by tariffs. (Screenshot)
The tracker projects an average increase of $488.4 per second across Michigan in statewide tariff costs. That number is a calculation, not a demonstration of constantly updating data — it divides the last confirmed total from the National Taxpayers Union Foundation, $23 billion, by the 545 days in that data period, to find the average per-second cost, and projects that amount forward.
The website also notes that the tracker was created using artificial intelligence.
The group also released the results of an early July Ipsos poll of 559 likely voters, which showed that, across party lines, voters were in strong support of statements that they would be more likely to support a candidate who says, “I support smart trade that protects Michigan jobs” and support congressional action to increase trade with trusted allies such as Canada and Mexico when it protects jobs and lowers costs.
“Anyone who is running for office right now should consider themselves on notice: Voters in Michigan across the political spectrum want smart trade and an end to erratic trade policies that raise prices and make it difficult or impossible for businesses to plan for the future,” Mark Fisk, another spokesperson for the Michigan Smart Trade Alliance, said. 
Another poll commissioned by the organization and conducted by EPIC-MRA in June showed similar pushback on tariffs, with a 70% to 20% margin saying that “state and federal lawmakers should pursue a different trade policy that reduces tariffs and lowers costs for consumers.” 
However, opinions in that earlier poll varied along party lines — “A 79% to 12% majority of Democrats, 58% to 31% of Independent voters oppose tariffs, while an 81% to 13% majority of Republicans said they support tariffs,” according to the alliance’s website.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. unemployment agency ‘mismanaged’ call center performance, ‘failed’ to quickly pay claimants, auditor concludes
description: The auditor’s report unveils how even before the agency was thrust into turmoil with record-breaking poor performance during a time of a relatively stable job market, out-of-work Massachusetts residents weren’t receiving the help they needed in a timely fashion.
text:
IN THE MONTHS AFTER Massachusetts adopted a new platform meant to improve the unemployment assistance system for both jobless Bay Staters and state workers managing claims, disbursement of those benefits trickled to a nation-leading low. 
The issues, as it turned out, had been festering in the years before that 2025 system update, a new report from Auditor Diana DiZoglio reveals. 
Those snags ranged from claimants stuck on hold for over an hour to poor access to in-person assistance in communities around the state to long lags in the issuance of payments for qualified residents staring down unemployment. 
As a result, the report concludes, Massachusetts risks losing federal funding as well as saddling vulnerable claimants with delayed access and lost trust. 
DiZoglio’s review of the Department of Unemployment Assistance was mainly limited to two years between 2022 and 2024. That’s before the agency implemented a new benefits system which, as chronicled by CommonWealth Beacon this year, led to the slowest rate of payments in the country. 
Lengthy delays at DUA have reverberated around Beacon Hill, where lawmakers report being inundated with complaints from constituents about the agency’s lack of responsiveness.  
However, legislative leaders have done little to tackle the problem. A pair of first-term lawmakers have been pushing for months to convene a special commission that would examine the issues, but it now appears even that modest proposal is dead until the start of the new term in 2027 at the earliest. 
Yet the auditor’s report unveils how, even before the agency was thrust into more recent turmoil with record-breaking poor performance during a time of a relatively stable job market, out-of-work Massachusetts residents for years weren’t receiving the help they needed in a timely fashion. 
“When hardworking people lose their jobs, unemployment insurance becomes a lifeline that allows them to continue to pay bills while they search for a new job,” DiZoglio said in a statement. “When those benefit payments are delayed, job search resources are unavailable, and complaints are not tracked and prioritized appropriately, the system fails job seekers and taxpayers alike.” 
Matthew Kitsos, a DUA spokesperson, said the agency is “committed to improving customer experiences and ensuring eligible claimants receive benefits in a timely fashion.” He added in a statement that DUA has “taken significant steps to address challenges head-on,” including launching a pilot program to process claims more efficiently and hiring more adjudicators and seasonal staff. 
For the vast majority of claims, DUA did not meet the federal performance standard that calls for issuing 93 percent of benefits within 35 days of a claim in any of the 24 months that DiZoglio reviewed. In April 2024, that number dropped below 70 percent, the lowest month included in the audit. 
The agency implemented a new system in May 2025 that Gov. Maura Healey vowed would catapult the state into “national leadership” for the delivery of benefits. But the percentage of payments issued to claimants within 35 days only plunged deeper to 42.5 percent last September, an all-time state low. The data has since improved over time, with 83 percent of benefits now paid within 35 days as of July, the most recent month with data available.  
Unemployment benefits themselves are paid through a tax on Massachusetts employers, while the federal government funds the administration of that assistance across the states. 
On call wait times, DiZoglio’s report criticized DUA for a failure to demonstrate that “call log data was being monitored at all” to evaluate performance.  
Out of more than 700,000 calls over a one-year period, the report found that it took 30 minutes to respond to about half of all inbound calls either from a call center agent or an automated voice prompt. Wait times exceeded an hour for about a quarter of the calls. 
Claimants hung up on DUA call centers around 30 percent of the time during some months in 2024 — six times as much as the 5 percent standard, “indicating challenges in managing call volume and access to service,” the report notes. 
Kitsos said that call wait times are now down from an average of two hours to between four and 11 minutes. 
DUA, citing budget and staff constraints, also failed to offer in-person assistance at three regional offices in Brockton, Springfield, and Lawrence, which were used for appeal hearings, during the audit period. 
That meant claimants had to travel in some cases 200 miles roundtrip to Boston, further increasing wait times and delaying access to benefits, DiZoglio noted.  
Rep. Joshua Tarsky, a first-term Democrat who co-sponsored the legislation to establish a special commission on unemployment insurance, said in an interview that the auditor’s report further validates the push to scrutinize the system – even though his bill likely won’t advance this year, he conceded. 
“These unemployment benefits aren’t abstract,” said Tarsky, who plans to re-file the bill alongside Rep. Hadley Luddy next session. “They are monies for people who are wanting to buy food, diapers, pay for their heat. It’s something that you can’t just, if it’s working inefficiently, let it go. We need to actually fix this so that our constituents can get the money they need and get the benefits that they’re entitled to.” 
The auditor also alleged that DUA violated state public records law by only retaining call log data for 13 months instead of three years, limiting the agency’s ability to “review and evaluate its call-handling performance.” Kitsos said that DUA disagrees with the auditor’s interpretation of records retention requirements and maintained that the agency is in compliance with the law. 
Nor did DUA take necessary steps to guard against fraud, which has become more prevalent since the 2020 pandemic. The agency didn’t complete the required number of claim reviews in fiscal years 2023 and 2024 — DUA cited a reassignment of six staff investigators to support the launch of the new system as the reason — which “could increase the risk of DUA not identifying improper payments.” 
And DiZoglio zoomed farther out, reaching back to a major Gov. Charlie Baker-era mishap in which the prior Republican administration erroneously spent more than $2 billion in federal Covid funds for unemployment benefits.  
Despite an agreement between Gov. Maura Healey and the feds to pay much of that money back over 10 years, DUA has not sufficiently kept the US Labor Department updated after the new platform launched — a problem “given the exorbitant amount of taxpayer dollars involved,” the report finds. 
To course correct on the issues that DiZoglio identified, the report recommends that DUA should routinely review call log data, implement system alerts for missing information from claimants, offer in-person assistance at regional offices, identify the underlying issues driving delays in benefit payments, and consider hiring additional staff members.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Poll finds opposition to Maryland redistricting ballot question
description: Roughly 4 in 10 voters said they oppose Question 3, according to a poll released by Protect Maryland Votes, a group that is opposing the proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution. The poll comes just as mail-in ballots begin to go out to Maryland voters and roughly a month before early voting begins.
text:
A proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution that could remove state standards for redrawing congressional districts faces a plurality of opposition according to a poll released by a group that opposes the ballot question. (Maryland Matters illustration)An effort by Democrats to re-write the standards for future Congressional redistricting efforts isn’t sitting well with a plurality of Maryland voters.
Roughly 4 in 10 voters said they oppose Question 3, according to a poll released by Protect Maryland Votes, a group that is opposing the proposed amendment to the Maryland Constitution. The poll comes just as mail-in ballots begin to go out to Maryland voters and roughly a month before early voting begins.
“This poll confirms what we have always believed, that Marylanders across party lines understand the difference between right and wrong,” Yuripzy Morgan, Republican voter and leader of Protect Maryland Votes, said in a statement.
The poll of 600 likely Maryland voters was conducted between Sept. 10 and 13 by two firms: Ragnar Research Partners and Lincoln Park Strategies, Republican and Democratic polling firms respectively. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus 4%.
In August, Democrats in the General Assembly pushed through an amendment to the Maryland Constitution.
Democratic super majorities in both the House and Senate easily passed the amendment along party lines.
The proposal would supersede a ruling by Judge Lynne Battaglia in a 2022 congressional redistricting challenge. Her ruling — which is not precedent — tied the recasting of congressional districts to compact and contiguous requirements in the Maryland Constitution.
Circuit Court judges in Anne Arundel and Dorchester Counties found problems with the question and ordered it stricken from the ballot. The Maryland Supreme Court similarly found problems with the question but opted to re-write it and allow it to go to voters.
Those who participated in the poll were read the question as it will appear on the ballot.
Forty-one percent said they would oppose the question while 28% said they would vote for the amendment to the Maryland Constitution. Another 3-in-10 voters said they were undecided.
“When voters hear what this amendment actually does, they reject it.,” Morgan said in her statement. “Stripping over 50 years of constitutional protections for fair and compact districts so partisan politicians can draw maps that can never be challenged in court again is wrong, and Marylanders know it.”
This story will be updated

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Most residents think Massachusetts is a great place to live, and also unaffordable
description: People who are finishing their education are almost twice as likely to consider leaving Massachusetts in the next five years, quantifying a dynamic many have long suspected in a state that welcomes crowds of college students every year.
text:
IF MOST MASSACHUSETTS residents had to come up with a new state motto, they could probably agree on something like: It’s a great place to live, if you can afford it.
Heading into an election season in which “affordability” is the defining issue, a majority of Bay Staters agree that Massachusetts is a better place to live than most other states and, simultaneously, that it remains too expensive, according to newly released polling data.
The latest survey from the MassINC Polling Group, conducted as part of the Massachusetts Taxpayers Foundation’s annual assessment of state competitiveness, builds on a well-established thematic foundation. The Bay State has some of the highest incomes in the country, but with the costs for basics like housing and utilities growing at a much faster pace, many families are feeling the pinch. 
Sixty-three percent of respondents rated Massachusetts as “one of the best” places to live or “above average” compared to other states, a rate unchanged from when pollsters asked the same question a year ago. At the same time, only 19 percent dubbed the Bay State one of the best or above average on “overall affordability,” compared to 56 percent who said the state is below average or one of the worst for affordability.
Doug Howgate, president of the Mass. Taxpayers Foundation, said polling would likely find affordability to be a top concern in “49 other states.” But in the years since the COVID-19 pandemic, he thinks concerns about the high cost of living in Massachusetts have “ratcheted up a little more compared to other states.”
“When you look under the hood at how people feel and these cost pressures that are weighing on them, and weighing on their location choices, that’s why we need to keep our foot on the gas,” Howgate said. “This is not a mirage.”
People with higher incomes and higher levels of educational attainment tend to feel better about their home state, according to the poll of nearly 1,000 residents, which was conducted in June and July. Nearly eight in 10 respondents who earn $150,000 per year or more rated Massachusetts a better place to live than most other states, compared to 53 percent of those who earn $50,000 per year or less.
When pollsters asked about different ways of comparing Massachusetts to its peers, they found strong reviews for the services offered in Massachusetts. Most respondents think the state’s health care, education, and public services are top-notch.
There was one clear loser: overall affordability. Far more respondents said the state is less competitive on that front.
MassINC Polling Group president Steve Koczela pointed out that high costs are a unifying issue for Democrats and Republicans alike, both of whom were likely to name rising prices among the top issues facing the country.
Affordability concerns, he said, “show up everywhere.” (The Polling Group is partially owned by MassINC, the nonprofit that publishes CommonWealth Beacon.)
Democrats dominate electorally in Massachusetts, and the actions of the Trump administration and a Republican-controlled Congress seem to make a sizable number of Bay Staters happier about where they live. An even 40 percent of respondents said actions at the federal level make them feel better about residing in Massachusetts, the poll found, up from 29 percent a year earlier.
Another year-over-year change suggests businesses are getting a bit more anxious. Fifty-one percent of those polled said Massachusetts is among the better places to do business, down from 59 percent in 2025.
Other indicators have shown significant concerns among employers, too. The monthly business confidence index published by the Associated Industries of Massachusetts spent much of the year in pessimistic territory, and fell again in August amid fears of an escalating trade war with Canada.
About two in five residents are considering leaving Massachusetts in the next five years, most often due to the high cost of living, the poll found. That rate is roughly twice as high for people between the ages of 18 and 29, and those who are working on their education.
“We found a very strong relationship between thoughts or intent to leave Massachusetts and if you’re either currently working on education or recently finished it,” Koczela said.
For Howgate, who leads a business-backed think tank, the trend of Bay Staters being more likely to leave as or just after they finish education is at once “a cause for concern” and “an opportunity.”
“Smart people connecting to our economy has been the engine of Massachusetts, and we have always lost a lot of folks who come here for education and then leave afterwards,” he said. “If you’re on Beacon Hill, if you’re interested in economic development, we need to be laser-focused on how to change the math or change the perception for that population to keep more of those people in Massachusetts.”
The Massachusetts Taxpayers Foundation will soon supplement the survey data with the release of its latest Competitiveness Index, which assesses how Massachusetts fares on a host of metrics from venture capital funding to average child care costs.
Now in the third year of publishing the index, Howgate hopes to give policymakers a “baseline and common language” to better measure which areas need more attention.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Q&A: Why schools have more money, but teachers aren’t making more
description: There’s been a puzzling trend over the last few decades: Adjusted for inflation, school funding has increased substantially, but teacher salaries have not. text:
(Getty Images) 
There’s been a puzzling trend over the last few decades: Adjusted for inflation, school funding has increased substantially, but teacher salaries have not. In recent years, real teacher pay has actually dipped as inflation surged.


Pay matters for every profession, including teaching, for obvious reasons. It shapes who enters and stays in the work. Talented people might not consider teaching or might leave after a few years because they’re not happy with their salary.


Teachers have never been paid especially well, but the pay gap between teaching and other college-educated professionals has grown in recent decades. And now there’s a new challenge: Many other white-collar jobs offer remote work perks that aren’t available to educators. 


Meanwhile, more teachers have left the classroom in recent years and fewer young people aspire to become teachers.


So why has teacher pay been stagnant? Again, it’s not because school budgets have been flat. Rather, as school districts have gotten more money, they’ve used it for other matters, including hiring more staff. Schools have brought on new people for a variety of reasons: to serve a growing number of students with disabilities, to address demands for more security, to lower class sizes. (More money has also gone toward non-salary benefits, like health insurance and retirement, for teachers and other staff.)



This “staffing surge” may have been valuable, but a number of policy analysts have raised pointed questions about whether dollars could have been better used elsewhere. One of them is Aaron Garth Smith, director of education reform at the Reason Foundation, a libertarian-leaning think tank. In a recent piece for Education Next, Smith dug into school staffing data in helpful detail.


I recently spoke with Smith to understand how schools are using their money and how strong the case is that they should spend it differently. 


Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.


 Tell me what you found about how American public schools have spent their increased resources?


In the last couple of decades [between 2002 and 2023], enrollment is up by about 4% but staffing went up by about 15%. One of the drivers of that is non-teaching staff. It’s not central office staff that’s driving this growth. It’s primarily school-level staff, in particular instructional aides and student support staff, including positions such as social workers, psychologists, audiologists, and several other categories of positions. I estimate that about 40% of the overall staff growth can be attributed to special education. The two main [special education] categories where we see growth are autism and ADHD. 


 What else do you think is driving staffing growth?


There could be a lot of reasons. You could point to things like testing and accountability post-NCLB. And technology, of course. You need more tech staff in the central office and in schools. Security can’t be overlooked. Another one is the whole-child model of K-12 education, which includes community schools.


 I’ve made the argument this staffing surge is probably fiscally sustainable because a growing economy can bring in more tax revenue without raising tax rates. What do you think? 


The question is what is the appetite for state legislatures to continue investing money in public schools while enrollment is falling. I had a legislator from a very red state tell me last week that even though enrollment is declining for various reasons, it would be political suicide to decrease appropriations. But I think it’s going to vary by state. Some will maintain or even increase appropriations, while others will allow funding to track closer to enrollment.


 What do you make of this increased staffing? Is this a positive trend, a concerning trend, or somewhere in between? 


My instinct is that this is probably not the best use of funds. The strongest indicator of that would be teacher salaries. Despite the fact that inflation-adjusted per-student spending has increased by 36% [in the last two decades], teacher salaries have fallen. 


 What makes you say that’s a better investment than all the other things you could spend scarce resources on?


Because teachers are the most important in-school factor for student learning. That’s not saying that school counselors aren’t valuable. But you only have a finite number of dollars to spend, and that money is not making its way to teacher paychecks. That seems pretty alarming to me. 


 I wonder if school district leaders might think, “Oh, yeah, we have new money. We’re putting a chunk of it toward teacher salary,” but actually, that is just keeping up with the inflation treadmill.  


That explanation makes sense.


 You offer a degree of skepticism about community school programs (which try to address challenges students face outside of school). Why?


I’m not saying that they don’t provide any value. I think the point is more of: Is this the best use of scarce resources and time? There are studies showing that they add value in several ways, but as far as I can tell, the evidence base seems a little thin compared to what’s being invested. 


 Anything else you want to add? 


I talk about the importance of increasing teacher salaries, but I think the real value isn’t just in accepting the status quo and paying teachers more based on years of experience and educational attainment. You need structural changes to accompany new investments in teacher salaries. There are some interesting examples out there with states like Texas trying to find ways not just to boost teacher salaries but to do so in a way that focuses on attracting and retaining the best talent.


Reach Barnum at mbarnum@chalkbeat.org.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Where do Alaska’s four candidates for governor stand on abortion?
description: On Tuesday, the advocacy arm of Planned Parenthood will endorse Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins to be Alaska’s next governor, according to an advance copy of the endorsement provided to the Alaska Beacon. Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates Alaska called JKT “a proven advocate for reproductive health and LGBTQ2S+ rights,” and labeled his three[...]
text:
Former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson speaks at a gubernatorial candidate forum on Sept. 16, 2026, while former Attorney General Treg Taylor, Anchorage business owner and talk-show host Bernadette Wilson and former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins listen. At the lecturn is Jared Kosin, president of the Alaska Hospital and Healthcare Association. The organization held the forum in Girdwood, and the event was focused on healthcare issues. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)On Tuesday, the advocacy arm of Planned Parenthood will endorse Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins to be Alaska’s next governor, according to an advance copy of the endorsement provided to the Alaska Beacon.
Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates Alaska called JKT “a proven advocate for reproductive health and LGBTQ2S+ rights,” and labeled his three, anti-abortion Republican opponents — Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor — as “three extreme, out-of-touch politicians who are intent on rolling back Alaska’s constitutional rights.” 
Morgan Lim, the Alaska state director for Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, said by phone that JKT was “a clear choice for us, and it’s a clear choice for folks who support access to abortion.”
Alaska Family Action, the most prominent antiabortion group in the state, is not making an endorsement in the governor’s race, said its president, Jim Minnery. 
“Essentially they’re the same in many ways, if not most ways, in regard to our issues,” Minnery said of Wilson, Bronson and Taylor.
In place of a single endorsement, Minnery said, his group is instead urging voters to “rank the red” and choose all three Republican candidates in Alaska’s ranked choice general election system.
In Alaska, the state supreme court has repeatedly ruled that the right to an abortion is protected by the privacy clause of the Alaska Constitution.
As a result, Alaska has no legal limits on abortion, but in practical terms, access is limited. Few medical providers here offer abortion services, and public data indicates most abortions take place before the 10th week of pregnancy and are performed through medication. 
In May, polling by Alaska Survey Research on behalf of Planned Parenthood found that 62% of Alaskans 18 and older believe that abortion should be legal in all or most cases. 
The percentage rises to 71% among voters registered as undeclared or nonpartisan, those considered political independents.
Kreiss-Tomkins, who served in the Alaska House for 10 years, repeatedly voted against legislation and budget items that attempted to limit access to abortion. 
In 2014, he voted against a law — later ruled unconstitutional — that would have restricted abortion to cases of rape, incest or medical necessity. 
He has said he would continue backing the Supreme Court’s position if elected governor, stating in a May discussion on the website Reddit, “Medical privacy and reproductive freedom should be fundamental personal freedoms in America and Alaska. Our administration will treat them as such.”
Two of the three Republican candidates outlined their positions in a May forum hosted by Alaska Family Action. Bronson is a cofounder of the group, Minnery noted at the time.
“We, the state of New York and the state of California are the three worst states in the country for abortion,” Bronson said at the event.
“The important thing, the biggest tool the governor has, is a great big red pen. He vetoes any bit of money, any funding that goes towards abortion in any way,” Bronson said. 
Wilson said that if elected, she would appoint a “pro-life advocate directly within the governor’s administration to monitor pro-life issues,” similar to an action taken by former North Dakota Gov. Kristi Noem.
She also said she would encourage the state to advertise the risks associated with medication abortions.
“I really think that it’s time for the state of Alaska and for the Department of Health to start running an education campaign on these matters,” she said.
She said she also would want her attorney general to create a restrictive definition for “medically necessary” abortion care and should continue to fight with the state supreme court on abortion restrictions.
Bronson also said he thinks the state’s next governor should fight the supreme court on the issue and advocated for the state to get rid of its current merit-based judge selection process, replacing it with judges appointed by election.
Taylor did not attend the May forum, but he has been open about his opposition to abortion and worked to restrict it while serving as attorney general under Gov. Mike Dunleavy.
In 2023, Taylor sought to restrict the use of Mifepristone, a common medication used for abortions in early stages of pregnancy and has defended a state policy that restricts prescriptions for the drug through telehealth appointments.
Lim of Planned Parenthood said the group believes Alaskans will be more likely to support a candidate that supports abortion care than a candidate that opposes it.
“We’re about letting folks know where people stand on the issues that they care about, and the reality is that in this race, it is three anti-abortion extremists up against a proven champion, and that’s what the people of Alaska want to know,” Lim said.
