text:
A hot hazy day in Minneapolis, July 15, 2026. Wildfire smoke has moved south from fires in northeastern Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)Back in 1990, I attended a talk by Jim Hansen, a lead climate modeler and director of the NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies. He concluded that the models were working well and could now reasonably predict global warming trends. An audience member asked when the public would believe the results of climate modeling. My recollection is that his response was “never,” before adding, “They won’t believe it until they personally experience it.” 
Thirty-six years later, nearly all climate scientists believe that climate warming has occurred as the result of human activities, but do you see it and feel it, plainly? Do you believe it?
Even before the multiple climate crises of 2026, majorities of Minnesotans surveyed in 2025 agreed “that global warming is caused mostly by human activities,” and they were “somewhat or very worried about global warming.” Majorities of Minnesotans also responded that global warming affects sea levels, flooding, droughts, wildfires and extreme heat.
In the past few years, the soot has hit the fan. Minnesota has been smothered by smoke produced by wildfires in Canada and the western U.S. for several years. Smoke from the 2026 Canadian wildfires caused the air quality index in Grand Portage to reach the highest level ever recorded in Minnesota (800, on June 2). For young children and Minnesotans with respiratory diseases — including 5% with COPD and 8% with asthma — this is a crisis. Many who are less vulnerable still suffered for our affected friends and families. Have you seen the smoke? Have you heard the coughing and wheezing? Did you take someone to an emergency room? Did you buy an air filtration device? 
Do you think wildfires in recent years have become more severe because of climate warming? Older readers: Do you remember smoke events as severe as our recent events 20 or 50 years ago? Probably not. More than half of the total acres burned by wildfires in the US over the past 41 years occurred in the most recent 15 years. The trend is less clear in Canada, but the area of wildfires in the memorable 2023 season was more than twice as high as any prior year since 1983.  
In Europe, the wildfire situation this year was far worse. As of mid-July, an estimated 300,000 people had been evacuated from wildfire areas. An estimated 440 deaths were attributed to the fire, either directly or indirectly.  
Do you remember the vivid photos of the 2025 Los Angeles area fire? It forced the evacuation of 200,000 people and destroyed 17,000 homes and businesses. Minnesota’s wildfires earlier this year forced “only” 8,000 evacuations because the 2026 wildfires were in sparsely populated areas. But what about future years? Perhaps in outer ring suburbs on the edge of combustible wildlands? Many Minnesotans grew up learning about the 1893 Hinkley fire, which virtually destroyed the city and killed more than 400. 
Extreme heat in Europe has also caused a surge of deaths in recent years, mostly in cities. Heat waves in 2025 caused 24,400 estimated heat deaths, with climate change being responsible for 16,500 of these. 
Should this be a cautionary tale for Minnesota? Maybe. Throughout Minnesota, the number of days per year with a heat index (a measure of how heat feels) over 90 increased between the periods 1986-1995 and 2016-2025. For example, in Hennepin County, it went from 18 days to 30 days. Several counties in southern Minnesota now have 35 days with heat indexes over 90. Have you felt the summers get hotter in recent years? Do you avoid going out for a walk on these hot days? Do you start to feel overheated doing a half hour of light gardening? Are your kids’ soccer games being canceled? Remember when the Twin Cities marathon was canceled in 2023? 
The high death rate during Europe’s 2025 heat wave occurred in part because most Europeans do not have air conditioning, which would have prevented many of these deaths. In contrast, about 95% of Minnesotans have air conditioning. This gives us a false sense of security — our power supply could be interrupted at the time it is most needed. Would some of our most vulnerable Minnesotans, especially the very young and very old, die in a heat wave, as they did in Europe? Should we be upgrading our electrical grid to improve its reliability?
Is this the year that the soot hit the fan? Thirty-six years after Hansen’s talk, have our eyes and ears and our experiences finally shown us that climate warming is very real and very dangerous, even in Minnesota?

name: Mississippi Today
title: Survey ordered by Gov. Reeves shows many Mississippi agencies are embracing AI use
description: Cover art of Mississippi Agency AI Inventory survey report.
text:
As Mississippi’s state government agencies embrace artificial intelligence, or AI, in their work, officials say human oversight remains essential.
Mississippi defines AI in part as “a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.“
In January 2025, Gov. Tate Reeves issued an executive order directing the Mississippi Department of Information Technology Services to survey and evaluate state agencies’ use of AI and develop AI use policy recommendations. For the survey, called the Mississippi State Agency AI Inventory, each state agency had to submit either a standardized report listing current and potential AI use or a letter stating no plans to use any. 
Out of 98 entities that responded, a little over half were using or planning to use AI. 
The Mississippi Department of Transportation, for instance, is working on AI projects for querying crash data, automating quality control across documentation and more.
The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality uses Grammarly, ChatGPT, Microsoft CoPilot and other programs for things such as research, drafting emails and calculations. The agency also uses several cybersecurity services, including Rubrik, Proofpoint and Silversky.
A cumulative total of 243 active or planned AI projects were reported across 44 agencies. The majority of AI projects, or 82%, were rated low-risk, and 69.5% relied solely on human decision making.

MDOT and MDEQ are among the five agencies that, when combined, account for a significant amount of AI usage across all state agencies, or 35%. The other three are the Department of Employment Security, the Department of Information Technology Services and the Mississippi Arts Commission.

Mississippi Today made a public records request for the completed inventory surveys from the these five agencies, and asked further questions about their AI use. 
ITS did not fulfill the public records request, citing an exception in the executive order. The Department of Employment Security and the Arts Commission provided their completed surveys, but did not respond to detailed questions. 
“Our annual AI inventory is designed to capture a point-in-time snapshot during the second quarter of each calendar year,” explained ITS chief strategy officer Stephanie Hedgepeth. “We then analyze the data during the third quarter, with the report targeted for publication on the ITS website early in the fourth quarter.”
Stephanie Hedgepeth, chief strategy officer for the Mississippi Department of Information Technology Services at MDITS headquarters, Thursday, March 19, 2026, in Jackson. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Hedgepeth said that while AI isn’t new, what is new is how accessible it’s become because of generative AI tools. Generative AI is an advanced form of AI that can create new content.
She, as well as leaders and spokespeople for the departments of Environmental Quality and Transportation, emphasized that AI is a tool to assist humans, not replace them. 
Paul Katool, MDOT’s deputy director of public affairs, explained that AI use is rapidly growing across the agency. 
“It enhances efficiency, enabling our existing staff to complete more work – often faster – without increasing headcount or overall labor costs,” he said.
“The reality is that we have fewer staff than we have ever had historically,” said Chris Wells, the Department of Environmental Quality’s executive director. At the same time, their workload has arguably increased. 
A 2025 national report found that MDEQ’s staff decreased by 17% between 2010 and 2024, and funding decreased by 71% in the same time frame. Records show that the agency’s total appropriations, including state funding and fees collected for services, dropped by over a quarter between fiscal year 2011 and fiscal year 2025.
Though most AI projects took a careful approach, the report found that governance hasn’t kept pace with adoption. The findings include recommendations for improvement, such as stronger protections for confidential data and communication, stronger accessibility and mitigating bias and misinformation for public-facing AI tools.
“Each agency is responsible for governing its use of AI in accordance with applicable laws, regulations, policies and requirements,” wrote Hedgepeth in an email.
ITS adopted the Acceptable Use Policy for Artificial Intelligence, which is meant to be a resource for state agencies to create their own AI policies.
The Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Regulation Task Force was established in 2025 to analyze all things related to regulating AI in Mississippi until 2027, and to report its findings and recommendations to the state Legislature annually. One of the recommendations the task force adopted was that state agencies disclose to citizens when they are engaging with an AI system.
The Department of Transportation issued its AI use policy in February. The Department of Environmental Quality and the Arts Commission are still developing theirs. 
Even without an AI policy, agencies still have rules. For the tools identified in their AI inventory report, employees at the Department of Environmental Quality are responsible for reviewing AI-generated information before using it. AI is not used to make decisions, either. The Arts Commission recently started requiring grant applications to disclose AI use.
Mississippi currently has a handful of AI laws, but the attorney general’s office determined that Mississippi has no overarching AI framework, according to the state’s Artificial Intelligence Regulation task force’s report.
Last year, President Donald Trump issued an executive order seeking to limit states’ ability to regulate AI. 
Republican Sen. Bart Williams of Starkville, co-chair of the Artificial Intelligence Regulation task force and chair of the Mississippi Senate Technology Committee, doesn’t believe the president’s executive order will impact AI regulation in Mississippi.
“I think we’re gonna look at what’s best for our citizens and what we need to do for them,” he said.
Williams said AI will definitely be a topic of conversation in the 2027 legislative session. Many legislators are concerned about AI as it relates to children’s safety online and the workforce. However, he doesn’t know if it will be regulated.
The task force’s panelists recommended taking a “wait and see” approach. The report states the AG’s office recommended monitoring how the order impacts existing computer-related state laws that do not mention AI specifically.
Kollin Napier is chief AI officer of the Mississippi Artificial Intelligence Network, the nation’s first statewide AI initiative. MAIN is in partnership with ITS to spearhead usage and adoption. It does not have a regulatory role.
Napier spoke about the importance of governance.     
“That comes as acceptable use. It comes as a statewide framework, structured pilots and so much more. So that way, you don’t have agencies just sort of experimenting in the dark, so to speak,” he said.
The AI Innovation Hub, established by ITS, Amazon Web Services and MAIN, has student teams work on solving AI use cases for state agencies. The teams presented their work at a showcase in May. 
Napier said the return-on-investment for the innovation hub and MAIN’s workforce development efforts are “tremendous.”
Mississippi governmental agencies are part of a growing trend. AI use is prevalent in governmental agencies across the country.
A 2024 survey found that 51% of state, local and federal government employees who responded used AI daily or several times a week. In a Google Public Sector survey of 250 federal IT professionals, 90% said their agencies were already using or planning to use AI.  
Federal agencies are using AI for a variety of projects, from facial recognition systems to helping the public search through historical records.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri’s ‘unprecedented’ budget vote leaves schools around Kansas City in the lurch
description: School districts around Kansas City know it’s possible, maybe even likely, that Missouri’s governor and lawmakers will choose to not fully fund public schools next year. The state’s foundation formula, the calculation of how much money schools should receive, is enshrined in law. That doesn’t mean lawmakers always choose to provide the full formula amount, [[...]
text:
A student at Ingels Elementary School in the Hickman Mills School District. Superintendent Dennis Carpenter said he’s disappointed by the Missouri State Board of Education’s decision not to request full funding for schools (Vaughn Wheat/The Beacon).School districts around Kansas City know it’s possible, maybe even likely, that Missouri’s governor and lawmakers will choose to not fully fund public schools next year.
The state’s foundation formula, the calculation of how much money schools should receive, is enshrined in law. That doesn’t mean lawmakers always choose to provide the full formula amount, especially when money is tight. The most recent statewide school budget fell $190 million short.
Still, some local and statewide education leaders were caught off guard when the Missouri State Board of Education at its Sept. 15 meeting approved a budget request that didn’t even ask for the full amount required to fund the formula.
They said the decision is unprecedented, to their knowledge, and undersells how much money schools need according to the framework that the legislature itself created. 
Instead, the state school board’s request asks the governor and the legislature to keep foundation formula funding flat compared to the current year’s already underfunded budget. That means that in the coming fiscal year, state school funding would fall more than $270 million under what is laid out in state law. 
Hickman Mills Superintendent Dennis Carpenter said he’s disappointed by the board’s decision, suggesting the move gives lawmakers an easy pass to continue depriving Missouri schools of deeply needed resources.
It “makes it more likely that we’ll get less than we received last year, because we remove the ability to have a strong conversation about the foundation formula not simply being something that’s on a spreadsheet,” he said. “It represents what the state determined was necessary to effectively educate children.”
The latest decision is just one way school funding is “under assault” at the local, state and federal levels, Carpenter said.
Jackson County schools are preparing for property tax refunds to cut millions of dollars out of their budgets, and schools have seen federal funding delayed, cut or threatened.
“We keep asking the system to do more with less,” Carpenter said. “At some point, the system can’t function at a level that we all can be proud of.”
 The board’s discussion

The decision came after the state board voted 4-4 on a budget recommendation that did include full foundation formula funding. The tie meant the proposal did not pass.
Democrats Jordan Bradberry and Vincent Schoemehl Jr., Republican Kerry Casey and Jon Otto, an independent, voted in favor of full funding. Republicans Kenneth “Brooks” Miller Jr., Michael Matousek and Robbie Myers, along with independent Gretchen Shull, voted no.
The board also has a new nonvoting member, Mike McDonald, who is a math teacher in the Park Hill School District.
Board members are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Missouri Senate. Their political affiliations are reported because no more than four may belong to the same party.
Matousek, a member from Kansas City, called for the board to disregard the funding formula, arguing that the department shouldn’t request a funding increase at all while it lacks a strategic plan and a permanent commissioner.
“I think we’re asking for a lot of money without a real justification for spending it,” he said.
“This board, this department, has a credibility problem, and I think sending over a nine-plus billion dollar budget to people who make these decisions doesn’t help.”
He said that while state law requires the department to calculate the full foundation formula amount, it doesn’t require that the budget request match.
“I think we’re asking for money that doesn’t exist,” he said, alluding to a tightening state budget.
In June, Missouri Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick warned that the state’s general revenue surplus is being depleted.
Casey said it isn’t the board’s role to determine whether funding is available. That’s the responsibility of the state’s legislative and executive branches.
“It’s our job to present the need,” she said. The governor and legislature “are the ones to determine how that works in the scheme of all of the bigger priorities within the budget. That is not our job.”
After the tie vote, the board reached a compromise to leave in budget requests tied to new initiatives ordered by Gov. Mike Kehoe, the legislature or the courts. Those include a plan to grade public schools and districts on an A-to-F scale, new antisemitism reporting requirements and increased oversight of athletics.
It approved a nearly $4.3 billion request for the foundation formula, the same as formula spending in fiscal year 2027. That’s $270 million less than full funding for the formula.
McDonald clarified that the only change from the budget the board voted down was a cut to school budgets.
“I guess my concern is that the easiest place to cut is from the funding of the districts,” he said.
 Local impact

Carpenter, whose south Kansas City district is digging itself out of a financial hole and fighting to earn full accreditation, said it’s striking that the board voted to underfund schools shortly after approving a framework to grade them on an A-to-F scale.
“I think it’s pretty interesting that we literally up the ante on accountability,” he said, “and we reduce the ante on the resources necessary to be successful.”
The foundation formula isn’t just his personal opinion about how much schools should receive, Carpenter said. “The state made that determination, and now we’ve gotten so comfortable with underfunding it that we’re now comfortable for not even asking for full funding.”
In the Lee’s Summit School District, about 28% of funding comes from the state, said Chad Hertzog, assistant superintendent of business services. 
When state funding lags, the district has to rely even more on local funding, he said, including potentially raising residents’ property taxes. Once the district hits the tax rate ceiling set by voters, it has to reduce expenses such as by cutting supplies, services and staff.
The district could also ask taxpayers to raise the tax ceiling.
“It’s not (an option) that we like to consider because again, we’re asking our local voters to ultimately fund shortfalls at the state level at even a higher rate than they already are,” he said.
Hertzog said the district’s most pressing problem is Jackson County property taxes, but state funding reductions add to budget concerns. KCUR reports that the district is anticipating a revenue reduction of $7 million to $10 million this year after it reduced the tax rate in 2023 in response to growing property assessments.
The county has since determined that those assessments were handled incorrectly and is planning to refund money to taxpayers, cutting into schools’ revenue.
Hertzog said the difference between full formula funding from the state and what the district is actually receiving is nearly $7 million. The district’s overall operating budget is more than $280 million.
Carter Taylor, a Kansas City Public Schools elementary teacher and legislative chair of the Kansas City Federation of Teachers union, said the state board’s decision felt in line with “the current era in Missouri politics.”
“This is just another move that says public education doesn’t deserve support or funding,” she said. “It is another not-so-subtle attempt to say that we shouldn’t really exist.”
School districts’ percentage of state funding varies widely depending on factors such as the value of property that can be taxed locally. KCPS is one district that receives relatively little from the state, but Taylor said that every dollar counts.
“We take the least, and we try so hard to put in the most, but there’s only so much that a good teacher can do,” she said.
Matt Michelson, director of education policy for the Missouri State Teachers Association, said that even flat funding represents a practical decrease for schools as costs rise.
“I think all of us see in our daily lives everything is getting more expensive,” he said. Schools are “not immune to those increases in costs that everyone’s experienced over the last year,” including raises for teachers who also experience the effects of inflation.
Sarah Laub, a parent of two in the Blue Springs School District, said she’s concerned that state funding decisions could lead to her kids losing teachers and extracurricular activities. She’s also worried rural school districts — like the one she left in search of more educational opportunities for her kids in a better-funded district — could be hit the hardest.
Laub was referred to The Beacon by the Will of the People PAC, which aims to flip Missouri legislative seats. She also worked to oppose Amendment 5 with Parents for Missouri Public Schools based on its predicted impact on school funding.
She said the board’s decision should be seen in the context of a political climate where Kehoe and the legislature haven’t supported full school funding.
“It sounds like the board made their decision to not request that funding, not based on the belief that the schools don’t need it, but instead based on the belief that they no longer have faith that the lawmakers would listen to them or provide it,” she said.
But she thinks the board’s decision could contribute to lower school funding.
“I am concerned that this has created a vicious cycle where now the legislature will use it as a reason to cut even more funds,” she said.
 The message to lawmakers and the public

Lindsey Baker, research director with the Missouri Budget Project, a center-left think tank, said there are plenty of historical examples of fully funding the state’s formula and the lack of full funding. But whatever the ultimate outcome, the education department always requested full funding from lawmakers.
“This is not something I have ever seen, certainly, and I’ve talked to many other people who have been around a lot longer than I have, who have never seen this before either,” Baker said.
“I think this is an indication that this is going to be a very painful budget year.”
Baker attributed state budget issues to years of tax cuts that she said have caused a “serious revenue problem.”
The board’s decision could have a mixed reception in the legislature, said Caitlin Whaley, senior director of advocacy for the Missouri School Boards’ Association (MSBA). Those against higher school funding might use it to their advantage, while others won’t be pleased.
“It certainly gives legislators something to hang their hat on if they can say, ‘Well, why should we fully fund it if the very board that we confirmed to oversee public education doesn’t think this funding is necessary?’” she said.
But “there are absolutely supporters of public education in the legislature,” she said, “that will now have a decidedly more negative view of the state board.”
Whaley said lawmakers shouldn’t be surprised by increased costs because the legislature had projections of the financial impact when they voted on the changes that have caused some of the increases to the foundation formula. Those changes include incentives for five-day school weeks and relying less on attendance when computing enrollment for funding purposes.
Attendance-based calculations of enrollment tend to penalize schools that have higher poverty rates.
A task force is working on a proposal to modernize Missouri’s school funding formula, which could further increase the cost of the formula.
Whaley said that as the budget process continues, MSBA will highlight stories of school districts that are facing budget challenges and emphasize that the state should fulfill its commitments.
“If we’re going to pass legislation that says we’re going to pay districts money, that we need to, as a state, be responsible for those decisions that are made,” she said.
In an emailed news release, Missouri Association of School Administrators Executive Director Mark Penny also criticized the board decision.
“This is a failure of the board’s most basic responsibility: advocating for Missouri’s public schools and the students they serve,” the statement read in part. “The board’s job is to tell the governor and the General Assembly what our schools need. Instead, this board has made the unprecedented choice to recommend that public schools remain underfunded, an action that reflects a board increasingly hostile to public education.”
Michelson said he’s not sure how legislators will respond, but he sees the recommendation as a poor start to the budget process.
“It sends a horrible message to our educators, our kids and our communities that the state board doesn’t believe that it’s necessary to even ask the legislature to fully fund our schools,” Michelson said.
This article first appeared on Beacon: Kansas City and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.

name: WyoFile
title: Barrasso loves attention from the media, but not protecting press freedoms
description:
Wyoming’s U.S. senator backs President Trump’s ban  on news outlets that say negative things about administration, columnist Kerry Drake writes.
The post Barrasso loves attention from the media, but not protecting press freedoms appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming’s senior U.S. Sen. John Barrasso had a golden opportunity to defend the constitutionally protected freedom of the press Sunday. Instead, he predictably launched into a feeble defense of President Donald Trump’s White House ban on three news organizations that have criticized him.

Opinion

In an interview on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” Barrasso compared Trump’s vindictive action against CNN, MS NOW and Politico to the president being banned from Twitter (now X) and Facebook during his first term. 
“I didn’t see people come to his defense,” the senator said. “So, it goes both ways.”
I can’t believe Barrasso doesn’t recognize the difference between private corporations, which have the right to enforce their own rules for participating on their social media platforms, and the First Amendment’s mandate to allow the media to report the news without interference from the federal government.
Of course, he knows better. But Barrasso apparently views his job as the Senate’s majority whip, the chamber’s No. 2 leadership position, to defend whatever nonsense the president spouts no matter how much it lays waste to the guarantees enshrined in the Bill of Rights.
Throughout his 19 years in the Senate, Barrasso has been a frequent guest on cable TV news shows, including CNN and MS NOW (formerly MSNBC), whenever he wanted to express his views to a national audience. That usually included sticking it to the Democratic administrations of former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden, and bashing Trump’s critics.
It’s no secret to his constituents that one of Barrasso’s top priorities seems to be getting in front of TV cameras and next to powerful politicians. While climbing the GOP Senate leadership ladder, he always hovered over the shoulder of then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell at news conferences.
“We all respect and value the freedom of the press, it’s in the Constitution,” Barrasso told NBC’s Kristen Welker, but it was just lip service from a politician who has adroitly used the media to get free air time.
If Barrasso truly values a free press, why won’t he even criticize Trump’s personal war against members of the media, whom he disturbingly calls “the enemy of the people?”
If Barrasso truly values a free press, why won’t he call out the president for threatening last Friday to revoke the White House press credentials of other news organizations as he sees fit, creating a climate of fear and intimidation?
“The press has an obligation to report fairly,” Barrasso told Welker. “The president doesn’t see it happening that way.”
No, Trump just brands everything that doesn’t show him in a favorable light as “fake news.” He has a particularly cruel way of trying to humiliate women reporters who are just doing their jobs when they ask Trump valid questions.
Like Welker, who saw Trump storm off her “Meet the Press” set in June when she asked a follow-up question after the president made an unsubstantiated claim about U.S. elections being rigged.
Trump called her “either crooked or stupid.”
When Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey asked about the release of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the president of the United States said, “Quiet, piggy.” Katie Rogers of The New York Times wrote an article about Trump’s age and health — perfectly reasonable topics about an 80-year-old commander-in-chief — and Trump lashed out, calling her a “third-rate reporter who is ugly, both inside and out.”
This is the guy Barrasso trusts to assess the fairness of journalists? And decide which news organizations have the right to ask him questions?
Trump has played this game of yanking White House media credentials before, and lost. After a contentious exchange at a news conference in 2018, the president revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta’s press pass to the White House grounds. CNN sued, and a Trump-appointed judge overturned the restriction.
“What’s going on here is a flagrant violation of the First Amendment,” Connor Fitzpatrick of the free speech advocacy group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expressions told The Washington Times. “The precedent on this point is clear.” 
Barrasso was so at a loss for ammunition to back his argument on NBC, he resorted to pulling a 2020 campaign trope out of the mud: Hunter Biden’s laptop.
“When you take a look at this president, and you take a look at the Hunter Biden laptop,” he said, appearing confused, “if you want to really get into things where the press ignored the reality for a long period of time, said it was a Russian hoax.” Huh?
Then Barrasso abruptly summed up what seemed to be his main point: of course Republicans will win and stay in power.
“The bottom line on all of this is, this is not going to have an impact on an election 44 days from now,” he said. “People are going to go to the voting booth, they’re going to make a decision based on their life, their future, what they believe is best for them and their families.”
Barrasso said the choice is between “common sense Republicans and crazy Democrats.” He claimed Democrats are in “dire straits, as they’re even less popular than Republicans.”
Well, that’s a strange way to put it, since Barrasso admits that Republicans are unpopular. And it turns out to be fake news: A New York Times/Sienna poll last week showed that likely voters favored Democratic congressional candidates over Republicans by nearly 9 percentage points. It’s a metric, the New York Times reported, that is “closely watched by both parties as a leading indicator of political momentum.”
It appears Barrasso’s assessment of where this midterm election is going — which will largely determine Trump’s ability to get anything done in the next two years — is equal parts fake news and wishful thinking. That makes it, like his statements on Trump’s press ban, another example of Barrasso favoring the company line over the truth.

name: WyoFile
title: Wet ink: The forgery accusation that nearly wrecked Wyoming’s first Legislature
authors: by WyoHistory.org editors Kylie Louise McCormick and Leslie Waggener
description:
WyoHistory.org editors Kylie McCormick and Leslie Waggener revisit the chaotic 1891 night when a clerk’s “wet ink” note sparked accusations of fraud, vote buying and a political meltdown in Wyoming’s first Legislature.
The post Wet ink: The forgery accusation that nearly wrecked Wyoming’s first Legislature appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
In the early hours of a Sunday morning in January 1891, the chief clerk of the Wyoming House of Representatives stood up to read a few lines off the back of a bill, and the state’s brand-new government nearly came apart at the seams.
The big clock on the wall read 11:40 p.m. It had read 11:40 for hours. Lawmakers had stopped it on purpose, a trick still used today to keep legislating past a deadline. Other clocks around Cheyenne showed the real time: 3:15 a.m. Wyoming’s first state Legislature, in session since November, was supposed to have adjourned the night before. Instead, exhausted lawmakers were still grinding through bills and trading favors, with no idea that one clerk’s handwriting was about to ignite into a full-blown accusation of fraud.

Frank W. Mondell, who as a freshman state senator sponsored the 1891 apportionment bill, pictured in the 1903 volume “Progressive Men of the State of Wyoming.”

At the center of it all sat a bill that read like dry legislative housekeeping: apportioning House and Senate seats based on the new 1890 census. It was sponsored by Republican Sen. Frank Mondell, a freshman lawmaker from Newcastle who would later spend 13 terms in the U.S. House. Getting his bill passed came down to a technicality. If the bill had already received its required second reading, supporters had just enough votes to push it through outright. If it hadn’t, they’d need a two-thirds vote to suspend the rules, a vote they didn’t have.
Apportionment decided how many House and Senate seats each county held, and those seats would shape how the next Legislature would fill a U.S. Senate seat, a job that wouldn’t be left to voters for another two decades. The Cheyenne Daily Leader suspected the bill’s district lines were drawn to help keep Francis E. Warren, the state’s dominant Republican, in his U.S. Senate seat when his term expired in 1893 — an accusation the paper never proved. Whether that theory is right or not, it helps explain why a fight over apportionment could get heated enough to end in an accusation of forgery.

Francis E. Warren, the Republican senator at the center of the apportionment dispute, pictured in the 1903 volume “Progressive Men of the State of Wyoming.”

So, everything hinged on one question: Had the bill actually been read twice, or not?
Rep. Nat Baker, a Converse County Democrat, demanded that the clerk read the bill’s endorsement. Every bill carried one: a set of notes on the back, added by clerks as it moved through the Legislature, tracking exactly when it had been introduced, read and voted on. With obvious reluctance, Speaker A.C. Kellogg gave the order to Chief Clerk Ichabod S. Bartlett, who read through the notes in a low voice. Partway down, he stumbled, doubling back as though he’d forgotten something, then announced that the bill had indeed been read a second time. The Leader reported that the assistant clerk “went through a series of contortions that made it evident to close observers that he was suffering from some mental torture.”
Rep. William H. Brown was on his feet immediately. The Sheridan County Democrat had chaired the committee of the whole that considered the bill. He claimed he knew for a fact it had never gotten that second reading. The endorsement, he said, was false.
Brown moved to indefinitely postpone the bill, and the House plunged into an hourslong fight over parliamentary rules and unrelated business. In the middle of the uproar, Baker walked up to Speaker Kellogg’s desk and struck up a conversation. It looked friendly enough. Kellogg was clutching the bill tightly when the floor debate pulled his attention away. His grip loosened, and the bill slipped free. It had barely touched the desk when Baker grabbed it. He refused to give it back until he’d read the endorsement himself. He found what he was looking for. The ink on the “second reading” notation, he announced, was still wet. The docket said Jan. 8. The ink said minutes ago. 
The chamber came apart. Members shouted, demanding to know who was responsible. “Bartlett, the chief clerk,” Baker answered, according to the Leader. When the chamber pressed him on whether Bartlett admitted it, Baker said, “He does.” All eyes turned to Bartlett, seated near the rostrum. He nodded, without objecting, in front of the whole House.

Ichabod S. Bartlett, from “History of Wyoming,” ed. I.S. Bartlett (Chicago: The S.J. Clarke Publishing Co., 1918).

Then a second accusation tangled up the first one. Rep. Brown also claimed that Rep. Frank Bond of Laramie County had tried to buy Rep. Amandes Startzell’s vote, offering to slip a $5,000 appropriation for the Rawlins penitentiary into a separate spending bill if the Carbon County lawmaker backed the apportionment. Bond didn’t deny it. 
The apportionment bill died that night. Amid the debate, Rep. Edward Thorpe of Sweetwater County jumped on a desk and shouted: “There isn’t money enough in the Republican party to make me do a dishonest act. This is wrong and I’m against it to the last turn in the road,” the Leader reported. “I’m with you, my lad,” shouted a fellow Sweetwater County lawmaker. Brown then moved to indefinitely postpone the bill, in effect killing it, and the motion carried to a roar of noise from the floor.
Warren finished out his current term regardless — but the Legislature’s taste for gridlock wasn’t done with him. When his term expired in March 1893, a new legislature, now split three ways among Republicans, Democrats and Populists, couldn’t agree on a successor either, and Wyoming had only one U.S. senator for the next two years, until lawmakers finally sent Warren back in 1895. 
But the story doesn’t end there, and it doesn’t end cleanly.
The news accounts published two days later only went so far. It reported that the assistant clerk was cleared of complicity, since he’d written every endorsement on the bill except the disputed one. Yet nothing was said about Bartlett being cleared of anything.
Chief Clerk Barlett told his own version of events, but it didn’t hold together. In a personal defense published in the Leader, he insisted that the endorsement was procedurally sound, but his own account of how it got there kept shifting. He first said he’d personally written every notation on the bill, second reading included. Soon after, he instead pointed to the House’s official daily record, which he said already showed the second reading in the assistant clerk’s hand, and claimed his only failure was not copying that same notation onto the bill itself until later.
He also went on the offense, recasting the whole affair in a statement to the Cheyenne Sun as three sore-losing Democrats staging “mad ravings” to kill a bill they couldn’t beat honestly, and arguing the bill’s defeat would cost the young state a costly extra session. He further claimed Baker himself had moved that same night to exonerate him by unanimous vote, although that claim was not verified. 
Whether Bartlett was a forger, a scapegoat or something in between depends on whose story you believe. What’s clear is that Wyoming’s first elected lawmakers spent their final hours in office in a shouting match over a wet signature, with a U.S. Senate seat and a costly do-over session hanging in the balance.
Bartlett, for his part, landed on his feet. He went on to serve as managing editor of the Cheyenne Leader from 1906 to 1908, the same paper that had accused him of forgery in its pages a decade and a half earlier. Ten years after that, he edited the multivolume “History of Wyoming.” The man accused of doctoring the state’s legislative record ended up editing its history.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming chooses public lands at the ballot box
description:
Voters finally felt the threat to public lands had reached a critical point, observers say.
The post Wyoming chooses public lands at the ballot box appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Few issues matter more to Wyoming hunter Jeff Muratore than the fate of the public lands — where he tracks elk and deer to feed his family, where he seeks solace and taught his grandchildren to hunt. A lifelong Republican, Muratore is no liberal: He voted for President Donald Trump and stands by traditionally conservative values like smaller government and fewer regulations.
But in Wyoming’s August primary, he could not bring himself to vote for the Trump-endorsed gubernatorial candidate, Megan Degenfelder. He felt that one of her opponents, Eric Barlow, had a better record of championing the lands owned by all Americans and managed by the U.S. Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management and other federal agencies. In 2026, a year after Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee spearheaded an attempt to sell off roughly 3 million federal acres, saying the sales would encourage the development of affordable housing, Barlow, a state senator, crafted a successful resolution recognizing the importance of public lands to Wyomingites.
Muratore thought about the land and its future as he worked his way down the ballot. And he voted against his own state senator, Bob Ide, who drafted unsuccessful legislation in 2025 demanding that the federal government surrender its public lands to the state.
Muratore, who formerly led the Wyoming chapter of the nonprofit Backcountry Hunters and Anglers, wasn’t the only one to buck candidates viewed as hostile to public lands or wildlife.
Across the state, incumbents lost as voters favored more moderate Republicans like Barlow. In fact, the right-wing Wyoming Freedom Caucus lost its majority in the Wyoming House of Representatives; it now holds only 10 of 62 House seats heading into the next legislative session. Its allies in the state Senate, including Ide, faced similar defeats. The moderate sweep was a remarkable turnaround for a voting bloc that had sought to secure a supermajority.
Other issues — like the Freedom Caucus’ plan to defund parts of the University of Wyoming and its role in a statewide campaign finance scandal — influenced voters. But many observers say politicians’ public lands positions played a part in their fate.
“The threat level to our access to the lands that we own as citizens of the United States and the state of Wyoming finally hit a tipping point,” said Wes Allen, co-owner of Sunlight Sports, a multigenerational outdoor store in Cody. “When we had candidates locally and for statewide offices who stood up and said they believed in public lands and wouldn’t want to sell public lands, it was a powerful statement.”
Wyoming’s politics have long been conservative. The Equality State once elected moderate Democrats like Teno Roncalio, the last Democrat to represent Wyoming in Congress, and former Gov. Dave Freudenthal. But since Freudenthal left office in 2011, Republicans have occupied all of Wyoming’s statewide and federal offices as well as most seats in the state Legislature. Republicans currently hold 56 of 62 seats in the House and 29 of the Senate’s 31 seats, meaning that the most important battles aren’t often fought in November but in August, during the Republican primary. Recently, conservative, ideologically libertarian Republicans found themselves pitted against the socially and fiscally conservative Freedom Caucus, the coalition of firebrands who captured a House majority in 2024 amid a wave of anti-woke national sentiment.
But in 2025 and 2026, emboldened by its victories, the Freedom Caucus stumbled, said Gail Symons, a longtime Wyoming policy wonk who operates Civics307, a voter education website. The lawmakers targeted beloved institutions like the University of Wyoming and the Wyoming Business Council, an economic development outfit. The Freedom Caucus proposed cutting 11%, or about $40 million, from the university’s budget, and attempted to defund and dismantle the Business Council altogether.
Many of the legislators who lost in August voted for and even co-sponsored Ide’s public-lands transfer bill in 2025, though some, like Reps. John Bear, R-Gillette, and Rep. Chip Neiman, R-Hulett, also supported Barlow’s public-lands resolution in 2026.
“Once we have 100% of the resources and revenue from those public lands, we would double our revenue and be quite easily able to manage those lands.”Rep. John Bear, R-Gillette
Bear, the former chairman of the Freedom Caucus, lost his seat in the August primary and said that public-lands policy likely played a role in the outcome. But he believes the public misunderstood his position. While Bear believes federal lands should be transferred to the states, he doesn’t think the states, Wyoming included, would sell them off.
“Once we have 100% of the resources and revenue from those public lands, we would double our revenue and be quite easily able to manage those lands,” he said, adding that public-land supporters “duped people into believing that public lands were at risk.”
A 2016 study commissioned by the Wyoming Legislature found that state management of public lands would not only be costly, it would come with a “bureaucratic maze” of congressional laws and directives.
Some in the Freedom Caucus did not directly target public lands. Many, however, championed other controversial wildlife management bills, including legislation allowing landowners to sell valuable hunting licenses and mandating unlimited statewide mountain lion hunting. Another measure would have forced the Wyoming Game and Fish Department to give out free “bear coupons” allowing resident elk hunters to kill grizzly bears — which are still federally protected — as well as black bears outside of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem.
None of those measures made it to the governor’s desk, though Barlow’s public-lands resolution did. Voters paid attention to what their local lawmakers supported, Symons and others said.
“The Freedom Caucus misread quite a few things, not the least of which the degree to which Wyoming citizens of every political persuasion really, really feel strongly about public lands,” Symons said.
At the same time, opposition to the Freedom Caucus mounted.
A backcountry mountain guide named Zach Lentsch, the son of a Wyoming game warden, formed Protect Wyoming, the state’s first public-lands PAC. He believed that traditional nonprofits were too restricted — 501(c)(3) organizations are not allowed to advocate for or against candidates — so he and the group’s treasurer, Chris Allen, raised money, then held public events and knocked on doors, targeting the candidates with the most extreme views.
“All 33 candidates that we preferred — that were on our pro-public lands and wildlife slate — won,” Lentsch said.
Like Lentsch and Symons, Allen, the Cody business owner, has watched the pendulum of Wyoming politics swing back and forth, each time lilting more to the right, including on public-land policy. While Wyoming voters have historically voiced support for public lands in bipartisan polls, they have still backed lawmakers who favor transferring them to states or selling off national forests, parks and other federally managed land.
“The Freedom Caucus misread quite a few things, not the least of which the degree to which Wyoming citizens of every political persuasion really, really feel strongly about public lands.”Gail Symons
At the national level, that trend may have continued. Republican voters picked current U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman — who once proudly wore the tagline “Wicked Witch of the West” for her public-lands stance — over Sam Mead for U.S. Senate. In 2024, the congresswoman backed Utah’s attempt to return BLM land to the states, which failed in the Supreme Court. She has also advocated for overturning popular national policies like the Roadless Rule, which prevents road construction in some areas of national forests. Mead, in contrast, made protecting public lands one of his core platform positions.
Symons understands the dichotomy. In her view, voters decided to send a Trump-aligned fighter to D.C., while choosing more moderate candidates locally. Hageman also had significantly greater name recognition than Mead.
Allen credits the swing in local elections partly to concern over public lands, spurred to some extent by Sen. Lee’s push to sell them off.
“I don’t think it was widely accepted that our politicians would willingly give up protections for public lands,” he said. “But in the last couple of years, it became clear there were certain people who don’t believe we should have public lands, who believe we should give away most of our lands to other entities. And they’re not doing that because they think it’s good policy, but because they simply don’t believe in public lands.”
In Allen’s view, the August primary was the first time a majority of voters concluded that protecting public lands was one of their major issues. Neither he nor Symons and Muratore expect this to be the last swing of the public-lands pendulum. But, as Muratore said, “it is a pretty big bump in the road.”

title: Tennessee schools still miss farm-to-school grant eliminated in 2025 as USDA rolls out new programs

text:
Tennessee schools are still feeling the loss of Local Foods for Schools funding eliminated by the Trump administration in 2025. The U.S. Department of agriculture recently announced a new 'Harvest to Hallways' initiative, which offers guidance and funding for equipment, among other things. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)School Nutrition Director Vickie Dunaway has spent years transitioning the Milan Special School District in West Tennessee toward scratch-made cooking.
She used grant funding to purchase equipment needed to process whole foods in school kitchens, and she bought fresh corn, squash, tomatoes and local beef from farmers for student meals.
But in March 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture canceled the Local Food for Schools program that helped her district afford fresh local foods — more expensive than pre-processed commodities — amid the Trump administration’s efforts to slash the federal budget. 
“We were able to chop the tomatoes and shred the lettuce and all the squash and sweet potatoes and all the things,” Dunaway said. “We bought the equipment. Now I can’t afford the food.”
The U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Department of Health and Human Services announced a new slate of programs in late August aiming to bring more American agriculture products to school cafeteria trays. 

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The “Harvest to Hallways” initiative includes up to $70 million for schools to update cafeteria equipment and storage, and an additional $25 million infusion into Patrick Leahy Farm to School Grants, which support projects that connect schools with local producers. The USDA will also offer guidance to schools looking to use their existing school lunch federal reimbursement dollars on local foods. Another $32.5 million HHS program will help school districts test new approaches.
Dunaway said it’s a step in the right direction: Many schools need help building the infrastructure to handle fresh foods, and the local option for reimbursement dollars is helpful. But these things don’t change her budget’s bottom line. 
“We need both the equipment to process the fresh ingredients (and) a sustainable recurring revenue that helps make buying food possible long-term,” she said.
The USDA has yet to publish application requirements for the new grants. The Tennessee Department of Education is awaiting guidance from the USDA, Director of Media Amanda Chin said in an email to The Lookout.
If any of the opportunities provide funding to help purchase fresh, local food, Dunaway said she’ll be “the first one jumping in.”
Otherwise, she’d rather have the money go to schools that don’t already have the necessary equipment, she said. But that may also be difficult.
“For so many of us, writing that grant and staying on top of that grant is not something that a lot of the small districts can do,” Dunaway said. “They just don’t have the staff, and they don’t have the time to do all that.”
Grant-funded program to bring cooking labs, fresh local foods to Northwest Tennessee schools

The nonprofit Northwest Tennessee Local Food Network secured a $500,000 Patrick Leahy Farm to School Grant this year and is working with five school districts over the next two years to train cafeteria workers to work with fresh produce and introduce new foods to students. Dunaway’s school district is among those benefiting from that program.
The nonprofit’s co-directors Samantha Smith Goyret and Caroline Ideus said they are grateful to see the administration’s focus moving toward supporting more local ingredients in school meals but noted the federal grant process may be a challenge for smaller, less-resourced schools and organizations to tackle without experience.
“We worked with several smaller school districts to help write Farm to School grants this past cycle, but they weren’t awarded because they’re not strong enough, they’re not big enough,” Smith Goyret said. “So what the government is doing, it’s really fueling the organizations that already have that capacity.”
Barriers to offering more local food in schools boil down to three points: education, equipment and lack of funding, Smith Goyret said. The recently announced grants could help reduce some of those barriers, she said.
But the loss of the Local Food for Schools funding in 2025 “was a huge blow and still is,” Ideus said.
The program, which started during the COVID-19 pandemic, earmarked about $660 million for schools and childcare institutions to purchase locally produced foods in 2025 under outgoing President Joe Biden’s administration. Another $500 million was earmarked for local food purchases for food banks.
“That was a direct pipeline to the schools for them to use for local food, period,” Ideus said. “So these grants that they’re dibbling out are nice, but it’s not $1 billion.”
Having both the Farm to School grants and the Local Food for Schools funding would be the “ultimate” combination, she said.
Schools get reimbursed a set amount by the federal government for eligible meals and snacks they serve, but the budget is tight, and local foods can be considerably more expensive than commodity products, Smith Goyret said.
“Even wholesale, farmers still have to make ends meet. They’re not charitable organizations. They’re businesses as well,” she said.
Dunaway said the cost of even commodity foods is rising, but local farming operations can’t compete with bulk prices. Now, she’s only able to purchase sausage and beef from a local source “on special occasions.”
A spokesperson for the USDA pointed to USDA Foods, a program that allows schools to use preset federal entitlements to order domestically produced fruits, vegetables, meat and other foods procured by the USDA and delivered through a partnership with the Department of Defense’s logistics agency. The spokesperson also highlighted $45 million issued in 2026 through Farm to School grants, in addition to other programs that distribute locally sourced foods to tribal members.
In 2023, nearly two-thirds of school food authorities reported serving local foods to students, according to the USDA’s 2023 Farm to School Census. Those districts logged nearly $1.8 billion in local food purchases, about 16% of total spending. About half of that went toward local milk. That year, 42% of participating school food authorities reported challenges with availability of local foods, and 35% reported cost difficulties.
The next Farm to School Census is slated for 2027, according to a USDA spokesperson.

title: COVID vaccines for uninsured Tennessee kids in limbo amid federal delays
description: The federal government has yet to release information on when — or whether — it will continue to provide COVID-19 vaccines to low-income children through a free immunization program, raising alarms among some Tennessee health providers ahead of this Fall’s respiratory illness season. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccines for Children prog[...]
text:
The federal government has not confirmed it will release COVID vaccines for low-income children through its Vaccines for Children program this year, causing concern among healthcare providers in Tennessee where half of all children are vaccinated through the federal program. Pictured: Esmeralda Baravar, 18, winces as she gets her COVID-19 vaccine during a pop-up clinic at Our Lady of Guadalupe Catholic Church in South Nashville in 2020. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)The federal government has yet to release information on when — or whether — it will continue to provide COVID-19 vaccines to low-income children through a free immunization program, raising alarms among some Tennessee health providers ahead of this Fall’s respiratory illness season.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Vaccines for Children program routinely delivers immunizations to state and local health officials to be made available to children at public health clinics in all 95 Tennessee counties and other federally-subsidized urban and rural clinics across the state.
About half of all Tennessee kids — and 50% of children nationwide —  rely on the program for all or most of their vaccines, including COVID-19.
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved 2026-2027 COVID vaccines in August, and they are currently available to those with commercial insurance. 
But a statement released late last week by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services has introduced confusion and uncertainty about the federal government’s plans to get the vaccine to low income children this year.
“HHS and CDC have a responsibility to ensure responsible stewardship of taxpayer resources and that vaccines procured through federally funded programs are appropriate for the populations those programs serve,” read the statement, which was also shared on Monday with the Tennessee Lookout in response to questions posed to HHS about the government’s plans to make the COVID vaccine available to low-income children.
The CDC is “finalizing decisions regarding COVID-19 vaccine procurement” for the children’s program, as well as a separate program that provides vaccinations to low income adults, the statement said. “Additional information will be available soon,” the statement said.
Brian Haile, CEO of Neighborhood Health Centers, called the uncertainty and delay over COVID vaccine availability for children “deeply, deeply distressing.”
Neighborhood Health Centers provide medical care to adults and children regardless of income or insurance. Last week its clinics began offering flu vaccines. Ideally, Haile said, COVID shots would be provided at the same time, sparing busy families a second trip to a clinic. 
Offering seasonal vaccines, beginning in September and through November, provides “maximum protection for folks before the holiday season begins and they start spending more time indoors in close proximity to others, especially others that they might not see on a routine basis,” he said.
“This is a big deal,” Haile said. “We are worried we’re going to have much lower COVID vaccination rates than we could otherwise achieve if the federal government had simply taken timely action.”
“What we’re seeing this year is unusual,” said Dr. Michele Fiscus, chief medical officer for the Association of Immunization Managers, about uncertainty surrounding a COVID-19 vaccine program for low-income children. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Neighborhood Health is currently referring patients with insurance to local pharmacies, where COVID shots are free to those with coverage. “Neighborhood Health hopes to be able to provide COVID vaccinations to children and pregnant women later this year,” a flier for patients said.
Children also routinely get free COVID shots in public health clinics operated by the Tennessee Department of Health that are paid for by the federal Vaccines for Children program. The department did not respond Monday to questions about the impact of federal uncertainty or delay in offering the vaccines or provide its current advice to parents and caregivers seeking the vaccine for children.
It is not unusual for there to be a delay between when seasonal vaccines become available on the commercial market versus when they are made available through the Vaccines for Children program, said Dr. Michele Fiscus, chief medical officer for the Association of Immunization Managers, a membership organization for state and local public health vaccine programs. Fiscus was formerly medical director for Tennessee’s Vaccine Preventable Diseases and Immunization Program. 
That lag in approved coverage of vaccines between kids with insurance and those without has long been a source of frustration for pediatric providers, she said.
“You never want to have to tell a child that they can’t be protected against a disease because of their insurance status, and so that never feels good. And from an ethical and equity perspective, it is not ideal to have there be a gap in the availability,” Fiscus said.
But, she said, “what we’re seeing this year is unusual.”
“What’s happening this year is the anxiety around when the vaccines will become available just because of the environment that we’re all living in right now,’ she said.
Fiscus said her advice to parents is to “get their children vaccinated as soon as the vaccines become available.”
Editor’s note: Tennessee Lookout Editor J. Holly McCall serves on the board of directors for Neighborhood Health.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: As public splits over CHOOSE Act, so do Alabama political candidates
description: Alabama’s school voucher program is set to go universal at the beginning of next year, but public perception of the effectiveness of the program is split and candidates sort down party lines about its future. Under the CHOOSE Act, parents can claim up to $7,000 in tax credits  for education-based expenses including private school tuition, […]
text:
Students walk to class at Collinsville Elementary School in Collinsville, Alabama on Feb. 10, 2026. Candidates in the state's gubernatorial race have differing opinions on the CHOOSE Act, the state's effective school voucher program, and Alabamians are almost equally split on support of the school vouchers. (Eric Schultz for Alabama Reflector) 



  Key Points 


Alabama’s school voucher program, known as the CHOOSE Act, is set to go universal Jan. 1, 2027.
Proponents of the program argue that it allows parents the choice on how their children are educated while opposers say school vouchers take money away from public schools.
A 2026 survey from the Public Reseach Affairs Council of Alabama found that state residents are nearly split in half on support for the CHOOSE Act and that 42% of Alabamians think too much money is given to school vouchers.

 



Alabama’s school voucher program is set to go universal at the beginning of next year, but public perception of the effectiveness of the program is split and candidates sort down party lines about its future.
Under the CHOOSE Act, parents can claim up to $7,000 in tax credits  for education-based expenses including private school tuition, school supplies and tutoring. 
Currently, the program eligibility is capped at 300% above the poverty level, or $81,960. The program is set to be universal at the start of 2027, meaning anyone can apply regardless of income, leading some lawmakers to become concerned about the money that will be spent out of the Education Trust Fund budget in what could be an already tight fiscal year 2028. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The program has long split Democrats and Republicans, a split that has carried over into this year’s gubernatorial race. Republicans have touted the program as a way for students in struggling schools to have an option for a better education. Democrats said the program diverts funding from already-underfunded schools, and have cited the soaring costs of similar programs in other states, such as Arizona.
According to a survey conducted earlier this year by the Public Research Affairs Council of Alabama, 48% of Alabamians approve of the program while 50% disapprove. The survey also showed 42% of people think the state spends too much money on school vouchers, 24% think the state spends the right amount and and 17% think the state spends too little.
Ryan Hankins, executive director of PARCA, said in an interview Monday the split was mostly along party lines, but there isn’t a clear answer as to why support fell that way.
“A majority of Republicans supported it, a majority of Democrats opposed it, but that was not universal on either side,” Hankins said. “So I think we have some Democrats that support it, and we have some Republicans that oppose it. But we did not drill further down into you know the why as they what made respondents respond one way or another.”
A political divide
Most CHOOSE Act recipients will stay in the same type of school with voucher-like credit

When asked for comment, Republican gubernatorial nominee Sen. Tommy Tuberville’s campaign referenced an interview he did with the Trussville Tribune on Wednesday. During the interview, the senator, who has supported public funding of non-public school options, said he wanted to expand the CHOOSE Act and criticized Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones’ opposition to it.
“The CHOOSE Act is pretty simple, and I can’t believe anybody would be against it,” he said during the interview. “And obviously, Doug has got a different idea of education. He loves government schools and so do the democrats, but times change.”
In an interview Friday, Jones called Tuberville’s defense of the CHOOSE Act “absurd.”
“I think what it says is that the marketing for it has done a pretty good job of trying to fashion this as a parent’s choice when it is really not a parent’s choice, it is a private school choice,” he said. “They’re the only ones who really get the chance to choose which students that they take, and so I think it’s been a pretty good political marketing ploy by those who want to see money going out of public schools.”
Tuberville did not say how he would expand the program. Sen. Arthur Orr, R-Decatur, said in an interview Monday any expansion made to the CHOOSE Act would “need to be done slowly and incrementally as the revenues allow it.” 
“We need to move as far as the appropriation and the dollar amount only at a level which we can maintain,” Orr said.
Who applies for the CHOOSE Act
CHOOSE Act applications for the 2026-27 school year reached record numbers. Gov. Kay Ivey’s office reported 29,341 applications representing 48,927 students. That’s up nearly 7,200 applicants from the 2025-26 school year.    
  

Of the students who applied, over 70% are outside the state’s public education system. The governor’s office said 21,351 (43.6%) represented private school students; 13,425 (27.4%)  represented homeschooled students and 8,961 (18.3%) represented public or charter school students.
The percentage of public school students applying for CHOOSE Act money fell from 10,287 (27.9%) who sought the aid in the 2025-26 school year. That same year, 15,436 (41.9%) were from private schools and 9,070 (24.6%) students came from homeschools.
Hankins said that one issue with the CHOOSE Act is that there is no way to measure how the students who take the tax credit are doing. Orr said adding that into the legislation could happen in the future.
“When the bill was coming through the legislature, that topic was discussed and debated extensively,” Orr said. “We can always revisit it, but my opinion would be, let’s get the program going. We’re only what, (17) months in or so? Let it get going, and then we can always come revisit it.”
Rep. Danny Garrett, R-Trussville, who chairs the House Ways and Means Education Committee, said in an interview Friday he doesn’t mind private school students being the majority of applicants.
“This is giving parents all across the state the ability, if they’re in that income bracket, to make the best choice for their child,” Garrett said. “And maybe the best choice for their child is to go to a private Christian school, maybe to go to another kind of school, (like a) classical school. It may be for them to homeschool.”
Jones wants to stop accepting applications and phase the program out, saying he’s “opposed to using taxpayer dollars that are designated for public schools to be used for private schools.” 
“I don’t want to take away the choice of folks who’ve already made a choice under this act,” he said. “I don’t think that would be fair to those kids who have maybe transferred schools, but I think there’s a way to phase it out.”
Looking to the budgets
Multiple attempts to reach Democratic lawmakers were unsuccessful. In March, Rep. Barbara Drummond, D-Mobile, also criticized the CHOOSE Act for taking money away from public schools.
“The CHOOSE Act, as well as other initiatives that take money away from public education, it’s not making that system better. It’s making it worse,” she said. 
Alabama’s school voucher program might go universal despite budget concerns

Orr said some of the public school students receiving the vouchers are using it to attend other public schools.
“Many times, … it’s (students attending) another public school, but they have out-of-district fees, so they’re (students) taking CHOOSE Act funds as out-of-district fees for a child that doesn’t live in their district,” Orr said. “So to me, it allows an alternative, particularly for those families that cannot afford a private education, but it gives them that hope of a better education.”
Last year, 23,429 students received CHOOSE Act money. Of that number, 6% of them (1,442) planned to use the funds to go to a public school. The overwhelming majority of those students (91%) were already enrolled in a public school.
Garrett cited ongoing growth in Education Trust Fund revenues as keeping budgets whole. 
“We continue every year, even with the CHOOSE Act, to put millions, hundreds of millions of more dollars into public education every year. So we have not taken money away from public education. The budgets have grown, and we have continued to increase the contribution to public education,” Garrett said.
In fiscal year 2026 the Alabama State Department of Education received $733 million in the Education Trust Fund to the CHOOSE Act’s $101 million. In fiscal year 2027, ALSDE received $772 million to the voucher program’s $236 million.    
  

Hankins said given the warnings around the FY28 budget “everyone is expecting the next budget debate to be a pretty hotly contested topic.”
“Recent indications say the tax revenues are up, contrary to expectations. So it’ll be interesting to see how that shakes out by the end of this fiscal year,” he said. “But all indications seem to suggest that while costs are going up for governments, revenues are not, and that will be a complicated debate in the Legislature.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee officials approve plan to seek master developer for lots near Capitol, Boring tunnel
description: After a 10-day delay, Tennessee state officials approved a waiver to move forward with the next phase in finding a master developer for parking lots near the State Capitol.  The Tennessee State Building Commission unanimously approved a waiver allowing the Department of General Services to skip its normal disclosure process and seek bids for a […]
text:
An August 2026 aerial shot of the Boring Company's Music City Tunnel station under construction at the Tennessee State Capitol.
(Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)After a 10-day delay, Tennessee state officials approved a waiver to move forward with the next phase in finding a master developer for parking lots near the State Capitol. 
The Tennessee State Building Commission unanimously approved a waiver allowing the Department of General Services to skip its normal disclosure process and seek bids for a master developer for roughly 10 acres of parking lots surrounding the Capitol in downtown Nashville. 
The lots include the one on which Elon Musk’s Boring Company is building the first phase of its underground tunnel connecting parts of downtown to the airport with Tesla vehicles. 
State officials plan to choose a master developer to turn the parking lots into a mixed-use development with housing, hotels and retail. The chosen developer will also receive an option to redevelop the James K. Polk building, which currently houses the Tennessee Perfomring Arts Centers, and build a garage for state employees. 
The deal will be a land lease agreement, allowing the state to keep ownership of the land. 
Tennessee State Building Commission to vote again on mixed-use development in Nashville

Gov. Bill Lee, who made a rare appearance to chair the building commission meeting, said the overall plan focused on better “utilizing” the valuable land in Nashville.
“We’ve been working on this for some time,” Lee said during the meeting. “At the end of the day, the taxpayers will benefit from decisions being made here. It was something I was hoping to get done before I left.”
Lee is term-limited and will no longer be governor after January.
Two weeks ago, the building commission deadlocked in a 3-3 vote because Lee, one of the designated board members, did not attend the meeting. 
State Sen. Heidi Campbell and state Rep. John Ray Clemmons, both Nashville Democrats, opposed waiving the normal disclosure process during the meeting’s public comment period. 
Without a waiver to skip its normal disclosure, state officials would have to wait until spring 2027 to move forward with a bidding process.
Campbell said she favored redeveloping the lots, but was concerned that the state was moving too quickly and not getting a competitive deal on “$160 million in state-owned land.”
”The state wants permission to bypass the normal disclosure timetable and select one developer to negotiate a long deal… without first holding a competitive price stage,” Campbell said.
The next step in the process is for the Department of General Services to release a request for qualifications, allowing it to receive bids from those wanting to be the master developer of the land.

title: Idaho is built to lead our country’s next big energy transition
description: For nearly three years, the Idaho Advanced Energy Consortium has partnered with the Idaho National Laboratory, Idaho Environmental Coalition, colleges and universities, and dozens of industry organizations across Idaho and the greater region. We’ve done this because Idaho is one of the only places in the country with the highly skilled nuclear workforce, inf[...]
text:
Two men work at the Irradiated Materials Characterization Laboratory at the Idaho National Laboratory's Materials and Fuels Complex. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho National Laboratory)For nearly three years, the Idaho Advanced Energy Consortium has partnered with the Idaho National Laboratory, Idaho Environmental Coalition, colleges and universities, and dozens of industry organizations across Idaho and the greater region. 
We’ve done this because Idaho is one of the only places in the country with the highly skilled nuclear workforce, infrastructure and institutional knowledge to lead the nation into the next era of American energy. 
All of this resulted from decades of investment. The region’s nuclear engineering roots trace back more than 70 years, beginning in 1949 at what is now the INL site. In that time, Idaho has developed its workforce, supply chains and research capacity that, today, supports industry from small modular reactor development to hydrogen production and next-generation grid technology. 
Last year, the U.S. Department of Commerce formally recognized the region’s leadership, designating the Intermountain West Energy Corridor as the nation’s only nuclear energy focused Tech Hub. More than 45 organizations across Idaho and Wyoming are now working together to further develop the existing workforce and enhance manufacturing capacity to support America’s energy future. 
Idaho-Wyoming nuclear industry partnership set to receive $31M federal award 

This matters because the conversation surrounding the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus should be understood in this context. Whatever position individuals take on specific proposal details, the underlying opportunity cannot be overlooked. New research missions that help fuel America’s energy future represent exactly the kind of institutional growth Idaho has prepared to implement for years. 
Historically, new missions at the U.S. Department of Energy’s premier nuclear laboratory have supported durable careers and advanced technical fields that allow young Idahoans to remain in our state. These missions have established a research ecosystem that continues to attract global attention and private investment. 
We’ve watched this pattern play out for decades, and we’re continuing to build workforce pipelines and new infrastructure that prepares our communities for the next chapter of economic growth. 
As a nonprofit coordinating organization, the Idaho Advanced Energy Consortium does not advocate for or against specific proposals. It is our job to help our region position itself to benefit from whatever opportunities emerge and to make sure the benefits of this growth extend to communities across the region, not just around the laboratory’s front gate. This is the lens through which the energy consortium views the Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus opportunity and the broader advanced energy work happening in our region. 
We encourage anyone following this debate to look past the headlines and ask a more practical question: What does it take for a region like ours to prepare for the next generation of energy technology? This is the question our consortium exists to answer, which is why we convene partners across construction, manufacturing, transportation and education. 
It’s the reason we’ve spent the last several years building the workforce infrastructure this moment calls for. 
I’ve spent nearly two decades watching workforce investment transform communities across this state and one thing has been consistent: Building this kind of capacity doesn’t happen by accident. It takes sustained investment in people and institutions, the kind our consortium was established to support.
