title: Administrative judge sides with teacher punished for Charlie Kirk Facebook post
description: The state should drop charges, including an allegation of gross immorality, against a Duval County teacher who posted about Charlie Kirk after he was killed, an administrative law judge has recommended.  The decision came last week, addressing charges against Hope McMath, who was an advanced placement art history teacher at Douglas Anderson School of the […]
text:
People visit a memorial set up in honor of Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University in Orem on Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The state should drop charges, including an allegation of gross immorality, against a Duval County teacher who posted about Charlie Kirk after he was killed, an administrative law judge has recommended. 
The decision came last week, addressing charges against Hope McMath, who was an advanced placement art history teacher at Douglas Anderson School of the Arts, a magnet high school in Jacksonville, when Kirk was killed in Utah in September 2025. 
Her Facebook post positioned the shooting as “Karma,” referring to Kirk’s comment, “I think it’s worth to have a cost of, unfortunately, some gun deaths every single year so that we can have the Second Amendment to protect our other God-given rights. That is a prudent deal. It is rational. Nobody talks like this. They live in a complete alternate universe.”
Additionally, according to the state, she “posted or reposted an artist’s rendition of an individual holding the screaming severed head of what clearly is intended to represent the President of the United States, Donald Trump.”
Even so, Administrative Law Judge Garnett Chisenhall wrote that the state provided “no competent, substantial evidence that the social media postings at issue impaired Ms. McMath’s service in the community.”
“The social media postings did not reflect any use, attempted use, or threatened use of violence by Ms. McMath,” the judge wrote, adding that the state “has not argued that Ms. McMath’s post was a legitimate threat to sever President Trump’s head.”
Chisenhall recommended the Education Practices Commission dismiss the charges against McMath, which include gross immorality, personal conduct that seriously reduces effectiveness of an employee, violating the principles of professional conduct required by the Florida Board of Education, reasonably protecting students from conditions harmful to learning, and taking responsible precautions to distinguish between personal views and those of the institution.
Also in September 2025, the school board adopted a policy establishing that an employee’s “inappropriate or unbecoming Material on publicly accessible websites” “has the potential to disrupt the educational process, damage the reputations of the District, it’s [sic] teachers and staff, damages the District’s reputation and stature, and subject the District, its teachers and employees to ridicule.”
McMath’s post did none of that, Chisenhall concluded.
“In short, there is no evidence indicating that anyone could reasonably conclude that Ms. McMath’s sentiments were shared by her employers,” he wrote.
‘I was not celebrating’
The district issued McMath “a verbal warning” with “coaching/counseling,” and “a temporary reassignment to the School District’s Art Resource Center with no teaching duties.”
“I was not celebrating, and the language in that post and the intention behind that post was not celebratory,” McMath said during the proceedings, per the court record. She didn’t post the comments while on the clock at school.
A district investigation did not determine McMath had disrupted district operations. Furthermore, the evidence shows no teacher, administrator, or student complained, and no student viewed the social media posts.
According to the principal at the school, “The content of the posts never came up at the school. Students weren’t talking about it. Teachers weren’t talking about it. Parents weren’t talking about it. They were aware because it was in the news, but nobody ever brought it up as far as a concern of her being in front of their children.”
Shortly after Kirk’s killing, then-Education Commissioner Anastasios Kamoutsas wrote a letter to school superintendents statewide, reminding them that he has the power to discipline educators and sanction their certificates for probable cause, including “personal conduct that seriously reduces that person’s effectiveness as an employee of the district school board.”
McMath, according to the court record, has not been in the classroom since the incident.
“Content that trivializes a homicide and that generally depicts the decapitation of a national figure is a condition harmful to learning and to the mental health of the adolescent students who encounter it,” the state argued.
Chisenhall said he has seen no “persuasive explanation for why” McMath was reassigned away from students.
Federal lawsuit
McMath is plaintiff in a federal lawsuit against the Duval County school district, Florida Department of Education, and Moms for Liberty and its Duval chapter. “While not state entities, they are in some way managed, run or have significant influence on the individual Defendants herein,” that complaint says of the organization.
In that suit, she alleges retaliation, content and viewpoint discrimination, malicious prosecution, defamation, and tortious interference.
In May, the state settled with a state-employed biologist fired after posting about Charlie Kirk after his killing. The state owes half-a-million dollars to the now-former state employee.

name: VTDigger
title: Fund recovery, not active addiction
description:
Building a system with treatment on demand, not a safe injection site, is the real path to compassion.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Fund recovery, not active addiction.
text:
Dear Editor,
As a former three-term progressive Burlington city councilor who spent the last 12 years of my career working in the recovery field — as the executive director of both the Turning Point Center and Recovery Partners of Vermont — I feel compelled to write about the state of our city. 
I’m opposed to opening a safe injection site in Burlington. Our city is in trouble, and our viability as a destination for vacations and regional leisure activities like dining and shopping is in jeopardy. 
Instead of investing millions of dollars in supporting active addiction, I suggest we invest that money in building a treatment and recovery system that provides treatment on demand. If someone is ready to go to a treatment program, that request should be met with an open door for treatment at the point of request. Today, people must wait up to two weeks before a treatment bed is available. That is a huge barrier for someone who is ready to go and a delay that could — and has — cost many people their lives. 
We lost a 41-bed treatment program, Maple Leaf, about 10 years ago. The state has never made up that loss. It was not only a loss to the state but a huge Chittenden County resource lost. 
I drive by City Hall Park every day on my way to the YMCA. It is absolutely shameful that we have let things get this bad. The park that was redesigned for families is frightening and out of control. When I recently ran a booth as part of celebrating the nation’s 250th birthday, I was presented with a woman who pulled her pants down and urinated right in front of me on the grass. 

READ MORE

Battery Park is going in the same direction. Recently, I was giving a Burlington history tour, and we were confronted with a mob on the walkway at the front of the park. There was fighting, drinking and loud music. I could not get close enough to show my customers a special view of the beautiful lake and mountains. I was embarrassed. We stopped and turned away.
Adding a safe injection site where people can continue their active addiction will only bring us further down in a spiral that breaks my heart. Some say that if we have any compassion, we will open this injection center. I say building a more comprehensive treatment and recovery system is our way of showing compassion and putting the emphasis on recovery, not active addiction. 
People in recovery will tell you that they want to be held accountable for their actions. For some reason here in Burlington, we have decided accountability is not all that important. It seems to me it’s the bedrock of a civil society. We do no favor to people by bending and breaking the law. I hope that, as the guardians of this city, Burlington City Council will steer us to a better future. I’m certainly available for any discussions on this matter.
Gary De Carolis,Burlington, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Fund recovery, not active addiction.

title: Diesel prices shoot upward as top farm-state GOP senator begs Trump for export embargo
text: WASHINGTON — Diesel prices hit a record average of $6.51 a gallon Monday, and some in President Donald Trump’s own party are breaking their support for the ongoing war in Iran that has driven fuel prices to staggering levels in the United States and across the globe.Already House Republicans locked in tight races as the November midterms approach have distanced themselves from the president’s conflict and his administration’s stagnant negotiations with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passage for global petroleum products. Another major vote on Iran support is expected later this week in the U.S. Senate.The cost of diesel, which fuels the movement of goods through the United States, is up nearly $1 since last month, and up from just over $3.69 a year ago, according to AAA. The national average cost for a gallon of gasoline landed at just over $4.47 Monday, up more than a dollar from last year’s average at $3.18, according to the motor club’s daily monitor.Trump has an opportunity this week to potentially meet with Iranian officials, as leaders head to the United Nations General Assembly in New York City. Trump told Fox News on Sunday he is “open” to meeting with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian.Trump said he is in “deciding mode” about next steps in Iran, and that “big things” will happen in the “not so distant future,” he told the network’s Trey Yingst. Grassley wants diesel embargoLongtime Iowa Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley urged Trump throughout the weekend to embargo diesel fuel exports as costs impact farmers in his largely agricultural state. “W(ith) diesel $6.57 in Iowa why doesn’t Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on (agricultural) products bc food prices were inflated. High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME,” Grassley wrote Saturday on X, followed by two more posts on Sunday urging the president to put “AMERICA FIRST.”The administration does not have plans at this time to ban or restrict diesel exports, according to a White House official Monday. Seven House Republicans broke ranks last week and voted in support of stopping Trump’s war with Iran unless Congress approved further action. The Republicans included two vulnerable Iowa representatives, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, who are facing tough reelection bids in the fast-approaching midterm elections.Democratic senators are expected to move on a War Powers Resolution vote this week. Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Wednesday he will force the vote to continue applying pressure on Trump to stop the military campaign that has not been authorized by Congress.“We’re gonna force a vote to end this illegal war every week until we succeed,” Kaine said in a video posted to X. Two Republicans who will not serve in Congress next year, largely due to Trump’s public opposition to them, have also spoken out against the Pentagon leadership.House Republican Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who has consistently supported War Powers Resolutions on Iran, unexpectedly introduced articles of impeachment last week against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, citing his leadership during the Iran conflict. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina told reporters on Capitol Hill Thursday that Hegseth “needs to go.” Tillis has voted no on multiple War Powers Resolutions aimed at ending hostilities in Iran.Energy commodities up 16.3%Inflation continued a steady march upwards in August, with fuel leading the way, according to the government’s latest consumer price index. The cost of all types of gasoline and fuel oil rose 3.9% from July to August. All energy commodities and services, like electricity, shot up 16.3% over the past 12 months, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.Trump and his administration officials have downplayed the squeeze on Americans at the pump, and Trump has promised fuel prices will drop “quickly” once the conflict ends.On Monday he shifted the blame for skyrocketing diesel prices on to Russia’s war in Ukraine.“Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine. A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission. This ridiculous and never ending War with Ukraine must be ended,” he wrote on his platform Truth Social.Vice President JD Vance told reporters Monday that the administration “is doing everything we can” to reduce energy prices, and suggested that states should suspend gas taxes.“We're very cognizant of the fact that because the Iranians are terrorizing international shipping, energy prices are elevated,” he said.Meanwhile the conflict has expanded in the Middle East as Iran -backed Houthi rebels in Yemen fight for control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a key route for Saudi Arabian oil exports. The State Department issued a safety alert Saturday to U.S. citizens in the Middle East, warning “the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation.”“Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” according to the warning, which instructs American travelers to make sure cell phones are charged at all times and to “keep a low profile.”

text:
Emily Donovan, Clean Cape FearOne of the most important and worrisome threats to our natural environment and human health to emerge in recent decades is a group of chemicals commonly referred to as PFAS. Also known as “forever chemicals,” PFAS are especially pernicious because they’re toxic, cause all kinds of health problems, and don’t break down in the environment. For the last several decades, corporate polluters spewed vast quantities of PFAS into the air and water in southeastern North Carolina, thus contaminating public water systems and thousands of private wells.
Thankfully, one especially important and effective group that’s emerged in response to this problem is the nonprofit Clean Cape Fear, and recently Newsline caught up with the group’s co-founder Emily Donovan as she returned from testifying before the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva, Switzerland.
Click here to listen to the full interview with Clean Cape Fear co-founder Emily Donovan.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico general election 2026: Public Education Commission
description: Two races are on the ballot come November for seats on New Mexico's commission that oversees and approves charter schools. The District 2 race sees the incumbent Democrat face a Forward Party candidate and a Democrat and Republican face off for an open seat in District 7.
text:
Two seats on the New Mexico Public Education Commission, which oversees charter schools, have contested races in the Nov. 3 general election. (Photo by kali9/Getty Images)The New Mexico Public Education Commission approves public charter schools applications, and reviews and supports the over 100 charter schools currently in the state. The commission is administratively attached to the New Mexico Public Education Department, which supplies the commission with staff. Ten partisan commissioners serve four-year terms with no term limits representing 10 districts across the state.
Charter schools are public schools that are governed by an independent governing board instead of being administered by a school district like traditional public schools. 
In the Nov. 3 general election, the Democratic incumbent faces a challenge from a Forward Party challenger to represent the Albuquerque-area district.
Two candidates, a Republican and a Democrat will vie for the open seat in southern New Mexico’s District 7, and hope to replace Patricia Gipson, who did not run for re-election.
Source NM posed several questions to the candidates about their races. Their answers have been edited for clarity and concision.
District 3
District 3 covers western parts of Albuquerque in Bernalillo County. There are currently 14 public charter schools in the district, according to the PEC.
Dennis Dinge
Dennis Dinge, Forward Party candidate for the Public Education Commission. (Courtesy of Dennis Dinge)
Forward Party candidate Dennis Dinge is a physicist, researcher and educator who previously worked at Sandia National Laboratories and is state treasurer of the Forward Party, which was certified in May as a minor party in New Mexico. He previously ran for New Mexico’s first congressional district in the 2018 Democratic primary, but dropped out of the crowded race in 2017.
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
The PEC felt like a natural fit for my background in research and makes me a better candidate. I worked at the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, which was the largest database in the world that mapped galaxies. I want to bring that same data-centered approach to New Mexico’s public charter system.
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
Barriers like lack of charter school options and transportation. Public charter schools need to be available to all students in the state. There are rural areas of the state that could use them, and parents may lack the transportation to get their kids there. 
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
Public charter schools provide educational experiences that usually may not be offered in the state, such as ones that focus on trades or art. They have some wiggle room to experiment with different teaching methods, and if those methods are successful, lawmakers can consider adopting on a statewide level.
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
To cut funding for public schools is never a step in the right direction. Federal funding should not prioritize one type of public school over a different one — money is best spent helping all schools. It’ll be rare to find me in agreement with the Trump administration.
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order?
Prospective charter schools have to include how they will help affected Yazzie-Martinez students in their initial application. If they don’t, then an objection will be raised. The same goes for renewal applications, though it will be easier since the commission can look at the track record to see if the school has been successful in satisfying the court’s order.
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
I would like to see the Legislature promote charter schools in rural parts of the state and ensure that underserved populations are cared for. Virtual charter schools may be a way to address that. I want to also make sure that charter schools are not allowed to discourage unions in any way.
Jacob Trujillo
Public Education Commission District 3 incumbent Jacob Trujillo. (Courtesy of Jacob Trujillo)
Jacob Trujillo is the Democratic incumbent of District 3, appointed by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on June 17 after former commissioner Alan Brauer resigned due to moving from the state.
Trujillo cites his status as a charter school graduate — he attended  Albuquerque Institute for Mathematics and Science — as a point of pride. He has served as the chair of the Democratic Party of Bernalillo County since 2025 and as a field representative for U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.). 
Trujillo was appointed to the position by Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on June 17 after previous commissioner Alan Brauer resigned.
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
I feel a need to fill a gap of representation because the PEC consists of people who never went through the educational system they govern.
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
We need to better educate the public that public charter schools are not private schools. The charter schools under PEC are also public schools and do not hand-pick like private schools do.
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
Charter schools allow us to test out different education styles to see what is working and then implement at other schools. This improves the public education system as a whole.
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
I do not think that is a good direction. Republicans want to privatize education, and the way they start getting there is by promoting charters while cutting public schools. That is why charter schools need to be very well regulated.
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order? 
One of the things I took my oath on was a copy of the Yazzie/Martinez case. If applicant schools are not supporting the Yazzi-Martinez student population, I will vote against their application. They have no reason to be a school in New Mexico.
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
Funding in order to hire and pay staff for the PEC. Currently, the PEC doesn’t have its own staff. A dedicated staff would make the PEC have better technical assistance for schools, families and students.
District 7
District 7 primarily covers Doña Ana County and a portion of Otero County in southern New Mexico, including Las Cruces. There are eight charter schools in the district, per the commission. The current District 7 commissioner is Patricia Gipson, a Democrat, who also serves as chair, but is not running for reelection.
John Foreman
Republican PEC District 7 candidate John Foreman. (Courtesy of John Foreman)
Republican candidate John Foreman is a lifelong educator who taught high school history, social studies and economics in New Mexico public and private schools. He previously ran as a Republican for New Mexico House District 52 in 2022 and lost to state Rep. Doreen Gallegos (D-Las Cruces).
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
I have always been a fan of school choice and charter schools are the only version of that for parents in New Mexico. My background in the education system is extensive — teacher, coach, administrator — which makes me qualified to sit on the commission.
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
The challenge going forward is to keep charter schools autonomous so they can do their mission and not feel pressure from teachers unions or funding mechanisms.
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
They give parents a choice and fill a role that maybe wasn’t there before. Students interested in a specific trade or career can have the opportunity to learn the skills required through charter schools which can keep them engaged in order to graduate.
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
Some of the federal moves were in the spirit of competition and competition is good. We need to look on a case-by-case basis, regardless if a school is charter and public, and see who is succeeding and progressing and shift funds accordingly.
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order? 
I previously was a principal in the Navajo Reservation and I know that students in the Yazzie/Martinez population can accomplish great things with the right classroom leadership that starts with the teacher. 
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
I support legislation that supports the autonomy of charter schools and that promotes increased vocational training.
Fred Parker
Democratic PEC District 7 candidate Fred Parker. (Courtesy of Fred Parker)
Democratic candidate Fred Parker spent close to 30 years as a New Mexico public educator  prior to retiring. He started his career cleaning computers for an elementary school before becoming a teacher and later an administrator. This is his first time running for an elected position.
Why do you want to serve on the PEC and what makes you the best choice?
As a prior district level leader that oversaw a local charter school, I understand the intricacies and knowledge needed for the position. 
What is the biggest challenge charter schools face in New Mexico?
Declining enrollment rates, which we see across the country. We need to reengage families and students in a way that is responsive to their needs and get enrollment back on track.
What role do charter schools play in the larger educational landscape in New Mexico?
Since charter schools are smaller, they are more agile to respond to student needs and pivot if needed. They hit the niche needs for families that want something different. 
Do you think the Trump administration’s massive investment in charter schools while also cutting federal funds meant for public schools is a step in the right direction for national education policy? 
Federal funds being allocated for charter schools is, in some cases, a good thing since they do not have access to certain types of funding that our traditional public districts have. 
As the Yazzie/Martinez education equity case continues, how will you hold charter schools accountable for enrolling and serving the student populations affected in the case and satisfying the court’s order? 
Equity has to show up in actual opportunities and outcomes than just what comes from written plans in applications. The commission needs to track the outcomes during each charter school review on how well they’re serving Yazzie/Martinez student populations.
What type of charter-school legislation would you back/hope to see in the coming session?
I’d like to see some funding increases to support charter schools for lease reimbursement that is matched to inflation and a clearer mechanism for charter schools to acquire and build facilities.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Gulfport program helps nursing home residents stay connected
authors: Michelle Pinto, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center, Justin Glowacki, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center and McKenna Klamm, Roy Howard Community Journalism Center
description: Vanessa Welch uses larger equipment to make video calls because some patients have vision, hearing or accessibility impairments. Welch also uses large equipment to show more than one resident at a time how to operate phones.
text:
GULFPORT — Juanita Wallace has lived at Gulfport Care Center for six years. With several family members out of state, her phone helps her stay connected — but using it has not always been easy. 
“I really appreciate (Gulf Coast Connection Services) because I really needed (help), because I sure did not know how to operate my phone,” Wallace said. 
Wallace is one of the residents receiving help from Gulf Coast Connection Services. Founder Vanessa Welch helps residents make video calls, adjust accessibility settings and troubleshoot phones, tablets and computers. 
Her company aims to help nursing home and assisted living residents overcome technology barriers that can leave devices unused and make it harder to communicate with relatives who cannot regularly visit. 
Mississippi’s Digital Skills and Accessibility Plan identifies people 60 and older as one of several populations facing barriers to digital access. Among the challenges for older Mississippians, the plan identifies limited digital skills and cybersecurity knowledge and calls for expanded digital literacy training and technical support.
One-on-one assistance 
Vanessa Welch, founder of Gulf Coast Connection Services, goes to Gulfport Care Center twice a week to teach residents how to use technology or assist with technology questions. Credit: Michelle Pinto/RHCJC
Welch meets with residents at Gulfport Care Center on Tuesdays and Fridays, working with groups and going room to room to reach those who cannot leave their beds. 
Lisa Perdue, the center’s activity director, said the program provides one-on-one technology assistance that staff may not have time to offer. 
“One-on-one, for that amount of time, it is pretty impossible for a CNA to take two hours, an hour with a resident to help them with things like that,” Perdue said. “That’s where Vanessa comes in.” 
Welch developed the idea after volunteering at another local nursing home, where she saw residents struggling with isolation from their families. 
She started Gulf Coast Connection Services in June and began reaching out to assisted living facilities. Gulfport Care Center joined the pilot in July. 
Perdue, who has worked in nursing home activities for 26 years, said her experience during COVID-19 visitor restrictions drew her to Welch’s plan. 
“We gave iPads any way we could during COVID, to keep them connected with their families,” Perdue said. “That’s why I was so on board with (Welch), because I saw what the video calls did during COVID, what they did for families.” 
A 2023 systematic review published in JMIR Aging found video calls and other communication technologies were used in long-term care facilities during the pandemic to help residents maintain social connections and address isolation and loneliness. 
Although pandemic-era visitor restrictions have ended, Perdue said residents with limited mobility can still experience isolation. 
“Imagine that you cannot move. You can’t do anything for yourself,” Perdue said. “The only touch you get that day is from a CNA who is positioning you in a different way. You know, no hugs, no physical interaction with anyone besides care.” 
Staying in communication 
Welch arranges video calls through Google Meet. When a resident requests a call, she contacts the family member, explains the service and schedules a time. 
She also helps residents enlarge text, turn on closed captions and access games, digital books and audiobooks. She creates reference sheets for residents to use after lessons and teaches them to identify possible scams.
Linda LaHood, who lives at the center with her husband, Gerald, said she had learned previous phones on her own but struggled with her newest one. 
“She’s helped us learn this phone like we had never been able to learn before,” LaHood said. “It’s complicated for older people because we don’t know how it all works.” 
Welch said closed captions transformed one resident’s video calls with his sister. Because he has hearing loss, his sister normally used a whiteboard during FaceTime calls. 
“I was able to turn on the closed captioning so he could read it as she was saying it, and they were able to just have a conversation,” Welch said. 
For Lashona Lewis, the calls help close the distance between Texas and Gulfport, where her mother lives at the center. 
“You get a free visit. You didn’t have to travel to do it. You don’t have to take off from work,” Lewis said. “It’s not to replace your in-person connection, but in the event that the person has a family dynamic where there’s not a lot of in-person visitors, this video visit is really important.” 
Beyond the pilot 
Gulfport Care Center is part of the Gulf Coast Connection Services pilot program. The care center connected with Welch’s Gulf Coast Connection Services after Welch sent surveys to multiple nursing homes on the Gulf Coast.  Credit: Michelle Pinto/RHCJC
Welch volunteers her time, and the facility, residents and families do not pay for the service. Donations help provide chargers, phone cases and educational materials. 
Outside of her work at Gulfport Care Center, Gulf Coast Connection Services offers paid assistance to people living at home or in privately-owned assisted living facilities. 
Welch initially planned to serve several nursing homes for two hours at a time. But her experience at Gulfport Care Center showed her that there was not enough time to answer questions and provide individual assistance. 
For now, she is focusing on Gulfport Care Center while determining how to make the program sustainable. She hopes to expand to other nursing homes along the Mississippi Gulf Coast and eventually make the service her full-time work. 
For Wallace, learning to use her phone is about maintaining relationships with people who cannot always be in the same room. 
“Communication is the most important thing with family,” Wallace said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Federal appeals court rules Lafayette County permit policy violates First Amendment
description: Lafayette County Courthouse in Oxford as seen from the west side of the square.
text:
A federal appeals court panel last week ruled that Lafayette County’s policy prohibiting an Oxford filmmaker and professor from using the exterior of its picturesque county courthouse at night was unconstitutional. 
The opinion, written by Judge Andrew Oldham and joined by Judges Jaques Wiener and Kurt Engelhardt, said the county’s stated reason of protecting public safety was not enough to justify instituting a blanket nighttime curfew and violates the First Amendment.  
“The County has not shown the curfew provision is narrowly tailored,” Oldham wrote. “Even though trial evidence showed that nighttime activity on the town square varies, the nighttime ban applies from sundown to sunup.” 
The litigation began in 2020 when John Rash, a University of Mississippi film professor, applied for a permit to project art onto the exterior of the county’s courthouse. The county denied the application because it had a nighttime curfew and only allowed access during the day. 
John Rash
U.S. District Judge Debra Brown ruled in Rash’s favor and prevented the county from enforcing the curfew. But she said Rash did not have legal standing to challenge the other portions of the county’s permit policy.
Both Rash and the county appealed to the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which ultimately sided with the plaintiff in the ruling released Thursday. The three-judge appellate panel went further and ruled that Rash did have standing to challenge all portions of the permit policy and sent it back to the district court for further proceedings. 
The American Civil Liberties Union of Mississippi and private law firm Simpson Thacher represented Rash in the litigation. 
Joshua Tom, the ACLU of Mississippi’s legal director, said in a statement that Americans have the right to assemble, protest and debate the issues of the day in a public forum like that county courthouse. 
“Lafayette County tried to stifle that right,” Tom said. “With this ruling, the Fifth Circuit has reaffirmed it.” 
Attorneys for the defendants did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The county could ask the full slate of judges on the 5th Circuit to reconsider the case. It’s unknown when the trial court will schedule future legal proceedings.
Correction 9/21/26: The federal appeals panel ruling in this case was Sept. 17. An earlier version of this article had the incorrect day of the ruling.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Republican House candidate under fire for comments about Black women, Muslims
description: Republican candidate Chris Clagett, who is running in Berkeley County for a seat in the West Virginia House of Delegates, posted several racist posts on social media that targeted Black women and Muslims.
text:
Chris Clagett is the Republican candidate for House of Delegates District 91, which represents southern Berkeley County. (Photo courtesy of Chris Clagett’s campaign website)Republican candidate Chris Clagett, who is running in Berkeley County for a seat in the West Virginia House of Delegates, posted several racist posts on social media that targeted Black women and Muslims. 
Clagett is on the ballot in the 91st District in the upcoming November election. The district has seen a string of controversies involving its Republican House candidates, including a candidate arrested after making terrorist threats against sitting lawmakers. 
A lengthy list of Clagett’s social media activity is now under scrutiny. 
A screenshot of Chris Clagett’s social media post.
In January, Clagett posted on X, “Maybe because black women are the most ill-mannered, ill-behaved, loud-mouthed demographics on the face of the Earth. Does that clarify it for you … ?”  He responded to a post that said, “They always think saying I’m not doing anything means they’re not resisting arrest.”
That same month, Clagett posted on X “their children are roaming the streets,” in response to someone saying, “No black woman would willinging bring their babies to an active arrest situation.”
In an X post on Jan. 6, 2026, Clagett responded to a photo of the Confederate flag and called it “a beautiful flag compared to so many drab three horizontal or vertical bar flags.”
West Virginia Watch reached out to Clagett on Monday by phone, email and social media. He answered the phone asking for an interview later in the day, but didn’t return the second phone call.
Clagett fielded questions last week from radio hosts with Eastern Panhandle station WRNR about the social media posts. During that interview, Clagett confirmed that he posted it. 
Clagett told the radio hosts, “context is everything.” He later said the post he responded to with the words “ill-mannered” included Black women “behaving in exactly the manner I described.”
“It does represent me poorly … if I had been more accurate, I should have put liberal Black women and I should have described it that way,” Clagett said. “I was also guilty of not being even handed because the truth is the awful, white female liberals are just as bad. We’re talking about a world view and the behaviors that go with it.”
Clagett added that, “There are many Black women I admire greatly.”
There are other posts made by Clagett that were not discussed in that radio interview.
In a Facebook post in 2023, Clagett said, “I want to announce that I now identify as Trans … racial that is. As a penance for my heretofore underserved status as a privileged white male, I now identify as a Black man. May the police hunt me down.” 
West Virginia Republican Party Chair Josh Holstein declined to comment on Clagett’s comments at this time. 
West Virginia Democratic Party Chair Mike Pushkin. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Mike Pushkin, chair of the state Democratic Party, said Clagett’s social media posts include repeated references to African Americans as “savages,” and to Black women as “sheboons.”
“These statements are abhorrent and should receive universal condemnation,” Pushkin told West Virginia Watch. Pushkin also serves in the House of Delegates.
“That’s why I am calling on House Speaker Roger Hanshaw and West Virginia Republican Party Chairman Josh Holstein to state clearly whether they condemn this language,” Pushkin said. “West Virginians deserve to know where their political leaders stand when hate-filled statements like these are made by someone seeking public office. Silence on matters this serious implies consent, which is why a clear public response is warranted.”
House of Delegates Minority Leader Sean Hornbuckle, D-Cabell. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Ann Ali, communications director for the House, said she hadn’t yet been able to speak with Hanshaw on Monday about the situation. 
“I am unfamiliar with this candidate’s language, and while context is always important, Speaker Hanshaw has never condoned hate speech,” Ali said. 
House Minority Leader Sean Hornbuckle, D-Cabell, condemned Clagett’s comments on his own social media page. Hornbuckle is the first Black man elected to the Minority leader position in West Virginia.
“Personally, I could care less about how many members I have in my Caucus, party or any of that because I’m never going to sit back in silence on disgusting behavior. The seat, the control, all the things that come with just don’t mean that much to me that I’m willing to allow people to be dehumanized,” Hornbuckle wrote Monday on Facebook.
“To my elected peers of all walks of life, this is beyond ‘politics.’ This spits in the face of West Virginia … the state was created by literally separating slavery and the worst behavior we’ve seen in our country,” he continued. “Don’t wait ‘til Nov. 4 to act like you care because you were power hungry and acting selfishly when these things could happen.”
Clagett also made comments online about the country’s Muslim population, responding on an X post with a photo that said, “MAGA care more about their dogs than Muslim immigrants, is that right?” In response, Clagett said, “Depends on your definition of ‘care.’ If ‘care’ means ‘to have affection for,’ then yes, we care more about our dogs.”
Clagett clarified on the Eastern Panhandle radio show that the post “was intended as an insult to conservatives. “I reposted it because I said, yes, this is accurate,” Clagett said.
“They’re not here to assimilate to enjoy the American dream,” he said.
In a separate social media post on Jan. 27, Clagett said he supported banning all Muslims from entering the West.
Clagett’s campaign website describes him as an experienced Navy leader who served as a member of the U.S. Navy Medical Corps. He retired in 2019 after 34 years of service, according to his website. Clagett’s biography says he earned a medical degree.
His political platform focuses on medical freedom from vaccinations, immigration enforcement and curriculum reform in public school.
Clagett ran unopposed in the May primary election, winning 796 votes. David Michaels, the
Democratic challenge in the race, won 435 votes.
(Photo courtesy of David Michaels)
Michaels said he was appalled by Clagett’s comments.
“I’m surprised that you know the West Virginia GOP hasn’t stepped in and said, ‘Hey, this is enough.’ We need better candidates,” Michaels said in a phone interview.
“I feel bad for the minorities that have to hear that sort of language, and it saddens me that it’s still thick. It’s still in the United States, and it’s still in West Virginia,” he said.
Berkeley County district’s controversial candidates
Del. Ian Masters, R-Berkeley, currently holds the House seat for the district. He is not seeking reelection.
Last summer, Masters denied allegations that he was responsible for an antisemitic comment made by a private Instagram account that used his name and is linked to an organization he recently led.
House Majority Leader Pat McGeehan, R-Hancock, supported Masters in the ordeal, saying there was proof that Masters did not post it. McGeehan later said that Masters gave his old phone to a person who was “basically homeless,” living with substance use disorder and very ill and that individual had posted the antisemitic comment.
Gov. Patrick Morrisey had appointed Masters to the House seat after Republican delegate-elect Joseph DeSoto, who won the November 2024 election, was arrested and accused of threatening to harm and kill lawmakers ahead of the 2025 Legislative Session.
There were also concerns about whether de Soto was truthful about his military career or if he was actually a physician.
Joseph de Soto (West Virginia Division of Corrections and Rehabilitation)
House Republicans in January voted to vacate the seat instead of expelling de Soto, saying it was the correct way to deal with the seat since de Soto was on house arrest and never sworn in.
DeSoto had won the 2025 general election as a Republican but he further complicated the arrest fallout since he switched his party affiliation to Democratic shortly before being arrested.
The vacate move prompted a legal challenge from the state Democratic Party, who argued that the seat should have gone to Democrats due to de Soto’s party switch.
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals dismissed a challenge from the Democrats in one of their challenges over the seat. The party’s other appeal is still ongoing and will be heard by the Supreme Court this week.
Michaels had been on the Democratic list to replace de Soto before the seat was secured by the Republican Party.
He said the de Soto ordeal had inspired him to run since he thought the area, which he has called home for more than 40 years, deserved better candidates. Berkeley County is growing quickly, Michaels said, and he’s running on a platform of improving roads and instituting locality pay to keep teachers in the county.
The southern part of Berkeley County is very Republican, he noted.
“(It) looks like there’s very little vetting that’s done on the Republican side and their choice of candidates,” Michaels said. “Unfortunately, we have yet another candidate that is being lifted up by the GOP that says, ‘Hey, this is your choice,’ and that just really saddens me.”

text:
The office of Attorney General Dana Nessel in the G. Mennen Williams Building in Lansing, Mich., on May 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Attorney General Dana Nessel on Monday announced charges against two Michigan residents accused of making terrorist threats against public officials in unrelated incidents, including the mayor of Dearborn, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and members of the Michigan Supreme Court.
Alicia Choucair, 33, of Roseville, Michigan, and Anthony Dekinderen, 61, of Lake Orion, Michigan, were arraigned late last week, Nessel’s office said in a news release.
Choucair is alleged to have called a local police dispatch threatening violence against a mosque and Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud. She was charged with two counts of making a false report and a threat of terrorism, and one count of committing a hate crime. Choucair allegedly threatened the mosque and Hammoud by saying the threat would occur if “your people” weren’t kept out of town, a reference to Arabs and Muslims in the predominantly Arab and Muslim city. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Choucair was arraigned Sept. 17 before a Wayne County 19th District Court judge. She was given a $20,000 cash or surety bond and is scheduled to next appear for a probable cause hearing on Sept. 30. She remained in custody as of Monday afternoon. If convicted, she faces up to 20 years in prison for each count of a false report and threat of terrorism and a two-year sentence for committing a hate crime. 
Dekinderen is alleged to have sent two threatening emails to Michigan Advance, part of the States Newsroom network. The emails allegedly contained threats to kill members of the Michigan Supreme Court, Whitmer and Benson, Nessel’s office said.
Dekinderen was charged with nine counts of sending a false report or a threat of terrorism, the attorney general’s office said, each carrying a 20-year prison sentence. He was arraigned before an Oakland County 52-3 District Court judge in Rochester Hills on Sept. 19 and was granted a $5 million bond with a requirement to wear a GPS tether. 
Oakland County jail records indicate that Dekinderen was still incarcerated as of Monday afternoon. He is scheduled to next appear in court on Sept. 28.
“Thousands of Michigan residents answer the call to serve through elected office, be it as the local mayor or in statewide office. Unfortunately, hate crimes and threats of terrorism against officials at all levels of government are becoming increasingly common,” Nessel said in a statement. “Let these charges serve as a warning that Michigan takes threats of violence very seriously and will prosecute these cases to the fullest extent of the law.”
Denkinderen sent two emails to the Advance on Sept. 14, containing slurs and threats to a reporter and threats to the officials.
A message seeking comment from Dekinderen’s attorney was not returned at the time of publication. This story will be updated once a response is received.
“We take threats of violence seriously,” said Jon King, Michigan Advance editor-in-chief. “The emails our journalist received were alarming, so we turned them over to the Michigan Department of Attorney General’s office immediately. The safety and security of our staff and the public officials named is our top priority.”

name: VTDigger
title: UVM and USDA researchers hope to improve local agriculture
description:
The Food Systems Research Station is a long-term collaboration between the University of Vermont and the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Agricultural Research Service.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM and USDA researchers hope to improve local agriculture.
text:
The research warehouse at the Food Systems Research Station in Charlotte, Sept. 17, 2026. Photo by Tierney Flavin/VTDigger.
Matthew McIntosh’s family says he came out of the womb loving cows. 
Now, McIntosh, who works for the Agricultural Research Service in the U.S. Department of Agriculture, is trying to help Vermont farmers improve the quality and quantity of their cows through the University of Vermont’s new Food Systems Research Station.
At the station, researchers are seeking to innovate solutions to agricultural problems, sharing  what they learn with the rest of New England, Kirk Dombrowski, UVM vice president for research and economic development, said in an interview. 
“It’s one of those new collaborative spaces where we can get students with their hands literally in the dirt,” he said.
UVM opened the research station to a crowd of researchers, staff and stakeholders Thursday. Located on an approximately 400-acre former dairy farm in Charlotte, the research station is housed in an 18,000-square foot warehouse where researchers have begun studying crop behavior, livestock and food system challenges. The station is the first of its kind in New England, according to Food Systems Research Institute Director Polly Ericksen.
Ericksen, who coordinates research opportunities and collaborates with the USDA, said in an interview that the center’s researchers are able to alleviate some of local farmers’ burdens.
This includes dairy farm consolidation, which McIntosh is working to address with his upcoming research studying dairy and beef cow crossbreeding, as well as various other impacts on cow behavior and production performance. 
Limited research started at the station in May, including a study of cow grazing preference inspired by discussions with other scientists, USDA Agricultural Research Service research leader Chris Peters said in an interview.
The research station is the newest step in the collaboration between UVM’s Food Systems Research Institute and the USDA’s Agricultural Research Service. The partnership began in 2019 through a $3 million congressional appropriation.
In 2024, UVM signed a 30-year lease on Nordic Farm to establish the research station.
In the two years since the signing, UVM and USDA teams have been working to prepare the land, determine equipment needs, establish preliminary research needs and begin building a research barn and acquiring livestock, Ericksen said during Thursday’s opening remarks.
She said that she envisions more “field days” like Thursday’s, where community members, researchers and stakeholders can see what work is being done.
Food systems research adds to a long-standing practice of trying to understand how agriculture works from all angles, Peters said, adding that researchers can’t keep their “blinders on.”
“The work that we do is not just studying farm products but whole systems, multiple products at one time,” he said, “kind of getting to the whole picture writ large.”
The hope for McIntosh and other researchers is to help local farmers produce healthy food that can stay in the Northeast.  
“We could have a huge impact on keeping it local,” McIntosh said. “I’m just so delighted to be here.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM and USDA researchers hope to improve local agriculture.

title: Kansas Democrat Don Coover objects to U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt’s approach to unreleased Epstein files
description: TOPEKA — Kansas congressional candidate Don Coover expressed frustration with U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt’s refusal to help trigger a House vote on a bill pressuring the administration of President Donald Trump to release more documents in the Jeffrey Epstein case. Coover, a Democrat seeking to oust Schmidt in the 2nd District of eastern Kansas, urged […]
text:
Republican U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt, seen March 12, 2026, at the Kansas Secretary of State's Office in Topeka, refused to sign onto a procedural move to bypass House leadership and force a vote on legislation to bring transparency to the Epstein files. Democrat Don Coover, who is running against Schmidt, criticized Schmidt's decision. (Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Kansas congressional candidate Don Coover expressed frustration with U.S. Rep. Derek Schmidt’s refusal to help trigger a House vote on a bill pressuring the administration of President Donald Trump to release more documents in the Jeffrey Epstein case.
Coover, a Democrat seeking to oust Schmidt in the 2nd District of eastern Kansas, urged the Republican congressman to join more than 200 Democrats and a handful of Republicans working on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II. The bill was a response to the U.S. Department of Justice’s failure to fully comply with a 2025 law mandating disclosure of Epstein documents. Critics also accused the DOJ of heavily redacting documents to hide names of alleged Epstein associates.
Schmidt, a former Kansas attorney general, told constituents during a recent town hall that he wouldn’t sign the bipartisan “discharge petition” directing GOP House leadership to bypass normal committee procedure and bring the new Epstein bill to a vote of the House.
“Once again, Derek Schmidt decided to stand behind D.C. insiders covering up the Epstein files instead of standing with survivors of sexual abuse,” said Coover campaign spokesperson Lily Johnson. “Like many Kansans, Don Coover is disgusted with what is happening in Washington. He will be a strong voice for Epstein survivors.”
 Epstein was awaiting trial on federal charges of sex trafficking of minors when he died in his jail cell in 2019. During the 2024 presidential election, Trump vowed to voluntarily comply with public demand for release of government documents linked to the case. Trump later broke his campaign promise to make Epstein files public, calling the inquiry a hoax perpetrated by Democrats.
U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, D-Kansas, signed the 2025 discharge petition related to the initial Epstein transparency bill. No Republican member of the state’s congressional delegation joined her. Under political pressure, Trump reversed course to endorse that bill. In the House, the measure passed 427-1. It received unanimous backing from the Senate. Trump signed the legislation in November 2025.
The New York Times reported the president’s name appeared in the government’s Epstein files at least 38,000 times.
On Thursday, House sponsors of a discharge petition attached to the second piece of Epstein disclosure legislation said they secured the minimum 218 signatures to bring about a vote. The follow-up Epstein legislation likely wouldn’t reach the House floor until after the Nov. 3 election.
Schmidt’s congressional office didn’t respond to telephone and email requests for comment about the Epstein files, but he said during the town hall that he objected to the petition process because it was often driven by lawmakers intent on making Congress appear dysfunctional.
“I have not yet signed a discharge petition on any subject since I’ve been in Congress,” said Schmidt, who was elected in 2024. “I prefer to work with the leadership to get items scheduled on the floor. This has the potential to sound glib and I don’t mean it to, but there’s a lot of politics around this place.”
“On lots of issues,” he added, “what happens is folks join up and try to run over the leadership. Not only because they care about an issue, but because they want to render the place nonfunctional. They want to basically hijack the ability of the (House) speaker and the leadership to control the floor schedule and to do that, usually, for political reasons.”
Schmidt committed to voting on merits of legislation regardless of how it got to the House floor.
In terms of the latest Epstein disclosure bill, Schmidt said during the town hall that “I’d probably vote for it.”
Schmidt said his preference would be for the Justice Department and Attorney General Todd Blanche to meet obligations under the 2025 Epstein law. So far, the DOJ says about half of 6 million pages of documents have been released.
Blanche has been accused by Epstein victims of undermining DOJ transparency. U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan threatened Blanche with civil contempt if DOJ failed to meet court deadlines. While Blanche defended the DOJ, the state of New Mexico sued after the agency refused to release information relevant to a probe of alleged sex crimes at Epstein’s ranch.
“I’m not sure we have to have another law,” Schmidt said. “What we have to have is DOJ follow the one we’ve got. Don’t make us pass another law. Just release what you’ve got. I think it would be potentially quicker and maybe fruitful. I’m happy to be part of those efforts.”

It is not known if the bear was the same one involved in the human attack, but a Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks press release stated that the bear was feeding on a cow carcass just three miles from the attack last Monday.
The attack was determined to be a surprise defensive encounter, and the hunter sustained significant, but not life-threatening injuries.
The grizzly was an adult female without cubs, and was determined to have killed three cattle in the area.
Montana FWP, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and U.S. Department of Agriculture Wildlife Services made the joint decision to kill the bear.

name: Delaware
title: Eight proposed changes to Delaware Constitution await new General Assembly
description: Four amendments involve voting rules, while others address marriage, the death penalty and vacancies in the lieutenant governor’s office DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s next General Assembly will inherit eight proposed amendments to the state Constitution, including four that could change voting rights and election procedures. Vil Ramunno, a public policy researche[...]
text:
Four amendments involve voting rules, while others address marriage, the death penalty and vacancies in the lieutenant governor’s office
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s next General Assembly will inherit eight proposed amendments to the state Constitution, including four that could change voting rights and election procedures.
Vil Ramunno, a public policy researcher and Delaware LIVE contributing journalist, outlined the proposals during an appearance on “A Better Discussion,” hosted by former Delaware Attorney General Jane Brady for A Better Delaware.
The amendments already received the required approval from two-thirds of the members elected to each chamber of the 153rd General Assembly. However, none is part of the Constitution yet.
Under Delaware’s amendment process, the same proposed changes must receive two-thirds support in the House and Senate again after a general election. Unlike most states, Delaware does not routinely place individual constitutional amendments before voters for ratification. The governor also has no power to sign or veto them.
That means the lawmakers elected in November will decide whether the eight proposals become part of Delaware’s foundational legal document.
Four voting amendments
Ramunno said four of the pending amendments involve elections or voting rights:

Senate Substitute 1 for Senate Bill 2 would authorize 10 days of early, in-person voting before general, primary and certain special elections.
Senate Substitute 1 for Senate Bill 3 would create a constitutional right to vote by absentee ballot without providing an excuse. Voters generally would still have to request a ballot for each election cycle unless they qualify for permanent absentee status.
House Bill 180 would generally restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies after they are released from incarceration. It would prohibit making restoration contingent upon restitution or another monetary payment and remove obsolete residency and literacy provisions.
House Bill 430 would specify that only natural persons may vote in Delaware elections, preventing corporations and other artificial entities from being granted voting rights.

Ramunno said she did not immediately see significant negative consequences in the four voting measures, but emphasized that was her personal assessment.
Brady disagreed, raising concerns about the details lawmakers could later establish through statute. She particularly questioned the no-excuse absentee proposal and argued that voting rights should not be restored before restitution to crime victims has been addressed.
Their exchange demonstrated why the second round of legislative consideration could produce significant debate, even though each proposal secured the supermajority needed to clear its first constitutional hurdle.
Marriage, death penalty and state offices
The four remaining amendments would address other parts of the Constitution:

Senate Substitute 2 for Senate Bill 100 would establish marriage as a fundamental right that cannot be denied based on gender or another characteristic protected by the Constitution. It also contains language protecting religious freedom.
House Substitute 1 for House Bill 35 would constitutionally prohibit the death penalty. Delaware currently has no enforceable death penalty statute, but the amendment would prevent a future General Assembly from restoring capital punishment without another constitutional change.
Senate Bill 264 would establish a special-election process for filling most vacancies in the lieutenant governor’s office.
House Substitute 1 for House Bill 320 would make a series of technical corrections to the Constitution, including removing duplicated words, correcting punctuation and clarifying several provisions.

Brady cautioned against treating the Constitution like ordinary legislation, saying it should remain a foundational document that is changed carefully and infrequently.
Making legislation easier to follow: CivicDelaware.com
Ramunno’s analysis is informed by nearly a decade in public policy. She previously served as a senior editor at the Caesar Rodney Institute, where she worked to make policy reports accurate, readable and understandable in plain English.
She now covers government and politics for Delaware LIVE and conducts public policy research.
Ramunno also created Civic Delaware, a legislative information platform designed to help residents follow bills moving through Legislative Hall. Its primary tool, Dover Dash, tracks legislation from introduction through committee hearings, floor consideration and final action.
She said she developed the platform after watching complex bills move from introduction to passage in a matter of days during the final weeks of a legislative session.
Dover Dash uses automated updates from the General Assembly’s website and organizes bills according to the people most likely to be affected. Users can select profiles such as homeowner, parent, young professional, retiree, senior or veteran.
Instead of displaying only bill numbers, the platform gives proposals descriptive names, plain-language summaries, their official legislative synopses and current status. Users can also browse bills by subjects such as taxes, energy, alcohol and cannabis, and the state Constitution.
“You want to only know the ones that affect you, and it helps you to be more engaged,” Ramunno said. “And it makes it a little personal, too.”
She said Civic Delaware will archive legislation from the outgoing General Assembly when the new session begins. The eight proposed constitutional amendments will remain active because they must be considered again by the incoming lawmakers.
Ramunno said the goal is to help residents learn about proposals before they become law, ask informed questions and engage directly with their elected representatives.
“You can actually go on this web app yourself and look up what bills passed, what bills got introduced or what bill is in committee that is affecting you,” she said. “The purpose in this is so everyone would be more engaged.”





TO GO: Track legislation with Civic Delaware

What: Civic Delaware’s Dover Dash helps residents follow bills moving through the Delaware General Assembly.
How it works: Select a profile — such as homeowner, parent, young professional, retiree, senior or veteran — to find legislation that may affect you. Users can also browse bills by subject.
What you’ll find: Plain-language summaries, official bill synopses, legislative status updates and information about where each proposal stands in the lawmaking process.
Visit: CivicDelaware.com
Why it matters: Bills can move quickly through Legislative Hall. Civic Delaware allows residents to identify important proposals, follow their progress and ask lawmakers informed questions before final votes are taken.

title: Glacier Park: Rare disease detected in beaver
description: Glacier National Park officials announced last week a beaver discovered on the east side had tested positive for a rare but serious bacterial disease. Tularemia occurs naturally and can affect both wildlife, pets and humans, according to a press release from the park. The beaver was discovered between Upper and Lower St. Mary Lakes. The […]
text:
North American beaver, Castor canadensis. (Courtesy Glacier National Park)Glacier National Park officials announced last week a beaver discovered on the east side had tested positive for a rare but serious bacterial disease.
Tularemia occurs naturally and can affect both wildlife, pets and humans, according to a press release from the park. The beaver was discovered between Upper and Lower St. Mary Lakes.
The disease is most commonly transmitted through bites from infected ticks or flies, and can cause wildlife illness and death, especially in voles, rabbits, beavers and other small rodents.
Humans and pets can contract tularemia through contact with infected animals, contaminated food or water, inhalation, or tick bites. Person-to-person transmission is rare, but exposure can cause serious health risks.
Park officials said visitors can reduce reduce the risk of tularemia infection, by following these precautions:

Apply insect repellent regularly.
Wash hands thoroughly and often.
Keep a safe distance from wildlife.
Drink only water that has been treated or boiled.

In humans, tularemia can cause a wide range of symptoms, including fever and chills, joint pain, muscle aches, headaches, dry cough, chest pain, skin ulcers or sores at the site of a tick bite, and swollen lymph nodes. Anyone who develops these symptoms within two weeks of visiting an affected area should seek medical attention and tell their healthcare provider about possible exposure to tularemia. The disease is treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early.
For additional information on Tularemia visit Tularemia (U.S. National Park Service).

title: Delaware Art Museum exhibit reveals Howard Pyle’s British influences
description: New research connects two of the Wilmington museum’s most important collections and offers fresh insight into the development of American illustration WILMINGTON — A new Delaware Art Museum exhibition is challenging the long-held view that two of the institution’s most important collections tell separate stories. “Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites,” which opened[...]
text:
Photo: “Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites,” which opened Sept. 5, brings together works by Wilmington illustrator Howard Pyle and British Pre-Raphaelite artists whose detailed, romantic style helped influence his approach to visual storytelling.
New research connects two of the Wilmington museum’s most important collections and offers fresh insight into the development of American illustration
WILMINGTON — A new Delaware Art Museum exhibition is challenging the long-held view that two of the institution’s most important collections tell separate stories.
“Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites,” which opened Sept. 5, brings together works by Wilmington illustrator Howard Pyle and British Pre-Raphaelite artists whose detailed, romantic style helped influence his approach to visual storytelling.
The exhibition’s larger significance lies in new research showing that Pyle and Wilmington textile manufacturer and art collector Samuel Bancroft were more closely connected than historians previously understood.
Bancroft assembled what became one of the museum’s signature collections of British Pre-Raphaelite art. Pyle’s work formed the foundation of another.
Although the two men were related by marriage, questions remained about whether Pyle influenced Bancroft’s collecting, whether Bancroft introduced Pyle to the British artists or whether their interests developed independently.
The museum’s research indicates that Pyle was already studying and drawing inspiration from the Pre-Raphaelites before Bancroft began acquiring their work in 1890.
Two collections become one story
The Pre-Raphaelite movement began in England during the 19th century. Its artists rejected some conventional academic approaches to painting in favor of vivid colors, close attention to detail, symbolism and stories drawn from literature, medieval history and Arthurian legend.
Those qualities are also visible in many of Pyle’s best-known illustrations.
The exhibition places Pyle’s medieval and Early Renaissance scenes beside works by Pre-Raphaelite artists and their followers, including Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Edward Burne-Jones and William Morris.
Among the works displayed are Pyle’s illustrations for stories about the Knights of the Round Table and Rossetti’s “Water Willow,” Burne-Jones’ “Cupid’s Hunting Fields” and a Rossetti study depicting Lancelot and the Lady of Shalott.
The side-by-side presentation allows visitors to compare the artists’ compositions, subjects and storytelling techniques instead of simply being told that a connection existed.
A Delaware link to American illustration
The exhibit matters locally because Howard Pyle’s legacy is closely tied to Wilmington and the Brandywine Valley. His illustrations appeared in prominent books and magazines, and his teaching influenced a generation of artists who helped establish American illustration as a distinct art form.
The Delaware Art Museum itself traces its origins to the Wilmington Society of the Fine Arts, founded in 1912 to preserve Pyle’s work following his death.
By demonstrating that Pyle encountered Pre-Raphaelite ideas early in his career, the exhibition adds a new chapter to the story of how American illustration developed. It suggests that the dramatic, story-driven images associated with Pyle and his students had meaningful roots in an earlier British art movement.
The result is more than a comparison of artistic styles. It is an examination of how artistic ideas crossed the Atlantic, took hold in Wilmington and helped shape images seen by American readers across the country.
The exhibition also gives the museum an opportunity to connect two collections central to its identity: its founding collection of Pyle’s work and the Samuel and Mary R. Bancroft collection of British Pre-Raphaelite art.
“Pyle and the Pre-Raphaelites” was curated by Katherine Feldkamp, the museum’s curatorial associate. It will remain on view in Galleries 11 and 12 through Jan. 24, 2027.
Feldkamp will lead a gallery talk from noon to 1 p.m. Friday, Sept. 25, examining how Pyle incorporated Pre-Raphaelite art into his teaching and how his students also found inspiration in the movement. The program is free for museum members and included with general admission for other visitors.
