title: Report: Rep. Bennie Thompson demands national Dems get more involved in Colom Senate race
description: U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson speaks during a voting rights rally at the Jackson Convention Center, Wednesday, May 20, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson, Mississippi’s only Democrat in Washington, is pushing national Democratic groups to spend more money to support Scott Colom’s closely watched Senate campaign against Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, according to Punchbowl News. 
Thompson told the news outlet he blames Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the fundraising arm of Senate Democrats, for failing to seize an opportunity in Mississippi. 
“I think the DSCC is missing a golden opportunity,” Thompson told the news outlet. “A lot of folks keep asking why Sen. Schumer and the DSCC won’t get engaged on behalf of Scott Colom’s campaign.”

Colom told Mississippi Today in a statement that Democrat Party leaders in Washington, D.C., are starting to understand that Mississippi isn’t a lost cause, something that Mississippians “have known all along.” 
“We can win this November if Democrats double down on rebuilding our power in the South by investing in states like Mississippi,” Colom said. 
Mississippi Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks during a voting rights town hall at the historic Farish Street Baptist Church in Jackson on Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Sarah Warnock
Maeve Coyle, a spokesperson for the DSCC, said in a statement that Colom is a strong candidate “who knows how to win tough races, and he’s put Cindy Hyde-Smith on notice in Mississippi.”
The comments from Thompson, Mississippi’s only Black official in Washington, come after the DSCC excluded Mississippi and Colom’s campaign from a $40-million investment in 10 battleground states ahead of the November midterm election. 
However, two sitting U.S. senators have visited Mississippi to campaign with Colom, and Schumer attended a fundraiser for Colom this summer. US. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York who leads the DSCC, also hosted a fundraiser for Colom in New York City earlier this month.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Chatfield embezzlement trial adjourned indefinitely, witness admission headed to Court of Appeals
description: The trial of former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield for alleged financial crimes, which was scheduled to begin Tuesday, has been adjourned indefinitely following a request for a stay from Chatfield’s attorneys over the qualification and admission of an expert witness.   That witness, Michelle Gallagher, is a Certified Public Accountant and an expert in[...]
text:
Former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield speaks with his lawyer, Mary Chartier-Mittendorf, after a stay was granted in his trial for alleged financial crimes over the admission of an expert witness on Sept. 21, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.)The trial of former Michigan House Speaker Lee Chatfield for alleged financial crimes, which was scheduled to begin Tuesday, has been adjourned indefinitely following a request for a stay from Chatfield’s attorneys over the qualification and admission of an expert witness.  
That witness, Michelle Gallagher, is a Certified Public Accountant and an expert in forensic accounting with Adamy Evaluation. A hearing on Monday, which ended in the stay being granted, centered on Gallagher’s admission of evidence, which assistant attorneys general for the state of Michigan were requesting. 
Gallagher’s admission as an expert witness will now go to the Court of Appeals, and the timeline for that decision is unclear. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Ingham County Circuit Court Judge Morgan Cole had initially denied a motion from Chatfield’s attorneys to exclude Gallagher as an expert witness and said that she would be permitted to testify as an expert in the field of certified financial forensic accounting.
In the high-profile case that was expected to be a hallmark of Attorney General Dana Nessel’s final few months in office, Chatfield faces 13 felony charges, including conducting a criminal enterprise and embezzlement from a nonprofit organization, his 501(c)(4) social welfare organization, the Peninsula Fund. 
Chatfield was first charged in 2024 by Nessel along with his wife Stephanie, who has since pleaded guilty to embezzling from a political nonprofit organization formerly controlled by Lee Chatfield — a deal which resulted in her avoiding a trial and prison time.
Chatfield has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges. 
Gallagher testified in a 2025 hearing to determine if the case would go to trial, as an expert witness who had compiled a report for the Michigan Attorney General’s office examining the Chatfields’ financial records.
Gallagher told the court at that time that, from January 2020 to April 2021, 99% of the more than $150,000 spent on the Chatfields’ personal credit cards was reimbursed by the Peninsula Fund.
She re-iterated those statements in Monday’s hearing, which focused on the findings of the report.
“I felt very confident that during this time period, of all the charges that were made, the Peninsula Fund had paid about 99% of the charges during that time period,” Gallagher said.
Gallagher also noted that the payments of those cards were “sporadic” in that they were not paid off consistently each month. Gallagher’s analysis was based on documents that she received from the attorney general’s office, including bank statements and credit card statements.
Mary Chartier-Mittendorf, Chatfield’s attorney argued Monday for the stay of proceedings.
“We cross-examined Ms. Gallagher, and while I respect the court’s decision, I believe that there is an arguable and reasonable legal basis to challenge Ms. Gallagher as an expert in this case, both because of her lack of experience with 501(c) organizations but also the methodology that she used in this case, which is essentially reviewing a policy in isolation and not in context with the people who are actually tasked, paid to enforce the policy and to make decisions about whether expenses are allowed or disallowed,” Chartier-Mittendorf said.
Cole in turn said that the court is required to grant a stay unless a motion is frivolous, and that the motion presented on Monday was not frivolous, given that Chatfield’s attorney “has an absolute duty to represent her client zealously, even if it is on the eve of trial.”
“The court has no other option but to stay this matter and adjourn the trial date until, and we receive a ruling from the Court of Appeals,” Cole said. “As soon as we do, we will get on the bus without scheduling immediately. Just knowing that this will take priority over all cases, it will end up being the oldest case on my docket. So when it does come back, it’s go time.”
The attorney general’s office requested that Cole deny the stay due to concerns about timeliness for the trial, though Chartier-Mittendorf insisted that “this is not a delaying tactic.”
Nessel, who initially charged Chatfield in 2024, will leave office at the end of December, meaning the decision on how to proceed with Chatfield’s case may likely fall to her successor — either Democrat Eli Savit or Republican Doug Lloyd. 
Monday’s hearing reviewed evidence previously heard by the court
Much of Gallagher’s questioning from Chartier-Mittendorf centered around her classification of car washes as personal expenses, who said in her closing statement, “the issue with the car wash, I think, highlights how flawed the analysis is.”
Chartier-Mittendorf argued that a car wash, if Chatfield were using that car to drive potential donors to the Peninsula Fund, could be a legitimate business expense, though Gallagher responded that she disagreed, and believed that two monthly car wash subscriptions would not be an appropriate expense for purposes of furthering the exempt purpose of the organization.
“It’s all contextual. She’s making these determinations essentially in a vacuum, and the government is trying to wrap that up as qualified expert testimony. That methodology is not reliable,” Chartier-Mittendorf said. “The people who can say whether expenses were allowed or not allowed are the officers of the Peninsula Fund, which she said that’s not within the scope of my work to even think about, or the Dykema Law Firm compliance team, which this court will find out at trial was paid to manage the Peninsula Fund.”
However, Gallagher and assistant attorneys general argued that the witness’ role was not to opine on whether or not fraud had occurred.
“Her job is to just calculate expenses,” Assistant Attorney General Dan Gunderson argued. “She already testified that she doesn’t look at criminal intent, and her report indicates that she’s not.”
Cole had also agreed that there were sufficient facts and data to support the factual foundation of Gallagher’s opinion.
“The fact that Ms. Gallagher put the categories in independent three separate categories: allowed, unallowed, and questionable, that analysis and summary of her findings furthers that it is sufficient data, and it’s fair and reliable, because she did not attempt to put anything that was questionable automatically into the unallowed expense,” Cole said in her initial decision to admit Gallagher as a witness. 
Chartier-Mittendorf also challenged the fact that Gallagher had adequate experience working with 501(c)4 organizations like the Peninsula Fund, after Gallagher said that she had advised individual clients in a “handful” of cases on what would qualify as allowed 501(c)4 expenses, which she later said to be less than five cases.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Midterms: Voters weigh in on their top issues ahead of midterms
description: A voter marks his ballot at Fondren Church in Precinct 16 during primary voting, Tuesday, March 10, 2026, in Jackson.
text:
Midterm elections in November will determine control of both chambers of Congress and how much power President Donald Trump will have to enact his agenda for the final two years of his term.
Republicans control the House and the Senate, but they face an electorate that, according to many polls, has soured on Trump and his party by extension.

In Mississippi, a U.S. Senate race tops the ticket, which includes contested general elections for all four of the state’s U.S. House districts. Recent elections indicate that Mississippi continues to be a deep red state, and most pundits and prognosticators have the state’s midterm federal elections firmly in the “noncompetitive” category. 
Most incumbents are poised to sail to reelection in November, but challengers are putting in the shoe leather, traversing the state and bombarding social media. Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, has raised significant amounts of campaign cash and appears to be mounting a strong challenge to incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde Smith. Ty Pinkins, an independent, is also running. 
Ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms, Mississippi Today asked voters what issues were top of mind as they prepared Election Day nears. Here is what they said. 
The cost of living
Former President Joe Biden, a Democrat, saw his approval rating slump as he struggled to tamp down inflation. A promise to lower prices was a central plank of President Trump’s 2024 campaign, and he rode a wave of voter discontent with the economy among other issues back into the White House.  
But as the midterms approach, the cost of living might lead to a blue wave, with voters lamenting the rising price of groceries, gas and other consumer goods. Many voters blame Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran for exacerbating an “affordability crisis.”
Shirley Miller, 68, a retired Mississippi Department of Mental Health employee from Jackson, said she has to buy less at the grocery store and limit her driving to cope with rising prices at the gas pump.  
“I can’t believe a head of lettuce is $5,” Miller said. “It’s impacted me because things I used to buy, I don’t buy anymore, or I use a cheaper version.”
Miller’s car requires premium gas. Before the Trump-led war in Iran, Miller said she remembers paying $3.29 a gallon. The last time she filled up, about a week before she spoke with Mississippi Today, it cost $4.49.
“I have places I go. I go and come back, and I don’t do a lot of travel between that time frame,” Miller said. “I just get in and do what I got to do and come back.”
Miller said she plans to vote for Democrats up and down the ballot in November. 
But other voters believe rising prices are temporary and pale in importance to winning the war with Iran. 
Mary Sellers, 87, a retired hospital switchboard operator who lives between Hattiesburg and Petal, said she believes Trump is on a divine mission to defeat the Iranian regime.  
“I’m not worried about the price of gas or the price of eggs at the store, because God has other things in mind for us to pray to him about,” Sellers said, “and that’s our faithfulness to Israel and our faithfulness to his word, the Bible.”
Sellers said she is voting for Republicans this November because they better represent her values. 
For Camille Wright, 66, a retired appraiser who lives just outside the Jackson Metro area,  electing a Democratic Congress that would repeal Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” or what she calls the “One Big Ugly Bill,” is a top priority. 
Wright believes the legislation will trigger the closure of multiple rural hospitals and nursing homes. She also fears changes to Medicare, Medicaid and SNAP funding could harm the state’s most vulnerable residents while also leading to higher health care costs for everyone. 
Wright believes these issues are particularly salient in Mississippi, long one of the poorest states with some of the worst health outcomes in the country. But she blames Democrats for failing to translate these realities into political victories, a concern that persists heading into this year’s election.  
“I blame part of this on the state Democratic Party because again and again they fail to stand up to the challenge,” Wright said. “I don’t know why that is, but they’re partly to blame because they have so much ammunition to go after the Republicans with.” 
Political corruption and self-dealing 
Several voters believe Trump’s conduct during his second term should bring about more scrutiny of the way elected officials use their positions to enrich themselves. 
Bo Alawine, 62, a Democrat who works for a defense contractor in Gulfport, said Republicans in Mississippi haven’t pointed out Trump’s multi-billion-dollar self-enrichment, even as they point out fraud in Democratic-led states. 
Bo Alawine, 62, a Democrat who works for a defense contractor in Gulfport, said Republicans in Mississippi haven’t pointed out Trump’s multi-billion-dollar self-enrichment Credit: Bo Alawine
“The personal enrichment of Donald Trump has increased his bottom line, his personal wealth, at the expense of others during his time in office, which is unheard of in modern times, at least,” Alawine said. “The fact that I don’t see any Republican member of our congressional delegation uttering a single peep of concern about it, I have a problem with that.”
Alawine said he hopes Democrats reclaim a majority in the U.S. House “to exercise oversight and investigations of the administration and hold members of the administration accountable.” 
Bryan Champlin, 48, an audiovisual systems specialist from Brandon, said corruption exists in both parties, though he believes it currently leans more endemic on the right.
“Politicians appear focused on themselves, donors and wealthier interests,” he said, adding that 
Religion and its influence on politics 
For Sellers, Democrats have done little to stop what she said was a growing threat posed by the influence of Islam in the United States and in Mississippi.
“Islam is an enemy, and they are trying to come in and take over,” Sellers said. “I have great-grandchildren that I’ve invested my life in, and I don’t want them to have any influence of this ungodly … it’s not a religion. A religion doesn’t require people to live like they live. Islam is a cult, not a religion, and so we don’t have to give them freedom of religion.”
Bryan Champlin, 48, an audiovisual systems specialist from Brandon, said corruption exists in both parties, though he believes it currently leans more endemic on the right. Credit: Byran Champlin
By contrast, Wright took aim at Mississippi politicians who she said invoke Christianity while pursuing an agenda that she said is at odds with Christian values.
“Mississippians want to say that they’re so Christian. No, they’re really not when it comes to their politics. They are hypocrites,” Wright said. “Mississippians are religious, but they are not Christian in their actions, because if they were, they would never support such a corrupt administration.”
The U.S. Senate Race 
Miller was sharply critical of Hyde-Smith, saying she hasn’t seen visible contributions to the state from the senator and plans to vote for Colom, who is “looking at the hoots and the hollers of Mississippi, the back roads, the interstates, the state highways, and not looking at what our current president thinks is important.”
Sellers said she didn’t know who Hyde-Smith was running against, but felt ads she’s seen attacking Hyde-Smith’s past remarks about rising meat prices have been misleading. Even still, she said Trump’s endorsement alone won’t sway her vote.
“I haven’t seen anything other than that she’s endorsed by President Trump. But that doesn’t mean that I’m going to vote for somebody because President Trump endorses them.”
Hyde-Smith is still a likely favorite in ruby red Mississippi. Colom has outraised Hyde-Smith for two fundraising quarters this election season, but a recent report showed Hyde-Smith with $2.54 million cash on hand, and Colom with $847,000.
Mississippi’s federal midterm Election Day is Nov. 3. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

description: TOPEKA — Kansas joined a growing list of states nationwide reporting measles cases with two cases apparently related to travel outside the state, a health agency said. The Kansas Department for Health and Environment reported two measles cases on its Infectious Disease Dashboard, which is updated on Wednesdays. These are the first measles cases reported […]
text:
Vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy on Jan. 26, 2015 in Mill Valley, California. (Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)TOPEKA — Kansas joined a growing list of states nationwide reporting measles cases with two cases apparently related to travel outside the state, a health agency said.
The Kansas Department for Health and Environment reported two measles cases on its Infectious Disease Dashboard, which is updated on Wednesdays.
These are the first measles cases reported in Kansas since an outbreak of 91 cases in 2025.
“Both cases are domestic travel-associated, meaning the individuals were exposed to measles while traveling within the United States, outside of Kansas,” KDHE said on its website.
Measles activity is elevated in the United States and globally, KDHE said. As of Thursday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 3,471 confirmed measles cases in the United States, occurring in 46 states and the District of Columbia.
Measles outbreaks, which means more than three measles cases related to each other, account for 95% of the cases being reported, the CDC said.
The percentage of caregivers claiming an exemption from vaccinations for kindergarteners continued to rise in Kansas, according to KDHE data. In the most recent data from the 2025-26 academic school year, the total exemption rate was 4.46%, with .33% attributable to medical exemptions and the remainder to religious exemptions.
In the 2019-20 academic year, total exemptions from vaccinations was 2.12%, with .26% from medical exemptions, KDHE data said.
Seven counties in Kansas report fewer than 75% of students received the measles vaccination, which is part of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccination.
Jewell county in north-central Kansas reported the lowest measles vaccination rate for kindergarteners at 64.56%. In the 2022-23 school year, the county reported 99.12% of kindergarteners were vaccinated against measles.

title: CNN, MS NOW, POLITICO sue Trump over White House ban
text: WASHINGTON — The three news organizations that President Donald Trump has barred from entering the White House filed a lawsuit against the administration on Monday.CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO wrote in a joint statement the suit is intended “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”“Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists’ credentials because it objected to our reporting,” the statement continued. “Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public’s right to independent journalism free from government interference.”Trump announced last week on social media that he intended to bar journalists from those three news organizations, airing a years-running grievance that he doesn’t believe their reporting is accurate.“I am proud to announce that, effective immediately, I am banning Fake News CNN, MSNOW (who recently changed their name from MSNBC due to lack of viewership and credibility!), and Politico (The recipients of an illegal and ridiculous $8 Million Dollar subscription, an All Time Record, directly from the United States Government, under Crooked Joe Biden, in order to keep them “alive.” Seems like corruption to me!), from the White House as a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS!” he wrote. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America. Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow. Thank you for your attention to this matter! President DONALD J. TRUMP”First Amendment citedThe lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, argued the “ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles.” The lawsuit says White House reporters from those news organizations had their press passes, which must be scanned to get through a Secret Service screening, deactivated. The news organizations say the ban violates the due process clause, “retaliates against protected newsgathering and speech in violation of the First Amendment” and that it bars journalists “from a nonpublic forum for unlawful reasons.”The president’s decision to exclude those reporters from the White House “inflicts irreparable harm to these news organizations,” according to the lawsuit.“The organizations, whose very purpose is to report national news, depend on individual reporters to gather information firsthand at the White House,” it states. “As a result of the ban, they have lost the ability to perform essential newsgathering at the seat of the Executive Branch, where critically important newsworthy events occur every day. “The ban irreparably curtails the organizations’ speech—preventing them from being able to publish stories they otherwise would—each day it remains in effect. The ban also impermissibly chills the speech of other news organizations and journalists, who must now balance conducting their constitutionally protected and vitally important work of reporting on the White House against the risk that coverage the President 'dislike[s]' will condemn them to the same fate.” The case was assigned to Judge Timothy J. Kelly, who was nominated by Trump during his first term and confirmed by the Senate in September 2017 following a vote of 94-2.TV network coverage of TrumpTrump wrote on social media on Monday morning that the “White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish.” “It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote. “It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP”Major television networks don’t plan to fill in for CNN as the television pool covering Trump on Monday, according to an email the network obtained from Fox News Washington Bureau Chief Bryan Boughton, who chairs the TV pool.“This follows the White House’s position preventing CNN from fulfilling its assigned pool duties,” Boughton wrote, according to the CNN article. “There will be no replacement pool put in place.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Election 2026: New Mexico attorney general
description: Incumbent New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, a Democrat, faces Republican challenger Samuel Kane, a Las Cruces-based personal injury attorney, in the Nov. 3 general election. Source NM spoke with both candidates about their visions for the office, which has garnered national attention for its lawsuits against Meta and the Trump administration.
text:
Incumbent New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, a Democrat, will face Republican challenger Samuel Kane, a Las Cruces-based personal injury attorney, in the Nov. 3 general election. (Courtesy photos)The New Mexico Department of Justice in recent years has garnered national attention for repeatedly taking the Trump administration and global companies such as Meta to court.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The office has also overseen a number of high-profile local cases, including criminally prosecuting police officers who used fatal force and seeking to claw back an alleged “golden parachute” for a former university president.
Incumbent Democrat Attorney General Raúl Torrez has found himself at odds with other state agencies. He has been highly critical of the troubled Children, Youth and Families Department under Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s leadership, and recently sided with two environmental groups in their legal challenges against state agencies including the New Mexico Environment Department and Office of the State Engineer relating to the Project Jupiter data center.
He and his Republican challenger, Las Cruces-based personal injury attorney Samuel Kane, hold differing stances on the role of the attorney general. While Torrez has often taken on national cases, Kane told Source NM he would discontinue the office’s practice of signing onto multi-state lawsuits against the Trump administration.
The two will face each other in the Nov. 3 general election. The office comes with a $154,714 annual salary. Its prosecutors oversee a range of criminal and civil cases that broadly affect the state. While prosecutors in local district attorneys’ offices typically focus on trying individual crimes, the attorney general’s office is currently involved in litigation against Facebook for its alleged role in the Cambridge-Analytica data breach; the federal government for failing to release documents related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein; and the U.S. Department of Justice for records related to allegations that drug enforcement agents knowingly let fentanyl flow into the state.
Source NM spoke with both candidates about the race, their priorities for the office and how they hope to work alongside a new governor. Their answers have been edited for clarity and concision.
Samuel Kane
Samuel Kane, a Las Cruces-based personal injury attorney, is the Republican nominee for state attorney general in the race against incumbent Democrat Raúl Torrez. (Courtesy of Samuel Kane)
Samuel Kane has lived in Las Cruces for more than 20 years after moving to southern New Mexico from Arizona.
Kane has run his own law practice since 2004, after clerking for Senior U.S. District Court Judge Robert C. Brack, where he largely focuses on personal injury cases and has worked as a contractor for the Law Offices of the Public Defender.
While Kane has never worked as a prosecutor, he told Source NM he’s confident he has the experience needed to lead the New Mexico Department of Justice.
“I’ve spent over two decades working with folks that have been disadvantaged in a lot of different arenas; criminal defendants, injured folks, we did bankruptcies for a while,” he said. “I feel that I can come in and make a difference.”
What will be your top priority, if elected, for the New Mexico Department of Justice next year?
My focus would be exclusively on things that impact New Mexicans. I would say the single top priority would be crime.
We’ve got this revolving door. We’ve got police officers that are out making arrests only to find the person they arrested at the same location committing the same offense, like three days later.
What happens is the district court judges have very large dockets…I would propose bringing in a high level of technology where we can have a clerk upload all the information, sort of like an AI tool, streamline it and give a really quick synopsis for the judges to look at and make an easy determination on (pre-trial detention).
If elected, what bills would you support in the 2027 legislative session?
There is a bill that wants to increase the penalties for juveniles. If it’s a serious and heinous crime, absolutely. In full frankness, I have no experience on the prosecutor’s side. I’ve been a private attorney my entire career…it’s never been a desire of mine to see people put in jail.
I don’t want to come across as soft on crime, but I would put a lot of my energy on preventing it from happening in the first place. If it did happen, obviously we would want to make sure that they’re incarcerated.
But the bill that’s in the making of coming down more heavily on juvenile offenders, I think it’s certainly worth supporting because there are situations where if you kill in cold blood, then you need to be tried as an adult.
New Mexico will also have a new governor in January. How would you work alongside them?
I’ve read my duties and responsibilities vis-à-vis the statute and, really, it’s very limited. You’re working side-by-side with the governor and you’re essentially doing what she instructs you to do.
I’ve tried very carefully to remain neutral to the extent that I can. Obviously, I’m a Republican, but I think that I could work well with either one of them.
The New Mexico Department of Justice has been highly critical of the Children, Youth and Families Department, including publishing a lengthy investigative report and suing the department over allegations its staff left a foster child at the U.S.-Mexico border. What steps will you take if elected to continue oversight of that agency?
We do a lot of adoptions here in our office. I can tell you that a lot of the (CYFD) employees are overworked. They’re understaffed. 
What I think is the current pattern of the current attorney general is you wait until it’s a significant problem and then you research it, you write about it and you file a lawsuit and you have a news conference. But is anything really happening to address the underlying issue?
I would be more involved almost immediately to make sure that some of these things were being addressed, in conjunction with what the governor’s dictates would be.
What makes you a better choice for AG than your opponent?
My approach has always been to do the right thing when no one’s looking.
We don’t need to continuously file lawsuits against our own agencies. I think it could be handled less costly and more efficiently. I’m just going to get in and focus on areas where I don’t want you to hear about me. I just want to come in and make a difference.
The current AG has joined weekly calls with other Democratic AGs across the nation to determine which multi-state lawsuits to join. Is that a practice you’d continue? 
The New Mexico attorney general’s office is not like an unlimited, fully staffed agency. You just can’t do it all.
I wouldn’t be a part of that. I wouldn’t do it on the Republican side of it, either. My focus is: Let’s deal with the issues here in New Mexico.
The NMDOJ has also filed individual lawsuits against the federal government, including over unreleased Epstein files and allegations that the DEA let fentanyl cross into New Mexico. Would you continue to litigate those cases?
Yes, I would, but let’s keep politics out of it.
With regard to the Epstein files, you’ve got that happening right in New Mexico. In a perfect world, let’s take politics completely out of it. We’re not going to go after somebody that’s in a jet or that has any type of unrelated association to the abuse, including Trump…Let’s hold the perpetrators accountable, but let’s not make this a partisan issue.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez
(Courtesy of the Raúl Torrez campaign)
Raúl Torrez first won election as attorney general in 2022, after a stint as Bernalillo County’s district attorney. Before that, he served as a White House fellow under former President Barack Obama and worked as a prosecutor in the U.S. Attorney’s Office.
Torrez, whose father was a longtime federal prosecutor, began his career litigating child abuse cases.
After nearly four years in this role, he draws parallels between his early work and the recent cases that have largely come to define his time leading the New Mexico Department of Justice, such as lawsuits against the state’s troubled child welfare agency and against Meta, which have often focused on themes of abuse, neglect and exploitation.
“When I learned how much social media platforms generally, but Meta in particular, had become a breeding ground for that type of exploitation at scale, it really motivated me to do something about it,” he said.
What will be your top priority, if elected, for the New Mexico Department of Justice next year?
We have a lot of work to do in both modernizing our consumer protection and our laws that regulate big tech.
It is both engaging in impact litigation along both of those lines and protecting consumers and kids online, but also pushing policymakers to really step up and to update and modernize our statutory framework to better protect citizens.
If elected, what bills would you support in the 2027 legislative session?
It’s going to be the biggest modernization of not only our consumer protection law, but I think any state’s consumer protection law in the country, probably in the last 50 years.
New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act was passed in 1967 and hasn’t really been touched significantly. It doesn’t really address a lot of the harms that we see in the modern digital economy — surveillance pricing, data brokering, the way in which technology companies use asymmetric information to target and take advantage of consumers.
We’re also going to push for new authority to investigate civil rights and we’re deeply involved in the process of trying to redesign our child protective services and CYFD, based on the investigation that we did.
New Mexico will also have a new governor in January. How would you work alongside them?
I have a really good relationship with Secretary Haaland. I expect her to be the governor, and I think we’re going to have a very positive and constructive relationship.
I haven’t had a partner on the fourth floor to really lift up the work of the office…I look forward to the opportunity to kind of reset that dynamic and that relationship.
The New Mexico Department of Justice has been highly critical of the Children, Youth and Families Department, including publishing a lengthy investigative report and suing the department over allegations its staff left a foster child at the U.S.-Mexico border. What steps will you take if elected to continue oversight of that agency?
We need to strengthen the Office of the Child Advocate. There were a lot of amendments that were supported by the governor at the last minute that stripped a lot of the essential investigative infrastructure that the office was designed to have.
I also think that passing clear civil rights legislation to give us the power to better protect any violations of a child’s rights while in state custody will be very important. 
What is the most meaningful accomplishment of your first term as AG?
The litigation against Meta and the trial victory.
I think it’s added a lot to not only the ability of other states to secure their settlements, but it’s also put a lot more pressure on members of our Legislature and members of Congress to step up and act.
I’m also extremely proud of the work that we’ve done defending the state against the Trump administration. I think it’s 59 lawsuits — I’ve kind of lost track at this point — but we’ve recovered something to the order of $885 million and counting in proposed federal budget cuts.
Why have you made litigation against Meta a cornerstone of your term?
I got my start as a child abuse prosecutor.
I used to do this work on the front line, one defendant at a time. Now that I’m in this role, I have the ability to not just focus on one defendant at a time. I can go after the technological architecture that facilitates exploitation.
Your opponent has said you’ve been too slow to act when it comes to your involvement in cases that relate to CYFD, fentanyl trafficking and the Project Jupiter data center. How do you respond to that?
We took our time to do a comprehensive investigation and produced an over 200-page report and filed two lawsuits. I think we’ve been very aggressive and very detailed. When you’re going to wade into the dysfunction at the heart of an agency that complex, you have to get your facts right.
I think that’s exactly what we’ve done with respect to Project Jupiter. We have weighed in when the issues were ripe for our intervention. We, in our institutional capacity, have a role to play when the issues that came up with respect to the emergency water application and the air quality permit came up to the state. That was the opportunity for us to engage in those issues.
What we don’t do is circumvent the local governmental process from Santa Fe…I think it’s actually pretty unprecedented to have an attorney general side not with two state agencies, but with the two petitioners who have challenged two separate proceedings.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Ty Masterson se retira de dos debates; Cindy Holscher lo acusa de “esconderse”
description: Republican Ty Masterson is unwilling to meet Democrat Cindy Holscher in a pair of televised gubernatorial debates ahead of the Nov. 3 election.
text:
La senadora estatal Cindy Holscher, nominada del Partido Demócrata para gobernadora, critica la decisión del senador estatal Ty Masterson, candidato republicano a gobernador, de participar en dos debates televisivos. Esta es una imagen de Holscher durante el debate del 12 de septiembre en la Feria Estatal de Kansas, en Hutchinson. (Foto de Jill Hummels para Kansas Reflector)Traducido por Claudia Amaro.
TOPEKA — Los votantes en Kansas no tendrán la oportunidad de asistir a dos debates programados entre el republicano Ty Masterson y la demócrata Cindy Holscher en la competencia por la gubernatura.
Holscher y Masterson participaron en un debate de 90 minutos el 12 de septiembre en la Feria Estatal de Kansas en Hutchinson, que fue el primer enfrentamiento directo entre los dos candidatos de los principales partidos en la campaña de la elección general. Masterson y Holscher fueron invitados a debates televisados, planeados por Gray Media el 24 de septiembre y por Nexstar el 1 de octubre.
Holscher dijo que se comprometió a ambas apariciones en televisión, pero Masterson declinó.
“Ty ha debatido con Cindy Holscher y ha aparecido junto a ella en múltiples foros”, dijo Garrett Henson, portavoz de la campaña de Masterson. “Por el momento, no tenemos planes de aceptar más debates.”
Holscher, senadora estatal por Overland Park, dijo que estaba preparada para seguir el debate de la Feria Estatal, organizado por WIBW Radio, con el evento Gray Media, que se transmitiría por KCTV en Kansas City, KWCH en Wichita y WIBW en Topeka. Dijo que la aparición en Nexstar se transmitiría en seis estaciones de televisión que cubren el 95% del estado, entre ellas Fox4 de WDAF en Kansas City.
“Los habitantes de Kansas merecen escuchar directamente a las personas que piden liderar su estado, y por eso no tengo miedo de debatir en cualquier lugar y en cualquier momento”, dijo Holscher.
Holscher dijo que Masterson, un senador estatal de Andover, estaba “huyendo de los votantes y escondiéndose de los debates porque no puede defender su historial de menospreciar a las familias comunes de Kansas mientras cumple las órdenes de sus donantes corporativos y apoya los desastrosos planes de Sam Brownback. Los habitantes de Kansas merecen un gobernador que siempre aparezca, y Ty Masterson ni siquiera hará eso.”
El senador estatal Ty Masterson, candidato del Partido Republicano a gobernador, dice que no participará en los debates televisados programados para el 24 de septiembre y el 1 de octubre contra la senadora estatal Cindy Holscher, candidata demócrata a gobernadora. Aquí, Masterson habla en el debate para gobernador del 12 de septiembre en la Feria Estatal de Kansas. (Foto de Jill Hummels para Kansas Reflector)
La decisión de no participar en los dos debates televisados siguió a una afirmación del director ejecutivo del Partido Republicano de Kansas, Rob Fillion, de que Masterson ganó el debate de la Feria Estatal.
El sentimiento fue compartido por Henson, portavoz de la campaña de Masterson, quien dijo que Holscher pasó por alto su historial en el Senado de Kansas durante el debate.
“Ty publicó su Carta de Derechos de Propietarios para detener los impuestos prediales descontrolados”, dijo Henson. “Cindy Holscher tuvo una hora en el escenario más grande de Kansas y nunca dijo ni una sola palabra al respecto. Su palabra para alivio del impuesto predial es ‘truco’.”
Henson dijo que Holscher era la “candidata liberal más radical que los demócratas de Kansas han presentado.”
El representante de campaña de Holscher, Riley Osen, dijo que el debate en la Feria Estatal reveló por qué los votantes deberían rechazar a Masterson el 3 de noviembre.
“Cindy está corriendo para reducir los costos cotidianos y hacer la vida más accesible para las familias trabajadoras”, dijo Osen. “Ty Masterson quiere arrastrarnos de vuelta al mismo extremo de las políticas de Brownback por las que Kansas ya pagó el precio una vez. Luchamos demasiado para recuperarnos de ese desastre como para regresar ahora.”
Osen se refería al proyecto de ley de 2012, firmado por el gobernador republicano Sam Brownback, que reducía los impuestos individuales estatales sobre la renta. Brownback prometía un profundo crecimiento empresarial y de empleo como resultado de una “inyección de adrenalina” para la economía, pero el resultado fue una disminución de los ingresos estatales y enormes déficits presupuestales. El desastre presupuestario se agravó al aumentar el impuesto sobre las ventas del estado y al recortar los gastos en educación, transporte y otros programas estatales centrales. Gran parte del experimento del impuesto de Brownback fue derogado mediante una votación bipartidista de la Legislatura de Kansas en 2017.
En el debate de la Feria Estatal, Holscher se comprometió a trabajar para reducir los costos cotidianos de los habitantes de Kansas, a una moratoria en los acuerdos de centros de datos y a mejorar el financiamiento de la educación pública K-12. Criticó a Masterson por un “empleo sin presentarse de $217,000 al año en GoCreate” en el campus de la Universidad Estatal de Wichita.

title: Want to Know What Your School Board Is Discussing? Start Here
description: First State Educate’s August School Board Roundup brings local meetings together to show the issues taking shape across Delaware. DOVER, Del. — Decisions about student progress, district budgets, school buildings, and student support appeared across Delaware school board meetings in August. The details differed by district, but the discussions raised a share[...]
text:
First State Educate’s School Board Roundup, published monthly, brings together discussions from Delaware’s 16 traditional public school districts… and it’s free!
First State Educate’s August School Board Roundup brings local meetings together to show the issues taking shape across Delaware.
DOVER, Del. — Decisions about student progress, district budgets, school buildings, and student support appeared across Delaware school board meetings in August. The details differed by district, but the discussions raised a shared question: How will boards know whether their plans are meeting students’ needs?
First State Educate’s August School Board Roundup brings together discussions from Delaware’s 16 traditional public school districts. It gives residents a way to follow their own board while seeing how issues in one district connect to those facing others.
FSE publishes the School Board Roundup monthly. Readers can find the latest edition in the Knowledge Hub.
The August meetings raised questions about measuring student progress, explaining financial choices, addressing building needs, and reporting back to the public. Some boards made decisions; others reviewed plans that will return for further discussion.
Turning priorities into measurable goals
Some boards adopted measurable academic goals, while others outlined how they plan to review progress during the school year. Their discussions covered reading, mathematics, attendance, and school climate.
Setting a long-term target is one step. Boards also need information during the year to see whether students are progressing toward it. The superintendent and district staff develop and carry out strategies; boards establish the outcomes they expect and monitor progress.
The August discussions show why progress and continuing gaps belong in the same conversation. An improvement in one measure may be encouraging while results in another grade or subject still call for attention. Families and community members need both to understand the full picture.
Asking what spending should accomplish
School boards discussed how targeted funding can respond to student needs. Some considered plans or greater flexibility for resources supporting multilingual learners, students from low-income households, mental health services, and other needs.
Approving a spending plan does not yet show what students gained from it. Future reports can help residents understand which students the spending is meant to help, what result the district expects, and how progress will be measured.
Those questions help boards connect proposed investments to district goals while leaving the development and implementation of strategies to district leaders and staff.
Making district finances easier to understand
Financial discussions varied across districts in August. Some reported enough cash to cover near-term obligations. Others discussed projected deficits, use of reserves, delayed revenue, or the possibility of a future referendum.
A district may have enough money to pay immediate bills while budgeting to spend more over the year than it expects to receive. Several boards asked for clearer reports to help them and the public understand the difference between available cash and longer-term financial pressures.
Clear information matters when a district considers reducing spending or asking residents for additional revenue. People need to understand what is driving the need, how current funds are being used, and what choices the board is weighing.
Following building needs and state funding requests
Facilities were a recurring subject at August meetings. Boards discussed overcrowding, aging buildings, renovations, new construction, and how to finance proposed work.
Several districts are resubmitting projects that have not received state funding. Board members also raised questions about how the state prioritizes requests and how long documented building needs may wait.
Submitting a construction request does not mean a project or referendum has been approved. Knowing where a proposal stands helps residents understand what their district is seeking, what need it would address, and what decisions may come next.
Connecting student supports with learning
Attendance, behavior, mental health, special education, and academic support appeared in discussions across multiple districts.
Some districts described efforts to make services more consistent across schools. Others discussed wellness centers, family outreach, or ways to identify why students are missing class. Together, the discussions show how access to support can affect a student’s ability to participate in learning.
The meetings describe services being developed or put into place; they do not yet establish their effects. As districts continue this work, boards can ask whether services reach the intended students, whether they are delivered consistently, and whether attendance, engagement, or other outcomes improve.
Watching safety and technology policies take shape
School safety remained on board agendas in August. Discussions covered equipment and building procedures, staff training, emergency planning, student discipline, and communication with families.
Districts also addressed personal electronic devices, artificial intelligence, and the role of technology in classrooms. Some adopted policies; others began reviewing proposals or changing how existing rules will be carried out.
Boards discussed device distractions, expectations for AI use, and how technology supports instruction. Safety discussions likewise extended beyond equipment to training, procedures, and communication. Future reports can show how these decisions were implemented and whether they served their intended purposes.
Staffing and student pathways
Districts entered the school year with different staffing needs. Some reported relatively few general vacancies but continued to have difficulty filling specialized positions, including roles in special education and student services. Others discussed how vacancies and compensation decisions affect their budgets.
Boards also heard about opportunities intended to connect students with college and careers, including internships and career and technical education. These discussions raise questions about access: which students can participate, what they learn or earn, and how programs connect to opportunities after graduation.
Making board decisions visible to the public
Several boards discussed how residents can better understand decisions before and after they are made. Topics included clearer financial reports, publication of board priorities and calendars, public access to committee meetings, and opportunities for community input.
A proposed policy, a state funding request, and an approved district plan are different steps. Explaining what has happened—and what remains undecided—helps residents know when and how they can participate.
What is happening in your district?
The statewide themes are shared, but the decisions remain local. One board may be reviewing student goals while another is considering a building request, changing a technology policy, or seeking a clearer financial report.
By bringing the meetings together, the August Roundup helps residents see both their district’s decisions and the questions other Delaware boards are facing. Readers can use that context to follow what happens at the next public meeting.
