name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas GOP’s Marshall and Moran, Democrat Hamilton embrace agriculture legislation
description: Democrat Adam Hamilton and GOP Sens. Jerry Moran and Roger Marshall agree — Democrats on Senate Agriculture Committee should have voted for farm bill.
text:
U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kansas, pleads for Congress to recommit to bipartisanship when debating legislation relative to U.S. farming and ranching. He recently cast a vote for the Senate Agriculture Committee's farm bill, which also received endorsements from Kansas GOP U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall and his November election challenger Democrat Adam Hamilton. (Kansas Reflector screen capture from U.S. Senate video)TOPEKA — U.S. Senate candidates Adam Hamilton and Roger Marshall found consensus amid their combative Kansas campaign by endorsing farm legislation passed by a Senate committee without votes from Democrats.
The respective Democratic and Republican nominees for U.S. Senate criticized Democrats on the Senate Agriculture Committee for opposing the bill outlining revisions to federal law benefitting farmers or ranchers and delivering food aid to low-income Americans. The bill moved to the full Senate. The U.S. House passed its own version in April. The rival pieces of legislation were crafted to supplement a 2025 mega-bill that included agriculture and food policy.
Republican U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran of Kansas also urged lawmakers to find the courage to set party labels aside when considering bills pivotal to people tied to agriculture.
Federal farm bills historically have been revised every five years with bipartisan support, but political disputes inhibited passage of a new comprehensive five-year law since 2023.
“Fighting for people is more important than party,” Hamilton said. “I’m disappointed that committee Democrats voted against this critical bill to help our farmers and ranchers. I would have voted to advance it. When diesel prices are skyrocketing to record levels because of an unnecessary war, our producers need all the support they can get. Democrats must support this bill. Republicans must vote to end this war. And both need to come together to fix the cuts to SNAP, which has already led to food being taken away from 18,000 hungry Kansas children and would create additional costs to our state.”
Marshall, a member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, said Senate Democrats were responsible for delaying action on the bill. The Senate waited for return of U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, the Kentucky Republican who suffered a serious fall in June, to secure a 12-11 margin necessary to get it out of committee.
“For over a month, Senate Democrats blocked this bill, and then every single one of them voted against it — turning their backs on farmers, ranchers and rural families to score political points,” Marshall said. “Kansans don’t have the luxury of playing politics with their livelihoods, and neither should Washington.”
Moran, who also voted for the Senate Agriculture Committee’s bill, said it was important members stayed focused on the farm economy instead of future elections.
He said lawmakers should turn away from “broader political implications that occur in all of our lives about who gets the majority next year after the election” in November.
Moran said the Senate bill would permit year-round sale of E15 gasoline, which is produced with corn. It would adjust the conservation reserve program for benefit of livestock grazing, increase Farm Service Agency loan limits and double U.S. Department of Agriculture trade promotion programs.
It would permanently transfer the Food for Peace program to USDA. The program had been targeted for elimination in 2025 by President Donald Trump.
Meanwhile, Marshall said the legislation would defend in international trade negotiations the opportunity of U.S. producers to use generic terms such as “parmesan” and “black forest ham” in marketing. The Senate bill could boost local meat processing capacity by shrinking regulations. It would broaden USDA requirements to deter importation of diseased dogs and promote dairy purchases by people receiving SNAP, or food stamp, benefits.
Marshall said during a news conference that some people didn’t understand why the five-year federal farm bill was important to the nation.
“That five years of certainty is going to allow that Kansas farmer to plant a wheat crop this fall, despite maybe having had bad drought and lost their corn crop for the most part,” Marshall said. “When we have a constant supply of agriculture products, this lowers the cost of groceries for Americans. Americans pay one-third to one-half of what other developed nations pay when it comes to groceries.”
He said the lingering question was whether Democrats would fall in line with Republicans in the Senate to pass the bill.
“Will we get the Democrats to vote for this before we leave here in a couple weeks? Or, are they going to play politics and continue to make sure that Republicans don’t get any type of a win?” he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi Supreme Court raises the bar for patients to sue doctors. Here’s what that could mean for medical consent
description: Shani Brown holds her newborn daughter in 2018 after what she says was a traumatic birth. Although she was excited to see her daughter, Brown told Mississippi Today she was crying "not happy tears" here. Photo courtesy of Shani Brown.
text:
In August, the Mississippi Supreme Court dismissed a case of alleged obstetric violence. Experts say that decision set a precedent that could make litigating similar cases harder and more costly.
The case, Brown v. Dr. Barbara Davey-Sullivan and The Woman’s Clinic of Mississippi PLLC, began after the 2018 birth of Shani Brown’s third child. When she first arrived at the hospital, Brown signed paperwork agreeing to potential surgical interventions, according to her hospital consent form. During labor, her doctor announced she intended to perform an episiotomy, a surgical cut sometimes made during childbirth to widen the vaginal opening. Brown, who had a previous episiotomy, revoked consent, according to records. 
“Please don’t cut me,” Brown told her doctor, according to the legal filing.
The doctor performed the procedure anyway. She did not tell Brown why, according to records. 
In 2019, Brown sued her obstetrician-gynecologist for performing the episiotomy. In legal documents, Brown, now 41, said her healthcare provider performed the procedure “with neither consent nor explanation of any medical necessity.”

Seven years after the case began, the state’s highest court dismissed Brown’s case this summer because it said she failed to produce expert testimony. Legal experts say that decision could affect not only pregnant patients – but anyone who elects to withdraw medical consent in a hospital. 
“Brown gave consent prior to delivery and then withdrew consent during labor,” the decision of the Mississippi Supreme Court stated. “In such cases, it is not enough to establish that consent was revoked. The patient also has to show that stopping the unwanted procedure was medically feasible without causing harm … ” 
A spokesperson with Baptist Memorial Hospital in Jackson, where Brown gave birth in 2018, declined to comment on the case. Stephen Kruger, the defense attorney who represented both Dr. Barbara Davey-Sullivan and The Woman’s Clinic, where Davey-Sullivan works, told Mississippi Today that “as the Supreme Court pointed out, the plaintiffs could not produce a medical expert to say that it would have been reasonable to stop” the episiotomy when Brown revoked consent as the baby’s head was crowning.
Kruger told Mississippi Today he credited Dr. Sullivan’s judgment with the delivery of “a completely normal baby.”
“If she had not done the episiotomy and there had been complications, where do you think we would be?” he said.
In the U.S., 1 in 5 women report mistreatment during maternity care, according to a 2023 survey by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. One of the most common types of mistreatment women in the survey reported was “being made to accept unwanted treatment.”
Now, if Mississippians want to sue their physician for not respecting withdrawn medical consent during a procedure, they will need to do so under claims of medical malpractice, not battery, said Mary Ziegler, a professor and reproductive health expert at the University of California, Davis, School of Law.
“And therefore you need expert testimony, which is going to only really be available to people who either have the money … or someone whose injuries are grievous enough that it’s worth it for the attorney to shell out a bunch of money on the front end hiring expert witnesses,” Ziegler said. 
Medical consent cases that won’t be affected by this ruling are the rare ones where no consent was given, explained Ziegler. An example, she said, would be if a patient went to the hospital for a knee surgery and doctors took out an appendix. But the vast majority of cases are murkier than that, Ziegler said.
In Brown’s case, the Mississippi Supreme Court found that Brown withdrew consent during the procedure because the court defined the birth – not the episiotomy – as the procedure. Ziegler said this distinction will be confusing for patients in situations that require several interventions.
“What if you don’t consent to one of those things?” she said. “Which of them is the procedure? Is all of them the procedure? I think there’s ambiguity about how you define that.”
The cases that make it to court
The new requirement of expert testimony could stretch far beyond obstetric patients. But those suffering obstetric violence may fare the worst, Ziegler said, with fewer attorneys willing to take on those cases because they tend to result in lower compensation. 
Attorneys decide which cases are worth their time based on expected payouts, Ziegler said. Those payouts are calculated from medical bills, lost wages and diminished quality of life. In obstetric violence cases, patients aren’t necessarily harmed in a “classic, easy-to-value way,” she said. Those cases are usually about autonomy, Ziegler said, where the injury is “that you didn’t get to decide what happened to you.”
Fewer lawsuits could mean less incentive for doctors to respect patient autonomy, Ziegler said. 
Already, these cases are quite rare because of the costs, time commitment and difficulty of litigation. It’s not surprising Mississippi is only dealing with the issue now, explained Daniel Waide, a Hattiesburg-based attorney who represented Brown from 2022 until the case was dismissed. 
While it’s not clear how many states have litigated cases like Brown’s, Waide said he’s aware of a growing body of legal precedent. He highlighted a few examples, including a 2020 case that established a precedent for withdrawn medical consent in Massachusetts, a 2012 case that did so in Connecticut, a 2008 case in Nebraska and a 2000 case in Kentucky. Those cases weren’t specifically about obstetrics. 
“Every state just addresses it as it comes up,” Waide said.
The standard of care
Brown now lives with her husband and their three children on Alabama’s coast. Since she gave birth in 2018, she said she faces lasting trauma, nerve damage that requires medication and pain during intercourse and while using the bathroom. In 2022, she underwent reconstructive surgery to repair a weakened vaginal wall. 
“You have to have a medical expert identify that damage and then to say that that damage was caused by a wrongful act by Dr. Sullivan,” said Kruger, the defense attorney representing the physician and clinic. He added that Brown did not produce an expert witness. 
Brown’s court case is over, but she hopes by speaking out she can prevent other women from enduring similar anguish.
Shani Brown poses for a portrait with her husband and their three children in 2018.  Credit: Sarah Watson with Watson Photography
“My goal at this point is I desperately want people to know that that can happen,” Brown said. “I desperately want people to read their consent forms.”
If she had known her verbal withdrawal of consent would have been ignored, Brown said she never would have signed the hospital paperwork. She would have gone elsewhere, she said. It’s not clear whether her situation would have turned out differently at another Mississippi hospital. 
Brown said she remembers being in a state of shock and emotional distress after the birth of her third baby in 2018. It distracted her from feeling the physical pain of the episiotomy until hours after the birth. Her delivery room was filled with medical students, which she said she also didn’t consent to, worsening her trauma.
“I remember when (my daughter) was placed in my arms feeling just deep sadness, knowing what my body had just went through and what just happened to me,” Brown said. 
A year after the birth, Brown started a regimen of anxiety and depression medications to cope with her postpartum trauma. In Mississippi, maternal mental health disorders are a leading cause of pregnancy-related deaths, according to the Mississippi State Department of Health. Pregnancy-related deaths are those occurring during or within one year after the end of pregnancy. 
The Mississippi Supreme Court sided with Brown’s doctor. Still, birth justice advocates say violations of consent and obstetric violence happen too often in the U.S. and go unchallenged.
The gravity of violations to consent during childbirth is sometimes lost when filtered through the norms of medical care, said Jacqueline Hammack, a birth justice advocate who represented Brown between 2019 and 2021 before leaving the case for family obligations. While U.S. births primarily take place in hospitals and sometimes involve medical intervention, Hammack said, they are normal physiological events – not inherently medical. 
Most people in the U.S. perceive childbirth as purely medical, but that’s “historical happenstance,” said Hammack, adding that other countries have midwifery-centered models of care where providers treat patients more like partners. In the Netherlands, she said, midwives serve as the backbone of the perinatal care system, with obstetricians attending more complex births as necessary. That system has worked well for the Dutch: Maternal mortality in the Netherlands is more than four times lower than in the U.S. Mississippi has one of the highest rates of maternal mortality in the U.S.
The Mississippi Supreme Court classified Brown’s case as medical negligence. In doing so, Hammack said, it could set up other cases for failure. That’s because expert witnesses would be required to show that the physician in question deviated from the standard of care. The defendant in a case of alleged obstetric violence often hasn’t broken with the standard of care, according to Hammack.
“The sad fact is, obstetric violence occurs with such frequency … And what constitutes the standard of care is what the majority is doing,” Hammack said. 
Good solutions, according to Hammack, would involve hospitals adopting policies requiring ongoing consent for significant interventions, as well as making clear to patients that consent can be withdrawn. 
But meaningful change would go beyond consent policies, Hammack said, ensuring women can access midwives, doulas and other birth advocates. She also said educating lawyers and advocates to recognize violations is important. 
“The larger goal is a system in which clinical expertise and patient autonomy aren’t treated as competing values,” Hammack said. “Providers bring clinical expertise, (but) the person giving birth retains decisional authority over their body.”
Brown hopes that by the time her children are grown, things will be different. 
“I have two daughters and I just feel like something needs to change,” Brown said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Where organized labor hits the ballot
description: Organized labor has been out in force on ballot measures — recently literally trying to secure bargaining power through the ballot — and that means manpower, mobilization, and money funneling toward a set of policy measures that the Legislature has waved away. This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporter Jennifer Smith looks at unions and direct de[...]
text:
EPISODE INFO

HOST: Jennifer Smith
GUESTS: Nick Juravich, associate professor of history and labor studies and associate director of the Labor Resource Center at UMass Boston; Chrissy Lynch, head of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO







LABOR HAS BEEN showing up in ballot question debates for years, but the last decade has seen unions truly out in force behind some of the buzziest initiatives. So when and why does organized labor decide manpower, mobilization, and money should funnel away from Beacon Hill and toward direct democracy? 
This week on The Codcast, CommonWealth Beacon reporter Jennifer Smith looks at the past and present of unions and ballot measures with Nick Juravich, associate professor of history and labor studies and associate director of the Labor Resource Center at UMass Boston; and Chrissy Lynch, head of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO. 
While the last few years have seen millions pour toward pro-unionizing efforts, in the long run “labor is never really going to outspend its opponents, but it can be present on the ground,” Juravich said. 
Initiatives from the political right in the 1970s and early 1980s carved away at union power, Juravich said, and the 1980 ballot measure Proposition 2½ that capped how much municipal property taxes could be raised was “devastating for the public sector.”  
For the Massachusetts Teachers Association — the force behind last cycle’s ballot measure eliminating MCAS as a graduation requirement — Juravich said the shift toward getting aggressively involved in ballot measures began with the 2016 fight over raising the charter school cap.  After $46.6 million spent in support and $15.4 million spent in opposition, voters rejected the question with about 60 percent of the vote.  
Educators took the message to their immediate communities, and a postmortem memo for the pro-charter side found voters trusted teachers, Chalkbeat reported. The union came away with “a ballot muscle,” Juravich said. 
He said unions that lean toward the private sector, like health care workers, can have a tougher time making their case if they represent fields without as much daily contact with voters as educators.  
Lynch said the AFL-CIO weighs each question by how it affects members on and off the job with “a limited amount of resources” to spend. Lately, she said, its ballot work has been “more us reacting to things.” 
That includes Question 3, which would replace party primaries with a single primary open to all candidates, with the top two advancing to the general election. Lynch said her first reaction was, “I don’t think we’re gonna get involved in this.”  
After talks with member unions and a look at other states, the federation came to oppose it, describing the measure as “moving to a system where whoever comes in with the most personal money from the jump are gonna be the two most viable candidates.” 
CommonWealth Beacon, which has a guide on all nine current measures, will be hosting a debate on the all-party primaries question on Tuesday, October 13.  
Rideshare drivers won the right to unionize at the ballot in 2024, and employees of the Committee for Public Counsel Services, the state’s public defender agency, are asking for the same this year with Question 2.  
Lynch called the back-to-back measures “a symptom of the fact that people want a union in their life.”  
The direct-to-voters path, rather than waiting for lawmakers to expand or clarify the law is “not very common,” Juravich said, but he expects that to change. “We are in a moment of flux in labor law in this country,” he said. “That’s national, and that’s local.” 
Juravich on labor’s ballot history begins at 1:30. Lynch on how the AFL-CIO picks its fights begins at 21:00.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Pitched battle for Alaska’s Senate seat is enveloped in a fight over fish
description: Fish are central to Alaska’s economy, Indigenous cultures and identity. With critical salmon runs in Alaska rivers struggling, commercial operators squeezed by higher costs and stiffer market competition, fish are now at the center of the hard-fought campaign for Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat. For Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, who is seeking to unseat incu[...]
text:
Fishing boats line a dock at Kodiak's St. Paul Harbor on Oct. 3, 2022. Fishing issues have become a top campaign issue in the race between U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and his challenger, former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Fish are central to Alaska’s economy, Indigenous cultures and identity.
With critical salmon runs in Alaska rivers struggling, commercial operators squeezed by higher costs and stiffer market competition, fish are now at the center of the hard-fought campaign for Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat.
For Democratic challenger Mary Peltola, who is seeking to unseat incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, the fishing issues are deeply personal.
She is Yup’ik, grew up in rural Western Alaska on the Kuskokwim River and, as she has explained many times, has been fishing since she was 6 years old.
“I’m the only candidate on this stage who’s an Alaskan fisherman. Fish is in my blood, earned over generations on the water,” she said at the Sept. 12 fisheries-focused debate held by the Kodiak Chamber of Commerce.
Sullivan is emphasizing his record after 12 years in the Senate, which he said resulted in 63 bills signed into law so far, many of which concern fisheries, and has secured generous appropriations for agencies that support the industry, like the U.S. Coast Guard.
“Our fishermen deserve relentless focus and action, not just talk,” he said at the Kodiak debate.
According to the information clearinghouse govtrack.us, Sullivan was the prime sponsor on 31 bills that have been signed into law during his tenure. Over his career in the Senate, he has been a cosponsor of more than 1,800 pieces of legislation, according to congress.gov, the  online database for the nation’s legislative branch.
In comparison, Peltola was the prime sponsor of two bills that were enacted during her two years in the House, though her bills were converted into provisions that passed as parts of larger legislation, according to govtrack.us. During her tenure, which started with a special election victory in 2022, she was a cosponsor of 348 pieces of legislation, according to congress.gov.
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, shakes hands with former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, at the Sept. 12, 2026, fisheries debate held by the Kodiak Chamber of Commerce. (Photo by Brian Venua)
Battle over bycatch
At the top of the Peltola-Sullivan fish fight is the hot-button issue of bycatch, or the interception of salmon and other nontarget species in the nets deployed by the huge trawling vessels that harvest pollock and other groundfish species in the Bering Sea and Gulf of Alaska.
Many in Alaska blame the poor conditions of certain salmon runs and declines in halibut and crab stocks, at least in part, on trawler bycatch. The issue has divided fishery sectors and regions.
For Peltola and Sulivan, the fight over trawl bycatch has been particularly bitter, with attacks on each others’ characters.
As Peltola and her supporters describe it, Sullivan is in the pocket of out-of-state industrial fishing corporations that contribute to his campaign but hurt Alaskans.
“CASHING IN. . .WHILE ALASKANS PAY THE PRICE,” says the website of a political action committee backing Peltola. “Dan Sullivan is looking out for his rich donors – and it’s costing us.”
As Sullivan and his supporters describe it, Peltola, is dishonest, unaccomplished and, despite her Yup’ik heritage, has sold out to Lower 48 liberals.
“When you don’t have a record to run on, YOU BUILD YOUR CAMPAIGN ON LIES,” says a special Sullivan campaign website called peltolalies.com. It features images of two prominent New York Democrats, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
The prominence of the fish debate in this year’s Senate race is unusual, said Brett Watson, a University of Alaska Anchorage economist and natural resource expert.
Watson, affiliated with UAA’s Institute of Social and Economic Research, has been working on Alaska natural resource issues for about a decade. “I don’t recall a time over that period where these issues have played such a central role in a statewide or federal campaign,” he said.
He believes that the intensity of the fight over trawlers and bycatch may reflect larger social trends that go beyond fish.
 

A bumper sticker attached to a pole in downtown Seward, seen on June 27, 2026, carries an anti-trawl message. Bottom trawling, which uses nets that sweep across the bottom of ocean, has drawn particular opposition from small-scale Alaska fishermen and environmentalists. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	There is widespread skepticism of large corporations, sentiment that coincides with specific concerns of people like Indigenous subsistence fishers on the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers and some broader concerns about the environment, he said.
“It’s been kind of an emerging theme in populist-type politics maybe over the last 10 years or so that combined with, obviously, issues related to bycatch: subsistence harvest, sport harvest, commercial harvest, etcetera,” he said. “It has increased that issue’s salience to the level that we see it at today. I wonder if that’s maybe the secret sauce here.”
Gunnar Knapp, a retired UAA economist and emeritus ISER professor who is considered the dean of Alaska fishery economics, said he has also been struck by the role the issue is playing in the campaign.
“I think everybody agrees, certainly including these two candidates, that bycatch is undesirable, particularly of halibut and salmon,” Knapp said.
But in the heat of the campaign, “it’s harder to hear what either candidate is specifically saying,” he said.
Peltola, who is reviving her past “Fish, Family, Freedom” campaign slogan, is using some tough rhetoric.
She calls for full ban on factory trawlers, ships that combine harvests with onboard processing at sea, though she has also been careful to distinguish between out-of-state operators, not small Alaska-based operators.
“Our fight is not against small and mid-size boats that keep communities like Kodiak strong. It’s against the out of state corporate greed that leads to wanton waste and damage to our sea floor,” she said at the Kodiak debate this month.
Sullivan has been touting his official actions over the years, most prominently a bill he introduced this year that cleared the Senate Commerce Committee on Wednesday.
In one of his trademark “Hey Alaska” videos, posted Wednesday on social media, Sullivan called his Bycatch Reduction Act “the most comprehensive trawl bycatch reduction bill, really, ever.”
 

Signs seen Feb. 7, 2026, at a room in the William A. Egan Civic and Convention Center used by tribal organizations attending the North Pacific Fishery Management Council meeting. The groups won a victory at the meeting when the council approved its first-ever numerical caps on bycatch of chum salmon in the Bering Sea trawl harvests. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	“This is a really important issue we’ve been working on for a long time in different areas,” Sullivan said in the video, which shows him exiting a hearing room and talking as he walks — similar to his other “Hey Alaska” videos. “This bill I think’s going to have a hugely positive impact for Alaskan communities for our fishermen, for our Native populations.”
The bill is among several actions that Sullivan points to as his work to reduce bycatch.
He also takes credit for the first-ever numerical caps on chum salmon bycatch in the Bering Sea pollock fishery that the North Pacific Fishery Management Council approved in February.  He “went to the council last year to get the Western Alaskan chum bycatch limit implemented,” he said at the Kodiak debate. “That was another area where I was leading.”
Peltola sponsored her own bycatch bill. Two years ago, she introduced the Bycatch Reduction and Mitigation Act of 2024, which Sullivan did not support at the time.
There are areas of overlap between the Sullivan and Peltola bills, notably financial support for bycatch-reducing technology. But Peltola’s bill prioritized smaller operators, with vessels under 65 feet qualifying for the funding. Sullivan’s bill has no such priority.
Peltola’s bill drew opposition from trawling associations, indicating that it was tougher on the industry than Sullivan’s bill, which has drawn no significant industry opposition.
Much of Peltola’s advocacy for bycatch limits focused on her efforts to update the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act, the main law that governs seafood harvests in the nation’s federal waters.
Those efforts predate her election to Congress, and they have been largely from the perspective of subsistence harvesters in Indigenous communities in Western Alaska — like her own family — rather than the commercial industry.
As executive director of the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission, she articulated those concerns at a 2021 subcommittee hearing of the U.S. House Resources Committee.
“We are only trying to feed our own families. We’re down to 20% of what we historically harvested. We do not contribute anything to the gross domestic product or ex-vessel value. We’re just trying to feed our families,” Peltola said at the hearing.
 

Fish-themed posters for Mary Peltola’s Sente campaign are seen on Sept. 16, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaksa Beacon)
 

	Peltola led the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission from 2017 until 2022. The organization focuses on tribal comanagement, research, rural advocacy and fish conservation. At the time Peltola testified in 2021, House members were considering bills sponsored by the late U.S. Rep. Don Young, R-Alaska, and U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman, D-California, to update and reauthorize the Magnuson-Stevens act.
The act passed initially in 1976. It established the 200-nautical mile exclusive economic zone in which foreign-flagged vessels are prohibited from harvesting fish. It has been periodically updated through reauthorization, including with a name change that honors the late U.S. Sen. Ted Stevens, R-Alaska. But the last time that happened was 2006.
When Peltola was in the House, she joined with Huffman to try to pass reauthorization bills. Their legislation had provisions to protect subsistence users.
One such provision would have added tribal seats to both the North Pacific Fishery Management Council and the Pacific Fishery Management council, which has jurisdiction over U.S. West Coast waters. Her approach, as detailed in past bills, would also enshrine protection of subsistence — the traditional harvests for personal consumption — as a duty of the councils. On bycatch, there were provisions in the bill she cosponsored for expanded use of salmon-protection technology and for removal of the phrase “to the extent practicable” in the wording concerning bycatch controls.
Sullivan, however, has warned that an election victory by Peltola would, by helping Democrats take control of the body, elevate the power of senators from Washington state, where the trawling industry is based. He referred obliquely to Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington, the ranking Democrat on the committee that oversees fishery policy.
“My opponent would empower a Seattle, Washington-based senator to be the next chairman of the Commerce Committee. Any opportunity to get bycatch bills passed, including mine, would be automatically undermined if you had the chairman of the Commerce Committee being from Washington State,” he said at the Kodiak debate.
Knapp said the logic of Sullivan’s argument “cuts a little each way.”
If Democrats win a majority in the Senate, “Alaska might want to have a Democrat in there, influencing how that works, rather than somebody who’s shut out from it,” Knapp said.
Regardless of who is in leadership, bycatch is a concern in all coastal states. In areas from New England to Hawaii, bycatch is described as a major problem. Fishery managers, fish harvesters and conservationists are engaged in numerous projects to prevent incidental harvests of different types of fish, birds, mammals and sea turtles.
 

Fish-themed mailers urging support for incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, are seen on Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Even in Washington, where large trawling companies are based, there are conflicts over bycatch occurring in the West Coast groundfish harvests. Bottom trawling, the practice of using nets at the sea floor, is banned in internal Washington state waters and in most of the federal waters off Washington, Oregon and California. In Alaska, where bottom trawling does occur in a small percentage of state waters a bill that would have banned the practice in state waters failed to pass the Alaska Legislature this year.
International issues
Sullivan and Peltola also clash on the international aspects of Alaska’s fisheries.
Sullivan is a Marine veteran who has made national defense a major focus of his 12-year tenure in the Senate.
At the Kodiak debate, he took full credit for keeping Russian fish out of U.S. markets, saying his achievement in office included “single-handedly banning Russian seafood imports.”
Knapp said Sullivan deserves some credit for the import ban on Russian seafood that competes with Alaska seafood.
“There have been several issues that are related to Russia, and that, certainly Sullivan has worked hard to address these,” Knapp said.
But the import ban was a group effort, and it was rolled out in stages.
In 2014, President Barack Obama, along with the European Union, imposed sanctions on Russia because of that country’s annexation of Crimea. In 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine, President Joe Biden issued an executive order banning all imports of Russian seafood into the U.S. In 2023, Bident used a follow-up executive order to close a loophole that had allowed Russian-origin fish to get to U.S. markets through third-party countries, mostly China, where that fish was processed.
The executive order achieved goals spelled out in legislation sponsored by both candidates. Sullivan and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, sponsored a bill in the Senate that would close the China-processing loophole, and Peltola joined with Rep. Garret Graves, R-Louisiana, in sponsoring a House version.
Alaska’s seafood industry has been battered in recent years by several forces that put it into a “tailspin,” as one state legislative leader put it in 2024. Among the contributing factors have been glutted markets for salmon and other fish, low prices, high costs, climate change-related stock declines and other problems, including problems with salmon markets. The industry lost an estimated $1.8 billion from 2022 to 2023, according to a National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration analysis.
Russia played only a small part in that, Knapp said.
“What you might call ‘Gunnar’s Rule No. 1 of Salmon Markets’ is that, any given time, there’s about a dozen different factors affecting the salmon market,” he said. That includes exchange rates, tariffs, farmed fish production, the size of runs in Bristol Bay and other Alaska sites and myriad other factors, he said.
 

Signs for and against Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, are seen in South Anchorage on June 9, 2026. Sullivan’s critics have accused him of failing to push back against actions by President Donald Trump that they consider to be bad for Alaska. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Sullivan has also singled out China as a threat to Alaska because of what he described as unsustainable fishery practices.
At the Kodiak debate, he cited his work on illegal and unreported fisheries occurring in international waters. A bill Sullivan cosponsored with Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-Rhode Island, Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and numerous members from both parties addresses what is known as “illegal, unreported and unregulated” fishing, or IUU.
The Fighting Foreign Illegal Seafood Harvest Act, or FISH Act, passed the Senate in March. It is awaiting final action in the House.
But to Knapp, who listened closely to the Kodak debate, Sullivan’s attacks on China were a bit surprising.
“I was puzzled by what he was referring to,” Knapp said.
Unlike Russia, which is a direct competitor to Alaska, China is a “major market opportunity for all kinds of seafood.”
Watson had similar observations.
China is “not just a place where we send our fish to be reprocessed. That is an opportunity for a new final demand market,” he said. Incomes in China are rising, making Alaska seafood potentially attractive to consumers there, he said.
President Donald Trump’s tariff war with China has disrupted efforts to achieve that, however.
“It’s really when China retaliates against us that causes the most acute pain for the industry,” Watson said.
China in 2023 and 2024 was the largest buyer of raw Alaska fish by volume, but almost all of that was for processing and shipment elsewhere, according to the most recent annual seafood industry report by the McKinley Research Group.
 

Competing signs in the same Midtown Anchorage yard, seen Aug. 7, 2026, support the candidates for U.S. Senate in Alaska: incumbent Dan Sullivan, a Republican, and challenger Mary Peltola, a Democrat. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Tariffs pose big problems for the Alaska seafood industry, the report said. “Alaska seafood’s reliance on global markets leaves the industry acutely vulnerable to the direct consequences of new U.S. import tariffs and, even more so, the indirect consequences of retaliatory actions by trade partners,” it said.
So far, Sullivan has steadfastly supported Trump on tariff policies, even diverging on that subject from Murkowski, his Alaska colleague.
He continues to align himself with Trump. On his campaign website is a photo of himself standing with the president and giving a thumbs-up sign. And Trump is planning to travel to Alaska to campaign for the incumbent senator.
Peltola and the Alaska Democratic Party have faulted Sullivan for his support of both tariffs and the U.S. war in Iran. Those international actions have jacked up costs of fuel and other necessities, pinching fish harvesters and all Alaskans, she argues.
“We are being priced out of petroleum, and we’re being priced out of our lives in Alaska, because of the war in Iran,” she said at the Kodiak debate.
Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola speaks to audience members at the Sept. 12, 2026, fisheries debate held by the Kodiak Chamber of Commerce. Peltola is trying to unseat Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska. (Photo by Brian Venua)
Budgets, jobs and climate change
The Peltola campaign and the Alaska Democratic Party are tying Sullivan to another Trump policy that has been unpopular among fishing-dependent Alaskans: slashes to fishery science and the federal workforce that performs it.
At the Kodiak fisheries debate, Peltola criticized Sullivan for supporting “draconian” cuts to NOAA through an initiative led by billionaire Elon Musk.
The “Department of Governmental Efficiency,” or DOGE, imposed cuts that compromised NOAA’s ability to gather information needed to manage fisheries sustainably, she said.
“We are flying blind without the surveys and the research that NOAA does,” she said at the Kodiak event.
The cuts also affect the National Weather Service, putting Alaskans in danger, she said.
“We live and die by federal agencies and the federal employees who keep those agencies going,” she said. Sullivan “went right along with all these DOGE cuts, mowing down federal employees that we rely on.”
As of the end of 2025, Alaska had lost 101 NOAA employees, according to the state Department of Labor and Workforce Development. That was part of a Trump administration purge that resulted in a federal workforce in Alaska that was about a tenth smaller at the end of 2025 than it had been at the start of the year, according to the department’s analysis.
Watson, who has partnered with NOAA experts for several years, said he has felt the impacts personally. “Many of my contacts that I had prior to 2025 no longer work at the various NOAA offices for which I collaborated with,” he said.
NOAA is not the only fishery-related federal agency in Alaska sustaining deep cuts.
 

A photo of Sen. Dan Sullivan making a thumbs-up gesture as he stands with President Donald Trump is featured on the incumbent’s campaign website. (Photo from dansullivanforalaska.com website)
 

	The U.S. Forest Service, which is also responsible for fishery research and habitat-protection work, suffered deep cuts as well, according to the state analysis. In recent years, the Tongass and Chugach National Forests provided habitat for about a quarter of Alaska’s commercial salmon harvests, as well as habitat for sport and subsistence harvests, according to a Forest Service study. But the agency lost 180 employees in 2025, according to the state analysis.
In March, Sullivan spoke favorably about the DOGE initiative at his annual speech to the Alaska Legislature. In that address, he said the DOGE cuts were “making some noble progress” in reducing the national debt.
Musk, through his political action committee, is supporting Sullivan’s re-election campaign and those of other Republicans in close Senate races in other states.
While Sullivan’s critics have blasted him for his strong allegiance to Trump, the senator  has repeatedly characterized his ties to the president as beneficial to Alaska.
When it comes to fisheries, that resulted in the Trump administration creating an Office of Seafood in the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Sullivan said at the Kodiak event. That seafood office was created in connection with a 2025 Trump executive order aimed at achieving “American seafood dominance.” Much of the executive order directs federal agencies to loosen environmental protections to allow for bigger commercial seafood harvests.
A plan to enshrine the Office of Seafood in the Agriculture Department is proposed in a wide-ranging farm bill pending in Congress, Sulivan said. He took credit for that: “I wrote a lot of this to help our fishermen,” he said.
Sullivan has also defended his record on NOAA funding.
At the Kodiak debate, he said he is “a strong supporter of our surveys” and was able to help secure an additional $10 million in the last budget for NOAA to conduct those. He spoke about supporting over $100 million over the years for NOAA’s ocean acidification research.
He said he “provided pushback on the Trump administration on surveys as it related to the Oscar Dyson,” a NOAA research vessel.
DOGE-related firings put Oscar Dyson operations in jeopardy last year. But the ship managed to conduct its 2025 surveys and is operating again this year. It will go on hiatus after this season and be upgraded through a $95.4 million contract awarded by NOAA in June of 2025, for which Sullivan, at the Kodiak debate, took credit.
 

Former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, listens to keynote speaker Natasha Singh on Oct. 16, 2025, the first day of the Alaska Federation of Natives convention in Anchorage. At the convention, which was held months before Peltola announced her candidacy for U.S. Senate, the former House member made a speech about subsistence traditions. Peltola, who is Yup’ik, is the first Alaska Native to have been elected to Congress. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	The Trump administration has consistently sought to make deep cuts to NOAA, but Congress as a whole has resisted those.
The Congressionally approved budget for the current fiscal year includes $6.17 billion for NOAA, $1.67 billion above what the Trump administration had requested. That total was about the same as the previous year’s appropriation, though a reduction from the year before, according to Congressional records.
The Trump administration is still pushing for deep cuts at NOAA.
The administration’s request for the coming fiscal year proposes a $4.54 billion budget for the agency, with elimination of several programs important to Alaska fisheries and coastal communities. Among those are the National Estuarine Research Reserves System, which operates in Kachemak Bay, and the national Sea Grant program, which is important to the University of Alaska. The administration is seeking to cut spending on several other programs related to fisheries, including the marine observer program and a 20-year-old program that provides funding for technology to reduce fishery bycatch.
The Trump administration’s plans for NOAA reflect the president’s approach to climate change. He has repeatedly dismissed it as a “hoax.”
In contrast, both Sullivan and Peltola indicated in a lightning round during the Kodiak debate that they believe climate change is a problem for Alaska fisheries.
To Knapp, Trump looms over the Peltola-Sullivan contest.
“At stake in this election are vastly different ideas about the direction of the country and, and in particular, about the direction that President Trump is taking us,” Knapp said.
Even though he finds the debates about fishing interesting, Knapp said he hopes voters will consider more pressing issues.
That is true in the gubernatorial race, where there are stark differences in candidates’ approaches to budgets, education and other broad subjects. And it may be even more so in the Senate race, which could tip the national balance of power, he said.
“The issues are so much bigger than our Alaska fisheries,” he said.
A fishing vessel is docked in Seward is reflected in the water on June 26, 2026. Economic pressures and environmental disruptions converged in recent years to put the state’s seafood industry into a “tailspin,” as one legislative leader put it. (Photo by Yeeth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

title: Flu and flu-related sickness killed 36 Alaskans last winter
description: Influenza-related illnesses killed 36 Alaskans during the 2025-2026 flu season, the Alaska Section of Epidemiology said Friday in a regular annual report summarizing the prior flu season. The report was released alongside a bulletin recommending flu shots for all Alaskans that are at least six months old who do not have medical conditions affected by […]
text:
A poster in Juneau's Dimond Courthouse on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026, advises anti-flu measures. (James Brooks photo/Alaska Beacon)Influenza-related illnesses killed 36 Alaskans during the 2025-2026 flu season, the Alaska Section of Epidemiology said Friday in a regular annual report summarizing the prior flu season.
The report was released alongside a bulletin recommending flu shots for all Alaskans that are at least six months old who do not have medical conditions affected by a flu shot.
The state’s weekly flu report shows cases of flu have been on the rise since mid-August.
Flu season in Alaska runs from October through July, and in the most recent season, “Alaska experienced more influenza cases and deaths than during each of the previous 3 years,” epidemiologists said.
According to state data, only 22.7% of Alaskans that are at least 19 years old were vaccinated for the flu during the prior flu season, less than half the estimated national average.
That likely contributed to the severity of the last flu season as did a November spike in cases, which mirrored national trends, the report stated.
“The combination of concentrated transmission, circulating virus characteristics, low vaccine coverage rates, and decreased (vaccine effectiveness) might help explain the relative severity of the 2025–26 season,” the report said.
Influenza-related illnesses killed 25 Alaskans in the 2024-25 flu season and 10 Alaskans in the 2023-24 season. 
Precautions intended to halt the spread of COVID-19 almost entirely eliminated flu illnesses and flu-related deaths in 2020, 2021 and 2022.

title: Better policy for Michigan’s youth starts with better data
description: If we want to guarantee that Michigan’s youth are thriving, then we need greater investment in their education, their health and their economic well-being. This year’s Kids Count in Michigan Data Profiles from the Michigan League for Public Policy show that, despite some small wins, policy failures have left children in Michigan more food insecure, […]
text:
Vanessa Nunes/Getty ImagesIf we want to guarantee that Michigan’s youth are thriving, then we need greater investment in their education, their health and their economic well-being.
This year’s Kids Count in Michigan Data Profiles from the Michigan League for Public Policy show that, despite some small wins, policy failures have left children in Michigan more food insecure, worse academically and with less economic assistance than before the COVID-19 pandemic.
Child food insecurity in Michigan has increased by nearly 40% since 2019, rising in 82 of 83 counties. And Michigan’s wealthiest counties saw some of the greatest relative increases, showing a concerning trend that is affecting kids and families throughout the state. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Despite more and more households struggling to afford basic needs, the majority of Michigan counties have fewer children receiving benefits from Medicaid and the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC).
These trends are concerning, given that, during the same period, unemployment has increased and the median household income has remained stagnant after controlling for inflation.
Michigan’s kids also have some of the worst educational outcomes in the country — and they are not getting better. From third-grade reading to college readiness, nearly every county in Michigan is showing worse academic performance than from before the pandemic.
Fortunately, we already know the avenues we can take to tackle these challenges.
One of the positive outcomes in this year’s data profiles is the improvement in 1- and 2-year-olds who are being tested for lead in most counties. We are likely to see even greater improvements in the coming years, due to a law now in effect requiring physicians to test children for lead at 12 and 24 months.
We need similar policy change and investment across the various domains of youth well-being, particularly education and economic security.
New ‘Kids Count’ data shows drop in college readiness, education participation among young adults

For example, Michigan spending on public education instruction has struggled to return to levels at the turn of the century. However, just this summer, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer signed a budget that modestly increased per-pupil K-12 spending and a law that will implement professional development for K-5 teachers to improve youth reading outcomes.
At the federal level, cuts are going to continue to harm kids. Changes to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) funding have resulted in fewer children receiving benefits since the implementation of the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” 
Future federal budget proposals also aim to slash support for programs that help children access healthy, affordable food, such as the WIC cash value benefit for fruits and vegetables.
Given the need for intervention, measuring the progress in youth well-being is critical. Ongoing data tells us if families need assistance, if children are doing well in school and if policies are working.
In particular, Kids Count in Michigan aims to provide data on children’s outcomes for every county in the state, no matter how large or small. In this effort, we rely on data from state and federal agencies as well as national nonprofit organizations — but some of these data are at risk.
Among the staggering number of altered or discontinued federal surveys is the federal food security survey, which is the country’s gold standard for estimating the prevalence of food insecurity. Our county-level child food insecurity data from Feeding America’s Map the Meal Gap rely on this survey to create accurate estimates.
There are even greater changes coming to data from the U.S. Census Bureau. 
A recent administrative order banned the use of certain data privacy practices, which is already causing delays to the much-relied-upon American Community Survey. This order might result in less data for areas with smaller populations, which could impact rural areas here in Michigan. This is on top of the federal abandonment of a directive that would have enhanced the collection of race and ethnicity data, such as by creating a new category for Middle Eastern and North African individuals.
Just this month, the Bureau published a proposed rule that would exclude noncitizens and remove questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial Census. These two provisions could overhaul our ability to understand who lives where, to allocate appropriate funding and to equitably distribute political power — the exclusion of noncitizens from the Census is also widely considered to be unconstitutional.
These sweeping changes may hinder our ability to understand how young people, of all backgrounds and in all corners of the state, are doing.
In the meantime, the League will continue to advocate for policies that invest in the well-being of children and young adults here in Michigan. The data we have now shows that they need it.
You can explore all of the Kids Count in Michigan Data Profiles by visiting https://mlpp.org/2026-kids-count-in-michigan-data-profiles/.

A day after the Ratepayer Protection Act passed the U.S. House of Representatives in a 417 to 3 vote, Husted asked the Senate for unanimous consent to skip debate and pass his bill, which would direct state utility regulators to consider standards requiring data centers that draw more than 100 megawatts of power to pay the full incremental cost of the electricity infrastructure they need…
Democratic U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico blocked Husted’s effort.
Heinrich, who is the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee’s top Democrat, said Husted’s bill asks state regulators to consider making data centers pay their own infrastructure costs instead of requiring it.

Now those survivors want the federal government to formally acknowledge their existence.

title: Lombardo declines sit-down over firearm safety
description: A former member of the state board that regulates armed security guards and private investigators says he resigned from his position over what he calls a lack of regulatory oversight by the agency, the Private Investigators Licensing Board.  Rick Brown, a Northern Nevada polygrapher and former law enforcement official who was appointed to the board […]
text:
The governor's office told certified firearms instructors it won't be meeting with them any time soon about evidence of alleged regulatory lapses by the state board that licenses security guards and private investigators.  (Photo courtesy Nevada Association of Certified Firearms Instructors)A former member of the state board that regulates armed security guards and private investigators says he resigned from his position over what he calls a lack of regulatory oversight by the agency, the Private Investigators Licensing Board. 
Rick Brown, a Northern Nevada polygrapher and former law enforcement official who was appointed to the board in 2020, resigned in June after learning the PILB’s executive director Vincent Saladino failed to notify the board of “irresponsible and negligent” behavior by a firearms instructor who trained armed guards. 
Gov. Joe Lombardo, who previously served as Clark County sheriff and stakes his political bona fides on his reputation as a law and order candidate, is refusing to meet with certified firearms instructors who provided evidence of alleged violations by board licensees and staff, and are asking for reforms. The PILB’s five members are appointed by the governor.
Andrew Cowie, president of the Nevada Association of Certified Firearms Instructors, says he’s been asking to meet with Lombardo since March. Since then, Cowie told Lombardo in an email provided to the Current, that the board has “stopped myself and others from bringing forward legitimate public safety matters.”
Lombardo’s office responded with the formal equivalent of ‘don’t call us. We’ll call you.’ 
“Considering the extensive nature of what you’ve provided, and the status of this Office’s current projects and responsibilities, we will review and consider additional follow-up, as appropriate,” Lombardo’s deputy general counsel Dylan Tedford responded this month, adding later that “at least in the short term” the governor would not meet personally with the instructors.
Nevada security guards illegally carrying rifles and shotguns, lawmakers learn 

Brown, the board member who resigned, says instructors reported watching Stephanie Costello of Archangel Training Solutions “on a weekly basis walk out of the range when instruction is going on” and “allowing non-certified instructors to instruct,” which is against the rules. Additionally, according to Brown, Costello’s schedule indicated she taught concealed weapons and firearms classes for armed guards at the same time.
“You can’t do both at the same time,” said Brown. 
Costello did not respond to the Current’s request for comment.
Saladino, the PILB executive director, moonlights as an instructor at the Clark County Shooting Complex, and “was allowing this to go on,” says Brown. 
Saladino did not respond to requests for comment.
Brown noted that last year, without the board’s knowledge, Saladino initiated an investigation of Costello and meted out disciplinary action amounting to a “slap on the wrist.” 
According to state law, the board, not the executive director, determines whether to take disciplinary action. 
“When I was sent videos of what happened, I was shocked that a small slap on the wrist was the only thing that was done,” Brown says, adding he sent the videos to PILB Chairwoman Tammy Nixon, Chief Deputy Attorney General Rosalie Bordelove, and Deputy Attorney General Stephanie Itkin-Goodman, who is assigned to the PILB. Itkin-Goodman is also running for Clark County Public Administrator. 
“I told them that I wanted an agenda item added to the upcoming meeting, where we could discuss suspending this firearms instructor and possibly revoking her certification,” Brown says. “There was hemming and hawing and ‘you know, we want to make sure that we’re doing this right and it’s legal,’ and stuff like that,” he says. 
“We’ve been made aware the instructor is unsafe and negligent, and we didn’t take any action,” Brown says he told Nixon, Itkin-Goodman, and Bordelove. “If something Costello does or does not do results in injury or death, we are in that liability chain. I said if no action is taken, I’m going to resign to take myself out of that chain.” 
Spokesman John Sadler said the AG’s “job in regard to the PILB is to provide legal advice. Our client — the PILB in this case — makes decisions within the scope of its statutory mandate. We are neither the policy making nor the disciplinary body. We cannot comment on legal communications with our clients.”
In July, the PILB issued a cease and desist letter to Costello pending further action. This month, the board fined Costello $5,000 and suspended her certification as a firearms instructor for her failure to adhere to regulations during classes she instructed. Her suspension was slated to end Sept. 18. 
The incident is not the only alleged regulatory lapse on the part of the PILB, which allows security guards to carry shotguns and automatic rifles — a practice not sanctioned by the law, legislative authorities observed in June.
“That blew me away,” Brown told the Current of Saladino’s assertion that carrying the weapons is standard practice. “No one on the board, as far as I know, had any knowledge of that. Come to find out, watching the executive director testify, that it’s been going on for years.”
Cowie of the firearms instructors’ association wants the state to not only enforce the current law that does not permit security guards to carry rifles and shotguns, but to consider mandating more training for armed guards.
“Lives have already been lost and others seriously endangered in recent incidents involving security officers,” Cowie wrote to Lombardo, adding these incidents never reached the board “for consideration of reforms that could help prevent recurrence.”
During the pandemic, a security guard shot and killed a patron at a Las Vegas 7-Eleven store. 
Last year, a security guard who wasn’t permitted to be armed shot a tourist on the Strip. 
In April, a security guard at Atomic Golf shot a kitchen worker in the chest, and then barricaded inside an office as police responded. 
Cowie contends the incidents “are only a fraction” of the concerns that have failed to get the board’s attention. He asserts Saladino, the executive director, and Nixon, the chairwoman, are using administrative processes “as a barrier to reform.” The agency’s inactions, he told Lombardo, amount to ““a public-safety failure with the potential to cost lives.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Don’t use schools to justify more data centers
description: As a public school educator in the Clark County School District, I’m being told data centers are supposed to be good for my students because they might generate money for schools. I don’t buy it. I have a simple question: Why should funding for my classroom and students depend on Nevada building more data centers? […]
text:
The governor's office released this photo of Gov. Joe Lombardo reading to students in Carson City during Nevada Reading Week in March 2023. Last week Lombardo issued an executive order which described data centers as "an unprecedented opportunity" for the state. The order aims to no longer provide a tax break that redirects revenue away from schools, at least for new data centers. That tax break remains in place for existing data centers .As a public school educator in the Clark County School District, I’m being told data centers are supposed to be good for my students because they might generate money for schools. I don’t buy it.
I have a simple question: Why should funding for my classroom and students depend on Nevada building more data centers?
For years, educators have been told Nevada simply doesn’t have the money to properly fund our public schools. We’ve watched students sit in some of the largest classes in the country. We’ve watched educators leave the profession. We’ve watched Nevada remain thousands of dollars per student behind the national average. Now, suddenly, we’re being told there’s another way: build more data centers.
Data centers have become the latest industry that some are trying to turn into a cash cow for public education. But educators and students should not be used to make another corporate tax scheme more politically attractive. That’s what this looks like: tech interests using the good reputation of public educators to sell a policy that benefits their industry. Nevada absolutely needs to invest more in its public schools, but tying that investment to the continued growth of an industry already benefiting from enormous tax breaks is not the answer. 
Other states should serve as a warning. According to an analysis by Good Jobs First, tax breaks offered to data centers reduced Virginia’s state sales tax collections by more than $1 billion. Roughly a quarter of that lost revenue would have supported K-12 public education. Nevada should learn from that experience and repeal the abatements for data centers. 
Most importantly, we don’t need to invent another plan to fund our schools because we already have a better roadmap. The Commission on School Funding spent years studying how Nevada can sustainably fund public education. They recommend modernizing our property tax system by resetting depreciation when property is sold and updating our sales tax system to reflect Nevada’s modern economy. Those are serious, sustainable revenue solutions that do not make the future of our public schools dependent on building more data centers. 
Those ideas may not be as flashy as promising billions from the next “booming” industry, but they have one huge advantage: they don’t make the future of our students’ schools dependent on how many more of these data centers Nevada can build. 
That distinction matters. What happens if the data center boom doesn’t last? What happens if companies stop building them at the pace they are today? Our students shouldn’t have to worry about any of that. Their schools deserve reliable funding year after year, regardless of which industry happens to be booming at the time.
Nevada has tried the corporate giveaway approach many times before. We are repeatedly told that if we give enough public money to wealthy corporations, whether Hollywood studios, billionaire sports team owners, or data centers, the benefits will eventually trickle down to the rest of us. Meanwhile, our schools remain $4,000 behind the national average with the largest class sizes in the country. 
And Nevadans are skeptical. According to Emerson College Polling, a majority of Nevada voters oppose data centers being built in or near their communities. Attaching school funding and promising revenue doesn’t suddenly make their concerns about water, energy, noise and quality of life disappear. 
And educators shouldn’t be used to make those concerns easier to dismiss.
As a public school educator in CCSD, I believe deeply in technology, knowledge and innovation. But innovation isn’t an excuse for bad public policy. My students don’t need their schools’ future tied to how many more data centers Nevada can build. They should not have to hope an unpopular industry continues growing so their classrooms can finally receive resources they deserve. They need lawmakers to finally make the sustainable investment in public education they’ve been promising for years. 
The good news is that lawmakers already have the roadmap to sustainably fund our public schools.  Seriously, pass the plan

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: How to get overdose reversal drug naloxone, or Narcan, in CT
description: CT officials say overdose deaths have dropped and efforts to widely distribute naloxone, also called Narcan, have contributed to that.
text:
Distribution of the overdose-reversal drug naloxone is a key part of the state’s efforts to reduce overdose deaths in Connecticut.
Officials say there have been meaningful reductions in the number of overdose deaths that correspond to efforts to widely distribute the drug, widely known by the brand name Narcan.
The number of unintentional overdose deaths fell from a high of 1,524 in 2021 to 982 in 2024. Because naloxone is so effective at preventing overdose deaths if someone is nearby to administer it, a large proportion of people who are still dying from overdose are using drugs while alone.
Here’s what to know about what the drug does, how to use it and where to find it.
How does naloxone work?
Naloxone is an opioid reversal drug that comes in the form of a nasal spray. 
When someone is overdosing their breathing slows down, and if too little oxygen reaches their brain the result can be death. Naloxone works by knocking opioids off of receptors in the brain and taking their place.
Some naloxone kits require the user to put together pieces of a cartridge and then administer the spray into each nostril. A second type of kit is already assembled and the user administers the spray with a push into one nostril. After waiting two to three minutes for a response, another dose can be given in the other nostril. A short educational video from Hartford Healthcare can be found here with visual instructions about how to use each kind of kit.
After administering naloxone, you should always call 911. A person who has received naloxone should be monitored to ensure they don’t need another dose after the initial dose has worn off, or they could still die of an overdose.
Where can I get naloxone? 
Anyone can get naloxone for free from a variety of harm reduction programs in Connecticut, including organizations like The Root Center for Advanced Recovery in Manchester, the Connecticut Harm Reduction Alliance in Hartford and New Haven, and the Alliance for Living in New London.
Another way to get naloxone is from a local pharmacy, which state officials say is the most convenient way to get it. No prescription is necessary and the cost varies between $20 and $40 for two doses, they said. Some insurance covers the cost of naloxone, while other insurers require a co-pay.
The state is also working on creating free vending machines in some cities, where people will be able to access naloxone, along with other safe use supplies like fentanyl test strips. 
The state has funded its naloxone distribution effort with money from legal settlements, with around $9.2 million to “naloxone saturation” so far. In 2025, 77,304 naloxone kits were distributed, according to the Department of Mental Health and Addiction Services.
Are there negative consequences to administering naloxone?
Health officials say that there are no negative consequences of administering naloxone. The drug will have no effect if administered on a person mistakenly who has not taken opioids. And if a person does have opioids in their system, naloxone has the ability to reverse an overdose. Naloxone can also cause a person who is using opioids to go into withdrawal. Connecticut’s Good Samaritan laws also shield those administering naloxone from legal liability. 
“I think as the population of Connecticut gets more familiar with the issue and understands how easy it is to use — that it is just a nasal spray that goes in your nose, like an allergy medication, it’s not complicated — as more folks get used to that, they’re more likely to actually use it when they come across somebody who looks like they might be overdosing,” said Luiza Barnat, director of opioid services at DMHAS.
Barnat said that when the reversal drug first became available, there were concerns that it would simply enable drug use. “I would want people to hear that it does not enable continued use. We have plenty of studies that show people don’t use more just because you revive them,” she said.
While DMHAS’s goal is to also get people who are using into recovery, they emphasize that no recovery can occur when a person is lost to overdose. “Life is worth saving,” Barnat said
Who should carry naloxone?
Health officials say that it’s most important for people who have regular interaction with opioid use to carry naloxone. That includes both people using opioids and other types of drugs, since many drugs are now tainted with opioids like fentanyl. 
People with family and friends who may be using opioids should also have naloxone. Health officials also say that people who work in public spaces like libraries, restaurants, community centers and event venues should carry naloxone or have it readily available on site.
Some advocates go a step further, saying that everyone should carry naloxone because you never know when you might come across someone who needs it. 
“In my travels, out and about in everyday life, I’ve Narcan-ed someone before,” said Joe Maddalena, director of nursing at The Root Center, a behavioral health center that offers substance abuse treatment. At the time, Maddelena was in a Walmart parking lot and saw a man overdosing in a car as his girlfriend tried to wake him up. 
Does naloxone expire?
Naloxone generally comes with an expiration date of two to three years, and while advocates say it can remain effective past its expiration date, it’s a good idea to replace naloxone within a few months of that date. In 2024, Narcan-brand naloxone extended its shelf life from three to four years.
For more information on naloxone, the Connecticut Department of Public Health has created a free app called NORA.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ labor chief criticizes ‘river of misinformation’ about independent contractor rule
description: A rule set to take effect Oct. 1 has caused a furor among business groups and freelancers, but the state insists enforcement won't change.
text:
A rule set to take effect Oct. 1 has caused a furor among business groups and freelancers, but the state insists enforcement won't change. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)New Jersey’s acting labor commissioner said a “river of misinformation” is fueling opposition to a state rule used to determine whether a worker is an employee entitled to benefits or an independent contractor who is not.
Acting Labor Commissioner Kevin Jarvis told the New Jersey Monitor that the rule, adopted in May and set to take effect next week, makes no changes to the state’s worker classification regime. Claims to the contrary have become a source of frustration for the agency that oversees unemployment, workers’ compensation, and other workplace benefit programs, Jarvis said.
“There’s absolutely some frustration because we’re swimming upstream against a river of misinformation,” he said in an interview. “This is not a new test. This is not a change in enforcement. The reason the regulations were adopted is because the New Jersey Supreme Court recommended the department exercise its regulatory authority.”
The rule codifies court and administrative law decisions surrounding the ABC test, the three-pronged assessment that determines a worker’s classification status.
It has drawn concern and confusion from business groups and freelancers who worry their or their workers’ classifications could change as a result of the rule. Some legislators — including Senate President Nicholas Scutari (D-Union) — have urged the department to delay its effective date to allow even more months for a legislative fix.
As laid out in statute, the ABC test’s three prongs ask whether a worker is free from their employer’s control when performing their service, whether that service lies outside the employer’s usual course of business, and whether the worker is engaged in independent trade or business. Workers are presumed to be employees and are marked as independent contractors only if they meet each of the test’s three prongs.
One of the rule’s chief detractors on Thursday indicated the resistance may stem from opposition to the 90-year-old unemployment statute that lays out the ABC test’s three prongs.
“With remote work and the gig economy of today, applying a test from the 1930s to 2026 — I think that’s where we’re missing the mark here,” said Jack Kelly, a government affairs associate for the New Jersey Business and Industry Association.
Legislators’ consideration of bills exempting swathes of workers — like insurance brokers, certain truck drivers, and amateur sports officials — shows the flaws in the test, said Kelly, who pointed to laxer standards in other states and at the federal level.
California uses the ABC test to classify most workers but classifies some as contractors as a matter of law without applying the test. It uses a separate multi-factor assessment called the Borello test for some other workers.
New Jersey’s test is “flawed,” Kelly said.
“If everyone’s failing it and the Legislature needs to decide who’s exempt from its scope, why go through the exemptions when you can just fix the test?” he said.
Some freelancers and groups caution the regulations would cost them treasured flexibility, but Jarvis said that worry is a mirage.
“All the groups I keep hearing from who keep saying it’s going to take away their flexibility or it’s going to change how they do their business and it’s some sort of an expansion, I’ve asked on multiple occasions for someone — anyone — point to me what specific reg is different than the way it was before. I’ve yet to get an example,” he said.
Employers are not barred from giving employees flexible hours, Jarvis said, and law does not limit workers to a single job.
He cautioned misclassification has real fiscal and financial consequences. In audits conducted last year, the state found about 14,000 workers had been misclassified, resulting in $1.3 billion in underreported wages and $32.5 million in missed contributions to the state’s unemployment insurance and disability insurance funds.
This year, the department has issued stop work orders over misclassification to MCH Masonry Group, Fine Quality Builders Corp., and Kismet International Limo & Teaneck Taxi Service, and other firms. The department has issued more than 200 such orders since 2019.
Because rates for the unemployment tax that New Jersey levies on employers are set based on the health of the fund, missed contributions can increase other employers’ tax burdens.
The state’s unemployment insurance trust fund is still recovering after record jobless claims during the pandemic. Its recovery caused rates to decline last year, and Jarvis said rates could fall again next year, though he warned it is too early to say for sure.
It’s unclear whether the department can accede to calls to further delay the rules’ implementation.
“The regs that were adopted require they be implemented on October 1st. I don’t even know if we have the legal ability to delay their implementation,” Jarvis said.
The Legislature could step in with its own fix or Gov. Mikie Sherrill could blunt it through executive action, Kelly said.
The uproar over worker classification comes almost six years after public outcry defeated legislation that would have altered a leg of the ABC test and expanded it to cover all New Jersey employment laws.
Under present law, the ABC test flows from New Jersey’s Unemployment Compensation Law, though the New Jersey Supreme Court in 2015 ruled the test should also be used to gauge employment class under its Wage Payment and Wage and Hour laws.
The regulations don’t go that far, but they’ve still caused some consternation among lawmakers.
On Thursday, the Assembly Financial Institutions and Insurance Committee passed a bill to exempt some insurance brokers from the ABC test.
Assemblyman Roy Freiman (D-Somerset), the panel’s chair, said during that hearing that he was frustrated that the new rule had spurred calls for new or updated exemptions for workers he said are clearly independent contractors.
“We should not be wasting our time and energy to pass legislation to clarify what the independent contractor statuses are on various different industries,” Freiman said. “It is frustrating to me that we are spending time on something like this on industries, on professions that are so plain as day to the rest of us.”
